News.title: Labour MP whose husband faces ‘China spy’ probe enjoys secret trysts with married Holyrood figure
News.content:
A LABOUR MP whose husband is accused of spying for China has been enjoying trysts with a married Holyrood figure, we can reveal.

Joani Reid, 40, was spotted sharing cosy meals and staying overnight with the high-profile man in her East Kilbride constituency.



It comes as lobbyist spouse David Taylor, 39, remains at the centre of a Met Police counter- terrorism probe on suspicion of “targeting UK democracy”.

Reid revealed she had returned to the party’s ranks amid a China spying scandal hours after her overnight stay with the high-profile Holyrood figure.



The Scot announced she’d had the whip restored at Westminster four months after husband David Taylor was arrested on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service.

But we can reveal Reid, 40, had a series of public meet-ups in her East Kilbride constituency with a married man who is well known in the Scottish Parliament.

The revelations also come after she was accused of being “flirty” with two naval officers at Faslane nuclear subs base on the Clyde.

Details of her affair with the parliament-linked man sparked a claim Reid’s “reckless” behaviour could leave her open to “compromise and blackmail”.



She had voluntarily suspended herself from Labour’s Commons group on March 5 but revealed her return in an online statement on the evening of Thursday, July 30.

But just hours earlier Reid and the married man had been seen leaving her flat — the morning after they had dined out together.

The pair had been spotted at 7.30pm on the Wednesday at Zucca restaurant in East Kilbride, close to Reid’s office and home.

At 8.55pm, they were pictured together walking the short distance to her pad. Reid was wearing a pink North Face jacket and blue jeans.

The man had on a pair of jeans plus a beige jacket with hood.



He was spotted leaving the MP’s property at 8.45am the following morning in the same outfit.

Around 30 minutes later, Reid left in her motor and made the short drive to her constituency office. She wore a blue skirt with flat animal print shoes and a denim jacket.

And Reid appeared to have the same outfit on ten hours later as she announced her comeback in a video posted on social media.



She told her 1,202 followers on Instagram: “I just wanted everyone to know my suspension from the Labour Party has now been lifted and I’m back as a Labour MP.

“It brings to an end a really difficult period for me and I wanted to say thank you to all the people and constituents who got in touch with messages of support and kindness.

“And finally I just wanted to remind and reassure you that I have never been part of a police investigation, either as a suspect or even as a witness.”

The Scottish Sun also has evidence that the man — who we are not naming for legal reasons — met with Reid twice last month.

They were spotted inside East Kilbride’s Mata Hari restaurant, having joined Reid’s fellow Labour members at a bash to back MSP Joe Fagan’s bid to be elected as the party’s next Scottish leader.



Rocked by six months of turmoil BY CHRIS TAYLOR THE latest controversy involving Joani Reid comes just over two years after she became a Labour MP at the July 2024 General Election. She’d told earlier how she had been inspired to stand for the East Kilbride and Strathaven seat while watching TV with her gran — who said she was “very concerned” for the country’s future. And during the campaign, she told voters she knew “the challenges that local families face” and insisted that the “community deserves better”. After husband David Taylor was arrested in March over claims of spying for China, Reid said she was not part of his “business activities”. But accounts for her now-liquidated firm Reid Strategy revealed she received nearly £24,000 in interest-free loans from two companies where he was listed as a director. In 2022 her consultancy business had assets of just £2,870. A year later they were £442,103, with shareholders’ funds rocketing from £1,351 to £311,836. The firm was dissolved in August last year.

The pair later spent some time in her flat before the man left a short time later, wearing a baseball cap. He then made his way to his motor in a public car park. On one occasion he was also seen walking to the door of Reid’s flat while she took a phone call in the garden.

The apartment is a short distance from the four-bedroom family home in the town’s St Leonards that was searched as part of the ongoing investigation into her husband by the Met’s counter-terrorism cops.

A source said Reid was now “estranged” from Taylor, but the Holyrood figure she was involved with still lives with his wife.

Last night Scottish Tory leader Russell Findlay said: “Following her husband’s arrest over allegations that he spied for China, this Labour MP’s own conduct has already been under the spotlight. So for her to engage in such risky and reckless behaviour further calls into question her judgment and that of her party.



“Hostile states like Russia and China are seeking to undermine our country, which means all elected representatives have a responsibility to be alert to the risk of compromise and blackmail.”

We told in March how Taylor, 39, was one of three men arrested on suspicion of spying for China and “targeting UK democracy”.

The lobbyist was held in London while PR firm boss Matthew Aplin, 43, an a 68-year-old unnamed man were nabbed in Wales.

Reid — who is a granddaughter of the late shipyard union boss Jimmy Reid — has said repeatedly she never saw anything to make her suspect her husband had broken the law.

High-flyer influence REID is one of 11 MPs sitting on Westminster’s Home Affairs Select Committee, which has launched inquiries into organised crime, security and combating extremism. She joined the panel just months after being elected and continued as a member during her Labour suspension. The granddaughter of late Clydeside union legend Jimmy Reid graduated in politics and philosophy from Glasgow Uni before leaving the city to obtain a masters degree in public policy in London. Reid was a councillor in Lewisham from 2014-2022 but returned to Scotland to stand in East Kilbride and Strathaven. She got 22,682 votes in the 2024 election, securing a 9,057 majority over the SNP candidate Grant Costello.



The Metropolitan Police said in May that all three suspects would remain on bail.

Reid insisted in March: “I have never been to China. I have never spoken on China or China-related matters in the Commons.

“I have never asked a question on China-related matters.”

Her Welsh husband is director of policy at Asia House, a think-tank which say is dedicated to “fostering meaningful dialogue between Asia, the Middle East, and Europe”.

He was previously a special adviser to Labour Welsh Secretary Peter Hain from 2009 to 2010.



Last November Taylor was pictured shaking hands with former Chinese minister Jin Liqun, who was then boss of Beijing-based Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.

Reid, an MP since July 2024, went on: “I have never seen anything to make me suspect my husband has broken any law. I am not part of my husband’s business activities.”

It emerged this April that she had been accused of inappropriate behaviour with two senior Royal Navy officers. Reid allegedly was “all over” one of the men during a drunken night in the officers’ mess at the Faslane base in Argyll.

She left the Armed Forces Parliamentary Scheme following the alleged incident last year.

An MP said they reported Reid due to fears that information about Britain’s nuclear deterrent could end up in enemy hands.



But a senior source said they were satisfied there was “no link” to the China spy case.

Separately, it was reported that a married submarine captain stepped down following another probe into a suspected relationship with Reid.

Insiders said allegations of “flirtatious” messages were probed by Navy chiefs and the captain was not found to have broken any rules.

In April, Nats MP Kirsty Blackman said the China spying claims and later revelations were “a scandal of unprecedented proportions”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

At the time, a source close to Reid said allegations of national security concerns due to her behaviour were “opportunistic hypocrisy — as shown by the nearly a year gap between the events and the report”.



We approached Reid but she declined to comment, as did Labour. The man did not respond to requests for comment.

News.title: Javier Milei proposes using Hong Kong-style handover as model for bringing Falkland Islands under Argentine control
News.content:
ARGENTINA’S president has called for the UK to give them a Hong Kong-style handover of the Falkland Islands.

Javier Milei’s brazen demands come amid speculation the US may support Buenos Aires over their nonsensical claims to the British territory.



The Argentine tyrant called for a “consensus solution” and claimed his people “do not believe in war”.

But the nationalist firebrand announced on Thursday plans for a new military base and slammed Britain as a country “in decline”.



He told The Economist: “The UK did this with Hong Kong, so why not find the agreement so that sooner or later the islands return to Argentina? They’re ours.”

Milei appeared to be referencing the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration – an agreement between the UK and China to gradually put the city back under Beijing‘s control from 1997 onwards.



The former British colony was reintegrated into China’s national territory but has been allowed to keep its own political system for 50 years.

Hong Kongers were never allowed a vote on the deal.



China has also been accused of violating the Joint Declaration due to its authoritarian crackdown on political dissent.

It comes after Donald Trump suggested he would not back the UK if Argentina invaded the archipelago, citing the lack of support in the war on Iran.

The fears follow a leak of an internal Pentagon email in April implying the US may review its position on the islands.



Milei has recently insisted the islands are a crucial part of Argentina’s “future”, while announcing sanctions on oil companies working off the islands “under the British occupation”.

He warned the UK is facing “multiple crises” that are “unlikely to be resolved” while “Argentina‘s future is flourishing and will prevail”.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband denounced Milei’s outlandish claim, as he doubled down on Britain’s “unwavering position”.

And the Falkland Islanders themselves have put two fingers up to Milei by insisting they want to stay British.

They dismissed “threats and claims” as old hat on Friday and vowed to press on development – code for drilling for oil off the coast.



In a statement the islands Legislative Assembly said their right to be British was enshrined in law and would not be threatened by leaders’ hot air.

They said: “Our future is a matter for the people who live here to decide. That is a right grounded in international law, and it is not altered by the statements of any other government.”

A 2013 referendum saw 99.8 per cent of islanders voted to remain a self-governing Overseas Territory of the United Kingdom.

In Argentina, many have accused Milei of using the Falklands to distract the public from his political woes – including the struggling economy and accusations of corruption.

He has helped tame inflation and reduce welfare spending – but the path has left many jobless and without benefits.

News.title: Milei’s Falklands rant should be urgent warning to Labour to properly arm our troops & protect ALL Brits here and abroad
News.content:
Falk in the road

OUR new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has insisted he is “unwavering” about keeping the Falklands British.

Such a statement from a strong, principled Government backed by a powerful military should leave the Argies thinking twice about ever trying again to take what they call “Las Malvinas”.



Instead, Argentinian president Javier Milei smells weakness and decline. Like our enemies in Russia and China, he knows Britain’s Armed Forces have been hollowed out for years and most of our warships and subs are broken.

Milei will also have read depressing reports that the funding crisis is so bad that Army exercises have been scrapped.



Most of all, Milei knows Labour’s utter failure to ramp up defence spending has caused a bitter rift with our closest ally.

Donald Trump now publicly questions why he should back Britain over the Falklands when Keir Starmer refused to offer any help over the war on Iran.

The US — increasingly close to Argentina over oil — now sees the UK as an unreliable military partner.

For now, the only reason Argentina has confined itself to sabre-rattling is that its army is so small it probably wouldn’t be able to overwhelm British forces already stationed on the Falklands.

But that is no reason for complacency.

Or the time for weasel words from treacherous Foreign Office mandarins like former Permanent Secretary Lord McDonald, who suggested to the BBC yesterday the islands were too far away, too costly and too strategically unimportant to be worth the £500million-a-year cost of defending them.



No doubt Miliband is receiving similar advice from the Whitehall appeasers who persuaded Andy Burnham and Starmer to give away the Chagos Islands.

But the fact that craven politicians have left Britain with virtually no chance today of sending a Falklands task force of the size sent by Margaret Thatcher in 1982 is NOT a reason for more capitulation.

Milei’s rant should be yet another urgent warning to Labour to arm our military properly and protect ALL British citizens at home and abroad.

Not so slick

AS WITH so much from our new Prime Minister, the promise fails to meet the reality.

On the face of it, there is good news that he will finally approve drilling in the Jackdaw North Sea gas field — a sensible decision that Labour should have taken two years ago.



But in hock to the Net Zero loons, Burnham is still likely to block the Rosebank development because that contains mainly oil.

Norway has sunk 45 North Sea wells while Labour has delayed.

Britain needs BOTH to be operational as soon as possible AND to start exploration of new reserves.

Anything less will leave our energy security in as much of a mess as ever.

News.title: Why it’s party over for Reform after latest saga – unless Nigel Farage can get a grip
News.content:
NIGEL Farage came pretty close to throwing in the towel this summer.

Seething about his family getting dragged into politics and shaken by threats and a torrent of abuse, he mooted packing it all in and going fishing.



The brutal murder of his colleague Ann Widdecombe could have rightly broken even the bravest of leaders, and it almost did after what I understand were tense talks with those closest to him.

Friends talk darkly about chilling information soon to enter the public domain that will shock even the Reform leader’s most ardent haters.



A chink of light at his inner thoughts was clear in some interviews where he couldn’t quite bring himself to say he actually wanted to be the PM.

But whether it was his sense of duty or ambition — or frankly just a love of the game — he hit the stump in Clacton instead and vowed to keep buggering on.

This weekend’s party conference was supposed to be the reset moment, where after the Starmer-destroying highs of 2025, Reform could put a summer of squabbles and wobbles behind them and actually focus on the policy.

In nearly 20 years of covering the man, Birmingham’s jamboree was on course to be the most professional gathering of his true believers that I had ever seen.

Corporate Britain was out in force, as were the big global firms, noses pressed against the glass, desperate to read the runes of a Reform government.

What would have been considered crackers just 18 months ago remains a moonshot chance: Nigel Farage, PM.



Though with exhibitors and power suits aplenty, like so many Farage-adjacent events there was still always a sense of the absurd.

Anyone lucky enough to remember the manic days of Ukip knows that more often or not, their events descended into carnivals of chaos.

So despite the veneer of professionalism, slick carpet and shiny signs, there remained a whiff of carnage — an unshakeable feeling things could go t*ts up at any moment.



There are more pyrotechnics on the stage these days, but it was always the fireworks elsewhere that caused the real scenes.

And so it came to pass. Once chastised by chin-stroking pundits for being too loyal to allies he should have cut loose, the axe swung at two in the morning.

After initially branding Channel 4’s Thursday night exposé a “hoax”, it became clear in the small hours that the damage could be mortal after a long summer of sleaze stories.

Long-term aide and part-time honorary son Dan Jukes was jettisoned after walking straight into a trap sprung by climate change activists posing as deep-pocketed foreign donors looking to bend the donation rules.

One too many negronis seems to have put paid to the political career of policy chief James Orr, who was seen slurring his way out of a job by promising a fake millionaire the world.



Now Reform can rage about it all being a globalist plot, and a co-ordinated deep-state stitch-up, a sophisticated attempt to bury them by their terrified establishment enemies.

And they probably have a point to some degree — the gloves are certainly off.

But they should know by now that this torrent was coming, and in asking to not just lead the country, but blow up half a century of political consensus, that it was part of the package.

They have been warned enough times by supporters and critical friends that the scrutiny was coming, whether it feels fair or not when the heat is on.

Though you might not know it from the airwaves, there was some serious meat from Reform yesterday.



A potential referendum on the House of Lords, ripping up how the judiciary is appointed and remarkable accord with the man likely to be France’s next PM that would see the French finally accept the return of small boat crossers.

But yet again all blown out of the water by entirely avoidable scandal.

This latest saga must be a reckoning for Reform — get a grip or give over to their claim to be the dominant force on the Right.

Despite the love in the hall, Farage felt the need to spell out to his adoring fans: “I am determined to lead Reform at the next election.”

And his problem is he may well get that wish sooner rather than later.



The odds of an early General Election have shortened dramatically in the last 48 hours.

With Reform beset by fresh chaos, a new wave of investigations and another bout of dire headlines about money, Andy Burnham may soon be laughing all the way to the Palace.

After Keir Starmer’s steaming leaving present on No10’s doorstep, if Labour can see off Wacko Zacko Polanski in the upcoming Holborn and St Pancras by-election, the case to go to the country will become irresistible.

The Left semi united, the Right deeply riven with a visceral loathing and mutual suspicion.

Worst-case scenario for Burnham, dopey Ed Davey has made clear with his slobbering all over the new PM that he’s open to doing business.



And that really would be a disaster for a country in desperate need of actual reform.

ED MILIBAND has been very tight-lipped about Chagos since taking over at the Foreign Office.

But that’s unlikely to survive the first big contact between the new government and Donald Trump later this month at the United Nations in New York.

The botched plan to pay Mauritius to take over our overseas territory in the Indian Ocean was dead in the water after the Americans scotched it over fears they would lose access to a vital airbase.



But now fresh efforts by the Foreign Office to resurrect the surrender deal have left Washington baffled.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Not least because at a time when Britain is in uproar over threats to the Falkland Islands – even while asking the Americans to slap down new Argie sabre-rattling – our government seems so willing to give up other territory willy nilly.

My mole says things are set to come to a head again when the new PM heads Stateside in a few weeks’ time.

News.title: Andy Burnham ‘set to give green light’ to new North Sea gas drilling this month
News.content:
ANDY Burnham is set to give the green light to new North Sea gas drilling this month, it’s been claimed.

The PM is expected to give his backing to the Jackdaw project off the Aberdeen coast following hold-ups from environmental groups.



The scheme could provide 3,500 jobs while being constructed and then 880 when its up and running.

The approval could come in the middle of the month before Parliament heads into recess for the party conferences, the BBC said.



A formal decision is set to be made by Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh who is also considering the Rosebank oil field.

Both projects were approved by the Tories but a court challenge struck them down after a legal bid from green campaigners, with Ministers not considering their full environmental impact.



Shadow Energy Secretary Andrew Bowie said approving the Jackdaw project is “just common sense”.

He said: “Approving the Jackdaw gas field is just common sense and should have been given the green light years ago.

“Labour’s ban on new oil and gas licences has been disastrous for the North East and cost thousands of workers their jobs as they continue to dither over a decision on these projects.”

The PM has previosuly said that using oil and gas could pay for the transition to Net Zero.



He has said: “We won’t be able to stop using oil and gas for some time, that’s just a fact.

“ The question is whether we can accelerate use of it so that we pay for the transition, and one thing helps the other … whether that extraction can be the bridge to the clean energy future we need, and bring it forward. It’s about a pragmatic approach to both of those.”

Downing Street said they didn’t have an update insisting it was a “quasi-judicial decision”.

A government spokesman said: “We do not comment on speculation.”

News.title: Donald Trump threatens to hit Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain nuke lair ‘very soon’ as he labels war ‘small potatoes for us’
News.content:
DONALD Trump has declared he may strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain “very soon” after months of threatening to blitz the key nuclear site.

The US president also described the spiralling war with Tehran as “small potatoes for us”.



He said on Friday: “We may hit Pickaxe Mountain very soon… if there is anything going on with Pickaxe.”

Speaking on the Iran war as a whole, Trump added: “A lot of people don’t call it a war.



“I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us.”

Trump previously said in July he was mulling strikes on Pickaxe Mountain.

Israel believes Iran has moved thousands of uranium-enrichment centrifuges into tunnels deep inside Pickaxe Mountain, officials told the Wall Street Journal.

The facility lies more than 300ft beneath Kolang Mountain near the Natanz nuclear facility.



It is a heavily fortified site that hosts two deeply buried tunnel complexes.

The regime is believed to have made the transfer after the 12-day war in June 2025, when US and Israeli strikes pummelled Iran’s three main nuclear sites.

When asked what is going on beneath Pickaxe, Iran has said: “It’s none of your business.”



Satellite images previously revealed tunnels feeding into the mountain and leading to a deep-buried operation.

Experts say it could be more secure than any of the facilities struck by the US and Israel.

Trump has previously left the site untouched while bombing Iran’s other major nuclear bunkers.

In July he warned the US would strike the area “pretty soon” and “very heavily.”

It comes as the war with Iran continues to spiral with no clear end in sight after months of failed negotiations and broken ceasefires.



This week, Trump declared the US controls the Strait of Hormuz and suggested it should be renamed in his honour as “Trump Strait”.

The US president wrote on Truth Social: “Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???”

Control of the critical oil choke point has been fiercely contested over recent months.

Trump claimed it was US territory in August as he cut off all talks with the Iranian regime.

Before the US-Israeli war on Iran broke out, a fifth of the world’s oil passed through the strait.



Trump insists the regime has lost control of Hormuz – a wartime record of more than 17 million barrels of oil passed through on Monday, according to US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He also launched strikes on Iran just days ago following weeks of relative calm.

The US leader said the attacks were revenge for Iranian strikes on the critical shipping lane.

News.title: Dramatic fault jet on Gatwick Airport runway suffered seconds before take off causing flights to be grounded revealed
News.content:
ALL flights at the UK’s second biggest airport were grounded yesterday after a passenger jet suffered a technical fault at 138mph — seconds before take-off.

Passengers faced chaos after the aborted departure of a Norse Atlantic Airways flight from Gatwick to New York closed the runway.



Fire engines and emergency crews raced to the scene after the issue with nose wheels on a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner that can take up to 338 travellers.

Alice Kavanagh, 30, who was on the stricken flight said: “The whole situation was pretty scary.



“We were starting to speed off for take-off and all of a sudden, the pilot slammed the brakes on.

“They spotted a technical fault.



“It’s so lucky the pilot spotted it — God knows what would happen if we’d taken off.”

The terrifying incident meant the runway had to be shut for 50 minutes just after 1pm.

Thousands of passengers faced disruption as around 20 flights due to land were diverted — with knock-on delays all day.

Gatwick has two runways but they are too close to be in use together.



An airport spokesman confirmed the plane had to be “towed away” and said the runway reopened “after a full safety inspection”.

It is the latest issue to affect Gatwick after passengers were left without running water in July.

The Sun revealed how flyers were unable to flush toilets, wash their hands or refill water bottles for hours due to the outage.

News.title: 'I'd rather die than ring the police': Distrust and fear in Middlesbrough after A66 crash
News.content:
All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.

What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one.

"Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."

Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town.

"This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.

The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.

Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown.

"It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"

He blames drugs.

"It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.

Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.

What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.

Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.

In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.

On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.

On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.

One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."

Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.

I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife.

"No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."

Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.

Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying".

"Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."

The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.

The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.

Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.

But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.

There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.

News.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
News.content:
Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a fatal crash which killed seven people including two police officers.

In her first sit-down interview since the A66 crash, speaking exclusively to the BBC, Victoria Fuller said the force needed to become part of a larger force with greater resources.

She said her officers are dealing with some of the highest crime levels in the country akin to those faced by metropolitan forces, but with less than half the number of officers.

Multiple people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.

A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra Â£2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra Â£20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

At the same time, Fuller said Cleveland Police had experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fueling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

News.title: Farage threatens to overhaul Lords and judges to meet his pledges
News.content:
In his speech, which was light on new policy announcements, Farage said the country needed a government "that actually delivers on its promises" and "we're the only people capable of doing it".

He argued the Tories "had 14 years in power and failed absolutely miserably", while Labour's new Prime Minister Andy Burnham "says he needs 10 years", a reference to the PM's promise to set out a 10-year plan for the country later this year.

If Reform wins the next general election, Farage pledged to sack ministers who fail to deliver on their promises in their first 100 days in the job "and replace them with somebody else with the courage to do it".

Setting out his plans to call a "national emergency" if Reform wins power, Farage said: "Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, for six days a week until we pass the necessary legislation."

He said he expected the House of Lords to "honour" Reform's policy pledges but if they refused to do so threatened to appoint hundreds of new peers so the party had a majority in the upper chamber.

"And if that proves difficult, we will hold a referendum on the current composition of the House of Lords, and they would be swept away by a British public appalled by them," he added.

Identifying the judiciary as another possible "obstacle", Farage promised to remove the ability of judges to rely on conventions like the European Convention of Human Rights (ECHR), which critics blame for hindering some deportations.

"We don't want the courts striking down, do we, the will of the people," he said.

"Parliament makes the law, judges interpret the law. We will do whatever it takes, and perhaps have to consider how judicial appointments work in the future."

Meanwhile, he said civil servants who "try to obstruct us" would be removed from their posts and replaced by people from the world of business.

"I'm tired of being told what can't be done," the Reform leader said.

"That is not what the public want. The public want action, the public want genuine change, the public do not want any more of the same. And our attitude is can do, and will do."

Predicting that Burnham would call an early general election in spring 2027, Farage attempted to use his speech to convince the public Reform was ready to govern.

Stressing he now had a team of spokespeople with "frontline experience", he said the party was planning to broaden its expertise.

"There are more big jobs to fill, and I'm looking and working on defence, health, and the other areas," he added.

In his speech, Farage also hailed a "historic agreement" on small boat returns, signed earlier between Reform and France's hard-right National Rally party.

The deal sets out how a Reform government would intercept boats in the English Channel and return them to France using the Navy, with France "ordinarily" accepting those on board.

It was signed by the National Rally President Jordan Bardella, whose party is currently leading in opinion polls ahead of French presidential elections in April next year, after he gave a speech to the main conference hall.

Farage took to the stage after a long delay, which he told delegates was due to a "security alert".

He took the opportunity to walk through the crowd and greet delegates during the delay.

His speech was also interrupted several times by protesters, including two women who held up a banner reading "Reform works for billionaires".

They were booed by audience members who shouted "out", as they were removed by security.

Farage laughed off the disruption, chanting "boring, boring, boring".

Reform is no longer consistently topping national opinion polls, after more than a year of enjoying a comfortable lead.

Meanwhile, Labour's ratings have risen since Burnham entered Downing Street, and Reform has lost some support to Restore Britain, the new right-wing party founded by former Reform MP Rupert Lowe.

News.title: Oasis fans say cryptic codes in chip shop video point to Glasgow gigs next year
News.content:
Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.

The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.

Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.

It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.

It follows the Gallagher brothers' hugely successful reunion tour which saw them perform at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries.

This included three dates at Murrayfield Stadium, Edinburgh, in August 2025, when they played to 200,000 fans.

News.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather, minister says
News.content:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El NiÃ±o event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El NiÃ±o that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

News.title: 'We expect our sons to be killed,' father of teen shot dead in West Bank tells BBC
News.content:
Funerals have taken place for two Palestinian teenagers who were shot dead this week when settlers and soldiers entered a Palestinian village in the occupied West Bank.

The killing of Omar al-Naasan and Khalil Abu Alia comes amid near-daily attacks by Jewish settlers in the village of al-Mughayyir, south of Nablus.

"We expect that when our sons walk in the street, they are likely to return to you injured or killed," Mohammed Al-Naasan, Omar's father, told the BBC.

Israel's military says it fired on "instigators of a violent riot" and that the incident is under review.

The United Nations says more than 80 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the territory since the beginning of the year.

News.title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
News.content:
The tone over the Falkland Islands dispute has been sharpening in Argentina from well before President Javier Milei's late-night national address on sanctions earlier this week.

It's tempting to see a visual representation of the tension in the jubilant Argentine players celebrating their hard-fought win over England at the Fifa World Cup this summer holding a banner which read "Las Malvinas son Argentinas" - the Falklands are Argentine - in front of their deliriously happy fans. However, the ill-feeling has been fomenting for much longer.

President Milei began his Thursday address with a brief history of the Falklands, very much from the Argentine perspective. He repeated the refrain at the heart of their position: the islands "rightfully belong" to Argentina. The British had invaded and colonially occupied the islands in 1833, he said, violently wrestling the territory from Argentina's hands.

The UK Government would say he conveniently overlooked a few details: the islands â over which the European powers had interchanged control throughout the 17th and 18th centuries â were uninhabited at the time the British reoccupied the land. The Argentine settlement had been forced out two years earlier, not by the British but by the Americans. A warship, the USS Lexington, destroyed a fort established there in December 1831 amid a dispute over local fishing and sealing rights.

Still, if the Americans had a hand in forcing the Argentines out two centuries ago, they may now play a central role in strengthening the Argentine claim. President Milei certainly thinks so.

"Winds of change" were blowing, he assured the Argentine people, after President Trump said he was "re-evaluating" the US position on the Falklands.

News.title: Examining US official's claim that data centres 'don't use water'
News.content:
US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick suggested that data centres don't use water.

According to the International Energy Agency, a data centre in the United States uses around 2 million litres per day on average.

They have become a controversial topic for communities across the US in the run up to November's midterm elections.

Produced by Aisha Sembhi. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz.

News.title: Woman whose XL bully dog killed her cousin given suspended prison sentence
News.content:
A woman has been given a suspended prison sentence after her XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control, causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to the dog attack at a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, which belonged to Reed and her boyfriend, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

News.title: Transgender surgery halted over concerns patients were not properly assessed
News.content:
Gender-affirming surgery was halted because of concerns from an NHS committee over whether patients had been "appropriately assessed".

After meeting Welsh government ministers on Friday the NHS Wales Joint Commissioning Committee (NWJCC) said data showed the rate of surgery referrals made by the Welsh Gender Service was "significantly higher" than in England.

It also said the proportion of Welsh patients progressing from referral for some types of surgery was "significantly lower" than across the border.

The NWJCC is the body which instructed Cardiff and Vale University Health Board to halt new referrals and planned surgeries.

The health board is responsible for the running of the NHS gender identity clinic which provides specialist care and support for adults in Wales.

It confirmed on Tuesday that some patients who had been awaiting gender-affirming surgery were already in hospital for their procedures when they were told of the suspension.

The Welsh Gender Service provides referrals for patients living in Wales, but all NHS surgeries are carried out in England.

Gender-affirming surgery - includes both masculinising and feminising procedures. They are not reversible.

News.title: Cambridge launches review into support for Jason Arday before death
News.content:
The University of Cambridge has launched an independent review into its "decision-making and actions" in the period leading up to former professor Jason Arday's death.

The review will examine the support available to Arday before his death, as well as the wider context of his time at the university.

Arday, 41, was found dead at his home in London on 14 August, the week after resigning from his position as professor of sociology of education amid intense scrutiny over allegations of plagiarism. He had denied the claims.

Announcing the review on Friday, Vice-Chancellor Prof Deborah Prentice said the time since his death had been a "period of profound sadness and reflection for the university".

"We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus, but given the devastating outcome, we are still asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more," she said.

"This review will help us answer that question."

In a post on social media, the University of Cambridge said: "University Council took the necessary steps to launch an independent review into the university's decision-making and actions, with a focus on identifying shortcomings and areas for improvement."

The first part of the review will look at the "support, interventions and protections" available to Arday in the period before his death.

Those findings will be reported within three months, allowing recommendations for "urgent action" to be considered and implemented "without delay".

It will be led by Nazir Afzal, chancellor of the University of Manchester and former chief crown prosecutor for the North West of England.

Afzal said in a statement that "it is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity", adding "we must be willing to ask difficult questions".

The second part of the review will examine the wider circumstances of Arday's time at Cambridge, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, mentoring and support arrangements.

It will also look at the university's response to allegations of research misconduct and the support available to academics facing "extraordinary public and media scrutiny".

An independent external chair will be appointed to lead the second part of the review, with an expert panel "including individuals with lived experience" advising it.

It is expected to conclude within six months of the panel being established.

In a video message, Prentice said: "I am conscious that Professor Arday's death has deeply affected black staff and students, as well as our neurodiverse community.

"There has also been an unacceptable rise in racist, hateful, and abusive attacks on our staff and students in online forums and on social media."

In 2023, the sociologist, then 37, became the youngest ever black professor at Cambridge.

Arday had faced allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He denied the claims, but admitted errors in his work.

Arday said some errors arose because of his autism, as he relied on using mimicry to make sense of information. He said similar scrutiny would find comparable errors in the work of other academics.

The allegations emerged after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work.

Arday said the criticism had gone "far beyond scholarly disagreement".

Resigning from his post in August, he added: "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and those I love."

Following his death, his family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son".

They added: "The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone."

A vigil held in Trafalgar Square was attended by thousands, according to its organisers.

There have been calls for a public inquiry into media coverage of Arday before his death.

News.title: Controversial Jackdaw gas field set to be approved in weeks, sources say
News.content:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come in mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will account for 6% of UK gas output when at peak production but environmental groups say it will provide only 2% of UK use when imports are included.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and further estimates were put out for consultation in July.

News.title: Man who died near Notting Hill Carnival is named
News.content:
A man who died after jumping into a canal while fleeing from police near Notting Hill Carnival has been named.

Karnell Kelly, 25, died in hospital after entering the Grand Union Canal off Kensal Road, west London, while being pursued by police officers.

He had fled on foot after the officers attempted to stop him near Harrow Road as he approached the carnival wearing a face covering at about 15:20 BST on Monday, the Metropolitan Police said.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which is investigating, said it was reviewing body-worn video from officers who had chased Kelly down Hormead Road.

Officers and members of the public entered the canal to pull him from the water and he was rushed to a central London hospital, where he was pronounced dead at about 16:40.

News.title: Gavin and Stacey star Rob Brydon's regret at turning down Dolly Parton interview
News.content:
Gavin and Stacey star Rob Brydon says he "regrets" turning down the chance to interview Dolly Parton after choosing to stay on a family holiday.

Brydon fronted the BBC documentary series Honky Tonk Road Trip, where he travelled across the American South to celebrate 100 years of country music.

In it he visited Dollywood, a theme park created by Parton, where Dolly's relatives had traced the lineage of the Parton and Owens sides to Wales.

He was told he could interview Parton if he returned after filming had ended, but chose to stay on his family holiday in Arizona - an opportunity he now wished he had taken because he never got to meet her before she died.

Parton died peacefully in hospital in Nashville on 25 August following a brief battle with cancer. She was admitted to hospital four days before her death with kidney and autoimmune issues.

"I sort of regret it now," he told Lucy Owen during an interview on BBC Radio Wales.

"I kind of wish that I had gone back because I never met her."

News.title: Planes grounded at Gatwick after aircraft stuck on runway
News.content:
Flights at Gatwick Airport were brought to a standstill for nearly an hour after a plane became stuck on the runway.

A Gatwick spokesperson said the runway was closed for 50 minutes on Friday afternoon because of a "technical issue with a departing vehicle".

The airport said the plane was towed away from the runway, which "reopened shortly afterwards following a full safety inspection".

"As always, safety and security is our number one priority," the spokesperson said.

News.title: Sheep stolen from Clarkson's Diddly Squat Farm
News.content:
Eleven sheep have been stolen from Diddly Squat Farm belonging to presenter Jeremy Clarkson.

Thames Valley Police said it received reports on Wednesday that the animals had been taken from the farm in Chadlington, Oxfordshire, within the last 10 days.

It said officers spoke with Clarkson at the scene on Thursday, adding that no arrests had been made and anyone with information should get in contact.

The 66-year-old told The Sun, external he discovered the animals were missing when he went to count his flock with Clarkson's Farm co-star Kaleb Cooper.

A judge has cleared the way for former U.S. Sen. Kyrsten Sinema to be sued under North Carolina’s homewrecker law.

Sinema tried to argue she shouldn’t face a lawsuit over her relationship with a member of her security detail in North Carolina because she has no connection to the state.

U.S. District Judge David A. Bragdon rejected that claim and ruled that nine text messages sent to Matthew Ammel, her bodyguard, while he was in the state establish North Carolina's jurisdiction over her. He called it implausible that she was unaware of Ammel's whereabouts when texting him.

Steven Epstein, Sinema's attorney, did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

open image in gallery Sinema has acknowledged having a romantic relationship with Matthew Ammel but argued that she can't be sued in North Carolina because she has no connection to the state ( AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite )

The legal action, brought by Ammel’s ex-wife, seeks financial compensation from Sinema, who represented Arizona in the U.S. House and later completed a single term in the Senate early last year.

North Carolina is among a small number of states allowing jilted spouses to bring suits for "alienation of affection" to obtain damages from a third party deemed responsible for a broken marriage.

Matthew and Heather Ammel maintained "a good and loving marriage" with "genuine love and affection" prior to Sinema’s interference, pursuing Matthew Ammel despite knowing he was married, Heather Ammel alleges in her lawsuit.

Matthew Ammel joined Sinema's security team after retiring from the Army in 2022 and accompanied her on domestic and foreign travel, the complaint states.

In early 2024, Heather Ammel discovered "romantic and lascivious" messages exchanged between her husband and Sinema on the Signal messaging app. By that summer, he stopped wearing his wedding ring, and Sinema appointed him as a national security fellow in her Senate office as he continued working as a campaign bodyguard, the lawsuit states.

During a deposition in July, Sinema described their sexual encounters, testifying the relationship became sexual on May 27, 2024, during a trip to Napa, California. She stated they later had encounters in New York, Washington, Colorado and Arizona, but never North Carolina.

Matthew and Heather Ammel separated on Nov. 1, 2024.

Legislation banning child-like sexual abuse dolls has moved closer to becoming law after clearing its initial hurdle in the House of Commons.

MPs backed the Child-like Sexual Abuse Dolls (Offences) Bill on Friday, criminalising the possession, sale and manufacture of these dolls across England and Wales.

Owning such a doll is not currently a UK offence, though individuals importing them face prosecution under the Customs Consolidation Act 1876.

Liberal Democrat MP Munira Wilson, sponsor of the private member’s Bill, said the legislation closes a "dangerous" gap by equating possession with holding indecent child images.

The Bill passed the Commons without debate on Friday and now advances to committee stage.

Ms Wilson said: “I’m incredibly pleased to see this important legislation pass its first test. These dolls are simply vile and they should have been banned years ago. Anyone using these dolls quite clearly presents a danger to children and these items have no place in our society.

“As both a mother and an MP, when I discovered this gap in the law, I had to act. I very much hope the Bill will continue to progress smoothly through the Commons so that we can take one step closer to making our country safer for children.”

open image in gallery Under the Bill, police will be able to seize such dolls and offenders who are found guilty could face prison time as well as monitoring ( PA )

It will need the approval of both the Commons and the House of Lords for it to become law.

Speaking to the Press Association previously, Ms Wilson said she is “disgusted and horrified that these things exist” but we “mustn’t be squeamish about tackling this issue head-on”.

The MP for Twickenham said: “It’s a horrendous issue to work on, to talk about, to investigate, and people have said to me… ‘do you really want to be named for this issue?’

“One of the reasons I’m in Parliament is to protect and make life better for children, and this is clearly a dangerous gap that we’ve got in our legislation.”

Under the Bill, police will be able to seize such dolls and offenders who are found guilty could face prison time as well as monitoring.

It is drafted to include any doll which “resembles a child or any part of a child”, to prevent perpetrators getting around the proposed law, Ms Wilson said.

Abigail Gill, acting head of policy and public affairs at the NSPCC, said: “We are pleased to see this Bill pass its second reading in Parliament and strongly support its continued progress. The Bill, which seeks to criminalise the manufacture, distribution and possession of child‑like sexual abuse dolls, is an important step towards closing a dangerous gap in the law.

“There is no comprehensive evidence that the use of these grotesque dolls prevents potential offenders from committing contact offences against children. In fact, using these dolls or other realistic props could risk adults becoming desensitised, as is often seen among those who view indecent images.

“Anything that appears to normalise or mimic the abuse of children and young people is dangerous and unacceptable. We urge the Government to continue backing this Bill to ensure it becomes law so that no child is left at risk of harm.”

Dame Rachel de Souza, Children’s Commissioner for England, said: “I am horrified by the very existence of these dolls and this Bill is a long overdue step in addressing this harmful and disturbing practice.

“I meet children who have experienced sexual abuse in the online and offline world – the consequences to the child and their family’s life are profound, and we must take every possible step to protect young people from the threat of this significant harm.

“That means identifying and addressing harmful sexual behaviours wherever they occur, at the earliest possible stage. I urge parliamentarians to back this Bill so that it can be enacted as soon as possible.”

A group of Christian missionaries has claimed they were made to leave Burning Man festival in the middle of the night, alleging they were discriminated against for spreading their religion.

John Hinerman and his Christian group, who set up a camp named Shift the Atmosphere, explained in a series of Instagram videos that they attended the Nevada desert festival to “spread the word of Jesus” but were asked to leave by organizers.

“Burning Man is discriminating us and breaking their own rules of being ‘radically inclusive’ and KICKING us out for being Christians?!” Hinerman said in his post’s caption.

While at Burning Man, Hinerman had shared videos of him and his group setting up a camp where they played “Christian EDM” music and served coffee to others while trying to spread their message. They also claimed to have performed more than 600 baptisms during the festival.

He said in the video: “We have been asked to leave Burning Man. We’re packing up. They’re kicking us out. Satan’s mad. We have over 600 people who have given their lives to Jesus already, and Satan can’t do anything about it.”

open image in gallery John Hinerman and his Christian group have claimed they were asked to leave Burning Man festival in the middle of the night for expressing their beliefs ( Instagram via @johnhinerman )

The festival has said they removed the group for filming others without their consent, but Hinerman disputed the claims.

A spokesperson for Burning Man Project told The Independent: “A theme camp was removed from Black Rock City after repeatedly violating Burning Man’s media policies and failing to respect participant privacy.

“Burning Man takes participants’ right to privacy seriously. Seeking permission and consent before filming or engaging other participants in Black Rock City is a requirement and responsibility for anyone at the event. This camp received multiple warnings and opportunities to correct their behavior, yet continued to violate our policies and were therefore evicted.”

Burning Man’s website states that all people should ask for permission before filming other attendees.

In another video, Hinerman said they had three hours to pack up their camp and leave, and that other attendees had helped them clear up.

“WE LOVE the BURNERS. We had such beautiful time spending with the people here. Burning Man is WRONG for kicking us Out and the devil is MAD over 800 people gave their lives to Jesus and became a LIVING temple of the Holy Spirit. One of their #1 Rules, is “Radical Inclusion”. I guess it’s Radical inclusion for everyone EXCEPT Christians,” he concluded.

Hinerman also criticized the free-spirited nature of the festival, stating that festival-goers would walk around naked “without the consent” of the people around them, including children.

“These children didn’t give you consent to be walking around with your penises out in front of all these kids. It’s so wicked and sad,” he said.

open image in gallery Burning Man festival has said the Christian group violated privacy terms when filming other festival-goers ( Julie Jammot/AFP/Getty )

Burning Man, running from August 30 to September 7, is a cultural event where attendees build camps from scratch and set up their own installations and other forms of entertainment. It was founded on 10 core principles, which include “radical inclusion,” “radical self-expression” and “demodification.”

This year’s edition of the festival has been subject to criticism after the co-founder John Law — one of the early organizers who helped move the event to Nevada’s Black Rock Desert in 1990 — accused Burning Man of losing its “anarchist soul” and becoming a playground for the rich.

In an essay for the San Francisco Standard published on Saturday, Law said Burning Man started as “an anarchistic collaboration of equals, conjured into being by a few hundred people of goodwill” but had become a “fabulous Disneyland for the well-heeled.”

The United States, Britain, France and Germany have drafted a resolution for possible consideration by the Board of Governors of the U.N. nuclear watchdog that seeks to refer Iran to the U.N. Security Council for failure to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations, diplomats say.

Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow inspectors of the Vienna-based International Atomic Energy Agency to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.

The diplomatic move has been under consideration since June 2025 when the IAEA board found Iran officially in noncompliance with its nonproliferation obligations for the first time in 20 years — one day before the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran’s nuclear sites.

The possible referral of Iran to the U.N. Security Council shifts the responsibility to a higher authority that is able to enact further legally binding measures, including sanctions or asset freezes.

But specific punitive measures by the U.N. are unlikely in this case since Iran’s allies Russia and China hold a veto power on the U.N. Security Council.

The draft resolution, which was seen by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Reuters, requests the IAEA director general Rafael Grossi “to transmit this resolution and the previously adopted resolutions … to all Members of the Agency and to the Security Council and the General Assembly of the United Nations, in accordance with the relevant provisions of the IAEA Statute.”

The resolution also “stresses its support for a diplomatic solution to the challenges posed by the Iranian nuclear programme and its implications for regional peace and stability leading to an agreement that addresses all international concerns related to Iran’s nuclear activities, and encourages all parties to constructively engage in diplomacy.”

Diplomats say that the resolution is still under negotiation and has not yet been formally submitted to the board. The text of the draft resolution may therefore still change, as board members still have the opportunity to suggest amendments.

Once formally submitted, it will be put to a vote during next week’s IAEA Board of Governors meeting in Vienna.

Referring Iran to the U.N. Security Council had been stalled to allow a final push for diplomacy, according to a senior Western diplomat, who wasn’t authorized to comment about the sensitive matter and spoke on condition of anonymity. The IAEA board now has to follow its mandate and act because not only has Iran not cooperated, but even communication is no longer happening, the official said.

Since Israel and the U.S. struck Iran’s nuclear sites during the 12-day war in June 2025, Iran hasn’t given IAEA inspectors access to nuclear sites that were affected by the strikes — even though Tehran is legally obliged to cooperate with the watchdog under the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty.

The agency also has been unable to verify the status of the stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the June bombing. Of course, that has been made much more difficult by more than six months of war that the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran on Feb. 28, including strikes that have been carried out by both Washington and Tehran this week.

The IAEA warned in Tuesday’s confidential report, seen by the AP, that continued denial by Iran to allow IAEA inspectors access to its nuclear sites and to verify the nuclear material constitutes a “proliferation risk” that needed to be “addressed with the utmost urgency.”

According to the IAEA, Iran maintains a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity — a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.

That stockpile could allow Iran to build as many as 10 nuclear bombs, should it decide to weaponize its program, IAEA chief Grossi warned in an interview last year with the AP. He said that it doesn’t mean that Iran has such a weapon.

The IAEA also reported in its confidential report on Tuesday that there has been no progress in its long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at various undeclared sites in Iran.

Western officials suspect that the uranium traces could provide further evidence that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons program until 2003.

Iran says that it’s not pursuing nuclear weapons, and its program is entirely peaceful.

A commercial spacecraft sent to extend a lifeline to NASA’s Swift Observatory succeeded in closing in on the decaying telescope and snapping photographs more than a week after the rescue attempt was abandoned.

But the three-armed robotic salvager was forced to turn away due to low fuel, according to Katalyst Space Technologies, which carried out the daring operation.

"We got so close, but so far," Katalyst CEO Ghonhee Lee told The Associated Press this week.

Katalyst's Link craft got within 15 kilometers (nine miles) of Swift last weekend, using its own sensors to gather data on the doomed telescope for NASA. Although the rescue effort had been called off in August because of Link's own troubles in orbit, the company wanted practice for future satellite service calls.

Katalyst Space’s spacecraft inside the SES (Space Environment Simulator) at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center ( NASA )

Link went into an uncontrollable spin soon after launching to Swift's rescue in July. Flight controllers managed to reduce the tumbling and stabilize the craft, using up precious fuel. Ultimately, there was not enough fuel remaining to boost the aging Swift to a higher, longer-lasting orbit so it could continue observing the cosmos.

Lee blamed Link's difficulties on the rush to get it flying. The mission was thrown together in just nine months, and engineers often had to grab whatever parts were available instead of waiting for preferred components, he said.

NASA paid the company $30 million to carry out the attempt, which was always going to be rushed. Both sides viewed it as an experiment with little to lose, although no one wanted a wreck that would unleash clouds of space debris.

"Unfortunately, it wasn't the outcome that we were expecting," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said following Sunday's launch of the Roman Space Telescope. "But that's exactly the type of missions that we should be flying at NASA. We will learn from that."

Isaacman said it makes sense to extend the life of a valuable spacecraft, especially if the cost to salvage it is less than to replace it. That is why the Roman telescope was designed to be refuelable even though it is headed toward an observation point 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) away.

It is unlikely that Link has enough fuel left to attempt another close approach to Swift, according to Lee. But it can keep exercising its 3-foot (1-meter) arms and provide important data before it reenters and burns up in the atmosphere in the next few weeks, he said.

Launched in 2004, Swift has a little more time remaining in orbit, depending on how active the sun is. Intense solar storms in recent years brought the telescope down much sooner than expected. As of Friday, its orbit had dropped to 208 miles (335 kilometers), barely half as high as when it set out to scan cosmic explosions.

NASA anticipates Swift will plunge through the atmosphere sometime between October and year’s end. The space agency resumed observations with the telescope last week after halting them early this year to save power.

Like Swift, the Hubble Space Telescope's orbit has also been shortened by solar activity. Katalyst is developing a next-generation spacecraft that could boost the 36-year-old Hubble to a longer-lasting orbit.

"Hubble does still have a few years of life yet, right? So the good news is this isn't imminent," Lee said.

Servicing old telescopes and other satellites used to be "a very, very niche concept," he added, "and we believe it’s going to become more and more commonplace."

Ulta Beauty is facing backlash from shoppers over the cosmetics giant allowing Flock Safety surveillance cameras at some of its stores.

The controversy started Wednesday when Atlanta comedian Lisandra Vazquez shared a video of her shopping at Ulta and alleged that “Ulta Beauty is one of Flock Camera’s biggest commercial customers.”

“Come with me to the Ulta-mate place for beauty and surveillance. Their shelves are so stocked, I don’t even mind being stalked. Hi, officer,” Vazquez said in the video, panning to a man who appeared to be a police officer standing in the store. It is unclear what Ulta location she is shopping at.

An Ulta spokesperson told The Independent that the company, which has more than 1,500 stores and overwhelmingly female shoppers, uses automated license plate readers at fewer than 1 percent of its stores to investigate elevated crime, particularly organized retail theft.

The cameras do not use facial recognition and access to the data is strictly controlled, according to the spokesperson. Flock camera use at Ulta was first reported by Retail Dive.

open image in gallery Ulta customers, many of them women, are calling on the beauty giant to stop using Flock cameras as at least 50 law enforcement officers have been accused, charged or arrested for misusing Flock and similar systems to stalk women ( Reuters )

At least 50 law enforcement officers have been accused, charged or arrested for misusing Flock and similar license plate reader networks to track and stalk women, including wives, partners and ex-girlfriends, The Washington Post reported last month.

The cameras are controversial because they use AI to automatically track and log drivers’ movements without a warrant.

Vazquez’s post caught the attention of civil liberties group UltraViolet, which launched a campaign titled “Hey Ulta: Mass surveillance isn’t pretty,” calling on the retailer to cut ties with Flock and deactivate the cameras.

“At a time when women seeking reproductive healthcare, immigrants, protesters, journalists, and others are increasingly being monitored and targeted, the consequences of Flock’s mass surveillance system are staggering,” the organization said in an Instagram post. “We shouldn't have to trade our privacy and safety for a trip to Ulta.⁠”

Meanwhile, customers flooded the comment sections on Ulta’s official Instagram, also expressing concerns over the alleged Flock surveillance.

open image in gallery At least 50 law enforcement officers have been accused, charged or arrested for misusing Flock and similar license plate reader networks to track and stalk women, including wives, partners and ex-girlfriends, The Washington Post reported last month ( Getty )

“Hey Ulta, we don’t want to be surveilled at your store. Also stop deleting comments about it,” wrote one person.

“Well aren’t we all just FLOCKING to ultra! My favorite part of makeup is when a cop stalks me because @ultabeauty wants women to be unsafe. Thanks guys!” another person wrote.

“I’m a regular customer at Ulta & I won’t be shopping here until you terminate your flock camera contracts. We deserve better from you,” a third said.
