Sports.title: Ipswich Town v Liverpool: Premier League – live
Sports.content:
now 16.51 EDT 90 min +2: Flemming and Davis combine cutely down the left, and for a split second look to have opened Liverpool up … but Nyoni nips in to intercept and calmly clear. He’s the real deal, and Liverpool, so short on defensive nous in their stock of midfielders, will need him over the coming months. Not sure why they didn’t act in the transfer window, but here we all are. Share

2m ago 16.48 EDT 90 min: … so having said that, Jacquet slips and nearly allows McAteer a run on goal. But his team-mates recover the situation. Then Koumas comes on for Wirtz, who has been ineffectual, bordering on poor. There will be five additional minutes. Share

3m ago 16.47 EDT 89 min: Enciso tries to release Greaves down the inside left, but Jacquet comes across to impose himself and shepherd the ball out for a goal kick. The young centre-back has recovered well after that shaky couple of minutes early in the second half. Share

5m ago 16.46 EDT 88 min: Barcola closes down O’Shea, and though the ball ricochets back off him and out for an Ipswich throw, he’s earned himself another appreciative cry from the Liverpool support. Share

6m ago 16.45 EDT 86 min: Wirtz has an opportunity to launch a counter, but misplaces the pass. Clarke is teed up, just to the left of the Liverpool D, and takes a whack. His shot deflects off his own man Diop, and sails wide of the left-hand post, but not by much. And Alisson, wrong-footed, was rooted to the spot. Share

8m ago 16.42 EDT 84 min: Gakpo romps down the right and looks for Wirtz, free in the box. His low cross isn’t accurate, forcing Wirtz wide, and then the flag pops up for offside anyway. Then Mac Allister is subbed out for Nyoni. Share

10m ago 16.41 EDT 83 min: A bit of space for Davis down the left again. He looks for Flemming in the middle, but Araujo deflects the cross back to Alisson. Araujo has had a good game in (one of) Liverpool’s problem position(s). Share

12m ago 16.39 EDT 81 min: Greaves slips a cute pass down the inside-left channel to release Davis, who enters the box only to be denied a chance to shoot or cross by Araujo. But it will be a corner to Ipswich, which Lukic takes … only to fail to beat the first man. What a waste. Share

14m ago 16.36 EDT 79 min: Another double Ipswich change, as Palacios and Fatawu are replaced by McAteer and Ouattara. Share

15m ago 16.35 EDT 77 min: Flemming curls a weak shot in from the left. Alisson claims. Liverpool counter through Barcola, who dribbles into the box from the left and rolls unselfishly across for Szoboszlai … only for Gakpo to nip in and butcher a shot over the bar. Share

17m ago 16.34 EDT 75 min: Fatawu dribbles dangerously down the right and enters the box … only to be denied by a characteristically haughty intervention by Van Dijk. “Jan Molby and Mike Dean!” purrs Niall Mullen. “Two football legends who could run a game from the centre circle.” Share

19m ago 16.32 EDT 74 min: Flemming strides down the right and delivers a low cross through the Liverpool six-yard box. But there’s nobody in Ipswich blue making a run, allowing Araujo to flick clear, and in any case the flag pops up for offside. Share

20m ago 16.31 EDT 73 min: The pace drops. Both teams unable to put much together at the minute. Share

21m ago 16.29 EDT 71 min: Barcola chases a pass down the left but Scherpen comes out of his box to deal with the danger. “I saw Jan Molby play centre back in a Goodison derby,” writes Gary Naylor. “He never got as far as the centre circle. Still ran the game though.” Share

23m ago 16.28 EDT VAR: no penalty 70 min: It would be a penalty for sure … Davis clipped his man … but it turns out Szoboszlai was marginally offside in the build-up. A huge let-off for Ipswich! Portman Road roars its approval. Share

24m ago 16.26 EDT Penalty to Liverpool? 68 min: Szoboszlai gets in ahead of Davis down the inside-right channel. He’s caught by the Ipswich man from behind. Szoboszlai goes over. The referee waves play on, but it looks like the Ipswich man clipped his opponent’s boot. VAR will get involved … and sends the referee over to the screen. View image in fullscreen Liverpool's Dominik Szoboszlai reacts after a challenge from Ipswich Town's Leif Davis before a VAR penalty review. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters Share Updated at 16.41 EDT

26m ago 16.25 EDT 67 min: Barcola’s first couple of touches, jinking in elegantly from the left, draws oohs and aahs from the travelling support. His third, an attempt to one-two with Wirtz, doesn’t come off. Share

27m ago 16.24 EDT 66 min: Ipswich respond with a double change of their own: Emersonn and Maeda are replaced by Clarke and Flemming, who like Barcola is also making his debut tonight. Share

28m ago 16.23 EDT 65 min: Had Isak remained on, it would have been the first time in football history that three £100m players were on the same pitch for the same team at the same time. But we must wait for that particular modern-day pleasure. Share

29m ago 16.22 EDT 64 min: Liverpool make a double change. Isak and Munoz make way for Gravenberch and the new man Barcola. View image in fullscreen Liverpool's Bradley Barcola Photograph: David Klein/Reuters Share Updated at 16.31 EDT

30m ago 16.20 EDT 62 min: Fatawu goes long down the middle. Emersonn is never getting the better of Jacquet and Van Dijk, the latter finally heading back to Alisson. Still a sense that there’s something in this for Ipswich. Share

32m ago 16.18 EDT 60 min: Looks like Barcola is receiving some tactical instruction from the Liverpool coaching staff. We might see him soon. Meanwhile on the pitch, Enciso curls softly towards the bottom right. Alisson, who hasn’t looked his assured self tonight, blocks but allows the ball to squirt away. He eventually claims, but is fortunate Emersonn wasn’t sniffing around. Share

34m ago 16.16 EDT 58 min: Wirtz tries to combine with Isak down the inside-left channel, but his attempt to spin into space on the edge of the box is no good. Still, some much-needed possession for Liverpool, who haven’t looked settled since the restart. Share

36m ago 16.14 EDT 57 min: Kerkez slides in recklessly on Fatawu, and that’s a no-brainer of a booking. Liverpool suddenly look a little ragged, and panicky at the back. Share

37m ago 16.13 EDT 56 min: Fatawu cuts in from the right and curls towards the top left. Well wide, and Alisson had it covered. But Ipswich are threatening to get back into this game. Share

37m ago 16.13 EDT 55 min: Scherpen dallies with the ball at his feet, then miscontrols, and is fortunate not to be closed down by Munoz. Share

39m ago 16.12 EDT 53 min: Munoz skedaddles down the right but he’s quickly surrounded by five players. Ipswich counter, and Jacquet once again catches Emersonn. That could easily have been a second booking in as many minutes, but the referee shows the young man some mercy. Lucky Jacquet. Share

40m ago 16.10 EDT 52 min: Szoboszlai curls in from the right. If Wirtz controls, he’s shooting from six yards. He doesn’t control and Diop clears. Emersonn challenges for a high ball on the halfway line, and is high-kicked for his trouble by Jacquet, who goes into the book. Share

42m ago 16.09 EDT 51 min: Liverpool enjoy some sterile midfield domination. Arne Slot would have been proud. Meanwhile Andrew Goudie, of half-time postbag fame, has got Jon Taylor reminiscing: “There were a few games in the 90s when Jan Molby played central midfield alongside John Barnes in his late-era, deep-lying and decidedly-less-svelte years. The two of them sat in the centre circle dictating play: it was like watching a binary solar system with two suns and the rest of the players orbiting around them.” Share

44m ago 16.07 EDT 49 min: All a bit scrappy at the moment. In lieu of anything exciting happening, Kerkez celebrates winning a throw like he’s just scored from 30 yards. Share

46m ago 16.05 EDT 47 min: Szoboszlai delivers from the right. Mac Allister, free six yards out, flaps a weak header goalwards. Easy for Scherpen. Mac Allister should have done so much better. Share

47m ago 16.04 EDT 46 min: Mac Allister and Van Dijk confuse each other, nearly allowing Enciso to romp clear. Alisson comes out of his goal to whack clear. Up the other end, Wirtz shoots from the edge of the D, and his shot is deflected wide right for the first corner of the second half. Share

48m ago 16.03 EDT Ipswich get the second half started. No changes as of yet. Share

55m ago 15.55 EDT Half-time postbag. “xG is one of those analytics stats that has breached containment and is now polluting football discourse. Unfortunately, like pollution, it’s difficult to clear up once it’s out there so we now have to live with it. More seriously, it’s only really meaningful over the long term. If a term is outperforming its xG, then it’s really taking its chances, but if it’s underperforming, then it needs to work on its finishing. In a single game, it tells you very little. As a statistic, it’s better than shots on target, as it at least tries to take into account the quality of them, but that’s a really low bar to get over” – Andy (Not That One) Flintoff “I’ve been trying to squeeze ‘No 6 collaborations project’ into a reply to Peter Oh (17 min) which is still relevant to the match, but I’ve got nothing. I will be watching closely at the end though to see if Issa Diop and Milos Kerkez have a long chat. You never know” – Rob K “All the palaver over Mike Dean this week reminded me that the great Jan Molby didn’t leave the centre circle for years” – Andrew Goudie “Gakpo and Isak. Shall we call this partnership GakSak?” – Paul Waite “Good to see Isak reviving Suarez’s beef with all things East Anglian” – Ian Copestake Share

1h ago 15.47 EDT HALF TIME: Ipswich Town 0-2 Liverpool Ipswich have responded well to the early double whammy administered by Alexander Isak … but Liverpool are nevertheless in control at the break. Share

1h ago 15.46 EDT 45 min +1: The game suddenly slips into Basketball Mode. Gakpo tears down the left but can’t find Wirtz with a poor pass infield; Palacios quick-breaks, but clanks his opportunity to release Fatawu down the right straight to Mac Allister. Both teams frustrated, Liverpool especially so as Fatawu had clipped Gakpo with the ball gone, just inside the area. But you’re rarely getting a penalty kick for that. Share Updated at 16.02 EDT

1h ago 15.45 EDT 45 min: … Gakpo batters clear. There will be two additional first-half minutes. Share

1h ago 15.44 EDT 44 min: The corner takes a while, because the referee allows Davis to retie his boot. When it eventually comes in, it’s Jacquet’s turn to slice a clearance, and Emersonn forces a corner that’ll come in from the right. Fatawu takes, and … Share

1h ago 15.43 EDT 42 min: When the free kick’s finally taken, Kerkez crosses from the left. Jacquet cushions the ball into the road of Wirtz, who carefully threads a shot towards the bottom right. But there’s no real pace on the ball, and it’s easy for the keeper. Ipswich go up the other end, Davis crossing from the left, and Araujo carelessly shins a clearance backwards and out for a corner. Share

1h ago 15.41 EDT 41 min: Gakpo is skittled 40 yards out. Mac Allister tries to take a quick free kick, only for Enciso to step in the road. He’s booked for delaying the restart. Share

1h ago 15.40 EDT 40 min: Szoboszlai, in space on the right, has the option of releasing Munoz into even more space … but opts to shoot instead. Scherpen once again parries clear. He’s had a busy – and mixed – evening so far. Share

1h ago 15.38 EDT 38 min: Alisson launches long. Diop misjudges, nearly letting Isak in on goal, but Greaves comes across to help the ball back to his keeper. Ipswich go up the other end, Enciso looking for the top-right corner from distance. He slices miles wide. It’s been a pretty open, easy-on-the-eye game. Share

1h ago 15.36 EDT 36 min: Liverpool coach Tommy Elphick is booked for telling it as he sees it. Share

1h ago 15.35 EDT 35 min: Maeda probes down the inside-left but Jacquet doesn’t give him much room to work with, and the eventual shot dribbles through to Alisson. Share

1h ago 15.35 EDT 34 min: Just before that disallowed goal, Emersonn gently nudged Van Dijk off balance while the defender was in mid air, and the Liverpool captain landed awkwardly. It should have been a foul, but the referee didn’t blow. Van Dijk, Mac Allister and Gakpo not happy with the official. Thankfully there’s no harm done. Share

1h ago 15.33 EDT 33 min: Wirtz turns down the inside-left channel into space, then rolls infield for Isak, who opens his body and calmly slots into the bottom right. But the flag goes up for offside, correctly so. It was close, though. Share

1h ago 15.32 EDT 31 min: Wirtz tees up Mac Allister, just outside the Ipswich D. Mac Allister pings a rising shot over the bar. Not by much, though Scherpen had it covered. Share

1h ago 15.31 EDT 30 min: Enciso nearly beats Mac Allister in a foot race down the inside-right channel. But not quite. Instead he crosses, looking for Maeda, who is denied by Araujo, who slices clear. Then Fatawu crosses from the right, Davis heading harmlessly over the bar from close range. Ipswich are knocking on the door, all of a sudden. Share

Sports.title: Chelsea hit bullseye with Morgan Rogers as Arsenal rue what might have been
Sports.content:
Chelsea thought they had little chance of signing Morgan Rogers at the start of the summer. Xabi Alonso and the club’s recruitment team had the England international as a priority target but a deal seemed unlikely. Chelsea had endured a disappointing season, missing out on European football after finishing 10th, and their expectation was that Rogers would leave Aston Villa for Arsenal.

It was towards the end of the World Cup that Chelsea were made aware of a window of opportunity. Although Arsenal could claim to be London’s top dogs after winning the Premier League they dithered in talks with Villa, raising the prospect of another club stepping in.

Mikel Arteta talked about being bold in the market after Arsenal’s defeat by Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final. Arteta wanted more in attack. A new option on the left was a priority; Leandro Trossard and Gabriel Martinelli were up for sale and everything pointed towards Arsenal making their move for Rogers at the end of June.

Yet the lines became blurred. Arsenal had a fee of £80m in mind, while Villa wanted more, particularly after Nottingham Forest sold Elliot Anderson to Manchester City for £116m. Time dragged on. How serious were Arsenal? There was also interest in Julián Alvarez, Vinícius Júnior and Bradley Barcola. Villa waited and the price for Rogers went up. Arsenal, beaten to the punch in the end, will have a look at what they could have won when Chelsea and Rogers visit the Emirates Stadium on Sunday.

Chelsea were decisive. They were tracking Rogers before he left Middlesbrough for Villa in February 2024. Joe Shields, one of Chelsea’s five sporting directors, worked with Rogers at Manchester City’s academy. The signing was not done on a whim. Chelsea have a good relationship with Villa’s owners and moved quickly after opening club-to-club talks a day after Rogers played in England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina. The fee was £117m and Chelsea did not struggle to convince Rogers. Alonso wooed him and the deal was confirmed five days after negotiations began.

View image in fullscreen Xabi Alonso has put a lot of smiles back on faces at Chelsea after last season’s player rebellions. Photograph: Alex Ferrelly/Crystal Pix/Sports Press Photo/Shutterstock

There was no last-ditch move from Arsenal. They signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge for £34m two days later and focused on other targets. When the window closed, though, Arteta’s options on the left looked a little light. Martinelli and Trossard left but only Tzolis arrived. Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke are alternatives. It is hard not to feel that Arsenal could have done with Rogers, even though Chelsea have paid a high price for him.

It remains to be seen whether the 24-year-old can prove he merits becoming the third-most expensive player in English football history. For context, the fee is the consequence of the market threatening to rise out of control and the money spent on many players starting to feel meaningless. It is worth pointing out, too, that money flowed back and forth between Chelsea and Villa all summer. Even so the price will follow Rogers around, so it is just as well he has made an excellent start.

Rogers has been involved in four of Chelsea’s seven goals in their first two league games. He scored in the 3-2 win at Fulham and later combined with João Pedro to set up Cole Palmer’s goal. He created Pedro Neto’s goal in last weekend’s 4-3 win over Brighton and played a key role when Jorrel Hato played in João Pedro to score.

Chelsea have thrilled in attack so far, João Pedro, Rogers and Palmer combining to devastating effect. Alonso, an adaptable manager, wants more control but his transitional football has been a delight. Chelsea were mannered and controlled during Enzo Maresca’s time in charge. It is felt that Alonso has recognised the Premier League’s shift towards power and athleticism. Rogers fits into the Spaniard’s system. Thomas Tuchel loves Rogers for his connectivity and pressing. It is significant that England’s energy levels rose in their quarter-final against Norway after the introduction of Rogers and Djed Spence late in the second half.

Chelsea needed more strength, more speed. Rogers, able to play anywhere in attacking midfield or as a No 8, looks a better fit in Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 than Enzo Fernández, sold this week to Manchester City for £125m. He has played with Palmer as one of the No 10s but has a responsibility to drift left, a role that is unlikely to have suited Fernández. Arsenal’s impeccable defence will be tested by Chelsea’s front three.

The Rogers-Palmer partnership has clicked. They are old friends and banter over the “ice cold” celebration. Rogers is a bubbly character and can get on with anyone. Chelsea are keen to improve the culture in the dressing room. It is felt that Alonso has shifted the mood after last year’s rebellions. The squad are united. It is one of the reasons why Chelsea decided to sell Fernández on deadline day. They did not need the headache of reintegrating the Argentinian.

View image in fullscreen Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, pictured celebrating Chelsea’s fourth goal against Brighton, have forged a promising relationship. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

This is a fresh start. The signing of Rogers, who was the Professional Footballers’ Association’s young player of the year in 2025, was a sign of Chelsea’s intent. Rogers was one of the best players in the Premier League last season. He grew under Unai Emery and scored when Villa beat Freiburg in the Europa League final in May.

It was one of Rogers’ less eye-catching goals: a clever jab at the near post from a low cross. There was a period last season when he could not stop scoring from long range but Rogers has spoken about wanting scruffier goals and he arrived at the far post to open his Chelsea account against Fulham.

Rogers is embracing the challenge. At Arsenal he would have been slotting into the finished article. Arsenal have reached the summit. Chelsea are beginning their climb under Alonso. Rogers, who has played in the Championship and had a loan in League One, rather liked the idea of starting lower down.

Sports.title: WSL transfer talking points: three things we learned from the data
Sports.content:
The Women’s Super League’s summer transfer window has closed before the start of the 2026-27 season. The finances involved are microscopic compared with the £3.4bn that Premier League clubs spent on new players but the data provides three key points of interest: which club has made the biggest improvement to their squad, who is banking on stability, and how the women’s game has outsmarted its male equivalent.

Arsenal have the most improved squad

Many transfers in women’s football occur without the fee being disclosed, which deprives us of the conventional shorthand for assessing player quality. Thankfully there is Soccerdonna, the arm of Transfermarkt that covers women’s football. It carries estimated market values of players in euros. Using these, we can see by how much clubs have improved their squads.

Arsenal’s new additions have a combined value of €3.9m, slightly more than the €3.5m of talent that London City Lionesses have gained this summer. The entire squads of eight of the 14 teams in the 2026-27 WSL are worth less than these figures, which highlights the impact the new players should have. Indeed, London City’s new two-time Ballon d’Or winner Alexia Putellas is valued at €1.15m, which is more than the entire Charlton squad and not far behind the roster at Crystal Palace.

West Ham could argue they have added the most to their squad as the combined market value of their new players (€1.02m) is more than the corresponding amount for the players who remain from last season (€0.96m). Having finished 10th after winning only three of their opening 19 matches, improvements were clearly required.

Clubs have kept more settled squads

While supporters are most excited by new signings, departees are just as relevant to the health of a squad. Or at least they are if they made significant contributions in the previous season.

West Ham had to make additions as they lost players that contributed 6,322 minutes in the 2025-26 WSL, 29% of their total. Chief among those leaving was the goalkeeper Kinga Szemik, who started 19 of 22 games. Only Martina Fernández (1,950 minutes for Everton) and Keira Flannery (1,891 at Charlton) left current WSL clubs and played more minutes last season.

Teams may have learned from 12 months ago. Brighton lost 9,584 minutes of playing time from their 2024-25 squad in the summer 2025 window and went on to finish two places lower last season. Liverpool also said goodbye to a higher share of their playing time than anyone has in this transfer window (6,406 minutes), and started the campaign very slowly.

Output could be a greater issue than time played. Manchester City and Aston Villa have both lost players who contributed at least 13 combined goals and assists last season in Kerolin and Kirsty Hanson respectively. The difference between these clubs is that the champions can absorb the cost of that exit far more easily. The 17 goal contributions Villa have lost from last season through players leaving constitute 36.2% of their total, the highest proportion of the teams who were in the WSL in 2025-26.

The WSL is far better prepared for transfer windows than the Premier League

The Premier League endured a ridiculous deadline day on Tuesday. Around a sixth of players signed by clubs in the latest transfer window completed their deals on 1 September. Just over a third of the money that went on transfer fees this summer was spent after the 2026-27 season had already begun.

Things have been rather more organised in the WSL. Granted, its window closed before the new campaign gets under way and they didn’t have a World Cup clogging up the summer this year. But where the Premier League had completed only 83% of eventual total signings when deadline day began, the WSL made that proportion four weeks ago.

The obvious explanation would be that lower-finance deals are easier to complete. Yet Fifa recently revealed global spending on transfer fees in women’s football had increased by 83.6% year-on-year. Spending on agents fees by WSL clubs grew by 75% in the year up to 3 February 2026 too. The transfer business remains efficient even while the sums involved are rapidly increasing.

Men’s football will always have much more money but it could benefit from the transfer expertise and planning in the women’s game.

Sports.title: Premier League news: Carrick warns no quick fix, Emery has ‘hard’ Harwood-Bellis chat
Sports.content:
1. No 'instant fix' at United, admits Carrick Michael Carrick has admitted one transfer window cannot provide an “instant fix” for Manchester United but said he was “largely happy” with the club’s business, despite being outspent by promoted Hull, Ipswich and Coventry. United spent £155m on central midfielders but failed to sign a left-back, leaving Luke Shaw as the only senior player in that position. United go to Everton on Sunday seeking their first away point, having lost at Hull. There were no signings in the final week of the window, despite a number of inquiries for left-backs. Everton asked about loaning Joshua Zirkzee on deadline day but United deemed it too late to source a replacement striker. “What squad’s ever the perfect squad?” Carrick said. “You’ve always got to find ways of adapting. When you’re building and trying to push, going through a period where we’re trying to get to the top, that’s the ultimate goal. You’ve got to make steps. It’s not going to be one hit where everything is [fixed] and I’m not just talking about players, individuals … I’m talking about the whole thing of improving as a group, improving as a squad. It’s not just an instant fix and you finish top of the league and you stay there.” Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba arrived to bolster the midfield, and Karl Darlow was brought in on a free as a backup goalkeeper. United start their Champions League campaign on Thursday and there are questions over strength in depth. “We went into the window wanting to come out stronger,” Carrick said. “From the group we had last season, we’ve added to that, we’ve done a lot of good work. The situation is what it is in terms of finances and what we can do. The players we brought in I’m delighted with; the quality and level we’ve got I’m really happy with. These other things you can do or could have done, that’s part of evolving the group and trying to push all the time. We had certain things we needed to fill and largely I think we’re in a good group. We’ve a good dynamic in the squad. We’ve got players that are flexible in the team and can play in different positions. Largely pretty happy.” Will Unwin

2. Emery leaves new signing Harwood-Bellis out of squad Unai Emery conceded omitting Taylor Harwood-Bellis from Aston Villa’s Champions League squad, two days after the defender joined in a £25m deal from Southampton, prompted a “difficult” conversation. Harwood-Bellis and the 17-year-old Brian Madjo were surprisingly left out of Villa’s 23-man squad. Emery spoke to Harwood-Bellis on Thursday to advise the 24-year-old, who has one England cap, that he would not be eligible to play in European competition. Madjo is not expected to play until October owing to a foot injury sustained after scoring in the Super Cup last month, but in that scenario would be injured only for Tuesday’s Champions League opener at Club Brugge. Harwood-Bellis, a deadline-day arrival, was the last of Villa’s 10 summer signings after being identified as a replacement for Ezri Konsa, who joined Arsenal in a £51m deal. It is understood there is no financial reason for the omissions, though Villa’s fight to meet Uefa’s squad-cost rules is ongoing. Emery said he hoped Harwood-Bellis would play in the Champions League later in the season, potentially in February if they advance to the knockout stages, but for now the midfielders Lamare Bogarde and Boubacar Kamara can deputise in at centre-back. “It was difficult,” Emery said of his decision to exclude Harwood-Bellis. “It is hard for him, it is hard for me to tell him my decision, but I did it yesterday. I spoke with Taylor and explained to him why. Of course, it was hard, but he understood it. For other players like Madjo and [Modou Kéba] Cissé, there are different circumstances, Cissé and Madjo are injured. Of course, hopefully Madjo will be available after the break and the next challenge is for him to get inside [the squad] in January.” In February 2025, Emery left Donyell Malen out of his Champions League squad, weeks after the Dutchman joined from Borussia Dortmund, for whom he played in the 2024 final against Real Madrid. In the same window the defender Andrés García, who joined from Levante and is on loan at Getafe, was also omitted. “Taylor arrived as the last one, and we can get the balance [in defence] with Lamare Bogarde, and we can even play Kamara," Emery said. "We tried to analyse it deeply. Taylor will be here for a long time, and hopefully, we will have the opportunity to play in Europe with us, after January maybe, and the next few years. Madjo is 17 years old and is so, so young. He will have, for sure, more opportunities to play with us this year and the next years in Europe.” Ben Fisher

3. City players delighted to have 'winner' Fernández, says Maresca Enzo Maresca has revealed Manchester City’s players repeatedly asked him whether Enzo Fernández was joining before the Argentinian completed his deadline-day move. Fernández signed from Chelsea for a British record-equalling £125m late on Tuesday. The deal ended a long-running saga, City having been linked with the World Cup-winner for most of the summer, and Maresca says the midfielder has immediately proved popular in the dressing room. View image in fullscreen Enzo Fernández is not regarded by his new manager as a potential Manchester City captain. Photograph: Manchester City FC The City manager said: “He’s a winner and when you belong to a squad and another winner arrives they are always happy. I can promise you that in the last four or five days four or five players in the squad were asking if he was coming or not because they wanted him to be with us. It’s very important that he is with us and we are 100% happy with that.” Fernández could go straight into the side to face Coventry at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday but will not be the captain. Maresca said last week he wanted to sign “one or two more captains” and had Fernández as a captain at Chelsea. “The four captains are Rúben [Dias], Erling [Haaland], Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma,” said Maresca. “But Enzo is ready. I know him quite well, I know what he can bring to the team. He’s a winner, he has a winner’s mentality. He knows how to win – World Cup, Club World Cup.” Press Association

Sports.title: Manchester City failed to land Spain pair in scramble for Miedema cover
Sports.content:
Atlético Madrid rejected a bid of more than £500,000 from Manchester City for the Spain midfielder Fiamma Benítez on the Women’s Super League’s transfer deadline day, the Guardian can reveal.

The WSL champions are understood to have tried hard to add attacking-midfielder reinforcements before the English summer window closed on Thursday at 11pm BST, largely in light of news that their No 10 Vivianne Miedema could be out for at least the rest of 2026 with a knee injury.

However, Atlético are understood to view Benítez as a key player and a future national team star and were not prepared to let the 22-year-old go. In 2022 Benítez helped Spain win the Under-19 Euros and Under-20 Women’s World Cup and she helped her country win the 2024 Women’s Nations League.

City then made an even later move for Everton’s Spain international Ornella Vignola, who can play in midfield or on the wing. A bid of about £400,000 is understood to have been turned down by Everton, largely because they felt they would not have time to source a suitable replacement but also because of Vignola’s importance to Scott Phelan’s side.

It was also widely reported that City attempted to bring in the Nigeria midfielder Jennifer Echegini from Paris Saint-Germain, but multiple sources have told the Guardian that PSG made clear they were not willing to sell the 25-year-old. PSG had agreed to sell the France defender Élisa De Almeida to Arsenal for a fee believed to be just over £500,000, and they were not prepared to lose two key players in one day.

City completed one deadline-day deal, bringing in England’s Anna Moorhouse on loan from Orlando Pride until the end of January, adding good-quality depth to their goalkeeping ranks after Khiara Keating moved to Liverpool on a free in July.

Although City were left scrambling unsuccessfully for a midfielder on Thursday, it was a positive summer for the club, not least because they began with their most important deal, retaining the services of the WSL’s Golden Boot winner Khadija Shaw with a lucrative new contract. Andrée Jeglertz’s side begin their title defence at home to promoted Birmingham on Sunday.

Discussing Miedema’s injuries on Friday, Jeglertz said: “It’s tough for her and of course for us, but her determination is to get back as quickly as possible. We need to keep assessing from week to week but we are fully aware that she will be out for this fall and then we will see where we are later this fall but we don’t expect her back in the coming weeks.”

West Ham have confirmed the signing of the Japan legend Saki Kumagai from London City Lionesses on a one-year deal, a move revealed by the Guardian on Thursday.

The 35-year-old, who scored the winning penalty for Japan in the 2011 Women’s World Cup final, is West Ham’s 10th summer signing. “The WSL is a very competitive league and I’m looking forward continuing my journey in England with West Ham United,” said Kumagai.

Meanwhile, Arsenal will face both of last season’s Women’s Champions League finalists during this season’s league phase after receiving the trickiest-looking draw of the three English sides involved.

Renée Slegers’s team, who won the Champions League in 2025, will travel to holders Barcelona and host runners-up OL Lyonnes as their two pot-one opponents. Chelsea travel to OL Lyonnes, Sonia Bompastor’s former side, and also host Paris Saint-Germain and Roma. City, who were in pot three, were handed home matches against PSG and Real Madrid, as well as a trip to Bayern Munich.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arsenal’s other ties include a visit to Milan to face Inter, who pulled off the surprise of the qualifying rounds by eliminating the two-time champions Wolfsburg on penalties. City will also be away to Inter, who finished second in Serie A last season.

There is a lot of similarity between Chelsea and Manchester City’s opponents; they both face PSG and Austria Wien at home and travel to Swedish side BK Hacken, who won last season’s inaugural Women’s Europa Cup.

The 18-team League phase gets under way on 22-23 September and the full fixture list is expected to be published within the next 24 hours. Each side plays six other teams overall – two from each of pot one, pot two and pot three. Teams from the same nation could not face each other.

The top four teams after the six matchdays in the league phase will qualify automatically for the quarter-finals, which begin in March. The teams finishing between fifth and 12th will contest the knockout phase playoffs in February, to fight for the four remaining quarter-final places. This season’s final will be held in Warsaw, Poland, in May.

The three English sides’ full lists of opponents:

Manchester City PSG (h), Bayern Munich (a), Real Madrid (h), BK Hacken (a), Austria Wien (h), Inter (a).

Arsenal OL Lyonnes (h), Barcelona (a), Benfica (h), Paris FC (a), HB Koge (h), Inter (a).

Chelsea PSG (h), OL Lyonnes (a), Roma (h), BK Hacken (a), Austria Wien (h), OH Leuven (a).

Sports.title: Nottingham Forest’s Liam Delap: ‘I play at my best on the edge of being horrible’
Sports.content:
“You can imagine it: he’s a centre-back, I’m a striker,” says Liam Delap, Nottingham Forest’s £45m club-record signing, smiling as he sets the scene. He is reliving taking on his younger brother, Finn, in the garden. These days, they are each other’s biggest supporters – Liam attended Finn’s victory for third-tier Burton on Wednesday – but as kids there was a friendly rivalry. The elder brother says: “There were probably a lot of tears, a lot of fights … whether it was playing Monopoly or football, it always ended in either the table being flipped or kicking the shit out of each other.”

It is a competitive streak that has stuck and Delap is determined to make his presence felt at Forest, for whom he could make his full debut against Tottenham on Saturday. It has been a testing 16 months; he left Chelsea a season into a six-year contract and after one goal in 28 top-flight appearances, a dozen of those starts. “It is never a linear path straight to the top,” Delap says, his right hand taking flight in the City Ground boardroom, the 1979 and 1980 European Cups shimmering behind him. “I just want to get my head down, focus and keep improving because I’m still so young and I have so much to learn. I even at times probably think I’ve been in football a lot longer than I have. I’ve still, hopefully, got a long career ahead.

“I think you just have to accept that sometimes things go bad, things happen … it might [prove to] be a good thing, I think. My first loans to Stoke and Preston [from Manchester City, across 2022-23] didn’t really go well at all and it was probably one of the best things that happened because I learnt so much from that season and went to Hull [for 2023-24] and kicked on from there. I’m still young, I’ve still got a lot of learning to do. Sometimes injuries happen, sometimes you don’t play. I don’t think anything is lost … Everyone has rocky moments. I’ve just got to use them to learn and kick on.”

Last summer, Delap was hot property. Oliver Glasner tells a story of Delap having proposals from 18 Premier League clubs and jests that the 23-year-old knows every top-flight manager owing to the various Zoom calls he held while deciding his next move. After all, one of those was with Glasner, then at Crystal Palace. Forest wanted him then, too. “It was a tough decision,” recalls Delap. “I remember the conversation we had, I was really impressed and I thought: ‘This guy [Glasner] is really good.’ He spoke incredibly well and you can see he has done really well with the strikers he has had in the past. That definitely stuck in my mind.”

Glasner wants Delap to play to his strengths: physicality, power and finishing. He doesn’t mean the forward’s hidden talent: cube roots. At the start of the year a clip of Delap showing off his maths skills went viral. “I didn’t enjoy maths one bit but I was always quite good at it. One of my friends taught me in school how to do it and I didn’t forget it. I hated school, [the] work, but I was always quite intelligent.”

The Austrian head coach said it was apparent in conversations with Delap this summer that the player had learnt lessons from a trying year: “I think it shows his attitude and his character that he said: ‘Yeah, I want a team and a club that values my strengths and wants to play to my strengths.’ Because I never want to change a player: it doesn’t make sense to say: ‘OK, now you should play like Messi: false nine, drop into midfield and combine play with one or two touches.”

View image in fullscreen Liam Delap scored once in 28 league appearances for Chelsea. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

A tally of 12 goals in the Ipswich side relegated in 2024-25 triggered widespread interest. At that point Delap was talked up as a potential heir to Harry Kane as England’s No 9. He has been capped by his country at every age group and was in the same under-16s team as Jude Bellingham. “As a little kid, all you want to do is play for your country,” Delap says. “So, of course, in my mind that’s where I want to get to. But it’s not as easy as that. I have to work hard and improve and that’s all I can do.”

An imposing 6ft 2in striker, Delap has long been viewed as the next big thing. He spearheaded Manchester City to FA Youth Cup victory over Chelsea in 2020, a couple of months after Pep Guardiola handed him his senior City debut aged 17. Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers, now teammates at Chelsea, were part of that same under-18s side, together with the new Aston Villa defender Taylor Harwood-Bellis and James McAtee, one of his best friends and now a clubmate again.

“He was a No 10 and quite often he would give me the ball and we just had that really good relationship off the pitch and it translated on to the pitch,” Delap says of McAtee. “If we didn’t win, we’d all be fuming. It probably instilled that winning mentality into us early. I think it’s worked because you can see from that team that almost everyone is playing somewhere in the Premier League, abroad, the Championship and that is probably because we pushed each other so much.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Delap made his Forest debut as a substitute at Anfield last weekend, his first notable action a quick throw-in that led to the penalty scored by Morgan Gibbs-White to earn a second-half lead. Only after the 2-2 draw did Glasner discover that Delap’s father, Rory, who played for Southampton and Stoke among others, knew a thing or two about throws. “I said: your father will be proud of you,” says Forest’s head coach. So, has Liam got a mammoth throw in his armoury? “No, I don’t think so,” he replies. “I would never, anyway: I’m a striker, I need to be in the box.”

View image in fullscreen Liam Delap was much in demand after impressing with a 12-goal league season at Ipswich. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images

Delap relishes the blood and thunder of battle. Glasner loves how Forest’s marquee signing stands up to centre-backs, making the point that defenders are hardly “hugging and kissing you all the time” in the heat of duels. But Delap, who spent a decade at Derby before joining City, says he has learned to harness his aggression on the field, after periods of getting into trouble when he was a youngster.

“You have to be careful, but not shy away from who you are,” he says. “I’m always going to fight for everything, always be aggressive, determined. It goes back to the point about my brother, being little kids in the garden, going at each other: that’s me. Sometimes you need to control it and sometimes you need to be careful, but I think I play at my best when I’m on that edge of being … being horrible.”

Sports.title: Chaotic Crystal Palace transfer window leaves Pierre Sage to run the gamut of emotions
Sports.content:
At least Pierre Sage did his research before joining Crystal Palace in June. Having stepped into Oliver Glasner’s shoes after the most successful era in the club’s history, it has not been the easiest transition for the engaging Frenchman following defeats against Everton and Manchester City to start the new campaign, and amid uncertainty surrounding the futures of some of the Conference League winners’ key players.

Ismaïla Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta ended up staying at Selhurst Park despite interest from Liverpool and Aston Villa respectively, while Palace brought in four new players after missing out to Sunderland for Malick Fofana in one of deadline day’s most dramatic storylines. But Sage is sanguine about experiencing a typically chaotic first transfer window in south London, and relieved to be able to concentrate on events on the pitch before Saturday’s trip to Fulham.

“I knew that and I had to deal and adapt to that,” Sage said when asked about Palace’s reputation for doing late deals, a trend that has led to them signing 10 players on the final day in the past three summer windows. “But at the end the most important thing is to have the player or the profile we choose and that’s the case. I think we are in line with what we need.”

Glasner, who has been joined at Nottingham Forest from Palace by Daniel Muñoz, made no secret of his dissatisfaction at having to wait until deadline day to bring in players after Palace signed four in his first summer at the club in 2024. It’s not Sage’s style to make a similar fuss, even if he is understood to have expressed frustration over their efforts to recruit a top-class replacement for Maxence Lacroix when the France defender was sold to Chelsea in July.

His favoured target was Ismaëlo Ganiou from Lens, the 21-year-old a key competent in the team that won the Coupe de France and finished second in Ligue 1 under Sage last season. However, Lens were reluctant to sell one of their prized assets and Ganiou signed a new deal at the start of August, forcing Palace to explore other targets.

A deal for Joel Ordóñez of Club Brugge broke down as the Ecuador defender is still recovering from a broken foot, while attempts to sign Augsburg’s Chrislain Matsima and Raphaël Le Guen of Brest also came to nothing. The arrival of Axel Disasi and the teenager Honest Ahanor on loan will help plug the gap, yet there remain major doubts over whether Lacroix’s leadership at the back has been fully replaced.

View image in fullscreen One that got away: Malick Fofana chose Sunderland over Palace on deadline day. Photograph: Jean Catuffe/Getty Images

Having failed to lure Mamadou Sangaré from Lens, with the Mali midfielder opting to join Brentford instead, Sage was the driving force in Palace’s attempt to bring in Fofana from another of his former clubs, Lyon. That ultimately proved futile despite a series of phone calls to the Belgium forward on deadline day. “I’m really proud and happy with what the club did for that,” Sage insisted. “We fight a lot and sometimes you cannot give more than this, but we give our best in this situation. At the end, the player chooses.” It remains to be seen whether the signing of the Chile forward Dario Osorio from the Danish club Midtjylland on an initial loan with an obligation to buy next summer for £26m makes up for the disappointment given he plays mainly on the right flank.

Palace are well stocked in attacking areas having also signed Dwight McNeil and Evann Guessand – who has been left out of the squad for the Europa League – and kept hold of Sarr. The return of Ben Chilwell and late addition of Quinten Timber to midfield will add depth and are believed to have gone some way to satisfying Sage, not to mention Palace’s rejection of bids from unnamed sides for Adam Wharton. Manchester City and Chelsea were believed to be among those who showed an interest. “The club was strong with the situation, and I think the player is completely in line with that,” he said.

But after breaking their transfer record twice in January, for Jørgen Strand Larsen and Brennan Johnson – who was swapped for McNeil, with Everton – Palace’s summer net spend of almost £40m in profit was the second lowest in the division behind Aston Villa. Over the past five seasons, Hull and Coventry have both invested more than Palace’s £90m despite being in the Championship.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Sage was quick to reject suggestions he is unhappy with Palace’s summer signings and instead drew on his experiences from watching his parents run their brasserie in Belley, a town in the Ain region of eastern France. “I’m not frustrated – we are not a bank,” he said. “We do with what we have. My parents had a restaurant and I prefer every day there’s a lot of clients but it was not the case sometimes and we have to deal with that every day. In football it’s the same.”

View image in fullscreen Pierre Sage said of Palace’s transfer window: ‘I’m not frustrated, we’re not a bank.’ Photograph: Malcolm Fell/Focus Images Ltd/Shutterstock

The absences of Sarr and Mateta, the latter of which had his hopes of leaving scuppered by a hamstring injury that will keep him out for another three weeks, will not help Palace’s chances against Fulham. Sage expects Sarr back from a groin injury for the game against Ipswich next Saturday but said the Senegal forward “needs time” after being affected by Liverpool’s interest, which led to his agent releasing a statement criticising the player’s treatment.

It will not have escaped Sage’s attention that Glasner won three times at Craven Cottage in 2025, including a quarter-final victory on the way to winning the FA Cup. After the week he has had, more of the same would do against another team who have yet to get off the mark in the league this season.

Sports.title: Football Daily | What you won’t see in the Premier League this weekend
Sports.content:
NOTHING TO SEE HERE

That icy wind rattling the rafters is the cold reality of what follows the closure of the transfer window, a hungover pall of regret. Despite £3.5bn shelled out in the men’s window, several things will not be happening in the Premier League when they might have been. When Arsenal host Chelsea for a most super of Sundays, Vinícius Júnior will not be playing in their attack, and neither will Gabriel Martinelli, whose lengthy social media disgrace farewells on his departure for Saudi Arabia pointedly made no mention of Mikel Arteta.

There will be no Enzo Fernández for Chelsea, with him joining what he called a “big club” in Manchester City and in his stead, Lamine Camara will not be lining up in Chelsea’s midfield. On Monday, the majority of Chelsea fans knew very little about Camara but now they yearn desperately, a love unrequited for the 22-year-old Senegalese tyro who, it says here, once played for Metz. Should the Gunners grind through the gears on Sunday, as is entirely possible, expect to hear criticism of sporting director Andrea Berta. A most modern phenomenon is suits having their names taken in vain. Liverpool travel to Ipswich later on Friday with fans wailing at a lack of cover at full-back. Richard Hughes, also off to Saudi, may well have ears burning when a year ago the Reds’ supporters were asking for his autograph. He will receive little thanks for Liverpool having the highest net spend in the league when the midfield is slow as a coach.

The same could be said of Jason Wilcox if Manchester United fans were able to scan his name into a song. Their red-shirted heroes will not feature Newcastle’s Lewis Hall when they face Everton on Sunday. Though having no obvious replacement should Luke Shaw suffer hamstring-twang is nothing on the personnel deficit at Hill Dickinson Stadium. Fans’ wishes for Harrison Armstrong to stay were met but he no longer has Iliman Ndiaye to pass to, while Thierno Barry is the sole striker available to David Moyes. That Everton currently own more stadiums than strikers has become a hoary old gag within days of the club’s deadline-day disasters. Folarin Balogun, the erstwhile Evertonian, will not be playing for Monaco against PSG this weekend, and neither will he play for the club in Tin Pot.

Richarlison, having hoped to return to Everton, will also not be playing this weekend for Tottenham at Nottingham Forest, having been tinned entirely from Spurs’ Premier League squad. His SMD post that “despite this turmoil, I am under contract at Spurs and will remain at the club’s disposal” was followed by them trying to dispose of him. Mohamed Salah’s Trabzonspor is a reported destination as well as the usual Saudi escape hatch. Balogun looks to be heading for the Turkish Super Lig or the Saudi Pro League, too. The funny thing about regret is that it’s better to regret something you have done than to regret something you haven’t done.

Join Scott Murray at 8pm BST for red-hot Premier League updates on Ipswich 0-0 Liverpool.

“[He] is in fantasy land!! The examination of performances assessors is forensic. When I was boss, referees’ performances were forensically examined. On my watch [he] could not have done what he said with the monitoring systems in operation … [I’m] satisfied he is talking nonsense” – Mike Hackett, the former head honcho at PGMOL, reckons former referee Mike Dean is full of … baloney with claims he tried to stay in the centre-circle while overseeing matches and would time how long he could officiate for without blowing his whistle.
