double quotation mark Re: yesterday’s Football Daily. Perhaps Messrs Vardy and James thought they had booked Jasper Carrott to kick off their hilarious podcast party. And got the not-so-funny doppelganger Mike Dean instead?” – Jim Arrowsmith.

double quotation mark With Premier League clubs now owned by a motley assortment of hedge funds, petrostates, billionaires and so on, perhaps the time is right to take a leaf out of pro cycling’s book and name the teams after their owners and sponsors. It will be a regular reminder to fans that the football entities they support are far removed from the community-based groups of like-minded individuals that the word ‘club’ denotes, and that they are instead cash-cow playthings of the mega-rich. As for me, I’ve been a fan of Fosun International Debet since they were known as Bhatti Brothers Manders Paints and Inks” – Neil Withers.

double quotation mark As someone who likes watching football rather than wasting time on transfers, this week has been boring, to say the least. Not so dull that it’s been enough to pick up a book, mind, but still. However, the result was that, after finding out that West Ham have a midfielder called Engels, I was sent down an internet wormhole and discovered that there is also a Brazilian midfielder called Marx Lenin (his real name, not just a nickname). Now, if only we could get them to play together, we would have something. Revolutionary tactics, no one in the centre or on the right wing, everyone on the left (a bit like Arsenal circa Henry, Pires and Ashley Cole), etc” – Noble Francis.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Neil Withers. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

Sports.title: Entitled influencers moan they were kicked out of US Open and stripped of free passes after breaking crucial rule
Sports.content:
The US Open's influencer controversy has reached boiling point. Amid the scrutiny surrounding the content creators invading Flushing Meadows, two have revealed that they were given the boot.

The Grand Slam has attracted new fans to the sport in recent years but this year's tournament has seemingly become increasingly overrun with influencers.

But the tournament found itself down a pair of the glamorous online socialites on Thursday when two were shown the door.

Meg Radice and Audrey Jongens, two NYC-based influencers who run the social media account The VIP List, claimed their credentials were revoked just hours after they committed a US Open cardinal sin.

The pair posted photos of their credentials on social media when they went to have dinner at a restaurant they had partnered with for the tournament.

'We post our credentials on our story. We go to our favorite restaurant. Have a nice steak dinner. We're downing Honey Deuces. We're having a great time, haven't even made it to court yet,' Redice told TMZ.

Two influencers have claimed that their US Open credentials were revoked this week

Meg Radice and Audrey Jongens said they were booted after posting their credentials online

'Within two hours of us leaving, we were told we could no longer use our credentials. We were heartbroken and we still are,' Jongens added.

Redice and Jongens received the passes through through a partnership with one of their favorite restaurants at the Open, then posted photos of the credentials to Instagram Stories this week.

They insisted that they were unaware they had broken any rules by sharing their credentials and have attended the tournament for the past three years.

The duo described themselves as 'diehard' tennis fans and said that they had intended to film content at the Grand Slam over the course of the two weeks, branding it a 'dream' opportunity.

'We were there to be respectful and follow the rules and just have a good time and show content to our followers about how amazing the US Open is,' Jongens added to TMZ.

'We were like, what do you mean? We had our credentials just stripped away within two hours before we even get to see a match. How does this happen?' Radice questioned.

'It was taken away like that. Just because we wanted to show how hot we looked in our credentials,' Radice added.

The pair pleaded with the USTA to allow them to return, saying: 'We don't even need an apology, we just want to go back.'

Radice and Jongens are NYC-based influencers who run the social media account The VIP Lis

They received the passes through through a partnership with one of their favorite restaurants

The duo described themselves as 'diehard' tennis fans, intending to film content at the event

They bemoaned the fact that they had cancelled plans for the two weeks and planned their outfits to be able to attend the event.

However, the USTA hit back at their version of events, saying that their access was revoked because they had been improperly submitted as vendor staff.

'These individuals were not credentialed as media or content creators,' Brendan McIntyre, the USTA's managing director and head of US Open, professional tennis and USA Tennis content and communications, said in a statement sent to The Athletic.

'They were improperly submitted for credentials on a staff list provided by a food vendor.'

This year's tournament has seen the number of influencers at the event almost boule with the USTA credentialing 100 content creators.

Yet, the impromptu photoshoot between points, chatting and moving around have caused quite the stir at Arthur Ashe, leaving traditional tennis fans disgruntled over the lack of etiquette.

Earlier in the week, Naomi Osaka was forced to wait until the chair umpire had chided a group of spectators in one of Arthur Ashe's hospitality suites.

'Guys, please, in the suite behind me, please thank you guys, please take your seat,' the chair umpire announced to the stadium, as the broadcast camera panned to a group milling freely within their prime seats, taking pictures and talking.

Guests of a US Open hospitality suite were told off by a chair umpire for taking pictures during a game, seemingly using a portable light (ringed)

One social media user called out 'influencers' for taking pictures while action was ongoing

Elsewhere in the stands, another spectator was heard calling out: 'The players are ready!'

When the stadium had stilled somewhat, Osaka returned to her serve but struggled with her ball toss, apologizing as she reset.

Footage captured from another spectator of the group on social media later showed them posing as a group, allegedly during a game, with a person who appeared to be a member of US Open staff holding up a portable light to help them capture the shot.

The social media clip showed another spectator on the same evening posing in front of the court with a portable light, also allegedly during live matchplay.

When contacted by Daily Mail Sport for comment on the incident, Brendan McIntyre, head of US Open communications said: 'We want our fans and guests to have an incredible time when they attend the US Open, but we also need to ensure that does not interfere with the action and competition on the court.

'These instances happen infrequently, and similar to when crowd noise reaches a certain level, our chair umpires have the ability to address the crowd when they occur.'

Sports.title: Inside Matthias Jaissle's first month as Newcastle boss: His letter to staff revealed, the double gym sessions, the training-ground action that he's banned, his deadpan humour and what the players REALLY think of him
Sports.content:
It was approaching tea-time but Matthias Jaissle was burning calories in the gym. Without the Newcastle head coach knowing, a handful of journalists stood nearby and watched him bench press a pair of 25kg dumbbells.

Noticing our presence, it was, for a moment, a little awkward.

‘Is that all you can lift?’ I offered, attempting to break the ice.

A colleague asked if I could manage the same load.

‘Looking at you,’ Jaissle intervened, surveying my unmighty frame. ‘I don’t think so.’

He had smashed the ice and my ego. In fact, exactly one month into the job, Jaissle has smashed through just about everything put in front of him.

Matthias Jaissle has made a great start to life as Newcastle boss with two wins out of three and a draw against Liverpool that deserved more

Anthony Elanga celebrates scoring against Tottenham in a match Newcastle won 2-0

‘The lads like him,’ said one source close to the players this week. ‘He’s got a swagger about him, but that’s fine if you can back it up.’

So far, Jaissle has walked the walk. Three matches, two wins and a draw against Liverpool that deserved more. It was not supposed to be like this, at least not through the sceptical lens of those on the outside. At 38, the German was an unknown who had never managed in a major European league, conveniently plucked from PIF-owned Al-Ahli in Saudi Arabia.

The truth is very different. Al-Ahli were, to quote a source, ‘massively p***** off’. Newcastle had to meet their £10million buyout and there was an acceptance that relations, for this summer at least, needed time to thaw.

When it was suggested they might return to Al-Ahli for 21-year-old midfielder Valentin Atangana, a Jaissle favourite, the notion was nervously laughed off by insiders. Newcastle chiefs already had their man and they were happy with that.

Indeed, at one of Jaissle’s interviews in Portugal, the club’s hierarchy were so taken with him that, after leaving the restaurant, they wondered whether they should turn around, walk straight back in and offer him the job.

What did the likes of chief executive David Hopkinson and sporting director Ross Wilson see? Leadership. Conviction. Energy. It helped that Newcastle chairman Yasir Al-Rumayyan agreed. What looked like a panicked and easy appointment to the rest of the world was, to Newcastle, a coup – and a thoroughly considered one at that.

It is early days, of course, and Newcastle is a club where emotions can move faster than Anthony Elanga. But the emperor’s new clothes appear to fit. In Jaissle’s case, that is a crisp white shirt whose stitching is tested by the biceps beneath.

The gym session we observed was his second of the day. He arrives at the training ground at 7.30am and, during his first fortnight at least, he was leaving under the cover of darkness, quite an achievement during a northern summer. He joked that the centre felt like his new home. Since then, though, he has explored.

It is early days but the emperor’s new clothes appear to fit. In Jaissle’s case, that is a crisp white shirt whose stitching is tested by the biceps beneath

Yoane Wissa labelled Jaissle ‘our best signing of the summer’ after last weekend’s win at Tottenham

Former Newcastle manager Graeme Souness used to book a table in the same Jesmond restaurant, Sale Pepe, every Saturday night. If the team won, he’d sit in the window. If they lost, he’d dine out the back.

It shows how well Jaissle has started that his most recent reservation was on the sea front! Riley’s Fish Shack, a grill tucked into a cove in Tynemouth and overlooking the beach, is hugely popular. And, four weeks in, so is Jaissle.

Shortly after arriving at the club, we can reveal, he wrote a letter to every member of staff. He introduced himself and pledged to do everything in his power to deliver success for the club – but stressed that anything achieved would only be done with everyone pulling in the same direction.

He recognised that for employees, working for Newcastle United was ‘more than just a job’. There was also a tribute to his predecessor, Eddie Howe.

When Jaissle then showed up, unexpectedly, at an all-staff ‘town hall’, there was a sense of a manager whose actions will support his words. His players have felt that commitment, too. Yoane Wissa labelled him ‘our best signing of the summer’ after last weekend’s 2-0 win at Tottenham.

And what of the football? Jaissle’s favourite moment from his first month has not come during a game. Rather, it was the realisation that the work done on the training ground would show itself in those matches.

‘I remember one or two training sessions where I had a huge smile on my face afterwards,’ he said. ‘That was because I felt these guys are so committed. I knew then we would develop fast. I could see us working as a unit on the pitch. These are the small steps where you can see we’re going in the right direction.’

Jaissle’s favourite direction is forward. In training, teams are penalised when a pass is played backwards in certain zones of the pitch. That is as much a psychological instruction as it is technical.

In training, teams are penalised when a pass is played backwards in certain zones of the pitch

From the outside, it all felt a little serious during his early days. But then, with time and exposure, there have been lighter moments

‘Guys, that's the rules. Understand it straight away,’ he told his players during week one in La Manga. He was likened to a military instructor by some and, as one supporter observing a clip online noted, ‘I’m knackered just watching this’.

Jaissle’s intensity on the grass is balanced by shorter video sessions. Clear instruction, perhaps aided by a slow and deliberate delivery in his second language, is the intention. His three non-negotiable values are said to be trust, respect and pure commitment, while his mantra last month was ‘control the controllables’.

From the outside, it all felt a little serious during those early days. But then, with time and exposure, there have been lighter moments – not least his quip on the back of his heavy lifting in the gym.

Deadpan is his humour, it seems. When one colleague asked him if Nick Woltemade’s struggles were psychological, he simply replied: ‘I don’t know, I’m not a psychologist.’

There have been more.

What percentage is your team ready heading into the season?

‘I’m not a mathematician.’

After shaking every reporter's hand at his unveiling, a warning not to expect it every week.

‘Just the first time, guys.’

On adapting to life in a new country.

'The biggest challenge is your dialect… and driving on the left side.’

The new Newcastle manager has already demonstrated his deadpan sense of humour

He has also poked fun at his animated touchline demeanour

He has also made fun, in private and in public, of his animated touchline demeanour. After taking the job, he asked staff how many yellow cards a manager was allowed in the Premier League before serving a touchline ban.

‘Only three?!’ he shot back when informed.

There has been little regard for the boundaries of his technical zone, either.

‘I had a longer touchline in Saudi Arabia, my GPS was quite high…’

Jaissle walked into a difficult situation post-Howe and the loss of several star players. Yet, he has hit the ground running. His partner, model Lisa Czetsch, was even dancing in the St James' Park reception in celebration of last week’s victory over West Brom in the Carabao Cup. They like folk who take that competition seriously on Tyneside.

A month is too soon for definitive judgement, but Jaissle has spent that time lifting the mood, expectations and, as I discovered, weights beyond my means. For this Newcastle manager, 50 kilograms feels just like the start.

Sports.title: Aryna Sabalenka stops play at US Open to complain about the smell of WEED after claiming a fan was 'smoking' during her third-round match: 'It was so strong'
Sports.content:
Aryna Sabalenka was forced to stop her third-round match against Kamila Rakhimova to complain about someone apparently smoking weed inside the US Open's Louis Armstrong Stadium.

The court is the second-largest of the tournament's showcourts, but despite the venerable setting, Sabalenka was so disturbed by the smell of what she believed to be marijuana that while serving in the third game, she called for umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore's attention after first speaking to her team.

'Someone is smoking weed,' she said as she paused play at 30-0 up to speak Asderaki-Moore. 'Would you mind to (tell them to deal with it) because it's so strong.'

The world No1, who went on to win in straight sets, had been serving at the south end of the stadium, close to where her team were seated in the players' box.

The chair umpire quickly radioed for assistance, making a mysterious snipping signal at her colleagues. Members of US Open staff then headed into the crowd in a bid to find the source of the smell.

The smell of cannabis is not unexpected around the grounds of the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, due to its position inside Flushing Meadows Corona Park, where weed can be smoked legally by those relaxing in the sunshine.

Aryna Sabalenka alleged that a spectator was smoking weed during her US Open match

It is however forbidden, along with all forms of smoking, inside the tournament. The US Open has been contacted for comment.

During qualifying and ahead of the start of the tournament, a number of British players noted the unique smell of the grounds, with Katie Boulter particularly disapproving of how the stink hung around Court 17 - referred to in the Danish media as 'hash court' for how strongly the smell lingers in the air.

‘I have experienced it,’ Boulter, who was knocked out on Wednesday by Karolina Muchova, shared. ‘You got down to the practice courts and down in the park courts, you do smell it a lot.

‘I’m not a huge fan of it. I know a lot of players have complained on specific courts. I’ve played on (Court 17) before and I did smell it during my match. It’s something that I wouldn’t like to smell in the middle of my match.’

In response, the USTA shared the following statement: 'While we can’t control what takes place off the grounds of the USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, we continue to be vigilant as we maintain this facility as a smoke-free environment.

'This includes enforcement by our security and guest services teams when they are made aware of any individual that may be smoking, making them aware that although it may be legal in New York, that smoking is not permitted on parks property, including the tennis center.

'We constantly work with the NYPD and Parks Department, and we believe this has helped to decrease smoking near our fenceline.'

Sabalenka brushed aside world No 92 Rakhimova to continue her straight-sets march

Sabalenka brushed aside world No 92 Rakhimova to continue her straight-sets march towards what she hopes is a third-consecutive US Open title.

And of the earlier incident, she later said with a smile: ‘I was like guys, you can do whatever, you can smoke whatever, you can relax however you want, but please try not to do it during a tennis match. It’s a bit tricky to handle the smell while you’re trying to compete at your best.

‘But come on guys, I think there is nothing more to say about weed. I’m just asking people not to smoke it next to the tennis court,’ she continued, only to add of her game: ‘Maybe it’s too fast for them, and they want to slow down!’

Despite the early distraction, Sabalenka was able to reset with the minimum fuss and continue to scythe through the opening set.

The second was another matter. Almost double the length of the opener, Rakhimova had grown into the match and tested Sabalenka from the off as she pushed her to deuce four times in her first service game.

Only a strong serving performance, with 10 aces struck across the match, kept her opponent from hunting down a crucial break.

Although joking with the press pack about how ‘high’ being in New York made her feel on Friday, Sabalenka has been a trickier subject after her matches in New York. Wound tight after a challenging summer that has seen her normally ultra-consistence form take a nosedive, her attitude has read as defensive.

In the second set, this mode switched to visible frustration. The world No1 shouldn’t have looked as frustrated as she did as Rakhimova continued to deny her opportunities to break her serve - the win was almost inevitable.

There is a growing sense however, that Sabalenka wants not just to keep going in the tournament, but to wrench back the feeling of dread her opponents would normally sense when seeing her in their section of the draw. Amid a summer of toothlessness as her level has dropped, that was not assured coming into New York.

Slowly but surely, however, she is clawing this back.

READ MORE - Inside the US Open's notorious 'hash court' - which Alexander Zverev once labelled 'Snoop Dogg's living room' - as British stars contend with 'one of the worst' smells at Flushing Meadows

Sports.title: Graham Potter makes thinly-veiled dig at Chelsea and West Ham after fan mocks his Pilates exercise
Sports.content:
Ex-Chelsea and West Ham boss Graham Potter appeared to take aim at 'dysfunctional' former clubs after a fan mocked his Pilates exercise on Instagram.

Potter is currently head coach of the Swedish national team after taking charge last October.

The 51-year-old had salvaged Sweden's World Cup qualifying campaign to guide them to the finals, where they were eventually knocked out in the round of 32.

Sweden's performance at the World Cup had helped Potter bounce back from underwhelming spells at Chelsea and West Ham.

Potter was sacked by Chelsea in 2023 after less than seven months in charge, having won just 12 of 31 matches.

He returned to management with West Ham in 2025, but was sacked just five games into last season.

Graham Potter responded to a fan who mocked a post of him doing Pilates on Instagram

Potter appeared to take aim at 'dysfunctional' former clubs after the fan hit out at his management ability

West Ham were ultimately relegated at the end of last season, with current boss Nuno Espirito Santo having overseen the majority of the campaign.

Potter had shared photos of himself on Instagram doing a Pilates session, writing 'Pilates session update! I have a lot of work to do!!'

One football fan responded with the jibe 'Hopefully you are better at Pilates than you are a football manager.'

Potter responded: 'I'll try not to do Pilates in a dysfunctional place and I will be okay.'

In response to a follow-up by a Hammers fan, Potter added: 'Easy tiger. I never mentioned West Ham or any club.'

When told to 'ignore the haters' in another comment, Potter conceded: 'Of course I am responsible for my part but unfortunately lots happen at football clubs to determine success or failure not just one man! COYI.'

Potter's spells at both Chelsea and West Ham came at times of boardroom upheaval at both clubs.

He had previously described his ill-fated spell at Chelsea as being the 'perfect storm', citing a fixture pile-up ahead of the winter World Cup in Qatar in 2022, before the club's new owners invested heavily during a staggering January transfer window.

Potter's brief spell at Chelsea came in the first season under the club's new ownership

West Ham fans had protested against their owners during Potter's ill-fated spell at the club

'If you are spending £300m on players coming from outside the Premier League, from countries having a mid-season break, then the reality is you can't just imagine they are going to hit the ground running and everything's going to be fine,' Potter said in 2024.

'But, obviously, if you spend £300m, the pressure on the team goes up and the pressure on the coach goes up.

'And people go: "Come on then, you've spent all this money." I think if I'd have spent it on Harry Kane and Declan Rice, fair enough, but at the time that was the decision.

'We tried to support it as best we could, but it left us with a challenge of a lot of players after January and then they can't go anywhere.'

Potter's spell at West Ham also came at a time with fans regularly staging protests against David Sullivan's ownership and former vice-chair Karren Brady.

Sports.title: Mike Dean responds to uproar at his claim he played 'minigames' while refereeing Premier League matches - as he prepares for appearance on Sky's Soccer Saturday
Sports.content:
Mike Dean has broken his silence on the furore surrounding his claims that he played 'minigames' when taking charge of Premier League matches. The former referee, appearing on Jamie Vardy's Having a Party podcast, said this week: 'There used to be games we would have for a laugh. It would kick-off, right; see how long we could go without blowing a whistle. 'I done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR, obviously. Went 20, 25 minutes without blowing the whistle.' Dean continued: 'I used to do another one in the Premier League, I used to stand in the centre circle and see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about. Got about 15 minutes once, in one game.' His comments have caused uproar in the football world, with fans questioning his integrity and former officials weighing in. And now Dean has issued a statement on Instagram, insisting he did always apply the letter of the law when he was an official. Past colleagues have turned on Mike Dean (pictured) after he admitted to sometimes trying to see how long he could go without blowing his whistle in a game 'Throughout my 25 years as a professional referee, I have always applied the Laws of the Game to the best of my ability,' he wrote. 'My approach as a referee was always to allow the game to flow and whenever possible I preferred to apply a high threshold for contact which the players liked. 'However, if I saw a foul challenge that needed me to take the appropriate action I would give it from the correct position. At no stage was it my intention to question, criticise or undermine the integrity of refereeing in this country. I have always respected the profession and the responsibility that comes with being a referee.' Dean is set to appear in his role as refereeing expert on Sky Sports' Soccer Saturday tomorrow afternoon, where he is expected to further address the controversy. His statement comes after his former boss and refereeing colleagues turned on him following his claims. Former referees' chief Keith Hackett, fellow ex-top flight referee Graham Scott and referee body ProRef have all moved to rubbish the claims of Dean, who took charge of 553 Premier League games in his career. Dean's former refereeing boss Keith Hackett (pictured) has suggested there is no way the controversial ex-referee could have got away with minigames Keith Hackett, who was a FIFA referee for more than two years and Dean's boss at PGMOL between 2004 and 2010, has looked to front that response. Hackett wrote on X: 'Mike Dean is in fantasy land!! The examination of performances assessors is forensic. When I was boss referee's performances were forensically examined. 'Dean on my watch could not have done what he said with the monitoring systems in operation.' Hackett added he was 'satisfied (Dean) is talking nonsense' and said: 'He clearly has damaged his reputation. The fallout does not help current refs.' Scott, meanwhile, who refereed in the Premier League between 2015 and 2025, rubbished Dean's claims and argued that his behaviour post-retirement has been questionable. 'I worked with Mike loads of times - they're not true stories,' Scott said on talkSPORT. 'I wish people wouldn't do this kind of thing. It's the audio equivalent of clickbait, isn't it? 'It's to try and get people interested and laughing. It's palpable nonsense.' He added: 'I found him quite shy, personally. I found him quite small when he was in a private situation. Graham Scott, meanwhile, said Dean has shown 'precious little' common sense since retiring Dean revealed his 'minigames' when speaking on Jamie Vardy's podcast, and his quotes have caused outrage 'What happened on the field, what happened in referee meetings, is he put on a persona that was way too far the other way, as a kind of coping mechanism.' Scott also wrote in The Athletic: 'For all his common sense on the field, he has shown precious little of it since retiring. Casual comments that harm former colleagues and employers do not disappear when the following day's newspapers are thrown in the bin, yet hang around forever to cause untold damage to all referees' reputations.' Daily Mail Sport understands Dean's comments have raised plenty of eyebrows within the current refereeing community too, with senior figures questioning the plausibility of his claim given the lack of detail. According to senior officials at ProRef, Dean provided no indication of when these alleged 'minigames' took place. He also claimed they occurred before VAR was introduced for the 2019-20 season, meaning any such incidents would have taken place under previous refereeing chiefs – and current bosses are insistent that 'integrity and impartiality' are at the heart of referees' decision-making. A number of fans, meanwhile, have taken to social media to voice their concern at Dean's suggestions. One wrote: 'Why the f***'s he admitting to this? "Oooh look at me I ruined the integrity of top level football matches while getting paid a f***ing fortune for a laugh." And people wonder why we all think refs are *****.' Dean has admitted, somewhat dismissively, that sometimes there was an element of wanting to be the 'centre of attention' when he was on the field. 'It's about wanting to be more a part of the game than what I should have been,' Dean said. 'If you play an advantage and it works off, you do celebrate it; if you get a decision right you kind of want to celebrate. 'I'd celebrate with the lads in my ear pieces and stuff. If you play an advantage and somebody scores, I think it's great. Love it.' But despite his prior explanations to Vardy, whom he officiated several times while the striker played for Leicester, fans didn't find his declaration amusing. Another fan added: '“Professional” referee by the way. This is something you would expect from a Sunday league keeper who’s earning pittance to get abused. ‘What an absolute f***ing ****. Always behaved like he was more important than the game being played around him.’ A different account wrote: 'How about, and I might be going out on a limb here, concentrating on officiating the matches properly rather than playing silly little games with yourself. Mike Dean thinking this makes him sound like a right lad is baffling to me.'

Sports.title: Football's most eye-catching new kit unveiling: Couples kiss to launch top European team's shirt 'inspired by a sense of connection'
Sports.content:
Austrian side FK Austria Wien launched their new third kit with a bizarre video that includes couples kissing in the strip.

A two-minute video, which has caught the eye of fans, begins with the words: 'Love takes many forms' on the screen, as a couple take a seat in what appears to be the club changing room.

Then comes: 'A kiss. A feeling. A moment. It brings people together. It connects generations. It creates memories.'

'Five stories and a jersey', is then shown, followed by 'which leads to an interpretation of its own.

'Inspired by a sense of connection.'

What appeared to be three couples and two sets of family members sat in front of the camera, and spoke in German.

Austrian side FK Austria Wien launched their new third kit with a video featuring couples kissing in the strip

The club said the message was to show how love can be expressed in different ways

Each duo then watched a screen showing off the club's new crimson third kit.

They were all then given a replica of the kit and asked for their thoughts before the video took a slight turn.

While those who were family members shared a hug, those in romantic couples embraced with a kiss, with footage shared in the video and more images shared after.

The club said: 'Together with our partner Macron, we are unveiling the new art-inspired kit. Inspired by the iconic patterns from Gustav Klimt's "The Kiss", the crimson third kit draws on the characteristic forms of this world-famous work of art.

'The artist and the club are united by a deeply Viennese sense of aesthetics: craftsmanship, attention to detail and the courage to forge their own path. The jersey will initially be available in 1,000 limited-edition boxes from Friday at 12:00 online and in the fan shop. Both the men's and women's teams will take to the court wearing it on Saturday at the Cup double-header in Traiskirchen.

'Love takes many forms. A kiss. A feeling. A moment. It brings people together. It bridges generations. It creates memories. Five stories and a jersey that inspires you to create your own interpretation.'

Sports.title: Furious soccer fans unveil Times Square billboard calling for Gianni Infantino to be ousted as they accuse embattled FIFA President of blackmail
Sports.content:
Angry soccer fans have taken to Times Square, unveiling a massive billboard calling for FIFA President Gianni Infantino to be removed after recent controversies.

Infantino sparked outrage long before the 2026 FIFA World Cup in the United States after giving President Donald Trump a newly created 'FIFA Peace Prize', before inviting Trump to present the trophy to the winning team.

Since then, his clandestine plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup to Joshua Kushner has been uncovered and faced huge backlash from fans around the world.

In the wake of The Times revealing the devious scheme, that would have banked him millions, Infantino has faced calls to resign and threats of boycotts from governing bodies, led by UEFA.

And soccer fans from around the world have now unveiled a Times Square billboard in New York City demanding he resign. The billboard went live at 6am ET on September 4, on the corner of 1500 Broadway and West 43rd Street.

Organizers said: 'We are football fans first and foremost and believe we echo the feelings of fans everywhere regarding Infantino and the threat he poses to the future of football.

Gianna Infantino is facing ongoing pressure in his role as FIFA President after recent revelations

Soccer fans have funded a Times Square billboard demanding Infantino be ousted from his role

Organizers of the billboard have accused the embattled President of 'blackmail'

'He deceived, blackmailed, and threatened FIFA, his team and the wider global football leadership in order to sell international football to people who have ties to deeply unsavory activities, and who have no interest in the fans except as profit centers.

'It is transparent to us that Kushner and his associates want to own the 'assets' of football – the fans and the players – to use as they wish while simultaneously wielding the soft power of international football as a tool of control.

'Infantino, who is meant to protect football from such grave dangers, enthusiastically offered it up on a platter, paving the way with a fake 'Peace Prize', and only stipulating that he gets a cut. Shameful.

'We call on fans everywhere to make it clear Infantino is persona non grata at their stadiums and to demand the confederations they're members of remove him as soon as possible.

'Until he is removed, we demand action: We call on federations and confederations to revoke invitations and/or ban Infantino from tournaments and matches

'We call on the football community to let Infantino know he's not welcome by demonstrating against him at matches and any football related events, by unveiling tifos calling for his removal and by boycotting FIFA events.

'Gianni Infantino is not a leader, he is a dealer who tried to sell the World Cup and more disturbingly, the children's World Cup. We should all be shocked and disgusted by the latter.'

FIFA recently accused UEFA of a 'smear campaign' after legal applications made to access documents related to FIFA's controversial private investor plan. UEFA is applying through the American courts for discovery of evidence and documentation linked to FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a private company which it was envisaged would run the World Cup and other FIFA competitions.

The billboard appeared on Friday morning in Times Square demanding 'Infantino Out'

Infantino and Trump made another public appearance at the FIFA World Cup Final in July

Infantino was recently tracked down in the Caribbean and confronted over calls to resign and claims he has 'betrayed the game'.

Not giving an answer to Sky News reporter James Matthews, he simply joked: 'You have a nice haircut.'

He repeatedly said 'thank you very much' as he neared the car. Then, as security personnel prepared to close the door, Infantino turned back towards Matthews and finished with another hair-related joke: 'I'll see you at the hairdressers.'

Sports.title: REVEALED: Jordan Cox to win £200k England central contract along with key bowler, and the latest on Ben Stokes' pay
Sports.content:
Jordan Cox’s reward for a breakthrough international summer will be to replace Ben Stokes on England’s central contracts list on October 1.

Essex batsman Cox has taken his opportunity by scoring half-centuries in both of the wins over Pakistan so far in a three-match Test series that concludes at Edgbaston from Wednesday.

Stokes, 35, quit international cricket in June but has remained on England’s wage bill beyond the customary one month for players announcing retirements and will only stop being paid in October. The arrangement is in recognition of his outstanding service over 15 years and 279 international caps.

The current £1million-a-year deal for Stokes – it includes a hefty bonus for being captain – was scheduled to run for a further 12 months but he has begun building a freelance portfolio for 2026-27.

A £210,000 contract with Adelaide Strikers – the Big Bash League’s limit for platinum signings – represents a start and he will also earn from commercial activities.

But with a finite pool of money from which to pay England cricketers, the saving on Stokes will more than cover 25-year-old Cox’s entry level salary of £200,000 and the return of Ollie Robinson to the roster two years after he last featured.

Jordan Cox will get an England central contract in October and will be paid the entry level salary of £200,000

Cox has taken his England chance by scoring half-centuries in both of the wins over Pakistan so far in a three-match Test series

Cox filled in for Ben Stokes at No 7 during the Oval Test defeat by New Zealand in midsummer, tasked with marshalling counter-attacks.

He has impressed since returning to the team, following omission in Nottingham at the end of June, covering the absence of Jacob Bethell at No3, highlighting his versatility and a willingness to scrap in challenging new-ball conditions.

Being able to fill a variety of roles will hold him in good stead when incoming head coach Stephen Fleming and captain Joe Root take stock of their personnel later this month, with the tour of South Africa in December and next summer’s Ashes in mind.

Bethell remains on the sidelines as he recovers from meniscus damage in his right knee incurred during the one-day series against India, and having had a scan on Thursday, continues to take a cautious approach to his rehabilitation programme.

ENGLAND WHITE-BALL SQUADS England T20 squad: Three matches v Sri Lanka, Sep 15 (Southampton), Sep 17 (Cardiff), Sep 19 (Manchester): H Brook (capt); Archer, Atkinson, Baker, Banton, Buttler, Coles, Cox, Dawson, Donald, Duckett, Jacks, Mahmood, J Overton, Rashid, Tongue. England ODI squad: Three matches v Sri Lanka, Sep 22 (Durham), Sep 24 (Leeds), Sep 27 (The Oval) Brook, Ahmed, Archer, Atkinson, Banton, Baker, Buttler, Cox, Crocombe, Dawson, Duckett, Jacks, J Overton, Rashid, Root, Tongue.

Already ruled out of the twin limited-overs series against Sri Lanka on home soil later this month due to recent surgery, the triangular white-ball tournament in Pakistan next month will also come too soon, meaning he is targeting a return to white-ball action in Australia in November, ahead of the three Tests against the South Africans from mid-December.

Although he says he would like to continue at No3, Bethell was an opening batsman as a schoolboy and could step up a place for that tour in the unlikely event that Emilio Gay’s form slump – 82 runs in five innings – sees him dropped.

Gay, 26, has not been alone among England’s batsmen in struggling this summer, but while he can count himself unlucky to have been out to a Mohammad Abbas grubber, two leg-side strangles have been partly down to a closed grip on the handle that means he tries to play off his pads or hip with half a bat.

That kind of vulnerability could be exposed on South Africa’s bouncy surfaces by an attack high in pace and only too willing to test opponents’ mettle against the short ball – one which Cox himself failed during his first incarnation as an England batsman in the Caribbean a couple of years ago.

England opener Emilio Gay is under pressure after scoring just 82 runs in five innings

If Gay is axed, Cox is an option to remain in the top three, although he would arguably provide greater value lower down the order

If Gay is axed, Cox could be an option to remain in the top three, although he would arguably provide greater value lower down, below Harry Brook, a position suited to his confident Stokes-like ball-striking.

The one potential stumbling block, however, is a lack of a Stokes-esque figure to balance the team.

Dan Lawrence has filled the all-rounder role at No6 against Pakistan, notionally offering some off-spin (it has not been used in any volume against opponents yet to make 200 in the series).

Debate about where Cox fits, however, is missing the point, because in a very short space of time he has shown that he fits somewhere. A central contract is testament to that.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
