World.title: Africa: Loza Maléombho Is Building An Industry From African Stories
World.content:
Internationally recognised after Beyoncé wore her designs, Ivorian designer Loza Maléombho is now looking beyond fashion. Through Pokou, she is combining Baoulé history, local craftsmanship and artificial intelligence to build an African-owned creative universe spanning clothing, film, art, architecture and digital experiences.

On the fourth floor of a building in Treichville, one of Abidjan’s busiest commercial and cultural districts, the world of Ivorian designer Loza Maléombho is expanding beyond the clothes hanging in her workshop.

Maléombho is developing Pokou, a creative universe inspired by Queen Abla Pokou, the legendary founder of the Baoulé people, and reimagined through science fiction, fashion and digital technology.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to tradition, Queen Pokou led her people from the Ashanti Kingdom towards present-day Côte d’Ivoire. When they were unable to cross the Comoé River, Pokou sacrificed her only son to save her people. The story, which symbolises courage, selflessness and communal survival, is also associated with the origin of the name Baoulé, often translated as “the child is dead.”

“It is a story that everyone knows in Côte d’Ivoire so people can identify with it. But it is also a story about sacrifice, and I think that is something any audience can relate to in family, work, and life in general,” she said.

Maléombho drew on this story for her YouTube Pokou series, which launched in June 2026.

Developed using generative artificial intelligence alongside Maléombho’s own research and design work, Pokou is intended to promote the clothing label while opening routes into film, art, architecture, craftsmanship and digital experiences.

The project represents the designer’s attempt to turn African stories into commercially valuable, African-owned intellectual property.

Maléombho is not starting from obscurity. Her international breakthrough came when singer Beyoncé wore pieces from her Spring/Summer 2016 collection in the “ Formation ” music video. She later created a custom outfit for Beyoncé’s 2020 visual album, Black Is King . The appearances introduced her work to a global audience and strengthened her reputation for combining contemporary silhouettes with West African materials and imagery.

Now she wants to take the label beyond celebrity recognition and luxury clothing.

“The idea today is not that we want to dissociate ourselves, but that we are evolving more toward a multicultural creative studio and toward cultural intellectual property,” Maléombho said.

“We are no longer focused solely on producing products for sale, but more on creating a universe as such. There are characters, there are clothes, there are art objects, there are interactive experiences, there are architectural concepts.”

The shift is partly a response to the limitations confronting fashion businesses based in African markets. A conventional label must design collections, source materials, maintain consistent production, organise distribution and find buyers. Maléombho says African brands often have to do this without the supply chains, finance and logistics available to established international companies.

Her own business has encountered difficulties sourcing raw materials, finding specialised workers, maintaining consistent quality, accepting online payments, securing finance and transporting finished products.

Côte d’Ivoire’s cotton industry illustrates one of these structural gaps. The country is a significant West African producer, with output forecast at 590,000 bales of cotton lint in the 2026/27 marketing year. However, only a small proportion is processed by domestic spinning and weaving businesses; most fibre is exported to textile-producing markets in Asia.

That disconnect helps explain why Maléombho can work extensively with Ivorian artisans while still importing some of the cotton used in her collections.

Rather than relying only on selling larger volumes of clothing, she wants to create several commercial entry points into the same cultural universe.

“It is creativity, it is cultural ownership, it is our cultural stories,” she said. Pokou could encompass clothing, art objects, interiors and architectural concepts, while enabling collaborations and licensing agreements with companies in other sectors.

Artificial intelligence has allowed Maléombho to visualise parts of this universe more quickly, but she rejects the suggestion that it is the author of the work.

“What is very important to specify is that I do not give creativity to artificial intelligence,” she said. “People tend to think that AI designs everything, and then creativity is lost. But artificial intelligence makes a huge number of mistakes in terms of storytelling or even mythology in our African traditions.”

The digital ideas eventually become physical objects in the Treichville workshop. Maléombho works with artisans to test fabrics, dyes, embellishments and accessories. Bronze workers make buttons and a signature gold-plated buckle inspired by a Baoulé mask.

Jute, ordinarily used in sacks for packaging and exporting cocoa, is transformed through dyeing, appliqué, beadwork and printing. Raffia, Baoulé cloth, Kita cloth and hand-dyed cotton also form part of the brand’s visual language.

Baoulé is a traditional Ivorian cotton fabric, handwoven in distinctive patterns and colours and often worn at ceremonies, while Kita is a West African textile handwoven in narrow strips of cotton and silk.

For Norou Sow, a leather craftsman and artisan who has worked with Maléombho for more than ten years, the collaboration has changed both his methods of work and his livelihood.

“She taught me to work in a group. She also taught me to develop my experience,” Sow said. “Many things changed in my life when I started working with her.”

The company employs 10 people directly and works with more than 50 artisans in Côte d’Ivoire. Maléombho says 90% of its inputs or production are local, while some cotton and some manufacturing are sourced internationally.

The label sells through outlets or concept stores in Côte d’Ivoire, the United States, Nigeria, South Africa, the United Kingdom and Tanzania.

Côte d’Ivoire-based fashion and tourism specialist Dorine Negou sees the larger challenge as persuading African brands and consumers to recognise the commercial value of their own cultural identities.

“I think the difficulty is that we Africans want to adopt European models too much,” she said. “We have so many things that can enhance our value and attract more attention to us. It is up to us to rely on our brands, on our nature, on where we come from, and know how to showcase what we have.”

Yapo Patrick is a visual and installation artist who has taught colour and textile techniques for more than 20 years at the Centre Technique des Arts Appliqués (CTAA), or Technical Centre for Applied Arts, in Bingerville, Côte d’Ivoire.

Patrick said Maléombho’s journey demonstrates how formal training must be combined with personal commitment and a willingness to take risks: “There will always be limitations and difficulties, but creators have to commit themselves personally. They have to dare and decide to act despite those difficulties.”

However, turning the success of individual designers into a stronger domestic fashion industry will require broader investment in skills and local production. Although Côte d’Ivoire is a major cotton producer, only a limited share of its raw material is transformed locally into finished textiles and clothing.

Patrick believes vocational training for designers, pattern makers and tailors could help expand production and encourage Ivorians to buy locally made fabric and clothing.

“We need more information, more initiatives and more people investing in professional training,” he said. “If Ivorians can produce and consume Ivorian products, including fabrics, that will generate revenue and encourage both the state and the private sector to develop an ecosystem in which the fashion industry can grow.”

Close 

Maléombho believes that Africa possesses a vast narrative and cultural inheritance but captures too little of its commercial value. The opportunity, in her view, is to turn stories, materials and craft traditions into products that retain a distinct identity while meeting international standards.

Her clothing label provides the initial commercial foundation. Its luxury pieces target customers drawn to the house’s craftsmanship and cultural references, while shoes, belts, jewellery and other accessories offer less expensive entry points.

Pokou would extend that model. A consumer might first encounter a garment in a film or digital world. A character could lead into a collection, while an imagined building might inspire furniture or another designed object. The story itself could be licensed or used in collaborations across different industries.

Over the next three to five years, Maléombho hopes to complete the transition from a fashion label into a cultural studio built around intellectual property. She believes the model could create jobs in traditional crafts, film, digital production and artificial intelligence.

“It is not just a clothing brand,” she said. “It is truly a multicultural studio that is in tune with the times and also knows how to innovate while keeping its roots in its history.”

From its base in Treichville, Pokou is attempting to bring Baoulé history into dialogue with artificial intelligence, craftsmanship with cinema, and clothing with architecture.

Maléombho believes the constraints facing African creative businesses can themselves produce innovation.

“The legacy I would like to leave would really be to show that, first of all, with very little, we can create much more value,” she said. “It is even within the constraints that we have the opportunity to innovate.”

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Connects Climate Solutions From Field To Factory
World.content:
As rainfall becomes less predictable, researchers are developing improved seed, testing more efficient irrigation and using digital tools to track water losses. Getting these solutions to farmers could protect harvests and provide Ethiopia’s textile factories with more locally grown fibre.

When the rains arrive late or stop too soon, cotton farmer Debalkie Abate can no longer depend on the planting calendar he once knew. But researchers and water specialists are working on an alternative: improved seed, better-timed irrigation and more accurate climate information that could help farmers continue producing despite increasingly unpredictable weather.

“The weather has become much less predictable than it was a decade ago,” Abate says. “Sometimes the rains arrive late, sometimes they stop too early. Without irrigation we cannot rely on rainfall alone.”

Ethiopia already possesses tools that could reduce that risk. Research in its cotton-growing lowlands shows how carefully timed irrigation can make better use of limited water. New assessments are identifying irrigation losses, while researchers develop varieties intended to improve productivity and fibre quality.



The challenge is to move those solutions from research centres into farmers’ fields, protecting livelihoods and providing Ethiopia’s textile industry with a more reliable supply of locally grown fibre.

The work reflects a wider continental shift. In February 2026, the African Union called for greater support to help smallholders—particularly women—access climate-resilient seed, irrigation and insurance. It also urged countries to share research and solutions involving digital agriculture, climate information and resilient infrastructure.

Using less water more effectively

The need to adapt is becoming more urgent. The Ethiopian Meteorological Institute’s 2025 climate projections anticipate continued warming under both medium- and high-emissions scenarios. Rainfall outcomes differ by region and season, with some areas potentially receiving more rain while others experience greater variability.

For farmers, the problem is not simply less rain. It is rain that can no longer be assumed to arrive when the crop most needs it.

At an AGRA agrifood-systems retreat in April 2026 , Ethiopia highlighted lessons from cluster-based approaches and digital advisory systems. It also identified stronger agricultural financing and greater climate finance for smallholders as priorities—support needed to move adaptation tools into farmers’ hands.

Research at Melka Werer in the semi-arid Middle Awash offers one possible response. Trials examined how cotton grown on heavy Vertisol soils performed under different irrigation schedules.

The study, available through the UN Food and Agriculture Organization , found that three strategically timed irrigations—at planting, flowering and boll formation—could produce a yield comparable with a far more intensive schedule while using about 40% less irrigation water, provided seasonal rain was normal and well distributed.

The research does not offer a ready-made prescription. The trials were conducted in the 1980s, relied partly on unpublished research-station data and involved specific varieties and soil conditions. Researchers would need to test the approach with current seed, weather patterns and farm conditions before recommending it widely.

Its value lies in showing what may be possible: improving productivity does not necessarily mean applying more water. Timing can matter as much as volume.

Finding where the water goes

More recent work is identifying another part of the solution—reducing losses before water reaches the field.

A 2025 International Water Management Institute assessment found that the Amibara irrigation scheme in the Awash River Basin was operating at just 32% overall efficiency, down from its original 49%.

Researchers combined remote-sensing information, digital mapping and field measurements to identify leakage, poor distribution and operational problems. They found that although water was available at the diversion point, supplies often fell short of crop needs farther along the scheme because of internal bottlenecks.

Digital water accounting can guide repairs and investment. It also shifts some responsibility away from farmers: advice on when to irrigate has limited value if ageing or silted canals cannot deliver water reliably.

IWMI says measures such as canal lining, improved furrows, low-cost moisture sensors and precision irrigation could raise efficiency. These interventions require investment, but could allow farmers to produce more with the water already available.

Getting improved seed to farmers

Water alone will not build resilience. Farmers also need varieties that can cope with heat, drought, pests and, in some irrigated areas, salinity without sacrificing the fibre quality manufacturers require.

At the Werer Agricultural Research Center in Afar, researchers have developed improved cotton varieties intended to raise yields and fibre quality. But limited capacity to multiply the seed has slowed distribution.

“Financial shortages and limited human resources have prevented multiplication of these improved varieties, leaving valuable research results underutilised,” says Berhanu Megersa, director general of the centre.

Recent research illustrates why seed access matters. A 2024 study of irrigated cotton in Ethiopia found that seed source, variety and planting rate significantly affected yields.

But a promising variety at a research station cannot protect Abate’s harvest. Seed must be multiplied and distributed, while extension officers help farmers select the right variety for local conditions. Seasonal forecasts also need to reach producers before planting and be translated into practical decisions about planting dates and irrigation.

Connecting farms and factories

Close 

The benefits could extend along Ethiopia’s value chain. Cotton must be ginned, spun into yarn, woven or knitted, and finished before a clothing factory can use it.

“If farmers cannot produce enough quality cotton, the entire manufacturing chain feels the impact,” Megersa says.

Abeje Menegesha, procurement manager at Amibara Agricultural Development PLC, says local fibre is preferred but its supply remains inconsistent.

“Our first choice is always Ethiopian cotton because it shortens supply chains and supports local farmers,” Menegesha says. “However, domestic production still does not consistently meet our requirements in quantity and quality.”

The work underway suggests Ethiopia does not need to wait for one transformative invention. It needs to connect several practical responses: repair irrigation systems, retest efficient watering schedules, multiply improved seed, deliver usable forecasts and give farmers a predictable market.

Farmer Abeje Selelew sees the opportunity in generational terms.

“I hope my children will see Ethiopian cotton processed into Ethiopian textiles and clothing sold across Africa and beyond,” he says. “When farmers receive fair prices and industries buy more local cotton, everyone along the value chain benefits.”

For Abate, the starting point remains his next planting season. The weather may be less predictable, but Ethiopia’s response does not have to be. Much of the knowledge already exists. The test now is whether it can reach his field in time.

World.title: Tunisia: Upheld Convictions in Mass 'Conspiracy Case' a Travesty of Justice
World.content:
In response to the Tunis Court of Cassation upholding the convictions and lengthy prison sentences against 34 defendants in the politically motivated 'conspiracy case', Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International's Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact, said:

"The Tunis Court of Cassation's decision to uphold these unjust convictions is a devastating blow to justice and an appalling indictment of the Tunisian justice system. By validating these draconian sentences, ranging up to 45 years, following a sham trial based on unfounded charges, the authorities have doubled down on their relentless campaign to eliminate political dissent and silence independent voices.

The Tunis Court of Cassation's decision to uphold these unjust convictions is a devastating blow to justice and an appalling indictment of the Tunisian justice system.Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International



"From the outset, this trial was severely compromised by grave due process violations, including forcing defendants to attend hearings remotely and stripping them of their right to be present at their own trial. The Court of Cassation had a final judicial opportunity to correct this injustice and yet instead today's verdict exposes the authorities' chilling determination to silence all remaining opposition.

"Those imprisoned include human rights lawyer Ayachi Hammami, opposition figure Ahmed Nejib Chebbi, and political activist Chaima Issa amongst many others wrongfully imprisoned. Tunisia's authorities must immediately quash these unjust convictions, drop all charges, and unconditionally release all those detained solely for exercising their human rights. The authorities must stop misusing the criminal justice system as a tool for political repression."

Background

The 'conspiracy case' involves the prosecution of prominent opposition figures, lawyers, and human rights defenders on politically motivated charges, primarily "conspiracy against state security." The trial has been widely condemned by international observers for severe fair trial violations, executive interference, and the denial of basic defense rights.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Fires Back At Critics of New Police Uniforms
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has defended Kenya's new police uniforms amid criticism over the design, saying the change is part of a wider plan to transform the National Police Service.

Speaking during the 59th Passing-Out Parade for Administration Police recruits at the National Police College in Embakasi, Nairobi, Ruto said the new uniforms should not be viewed as an isolated project.

"The new uniforms for general duty officers that we unveiled last week must be understood within this broader reform program," Ruto said.

"It is not a standalone intervention, but part of the comprehensive transformation of the National Police Service arising from the reform process."

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The President said the uniforms were developed after consultations with police officers and members of the public.

According to Ruto, the new design was meant to improve the professional identity of officers while also considering their operational needs and dignity.

"The uniform itself emerged from consultation with police officers and with the Kenyan public," he said.

He acknowledged that a uniform by itself could not change the police service, but argued that it plays a role in building a more professional force.

"A uniform alone cannot transform policing, but professional identity and pride are part of building a modern, disciplined, and effective police service," Ruto said.

The President also appeared to welcome scrutiny of the wider police reform programme, saying public resources must be properly accounted for.

"And because this entire reform program is undertaken in the public interest and financed with public resources, every aspect of it must withstand scrutiny," Ruto said.

"We welcome scrutiny of every decision and every shilling spent."

Ruto said Kenyans should ask questions about government decisions but warned against condemning individuals without evidence.

"We must demand answers without prejudice, question decisions without condemning people unheard, and expose wrongdoing wherever it exists," he said.

"Honest scrutiny strengthens institutions, safeguards public resources, and serves the greater public interest."

Ruto said the uniform changes are only one part of a much wider programme covering police pay, welfare, housing, training, equipment, technology and infrastructure.

He said the government had completed a three-phase salary review that increased the entry-level basic salary of a police constable by 36 per cent.

"There are corresponding adjustments across all the other senior ranks," Ruto said.

Close 

The President also said the government was expanding police housing, including projects in Embakasi, while improving healthcare through the Usalama Cover.

Other reforms, he said, include better mobility, protective equipment, specialised operational assets and air support.

World.title: Patrick Mahomes injury recovery motivation was being able to walk before his daughter
World.content:
Professional athletes are simply built differently than normal people, and sometimes that manifests itself in a serious competitive nature.

It's no secret that Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is a competitive guy, but I didn't realize just how much until a new report about his injury rehab over the offseason.

It turns out the thing that drove him to get through his recovery after knee surgery was trying to walk before his 11-month-old daughter.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

An article by The Kansas City Star's Sam McDowell talks about how Mahomes' season came to an end last December when he injured his ACL and LCL in a game against the Los Angeles Chargers.

The QB had surgery in Dallas, and after that the race was on to make sure he was back on his feet before his daughter was.

"After he returned to Kansas City later in the week, he shared with some of those closest to him a more immediate goal for his recovery," McDowell wrote. "He wanted to walk before his baby daughter, 11-month-old Golden."

Now, this is the reason (alright, one of many reasons) why Patrick Mahomes has won multiple Super Bowls, and you and I haven't.

PATRICK MAHOMES LEAPS PAST DAK PRESCOTT AS NFL'S HIGHEST-PAID QB WITH RECORD CHIEFS EXTENSION WORTH $504.75M

World.title: Trump lawyers target what Letitia James won’t say about evidence in $450M case
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump’s legal representation is demanding an answer to a key question in the civil suit that almost cost him $464 million.

In a letter filed with the New York Supreme Court on Thursday, Trump’s representation is arguing that James failed to comply with a court order that required her to present "the preservation practices" and "its preservation efforts." The demand is the latest objection Trump’s attorneys have used to argue that the case, which is being reconsidered, is full of errors.

Trump’s attorneys believe James may have key evidence she hasn’t turned over — communications with Michel Cohen, a former attorney for Trump.

DELETED EMAIL DETAILS ALLEGED TRUMP-TARGETING PUSH INSIDE LETITIA JAMES’ OFFICE: ‘FIND AND PURSUE CRIMES’

"In seeking the discovery, defendants rely on a January 16, 2026 article by Cohen, published on the online platform Substack in which he asserted that, in meetings with lawyers from [James’s] office, he had ‘felt pressured and coerced to only provide information and testimony that would satisfy the government’s desire to build the cases against and secure a judgement and convictions against President Trump," a court filing reads.

Cohen was a star witness in the civil suit.

During trial, he helped build the case that Trump had routinely misrepresented the value of his properties and testified that Trump had given him target net-worth numbers to meet.

Although the judge denied the request for additional discovery, the process where parties disclose relevant information about the case, he did require James to detail the process it has used to maintain and preserve information.

Trump’s attorneys maintain James failed to do so.

"[New York Attorney General’s Office] also carefully avoids representing one way or the other whether any requested materials in fact exist, and, if they do, whether NYAG has confirmed that they are being preserved," they wrote.

"Instead of actually complying with the Order, NYAG has simply recited in general terms that her ‘standard litigation hold procedures’ have been in place since the investigation phase of this matter."

The back-and-forth is the most recent development of the civil suit James brought against Trump in 2022, accusing him of habitually inflating the value of his property to a fraudulent extent.

LETITIA JAMES FACES SCRUTINY AFTER NEW YORK CITY SPENDS $81,700 PER HOMELESS PERSON AMID SHELTER SCANDALS

After being found liable, Trump was ordered to pay $355 million plus interest in disgorgement and was banned from applying for loans from any New York bank or financial institution for three years.

He was also banned from serving as an officer or director of any New York company for two years.

Although an appeals court later vacated the monetary penalties, James has appealed to reinstate them. Trump, for his part, has argued the case is fundamentally flawed and that it should be thrown out in its entirety

Earlier this month, Trump’s lawyers cited five key disqualifying weaknesses.

They argue that Attorney General James lacked the authority to bring the case, noting that the case involves private commercial transactions rather than harm to the public. They also contend that Trump’s valuations reflected subjective estimates that lenders independently evaluated rather than fraudulent misrepresentations.

"The only supposed 'victims' here are a handful of ultrasophisticated banks and insurers that have never claimed to be injured, were eager to do business with President Trump and his family, and made over $100 million from these transactions," the appeal states.

They further argue that the prosecution’s premise of overvaluation is based on the misguided idea that real estate has one objective value and that deviations from that value must be fraud.

"Under that breathtakingly broad theory, NYAG can second-guess any business transaction in this State on almost any imagined grounds," attorneys wrote.

And, on the penalties, Trump’s representation argues that the $450 million disgorgement is excessive, unlawful and even unconstitutional.

Finally, the appeal argues that the politically charged nature of the case, on its own, should have been enough to halt its consideration.

"NYAG cannot point to a single Section 63(12) enforcement action against similarly situated developers (or any other type of defendant) based on practices comparable to those alleged here," the filing states, referring to the state law Trump was accused of violating.

On the matter of its disclosures, James’ office pointed to its own letter in response to an inquiry from Fox News Digital, contending that it had met its disclosure requirements.

TRUMP BACKS REPUBLICAN CHALLENGER TO OUST LETITIA JAMES AMID ONGOING MORTGAGE FRAUD FEUD

"Insofar as Defendants have sought or are seeking more information about OAG’s specific preservation efforts, OAG objects to the demand for this extrajudicial discovery," the letter reads.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Moreover, OAG has completely satisfied its obligations under the Court’s Order for OAG to identify the preservation practices that existed and applied and continue to exist and apply."

World.title: Former Cal softball player files lawsuit against university, ex-coach over alleged sexual misconduct
World.content:
A former University of California, Berkeley softball player is accusing an ex-head coach of using her position of authority to pressure the player into a sexual relationship and allegedly threatening her playing time if she ended it.

The complaint, filed Aug. 24 in Alameda County Superior Court and obtained by OutKick, alleges Cal failed to intervene and allowed Chelsea Spencer to remain as head coach for months after athletic department staff learned of the alleged relationship.

Spencer ultimately stepped down last year in June, four months after agreeing to a multi-year contract extension. According to the lawsuit, a subsequent Cal investigation concluded that Spencer had violated campus policy regarding conflicts of interest in consensual relationships. The filing does not detail the dates when the probe started or ended. It also alleged Spencer was not cooperative in the process.

SJSU VOLLEYBALL COACH'S ALLEGED ASSAULT VICTIM SPEAKS OUT FOR THE FIRST TIME SINCE ALLEGATIONS SURFACED

In an email to OutKick on Friday, a Cal spokesperson declined to comment on the lawsuit or the school's investigation into Spencer.

The former softball player retained the services of Slater Slater Schulman law firm. Gizem Gures, an attorney at the firm, referenced Cal’s reputation and its response to the investigation in a statement to USA Today Sports about the lawsuit.

"Berkeley proudly holds itself out as the No. 1 public university in the world. That reputation comes with a responsibility to protect its students. As a Cal alum, it is deeply disappointing to see what our client experienced and how the University responded after its own investigation substantiated the conduct. Our client deserved better. Berkeley's students deserve better. The University needs to do better," the statement read.

The complaint further alleges that Spencer’s advances toward the former player started in fall 2023, after the unnamed player joined the softball team as an incoming transfer. It says Spencer contacted her daily, via phone calls and text messages. Those communications eventually took on a romantic tone.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

At one point, Spencer allegedly told the player, "you’re so beautiful" and "your girlfriend is so lucky." The complaint further alleges that Spencer shared details about her personal life and gave gifts in the form of cash.

Once the player effectively ignored the coach's messages, Spencer allegedly became angry and cut her playing time as punishment, the complaint claims.

"When Plaintiff did not provide Spencer the attention she demanded, Spencer yelled at Plaintiff, treated her differently, and reduced or withheld Plaintiff's playing opportunities," the complaint states. "Plaintiff thus began to recognize, even before the relationship became sexual, that Spencer's personal demands and Spencer's authority as Head Coach were intertwined."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The former player argued that Spencer’s conduct and the university’s alleged negligence caused her severe emotional distress and forced her to end her collegiate softball career earlier than she would have otherwise. She is seeking a jury trial and damages for personal injuries and other losses.

World.title: ICE officer pleads not guilty to lying about Minneapolis shooting involving Venezuelan man
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer pleaded not guilty Friday to charges of lying about a January shooting of a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis during the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration.

Christian Castro appeared in a Texas federal court where he faces six charges of making "materially false" statements to investigators, according to federal court documents unsealed Friday. He turned himself in to authorities Thursday evening.

A judge ordered Castro released on a $75,000 unsecured bond and required him to wear an ankle monitor.

DOJ CHARGES ICE OFFICER WITH LYING TO INVESTIGATORS FOLLOWING MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING OF VENEZUELAN MAN

The charges stem from the Jan. 14 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man who was shot in the leg. Moments earlier, Castro and his partner attempted to stop a vehicle.

The driver, also a Venezuelan citizen, fled, triggering a foot chase.

Castro caught up to the driver and a physical struggle ensued, according to the indictment. Sosa-Celis attempted to help the driver, and they both fled into a nearby apartment duplex and shut the door.

ICE AGENTS IN FATAL HOUSTON SHOOTING WERE NOT WEARING BODY CAMERAS, SOURCES SAY

Castro drew his service weapon and fired a single shot through the front door, striking Sosa-Celis in the leg, federal prosecutors said.

Two 1-year-old children and two women were inside the home when Castro opened fire, prosecutors added.

In an attempt to justify the shooting, Castro allegedly told investigators he was brutally assaulted by multiple individuals wielding tools, claiming he was hit with a broom and a snow shovel during the confrontation. He also claimed he was on his back when he fired toward the fleeing men, officials said.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION HAS LOST OR ABANDONED HUNDREDS OF LAWSUITS AGAINST ANTI-ICE PROTESTERS, MIGRANTS: REPORT

However, video evidence later contradicted those statements, prompting an investigation. Federal prosecutors said Castro was standing up when he opened fire, and they disputed his claim that he fought the suspect on the ground for three minutes, noting the struggle actually lasted about 11 seconds.

The shooting occurred amid a targeted crackdown on illegal immigration in Minneapolis.

Castro faces separate charges in Minnesota and was previously arrested in Texas in May.

ICE OFFICER CHARGED IN MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING RELEASED IN TEXAS AFTER JUDGE DECLINES TO INTERVENE

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

His case has sparked a legal battle involving Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who has refused to extradite him to Minnesota.

World.title: Robot dog could deliver your next package and an ad
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

We've covered robot dogs patrolling with police and training to handle terrain that could someday take them to the moon. We've even watched wheeled versions tackle some pretty wild ground. And whenever we show these machines, one question keeps coming up: What happens when they reach a flight of stairs? Well, Robot.com may have an answer.

Its new four-legged R-dog is built to carry packages where traditional wheeled delivery robots can get stuck. It can also show ads along the way, turning your future delivery into something of a moving billboard.

So, can R-dog really get your package closer to your front door while making the economics of robot delivery work? Let's take a closer look.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

ONE-WHEELED AI SECURITY ROBOT COULD PATROL YOUR PROPERTY

What is the R-dog robot dog?

R-dog is Robot.com's latest concept for autonomous delivery. The San Francisco-based company unveiled it on Aug. 11. The idea tackles one of the most frustrating parts of robotic delivery: the final stretch to your door. A wheeled robot may handle the sidewalk just fine, only to meet a curb or staircase it cannot cross. Robot.com designed R-dog to cover those final 330 feet with a mix of wheels and articulated legs.

Each leg ends in a wheel, so R-dog can roll efficiently across flatter ground. When the route gets more difficult, those flexible legs are designed to help it deal with stairs, curbs and other obstacles. The cargo compartment forms most of the robot's body. Robot.com says it can carry food orders and standard packages inside.

And yes, it definitely looks like a robot dog. There is even a tail, which gives the machine a friendlier appearance than your average delivery box on wheels. That personality may be more than decoration. Robot.com wants people to notice R-dog, interact with it and feel comfortable when it appears in public spaces. As you will see, that becomes especially important once advertising enters the picture.

Why stairs are such a headache for delivery robots

Getting a delivery robot across town can actually be easier than getting it from the sidewalk to your front door. Traditional delivery robots tend to perform best on predictable surfaces. Smooth sidewalks work well because wheels are efficient and relatively simple.

Then the terrain changes. A staircase can end the trip. A high curb can cause trouble. Even an awkward building entrance may force someone to step in. That creates an obvious weak point in a system that is supposed to reduce human involvement. Robot.com wants R-dog to keep going when a standard sidewalk robot would have to stop.

Its four-legged design could also expand the places where autonomous delivery makes sense. Campuses, apartment complexes and neighborhoods can all include routes that become difficult for wheels alone. Of course, getting over the obstacle is only useful if the package also reaches the right person. That brings us to R-dog's unusual delivery system.

How R-dog drops off your package

The cargo compartment can hold multiple items, including stacked food orders and e-commerce packages. Once R-dog reaches its destination, an unattended auto drop-off system releases the order. The robot can then continue to its next assignment. And yes, the visual is hard to ignore.

The package appears to slide out through the back of the robot. There really is no delicate way to say this: It looks a little like R-dog poops out your delivery. Funny visual aside, the system could have a practical advantage. You would not necessarily need to stand outside and physically unload the robot before it could leave.

Still, one question remains. Robot.com says the compartment can carry multiple orders, but its current materials do not explain exactly how the concept chooses the correct package when several items are loaded inside. That is one of the details I want to see explained as R-dog gets closer to real-world deployment. The company is still refining parts of the prototype, including its storage setup.

HUMANOID ROBOTS WORK NONSTOP IN PACKAGE TEST

Why R-dog also shows ads

Now we get to the part that makes R-dog more than a quirky delivery machine. The robot has two video screens connected to R-ads, Robot.com's advertising platform. Brands can remotely manage campaigns shown on the company's robots.

In other words, every trip can potentially earn money twice. The robot can perform a delivery while its screens carry paid advertising through the neighborhood. That business model makes some sense. People already ignore plenty of static advertising. A four-legged robot rolling past with a tail has a much better chance of making someone look.

You might stop to watch it. Maybe you pull out your phone for a photo or video. Someone else could share that clip on social media. From an advertiser's perspective, that kind of attention can be valuable. Robot.com also promotes natural voice conversations, allowing R-dog to respond when people interact with it. That could make the advertising experience more engaging than simply walking past another screen.

The company says R-ads also offers campaign analytics. However, its public R-dog materials leave some details about those measurements unclear. I would like to know exactly what the system measures when people interact with these robots and how that information gets handled. Those answers become more important if machines like R-dog eventually appear in busy public spaces.

How AI helps R-dog find its way

Of course, legs alone do not get a robot safely through a crowded neighborhood. It also needs to understand what is happening around it. Robot.com is working with FieldAI on the navigation stack planned for the production version of R-dog.

FieldAI's Field Foundation Models are designed to help robots operate in changing real-world environments without requiring prior mapping. That could allow R-dog to adapt when the route ahead looks different from what it expected, whether someone left an object in the way or the path suddenly changes.

Robot.com also runs its fleet through a platform called REMI. The company describes REMI as its fleet-management platform and physical API layer. The advantage here is that R-dog does not need an entirely separate operational system. Robot.com can plug the new four-legged design into technology it already uses across its fleet.

CEO and co-founder Felipe Chavez Cortes summed up that strategy when he said, "We built R-dog to run on what already exists."

Robot.com already has robots in the real world

R-dog may be new, but Robot.com has already spent years putting robots to work. The company was founded in 2017 and is headquartered in San Francisco, with additional offices in Colombia. Robot.com says more than 500 robots are deployed across the United States and Canada, plus Dubai and other MENA markets. Those machines have completed more than 2.5 million tasks.

Its lineup includes R-kiwi for sidewalk delivery and R-cargo for industrial logistics. Robot.com also develops R-noid, a humanoid platform aimed at workplace tasks. That existing fleet gives Robot.com experience to build on.

When and where will R-dog launch?

Robot.com says commercial deployments are targeted for 2027. The company's CEO has said college campuses will come first, although Robot.com has yet to announce specific campuses or cities. That makes campuses a logical proving ground. They offer lots of short deliveries, plenty of foot traffic and exactly the kinds of curbs or stairways that R-dog was designed to handle.

Robot.com already operates campus delivery robots in North America and expanded its autonomous delivery partnership with Sodexo in August 2026.

Pricing has not been announced. And do not expect to walk into a store and buy an R-dog for your house. At least initially, Robot.com appears focused on commercial delivery pilots and brand activations rather than individual consumers.

For now, businesses can 

NEW WHEELED ROBOT SAYS NO THANKS TO HUMANOID HYPE

What this means to you

If R-dog performs the way Robot.com hopes, robot delivery could get closer to your actual doorstep instead of stopping at the sidewalk. That could make autonomous delivery practical in more places and reduce the number of times a person has to step in to finish the trip.

But R-dog also gives us a preview of where the economics of robot delivery may be heading. Moving a package is one revenue opportunity. Selling advertising during the journey creates another. That means your future delivery experience could look very different. The same machine bringing dinner to your door might also be displaying a commercial as it rolls away.

Convenience will get plenty of attention, but I will also be watching the privacy side. Robot.com should be clear about what its advertising system measures when people approach or interact with R-dog.

Kurt's key takeaways

I have seen plenty of robot dogs that can climb, jump or show off in a demo. R-dog caught my attention because Robot.com is trying to apply those abilities to a very ordinary problem: getting a package all the way to your door. Wheels are great until the sidewalk ends. Giving a delivery robot articulated legs could help it complete routes that stop other machines short. The advertising angle may be equally important to whether this idea works as a business. If R-dog can earn money from an ad while it is already out making a delivery, that gives operators another reason to deploy it. Still, R-dog remains a concept heading toward commercial use in 2027. I want to see how it handles real stairs, crowded sidewalks and everyday weather before calling the problem solved. I also want more details about how multiple packages get sorted during unattended deliveries and what information R-ads collects from public interactions. Those answers will tell us a lot about whether R-dog becomes a useful delivery tool or simply a very clever way to get people to look at a screen.

Would you be comfortable with a robot dog climbing your steps to deliver a package if it was also showing ads along the way, or would you rather stick with a human at the door? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

World.title: Legendary sports agent talks about the Rams use of 'caponomics' to bring Aaron Donald out of retirement
World.content:
Aaron Donald officially made his return to the Los Angeles Rams earlier this week. But how did a team with so many expensive contracts fit Donald under the salary cap?

According to famed sports agent Leigh Steinberg, it's because the Rams do a great job with "caponomics."

The Rams did it by "creating cap room, redoing someone else's contract so that there's less salary involved and by giving that player a bonus," Steinberg told OutKick in a recent interview. "If a team is creative, they can move other contracts around and create cap space."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

After falling short against their NFC West rival, the Seattle Seahawks, in the NFC Championship Game last season, the Rams went on a spending spree this offseason.

They gave MVP-winning quarterback Matthew Stafford a one-year, $55 million contract extension, traded for Kansas City Chiefs star cornerback Trent McDuffie and signed him to a four-year, $124 million contract extension, signed cornerback Jaylen Watson to a three-year, $51 million contract, and acquired Cleveland Browns superstar Myles Garrett before signing him to a five-year, $208 million contract after redoing his deal following the trade.

Despite handing out all of those massive deals, the Rams were still able to sign Donald to a one-year, $20 million deal, despite being up against the salary cap.

So how, exactly, are the Rams making it work? Exactly as Steinberg said: by being creative.

For Stafford’s deal, the Rams have pushed his contract further into the future, spreading out the cap hit using void years, meaning Stafford’s contract will count against the salary cap in even though he won’t be on the team. Stafford’s contract is spread out through the 2031 season.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

As for McDuffie, the Rams backloaded his contract. This season, McDuffie’s cap hit is just $10.8 million, but that rises to $30.8 million next season and will hover around that figure for ensuing three seasons.

Garrett’s contract is structured similarly to both Stafford’s and McDuffie’s, with a lower cap hit in the first year and larger hits later in the deal while also using void years. The reigning Defensive Player of the Year’s contract runs through 2030, but his cap hits are spread through 2034.

Here are his cap hits each year through 2034: $8.4 million, $15 million, $27.57 million, $39.875 million, $48.17 million, $17.523 million, $11.5 million, $7.6 million and finally $3.3 million.

To fit Aaron Donald into their group of superstars, the Rams have pushed a lot of money into the future to make it work in the present.

Steinberg thinks the decision to acquire Garrett and bring Donald out of retirement will be well worth it.

"So let's imagine that you took a team that was already the favorite to win the Super Bowl because of their (trade) of the best defensive player in football, Myles Garrett. And you now add to him an unbelievably dominant defensive player in Aaron Donald," Steinberg said.

PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME MAKING MASSIVE OVERHAUL OF ITS SELECTION PROCESS FOLLOWING 2026 BILL BELICHICK SNUB

"It creates an impregnable line that's impossible to double team. The synergistic effect of this is that an opposing offense can't double team both Aaron Donald and Myles Garrett. So somewhere in there you're going to have this spectacularly dominant player on the loose."

Steinberg is also certain that Donald, who made the Pro Bowl in each of his 10 seasons in the NFL, would not have returned unless he felt he could play at an elite level.

"I am sure that Aaron Donald would not have come back except that he thought he could be dominant once again," Steinberg said. "I'm assuming that time takes its toll. Being outside of football takes its toll, but it won't take too long for Aaron Donald to be back in form. No other team has two players like this backed up by another three."

In addition to having Donald and Garrett, the Rams’ defensive line was already strong with Kobie Turner, Braden Fiske, Byron Young and Poona Ford. Steinberg said the Rams’ defensive line could be one of the best of all time, comparing it to the legendary line the Baltimore Colts had in the 1960s.

"I think the only thing that would be equivalent was the Fearsome Foursome that had Merlin Olsen and Deacon Jones and Rosie Greer. The Fearsome Foursome is back and as you said, they've got Poona Ford and Kobie Turner and Braden Fiske and Byron Young and they're loaded with gifted players," Steinberg said.

CAM SKATTEBO CONSIDERED RETIREMENT AFTER SEASON-ENDING ANKLE INJURY IN GIANTS ROOKIE YEAR

"The Rams do a better job of scouting players, drafting players, and then finding that one superstar that can be plugged into an already dominating defense or offense."

A front comparable to the Fearsome Foursome of Olsen, Jones, Greer and Lamar Lundy would give the Rams an excellent chance of getting to the Super Bowl and winning it all.

Steinberg, who was inducted into the California Sports Hall of Fame in 2017, has had many high-profile clients. Across football and baseball, Steinberg’s clients include Steve Bartkowski, Steve Young, Troy Aikman, Warren Moon, Bruce Smith, Thurman Thomas, Kordell Stewart, Jeff George, Ben Roethlisberger, Myron Rolle, Matt Leinart, Mark Brunell, Ricky Williams, Howie Long, Eric Karros and Dusty Baker, among others.

Steinberg was not surprised that Donald came out of retirement because so many of his clients wanted to as well.

"I had 64 first-round draft picks, 12 of the players in the Hall of Fame, and when they retired, they did it with class and dignity. But then a couple weeks later, the phone would ring and the player would say, ‘Do you think there's any spot for me? Do you think I can come back?’" Steinberg said.

The legendary agent said these were players who had peaceful second careers lined up and had all the money they would need, but that they simply missed the game.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They all want to play and when they're away from the game, players miss the structure, the fact that it gives them an itinerary that tells them what they're supposed to be doing every day, what they're supposed to be doing at this time of year. They have structure. They miss the camaraderie in the locker room with the band of brothers that are around them," Steinberg said.

"They miss the electric excitement of performing in front of packed crowds and or many of them from Pop Warner on this is all they've known and so, like the moth to the flame, professional sports is so intoxicating that players never really want to retire."

The Rams are certainly fortunate that Donald wanted to come back and play. The result could end with him holding another Lombardi Trophy.

The Ohio State University acknowledged that a former researcher had "inappropriate foreign affiliations" after agreeing to pay $2.1 million to resolve federal allegations that the university failed to share researchers’ ties to China while seeking and receiving taxpayer-funded research grants.

The Justice Department alleged Ohio State failed to properly disclose affiliations and financial support involving Chinese universities and state-run research organizations in applications and reports submitted to NASA and the National Science Foundation from 2012 to 2023.

The allegations included a principal investigator’s participation in China’s Thousand Talents Program.

Ohio State told Fox News Digital in a statement Friday that the university ultimately uncovered and investigated C.K. Shum’s foreign affiliations itself and reported them to federal authorities. Shum is no longer employed at the university.

HARVARD-CHINA LINKS UNEARTHED AS CONGRESS FINDS 140 PAPERS CO-AUTHORED BY CCP MILITARY UNIVERSITIES

"Ohio State uncovered and investigated C.K. Shum’s inappropriate foreign affiliations and self-reported them to NASA and the National Science Foundation," Benjamin Johnson, chief communications officer at The Ohio State University, told Fox News Digital in a statement Friday.

"The university suspended Shum’s principal investigator privileges, halted spending on the relevant federal awards, initiated disciplinary proceedings and repaid the federal grant funds in question. Shum is no longer employed at Ohio State, and the university has cooperated with federal authorities throughout the investigation.

"Ohio State takes national security seriously, and the university has long been recognized for its efforts to promote research integrity and security. Safeguards include dedicated research compliance and secure research offices, mandatory conflict-of-interest and research security disclosure systems and robust security and foreign influence training programs."

HARVARD TOPS NATION IN FOREIGN CASH HAUL AS COTTON DEMANDS PROBE INTO CHINA FUNDING

In a press release, the Department of Justice said the grant applications required OSU to share any ties to any foreign government.

"The settlement resolves allegations that OSU failed to disclose the collaboration and affiliation with, or funding received from, the PRC by certain OSU employees working on NASA and NSF grants," the press release said.

"Specifically, the settlement resolves allegations that, since 2014, annual Faculty Activity Reports submitted to OSU identified affiliations with PRC universities and state-run research organizations, but OSU did not disclose this information to NASA or NSF."

The press release also noted that Ohio State became aware in 2019 that a researcher tied to NASA-funded work was involved in China’s Thousand Talents Program but waited until 2023 to inform NASA and the National Science Foundation.

The federal government describes the program as a Beijing-backed effort to attract people with expertise in or access to overseas technology and intellectual property. The DOJ also said it found other OSU employees connected to the grants who had relationships with Chinese entities or received Chinese funding.

World.title: Maria Bartiromo’s lawyer says she was not fired from Fox News
World.content:
Maria Bartiromo’s lawyer on Friday said that the Fox News and Fox Business anchor was not fired from the company where she worked for more than 12 years.

“For many years, Maria Bartiromo hosted three No. 1-rated television shows on Fox channels,” said Bryan Freedman, Bartiromo’s attorney.

On Thursday, Fox abruptly announced in a statement that it had parted ways with Bartiromo, without offering any further details or context. The last episode of Bartiromo’s daily Fox Business show aired on Thursday. On Friday, those hours of programming came on the air with the same titles and graphics, but without Bartiromo’s name in them.

“The irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false,” Freedman said Friday. “Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise.”

He added: “Those reporting her firing or the incredulous facts supporting that fiction have exhibited a complete and utter reckless disregard for the truth.”

A Fox News Media representative, when asked about Freedman’s statement, said the company’s press release about parting ways with Bartiromo “speaks for itself.”

Before Freedman’s statement, on Thursday night the Status media industry newsletter reported that Bartiromo was fired after she had shared with the White House guidance from Fox management about claims made by President Donald Trump about recent elections. The New York Times and Wall Street Journal also reported later Thursday that she was dismissed after sharing internal Fox communications with the White House. NBC News has not verified those reports.

Immediately following Fox’s announcement on Thursday, Bartiromo’s bio and show pages were wiped from Fox’s websites.

Bartiromo had been Fox Business’ global markets editor since joining the channel in 2014. On Fox Business, she hosted “Mornings with Maria” on weekdays and “Maria Bartiromo’s Wall Street” on Fridays, while also anchoring “Sunday Morning Futures,” a business-focused show on the larger Fox News Channel.

For years, Fox News Media touted Bartiromo’s shows at ratings winners. She joined Fox after a trailblazing 21-year career at CNBC, where she hosted “Closing Bell,” a cornerstone of the business network’s programming.

Bartiromo drew attention for taking a more openly conservative turn in her reporting at Fox after leaving CNBC, where her work had been largely apolitical.

She also became very close to Trump, who appointed her to the board of the John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts. The center’s website still lists her as a board member as of Friday afternoon.

In 2021, Bartiromo’s comments and shows were cited as exhibits in a defamation lawsuit filed by the voting machine maker Dominion Voting Systems against Fox News. Dominion alleged that the cable network operator had knowingly broadcast false claims that Dominion had rigged the 2020 presidential election.

Fox News eventually agreed to pay $787 million in a settlement with Dominion.

Another voting machine firm, Smartmatic, also filed suit against Fox in 2021, naming Bartiromo as a co-defendant. The Smartmatic case is ongoing.

The Ghost Max, which earned the American Podiatric Medical Association’s Seal of Acceptance, has a curved outsole that makes your heel-to-toe transitions as smooth as possible, as well as a wide, stabilizing base.

Retailers drop prices on summer clothing during their Labor Day sales to get rid of warm weather apparel and make room for fall styles, says Vipin Porwal, CEO and consumer savings expert at Smarty, a shopping and rewards platform. The only exception is laptops. “Higher memory costs are putting pressure on notebook pricing, so if you find a strong Labor Day deal on the exact laptop you want, I’d take it seriously,” says Carls. “I wouldn’t assume November automatically gets you a lower final price.” Toys : Toy deals are the most competitive leading up to the holidays, especially during Black Friday and Cyber Monday, says Carls. If you’re already thinking about buying them as gifts, you’ll save the most if you wait to shop.

Fall and winter clothing, shoes and accessories: Retailers just rolled out next season’s fashion, so they’re not motivated to drop prices just yet. Wait until sales in October and November to save on denim, boots, coats and sweaters, for example, says Porwal. Are there better Labor Day sales online or in stores? There are comparable Labor Day sales online and in stores, especially at big box retailers, so you’re guaranteed to find strong deals wherever you shop. A few things to keep in mind while deciding whether to leave your couch: Shopping online makes comparing prices and stacking savings easier , letting you consider the total value of a deal, not just the sale price, says Ashley Feinstein Gerstley, a shopping and savings expert at Rakuten. Open a few tabs and search for the exact same product at a handful of retailers to weigh which one offers the lowest price and lowest shipping fee. You can also shop through cash back apps and browser extensions online, which help you find additional promo codes and rewards, she says.

Shipping fees add up, especially if you’re placing online orders at numerous retailers or buying big-ticket products that require installation. If your total goes up drastically once you consider shipping fees, see if you can buy online and pick up in store instead. When do Labor Day sales start? Labor Day sales have already started. Retailers typically consider the Friday before the official holiday, which lands on Monday, Sept. 7 this year, the start of the long weekend, so all sales are now live. When do Labor Day sales end? Plan for most Labor Day sales to end on the holiday, Monday, Sept. 7. Some may extend longer into the week, but don’t plan on it — aim to get all your shopping done by Labor Day, but shop sooner if you can, says Carls. “Summer clearance is already working with fewer sizes, colors and models, so the thing you actually want can disappear before the promotion does,” she says. “The discount may hang around, but your exact patio set, for example, may not.” How can you save the most money during Labor Day sales? All the experts I talked to agree that the best way to save the most money during Labor Day sales is to stack your savings. That means looking at the deal price as the starting point and combining it with additional offers to save even more, says Gerstley. For example, search for promo codes to lower prices further, shop through cash back apps and browsers to put money back in your pocket, and pay with credit cards that let you earn rewards as you spend. Additionally, make sure you’re comparing prices across retailers before buying anything, says Porwal. Since so many retailers are hosting sales right now, they’re all competing for your attention, and you never know when one might lower prices just a little bit more to give themselves an edge, or throw in extras that make a purchase more worthwhile, like free shipping, delivery, install or haul-away. Don’t be afraid to ask about price matching, too, says Carls. If a retailer really wants your business, they’ll be open to negotiating with you. Last but not least, don’t feel like you absolutely have to buy something if deals aren’t compelling, says Gerstley. As we enter the final quarter of the year, sales are plentiful with early Black Friday and Cyber Monday offers starting in October, and Amazon Prime Big Deal Days might be around the corner (it hasn’t been confirmed yet, however). There will be more promotional moments in the near future, and waiting might be key to maximizing your savings.

Labor Day sales historically offer strong deals across key categories like summer clothing and shoes, outdoor goods, furniture, mattresses and bedding, and appliances. Shoppers can save online and in stores throughout the holiday weekend at almost every major retailer. Labor Day sales are typically the last summer clearance events, causing brands to drop prices extra low to get rid of inventory before the fall.

World.title: Supreme Court backs Republicans in election ad rate dispute
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday handed a win to Republicans by ensuring that party committees paying for TV s in the upcoming midterm elections can take advantage of the same discounts that candidates get.

The justices blocked a ruling by the Richmond, Virginia-based 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals that had invalidated a recently announced Federal Communications Commission policy.

Only one member of the court, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, objected to the majority’s decision.

The decision means that the often sharply discounted rates will apply to committees and candidates alike as litigation continues.

The National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, with the backing of the Trump administration, had asked the Supreme Court to block the appeals court ruling.

In the unsigned order, the court said that the committees had shown they were likely to suffer “irreparable harm” if the appeals court ruling was not blocked because broadcasters have already started declining to offer them the discounted rates for ads.

Taken together with a Supreme Court ruling in June that lifted previous restrictions on committee expenditures, the latest decision represents a significant boon for Republicans.

In the June ruling, the Supreme Court struck down federal limits on “coordinated party communications,” caps that used to govern how much national party organizations like the Democratic and Republican Senate campaign committees could spend directly in concert with their candidates.

The two rulings allow Republicans to stretch their party committee dollars even further by allowing them to spend more committee money at lower rates. Democrats will have the same power, but the decision is of less help to them because their candidates are already, on the whole, better funded, and the Democratic National Committee has more than $100 million less in its coffers than the Republican National Committee does.

Several Democratic House and Senate candidates, including Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., challenged the March public notice issued by the FCC.

In an Aug. 25 ruling, the appeals court ruled that the party committees are not entitled to the same discounts as candidates.

Democratic candidates have generally raised significantly more money than their rivals for years, but Republican committees have far more money banked away for the fall, so the ruling allows the cash-flush GOP committees to help narrow that gap.

World.title: Trump says Lindsay Clancy "did a horrible, horrible thing"
World.content:
Shortly after the judge overseeing Lindsay Clancy's murder case declared a mistrial Friday due to a hung jury, President Trump called it a "terrible situation" and a "horrible tragedy" in his first public comments on a case that has drawn nationwide attention.

Asked by reporters if he is following the Massachusetts trial, the president said: "It's on television so much, it's hard not to follow it."

Clancy has admitted to killing her three children at home in the suburban town of Duxbury in early 2023, and her lawyers say she then tried to take her own life.

Prosecutors accused Clancy of first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children in their home in the suburban town of Duxbury in early 2023. Clancy has admitted to killing them, but pleaded not guilty, arguing she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis. The trial included testimony from a litany of psychologists and psychiatrists who weighed in on Clancy's state of mind.

Mr. Trump did not offer a strong view on what the outcome of the polarizing case should be.

"Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse," he said. "But you'll find out what the price to pay is. There'll be a price. It's going to be mental institution or jail or something."

He noted that another trial is possible, which he called "too bad."

The jury deliberated for 36 hours. If she had been found not guilty by reason of insanity, prosecutors could have asked a judge to commit her to a state hospital or mental health facility.

Jurors informed the judge several times that they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. After they remained deadlocked on Friday, the judge formally declared a mistrial. Local prosecutors have not said whether they will retry her.

The case was marked by an unusual bout of last-minute controversy. Clancy's attorney asked the judge to dismiss a lone juror who he alleged was ignoring the court's instructions, pointing to a note to the judge from the jury foreperson.

The judge rejected that request, but he held off on declaring a mistrial Friday so Clancy's legal team could appeal the matter to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court. When the state's highest court declined to intervene, a mistrial was declared and jurors were dismissed.
