World.title: Baja California Sur, Nuevo León and Querétaro lead new foreign investment in first half of 2026
World.content:
Baja California Sur, Nuevo León, and Querétaro emerged as the top destinations for new foreign investment in Mexico during the first half of 2026, even as new foreign investment in the country slowed overall.

According to new data from the Economy Ministry (SE), Mexico received US $2.7 billion in new investments from January to June — one of the three components of foreign direct investment (FDI) — down 13.4% compared to the same period in 2025. At the same time, total FDI grew as established ventures reinvested profits.

However, three entities maintained investor confidence.

Baja California Sur topped the list with US $524 million of new FDI, followed by Nuevo León with $473 million, and Querétaro with $410 million. Together, these three states accounted for nearly half of the funds allocated to new projects.

Baja California Sur’s tourism industry pushed it to the top of the list. In the first half of 2026, over 95% of the state’s total FDI was new investment. Of that new investment, over 97% ($511.9 million) went toward lodging services including guesthouses, boarding houses and furnished apartments with hotel services.

Meanwhile, Nuevo León registered a 190.1% annual growth in new FDI. The capital was concentrated in wholesale trade of trucks and auto parts, vehicle manufacturing and the iron and steel industries.

The result reflects the state’s importance as a manufacturing, logistics and automotive hub, favored for its proximity to the U.S. market and the integration of its suppliers into global supply chains.

Finally, Querétaro saw a 158.6% increase in new capital investment after receiving a boost of US $410 million. The main sectors receiving this investment include electricity generation and supply, confectionery, auto parts, and electronic components — sectors that confirm the state’s industrial diversification and its importance within the Bajío economic corridor.

These three states were followed by Jalisco, Quintana Roo, Nayarit, Chihuahua, Baja California, Puebla and Guanajuato, which received between US $100 million to $300 million in new capital investment apiece.

In contrast, Tlaxcala — the smallest state in Mexico — was the only state that saw no foreign investment.

Meanwhile, México state, Zacatecas, Sonora, Aguascalientes and Mexico City registered capital outflows.

With reports from El Economista

World.title: Marie, now a Category 2 hurricane, brings rain and flooding to Baja California Sur and the Pacific coast
World.content:
Rapidly intensifying Hurricane Marie reached Category 2 status off the coast of Baja California Sur on Friday, closing ports and suspending classes across the state.

A 10 a.m. social media post from the National Meteorological Service (SMN) said Marie was located 885 kilometers west-southwest of Cabo San Lucas, at the southern tip of the Baja Peninsula.

“It has maximum sustained winds of 155 km/h, gusts of 195 km/h and is moving west-northwest at 15 km/h,” the National Water Commission (Conagua) reported.

A Tropical Cyclone Advisory was issued by the SMN which forecast intense localized rains for the northwestern coast of Mexico, including the states of Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán to the south of BCS.

Civil protection authorities urged the public to take extreme precautions and heed the recommendations issued by the authorities of the National Civil Protection System.

Navigation is also severely restricted due to the extreme weather conditions. Maritime authorities have closed ports to small vessels in San José del Cabo and Magdalena Bay.

High waves are another risk factor along the western coastline, with waves of 1.5 to 2.5 meters (5-8 feet) in height forecast for the peninsula.

Conagua said Marie’s main threat is the extensive cloud bands which increase the likelihood of heavy rainfall and could cause more flooding in vulnerable coastal areas. This prompted BCS Governor Víctor Manuel Castro to suspend all school activities in the municipality of Los Cabos.

Cabo San Lucas was battered by high winds and heavy rain on Wednesday while Marie was still a tropical storm.

Legendary rock musician Sammy Hagar — owner of the resort city’s famous Cabo Wabo Cantina — said in an Instagram post that the storm caused a great deal of damage, asking his fans to pray for his club and the city.

In a Thursday Instagram post, Hagar praised the authorities for their quick reaction to the flooding.

“Cabo to the rescue,” he wrote. “Congratulations to the community for pulling the cleanup crew together so quickly.”

Hurricane Marie — along with the Mexican monsoon, low-pressure troughs, cyclonic circulations at high levels of the atmosphere and Tropical Wave Number 36 in southern and western Mexico — was also forecast to generate intense rains in Veracruz, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco on Friday.

Conagua said Marie is expected to weaken to a Category 1 storm on Saturday as it moves further out to sea.

Though it could soon thereafter be downgraded to a tropical storm, atmospheric instability is likely to continue interacting with low-pressure troughs in the interior of the country into next week.

With reports from Informador, El Universal and N+

World.title: Defense minister responds to US anti-drone border operations: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Zacatecas homicides down 85%: National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, an 85% reduction compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration. The 2026 daily average is down 96% versus 2021.

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, an 85% reduction compared to September 2024, the final month of the López Obrador administration. The 2026 daily average is down 96% versus 2021. 🚔 Thousands arrested since Sheinbaum took office: Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between October 2024 and August 2026 for high-impact crimes. He said that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period, while six meth labs were dismantled.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between October 2024 and August 2026 for high-impact crimes. He said that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the same period, while six meth labs were dismantled. 💰 Atizapán killings tied to money demand: García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings.

García Harfuch said one of two men arrested over the multiple homicide in México state had a “commercial relationship” with victim Jonathan Meléndez and had been demanding money from him before the killings. 🇲🇽🇺🇸 Defense minister addresses cartel drone reports: Responding to a Fox News report on U.S. operations against cartel drones at the border, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said the drones are mostly used by migrant smugglers to scout routes free of authorities. He didn’t confirm or deny Mexican military involvement in the U.S. takedown operations.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Guadalupe, a municipality that is part of the metropolitan area of Zacatecas city.

She was accompanied by Zacatecas Governor David Monreal and various members of her cabinet, including Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch.

Among Mexico’s 32 federal entities, Zacatecas has recorded one of the largest reductions in homicides this year.

At today’s mañanera, officials presented the latest security data for the state — statistics that allowed them to portray Zacatecas as an example of the success of the federal government’s national security strategy.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was García Harfuch’s remarks about the motive for a multiple homicide in México state.

Government reports 85% decline in homicides in Zacatecas

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa reported that there was an average of 0.17 homicides per day in Zacatecas in August, a reduction of 85% compared to September 2024, the final month of Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s presidency.

She said that the daily homicide rate so far this year is 0.2, a reduction of 50% compared to 2025.

Figueroa highlighted that the daily homicide rate in 2026 is down 96% compared to 2021, when an average of 4.5 murders per day were committed in Zacatecas.

In the first seven months of 2026, there were 51 homicides in Zacatecas, the eighth lowest total among Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

More than 3,800 arrests in Zacatecas since October 2024

According to data presented by García Harfuch, 3,824 people were arrested in Zacatecas between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum was sworn in as president — and Aug. 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes such as homicide, kidnapping, extortion and violent robbery.

He also reported that 1,240 firearms and 7.3 tonnes of drugs were seized in the state in the same period. In addition, authorities dismantled six clandestine methamphetamine labs in Zacatecas, García Harfuch said.

photo-harfuch

He acknowledged that “there is still a lot to be done” to improve security in Zacatecas, noting that rival criminal groups continue to fight turf wars in the state. García Harfuch said that federal authorities are “maintaining and strengthening” intelligence and investigation “actions” in the state as well as “territorial presence” and “coordination” with state and municipal authorities. The aim, he said, is to detain “generators of violence” in Zacatecas.

García Harfuch subsequently noted that three people were arrested in connection with a car bomb explosion outside a municipal police station in Ojocaliente, Zacatecas, last Sunday night.

García Harfuch: Multiple homicide in México state related to a demand for money

García Harfuch said that one of two men arrested in connection with a multiple homicide in México state this week had a “commercial relationship” with one of the victims, namely Jonathan Meléndez, keyboard player with the well-known band Camilo Séptimo. The security minister was referring to Diego Sebastián Rosen Ferlini, an Argentine national who was detained in connection with the murders of Mélendez, his pregnant wife, their three-year-old daughter and a domestic worker. The victims were found dead in an apartment in the municipality of Atizapán de Zaragoza late Tuesday.

Asked how much money the alleged murderer was demanding from Mélendez, García Harfuch responded:

“I don’t know but I’ll ask the [México state] Attorney General’s Office. What is a fact is that he was demanding money. There was a demand, there were certain threats and this terrible multiple homicide was committed.”

Defense minister: People smugglers use drones to locate routes that are ‘free’ of US authorities

A reporter asked the president whether she could confirm the “participation” of Mexican authorities in U.S. operations to take down suspected cartel drones at the Mexico-U.S. border.

His question was related to a Fox News report that was published on Thursday.

Citing a senior U.S. War Department official, Fox reported that the U.S. military “took down ‘approximately 100′ suspected cartel drones in August alone” at the United States’ southern border.

Citing the same official, Fox wrote that “each operation was planned and closely coordinated with the Mexican military and border authorities to prevent interference or unintended conflicts between forces operating on either side of the border.”

Operation Ardent Vanguard Update 11 cartel drones defeated by the Army’s Multipurpose High Energy Laser as of Sep. 4. More than 300 defeats using kinetic and non-kinetic systems this year, with more than 100 occurring in August. “JTF Southern Border’s combined arms approach… pic.twitter.com/KexEOvgM9D — U.S. Northern Command (@USNorthernCmd) September 4, 2026

Sheinbaum referred the reporter’s question to her defense minister.

“Firstly I want to highlight that the relationship with the armed forces of the United States has been very good, very positive,” Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said.

He said that U.S. authorities have informed the Mexican government that drones are mainly used in the border region by people who smuggle migrants into the United States.

“They are commercial drones. They only capture images … and what they’re seeking to find are routes that are free, where there is no presence of [U.S.] authorities,” Trevilla said.

The defense minister didn’t confirm or deny Fox’s reporting that the Mexican military was involved in the planning of U.S. operations to take down drones.

World.title: ‘Sexy and hot, like Mexico’: How Mexican beauty brand AORA is taking on the global market
World.content:
Pyramid-inspired palettes, bilingual packaging and vivid shades drawn from Mexico’s streets are just some of the hallmarks of AORA, a Mexican beauty brand that’s challenging the beauty industry with its plastic-free packaging and strong Mexican identity.

“We wanted to bottle the feeling of Mexico,” co-founder Rodrigo Peñafiel told Mexico News Daily. “We wanted to bottle that feeling you get when you visit a beach in Oaxaca; that feeling you experience when you visit Mexico City for the first time.”

Since the opening of its flagship store in Mexico City in 2022, the brand has expanded into major retail chains, landed collaborations with international celebrities including Sofía Vergara, and most recently, served as one of the makeup brands used during Bad Bunny’s 2026 Super Bowl halftime show.

International expansion, however, didn’t come as a surprise. For Peñafiel and his co-founder Nour Tayara, going global was always part of the plan.

“Why would we build a small local brand when we have the opportunity to bring something big into the world?” Peñafiel said.

Combining Tayara’s experience in marketing and innovation roles within L’Oréal with Peñafiel’s background in public relations, the pair set out to create a brand that offered more than just clean, high-quality products. They wanted to create a luxury product with a strong focus on identity.

“We do luxury makeup by working with the best factories in the world. Because if we want to compete, let’s compete with spectacular quality. But what we’re bringing — we’re bringing culture,” Tayara said.

The brand’s DNA: Mexico

Rather than downplaying AORA’s Mexican identity to appeal to international consumers, the founders have made it central to the brand, drawing inspiration from the country’s creativity, colors, architecture and connection to nature.

From the brand’s signature Mírame Eyeshadow Palette to their lipsticks, pencils and accessories, AORA’s products evoke Mexico’s cultural icons, historic landmarks and scenes from everyday life.

“In our palette, you can see a hint of Frida Kahlo, of Matías Goeritz, of Chichén Itzá,” Peñafiel said. “The shades inside our palette could evoke any street in Mexico with a yellow house and a green Volkswagen parked outside,” he added with a chuckle.

Launching the brand from Mexico also meant producing its marketing campaigns in the country. From their photoshoots to their male and female models, everything is done in Mexico with Mexican talent.

“Every detail about the brand reflects Mexico. We could not have created this brand if we hadn’t launched it here,” Tayara remarked.

A retail presence at Sephora

AORA’s authentic vision has propelled the company into a new growth stage after entering Sephora in the United States, making history as the first 100% plastic-free beauty brand sold at the retailer, and the first brand to use both Spanish and English on its packaging.

“Sephora is betting on a brand that’s very colorful from Mexico and is betting on its first plastic-free brand in its portfolio,” Tayara pointed out.

In a competitive market dominated by European and U.S. brands, AORA is disrupting the beauty industry and aims to demonstrate that luxury also stems from cultural heritage.

“We started something that didn’t exist before, which is creating luxury beauty in Mexico,” Tayara said. “We come to challenge the industry in the language, in the visuals, in the products and in sustainability,” he said.

For the co-founders, AORA’s debut in Sephora goes beyond having its products on the shelves of one of the world’s leading beauty retailers. It also signals support for a Mexican brand and recognition for the Latino consumer market in the U.S.

“I think there’s a recognition of the amount of people in the U.S. that are of Latino descent and speak Spanish. It is an amazing message and signal Sephora is sending to the industry,” Tayara acknowledged.

A growing curiosity in Mexican identity and design

AORA isn’t the first brand to place Mexican identity as the center of its appeal. In recent years, global brands have increasingly sought partnerships that draw on Mexico’s visual identity, cultural heritage and creative talent.

In 2025, cosmetic brand Rare Beauty, founded by U.S. actress and singer of Mexican descent Selena Gomez, launched an exclusive, limited-edition makeup kit in collaboration with the Mexican seasoning Tajín.

Back then, Gomez described the collaboration as a “celebration of what makes us unique — our culture, our energy and the moments that bring us together.”

Last year also saw H&M launch a collection in collaboration with fashion designer Lorena Saravia, marking the first time the Swedish brand collaborated with a Mexican designer.

Joining the trend is Mestiz, a design studio founded by Daniel Valero in San Miguel de Allende, which recently collaborated with French design house Hermès to design their shop windows in Mexico.

Mexico’s appeal to consumers

“Mexico is trendy,” Peñafiel said with a smile. “I think there’s a celebration of Mexican culture that hasn’t been seen before. The challenge was to pass the front page of the news that we see every day about the dangers of Mexico, because the reality is that when people come here, they are amazed and fall in love with the food, with the culture, with the colors, the beaches, the brands,” he said.

As AORA seeks to reshape perceptions of Mexican luxury abroad and share a positive image of the country, its founders say the brand’s ultimate purpose is more personal — to make consumers feel attractive.

“We buy beauty because we want to feel good about ourselves. Because we want to feel sexy,” Tayara said.

“Yes, we want our clients to feel sexy and hot, like Mexico,” Peñafiel said.

Gabriela Solis is a Mexican lawyer turned full-time writer. She was born and raised in Guadalajara and covers business, culture, lifestyle and travel for Mexico News Daily. You can follow her lifestyle blog Dunas y Palmeras.

World.title: No, September is not earthquake month in Mexico City
World.content:
One of the most visceral and profound fears we Mexico City residents have is the seismic alert going off. And that’s no exaggeration.

Particularly for those of us who lived through the September earthquakes — which, in an almost absurd coincidence, all occurred on the 19th of different years — that sound is a near-physical reminder of the catastrophe.

Born and raised in Mexico City, I grew up listening to my parents’ stories about the terrible 1985 earthquake, when Mexicans united to help the military and first responders rescue people from the rubble.

“The response from their community was immediate,” Gaceta UNAM magazine noted at the time, “and extended to the most diverse tasks, such as the distribution of medicines, food, drinking water and clothing, as well as transportation to shelters.”

Therefore, it is no surprise that my generation grew up attending drills at school. We learned about the seismic nature of Mexico City, largely due to the confluence of tectonic plates in our country and the presence of two magnificent volcanoes.

It wasn’t until September 2017, in my first year of university, that I truly understood what it was all for. The tedium of the drills turned into outright terror when the seismic alert sounded.

And yes, September is back. As it happens year after year, there’s this morbid expectation that another seismic catastrophe will shake the nation’s capital. And why not? On Sept. 19, it has become all but customary.

To avoid this irrational fear, MND put together this explainer about why it’s practically impossible to predict earthquakes (yes, even in turbulent Mexico City), and why it’s an infinitesimal coincidence that they’ve occurred on the same day in different years.

No, there is no way to predict an earthquake — but we can prepare for them

Ranging from 7.1 to 8.1 on the Richter scale, 1985, 2017 and 2019 are the years that have marked the strongest earthquakes in Mexico City’s recent history, as documented by the National Seismological Service (SSN). Leaving hundreds of thousands of people homeless and an uncertain death toll of hundreds on each occasion, it is understandable why these natural disasters instilled panic among the residents of the capital.

And, understandably, there’s a superstition that September is the month of earthquakes. Although fitting, it’s nothing more than a popular belief that science has taken pains to disprove.

In fact, SSN records show that there have historically been more earthquakes in December than in any other month. But what does this mean?

In Mexico, more than 15,000 earthquakes have been recorded so far in 2026, according to SSN monitoring. The number changes daily because the country has consistently high seismic activity.

Furthermore, this does not mean that all of the underground movement has been harmful to the population. Sometimes, it’s barely perceptible on the surface.

Although the records are accurate, they can only be taken after the telluric event. In other words, the technology we currently have is not predictive, but only serves to maintain a record of the country’s seismic activity.

This is because, according to the SSN, “not even the most advanced research has been able to develop a predictive technique for earthquakes, […] in the face of any seismic event, the only thing that can help us is prevention.”

This does not refer to the prevention of earthquakes per se, which are inevitable natural events, but to measures to mitigate the impact of these phenomena on the population. The drills we hated so much in elementary school are the best way to prepare for an event like this.

Tepeyóllotl, have mercy on us!

Through the National Center for Disaster Prevention, the Mexican government acknowledges that it is an extremely rare coincidence that the three strongest earthquakes in the country’s recent history occurred on the same day.

Almost ludicrous, and certainly grim, for those of us who live in the capital.

It’s almost as if the fearsome Tepeyóllotl, the great lord of seismic movements in the Mexica pantheon, were laughing at us and saying, “Let’s give the capital’s residents a little scare.”

So no, it’s not possible to predict earthquakes. We know why they happen, and that the movement of tectonic plates is inevitable. At best, it has given us our majestic Sierra Madre mountain ranges and the pair of magnificent volcanoes that crown the center of the country. At worst, it has left terrible death tolls across the territory, as part of the cost of living in a seismic country.

Let us entrust ourselves, then, to the lord of the mountains. Perhaps only he, with his guttural roar in the bowels of the earth, can calm the subterranean movements that plague the ever-unstable Mexico City.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: ‘A pact with organized crime’: Opposition’s response to Sheinbaum’s second year report
World.content:
Listen to this article

In a 67-minute speech at the National Palace on Tuesday, President Claudia Sheinbaum delivered her second annual government report. A month shy of completing her second year in office, she touted achievements across a wide range of areas and declared that her administration is “transforming public life in this country.”

Later on Tuesday, prominent opposition politicians presented a fundamentally different view of the state of the nation, asserting that Mexico, as a country, has not in fact improved under the leadership of Sheinbaum and her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador (2018-24).

While opinion poll results show that Sheinbaum is a highly popular president, millions of Mexicans oppose her government.

In speeches in a general session of Congress on Tuesday, two of Mexico’s best-known opposition politicians, Sen. Ricardo Anaya of the National Action Party and Sen. Alejandro Moreno of the Institutional Revolutionary Party, outlined some of the main grievances that they — and many other Mexicans — have with the federal government and the broader Morena party-backed “fourth transformation” political movement that was founded by López Obrador and is now led by Sheinbaum.

They included grievances about insecurity, even though the president on Tuesday touted a 51% reduction in homicides (in July compared to the final month of López Obrador’s term).

They included claims that the government is shielding a ruling Morena party governor accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel, even though Sheinbaum has said on repeated occasions that her administration won’t protect anyone who has committed a crime.

And they included accusations that the government is attempting to silence or censor government critics, even though the president says her administration will always respect freedom of speech.

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, national leader of the Citizens Movement party, also offered an appraisal of Mexico almost eight years after Morena first came to power. His remarks, and those of Anaya and Moreno, are covered below.

Ricardo Anaya, National Action Party (PAN) senator and former presidential candidate:

“It was said that Mexico is at peace, that homicides had already gone down. I wish that were true; it isn’t.”

In the Legislative Palace of San Lázaro on Tuesday afternoon, Sen. Ricardo Anaya told his colleagues that he was at the rostrum to “seriously respond” to Sheinbaum’s second government report, which he asserted was “unfortunately riddled with lies.”

In his speech, Anaya sought to demonstrate that the Morena party government is failing to uphold its own ethos: “Don’t lie, don’t steal and don’t betray the people.”

“First they promised not to lie. This morning it was said that Mexico is at peace, that homicides had already gone down. I wish that were true; it isn’t,” the senator said.

“And I don’t say it with my numbers, I say it with yours, with those of the Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System [SESNSP],” he said.

Mi respuesta al informe de Claudia Sheinbaum:

Maquillan las cifras, esconden el robo y protegen a los narcopolíticos. Prometieron no mentir, no robar y no traicionar al pueblo. Fallaron en las tres. pic.twitter.com/mNr6cx12NQ — RicardoAnayaC (@RicardoAnayaC) September 2, 2026

Anaya, who contested the 2018 presidential election as the candidate for the PAN, said that the average daily homicide rate before Morena took office in late 2018 was 70.

“In this six-year term of government, according to you, it’s 63. Seven fewer [homicides per day] is the apparent miracle,” he said.

“But this document — yours, not mine — has another column,” Anaya said as he held up a crime statistics report.

“It’s called ‘other crimes that threaten life and physical integrity.’ There are deaths listed there as well, but those — in a devious and deceitful manner — weren’t counted in this morning’s report. Those deaths, with you [in office], went from 15 to 40 per day,” he said.

Anaya also said that the number of daily reports of disappearances has increased from 16 to 31 under Morena’s rule.

“Disappearances doubled,” he said.

“So, do the math with me because it’s a primary school calculation. Homicides went down by seven per day in one column [but] went up by 40 in the other two,” Anaya said.

“Even though they fudge the numbers, in Mexico no one was brought back to life,” he said.

Anaya apportioned blame for the allegedly fudged numbers to authorities in Mexico’s 32 federal entities, the majority of which are governed by Morena. His claim that homicide statistics are being manipulated has also been expressed by security analysts and others.

Anaya proposed a “public and technical review of the methodology” used by the SESNSP — which compiles crime data it receives from state Attorney General’s Offices — “so that no dead person can change columns.”

“Counting correctly is not a technicality; it’s the first requirement for governing truthfully,” Anaya said.

The PAN senator also accused the government of seeking to silence critical voices with its General Guidelines for the Protection of the Rights of Audiences.

“Huachicol fiscal is the largest robbery in the history of our country.”

Anaya asserted that the government has also broken its “do not steal” maxim.

“Huachicol fiscal is the largest robbery in the history of our country,” he said, referring to a fuel smuggling/tax evasion offense in which high-ranking members of the Mexican Navy and customs officials were allegedly involved.

“And it’s not [just] the opposition saying it. The federal tax prosecutor said it in this chamber: 600 billion pesos (US $35.45 billion),” Anaya said.

“… Six-hundred billion pesos is the hospital that wasn’t built, it’s the medicine that wasn’t supplied,” he said.

“It’s a second promise broken,” Anaya said before proposing the creation of a “special commission to investigate huachicol fiscal,” a crime that Sheinbaum says her government has “practically” eliminated.

The commission, he said, should be “plural,” but chaired by “the opposition.”

Anaya said that the commission could begin by looking into allegations that a company called Portacelis is involved in huachicol fiscal.

“The company is called Portacelis and the name that appears again is that of the friend of Andy, Amilcár Olán,” he said, referring in the first instance to Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, a son of ex-president Andrés Manuel López Obrador and Morena’s former secretary of organization.

“The problem isn’t that Andrés Manuel López Obrador has been stripped of his [U.S.] visa. The problem is that you don’t want to ask a single question. … That is the country you’ve built — one in which your surname determines whether you’re investigated or exonerated,” Anaya said.

“Sovereignty isn’t impunity.”

Finally, Anaya asserted that the government hasn’t fulfilled its pledge to “not betray the people.”

“In a country ravaged by homicides, oppressed by extortion, the worst possible betrayal has a verb, the verb pactar,” he said, alleging that the federal government has a pact with organized crime.

To support his claim, Anaya referred to U.S. prosecutors’ drug trafficking accusations against Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya, a Morena politician who is currently on leave.

“A grand jury decided to bring criminal charges against Rubén Rocha Moya for drug trafficking. A federal judge issued an arrest warrant. The State Department formally requested his provisional detention for the purpose of extradition. Today marks 126 days, and they keep telling us there is no evidence,” he said.

Anaya asserted that there is indeed evidence linking Rocha to drug trafficking, citing an allegation that he met with Sinaloa Cartel kingpin Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada, among other supposed examples of proof.

“Proof is not lacking here. What we have in abundance is protection,” he said.

“… Sovereignty is not impunity,” Anaya said, referring to Sheinbaum’s assertion that Mexican authorities can’t detain and extradite Rocha unless they are satisfied that the United States allegations are supported by sufficient proof.

“… The same apparatus that protects Rocha Moya, imprisons Ernesto Ruffo,” he said, referring in the second instance to a former PAN governor of Baja California who faces organized crime, fuel theft and tax evasion charges.

Alejandro Moreno, national leader of the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) and a federal senator:

“Eight years after the Morena governments began, the outcome is a country that is divided, fractured, indebted, bogged down and engulfed in violence.”

Speaking before Congress on Tuesday, Senator Alejandro Moreno was also highly critical of the current federal government and its predecessor — i.e. the administration led by former President López Obrador.

“Eight years after the Morena governments began, the outcome is a country that is divided, fractured, indebted, bogged down and engulfed in violence,” he said.

Moreno, a former governor of Campeche, asserted that the Sheinbaum administration doesn’t have a “national project” or “answers” to the problems Mexico faces.

Although Sheinbaum has an approval rating of 68% according to the most recent El Financiero poll, the senator claimed that her government is rejected by Mexicans.

Claro, en MORENA sí “Juntos han hecho historia”, pero por haber hecho un pacto inconfesable entre el gobierno y la delincuencia organizada. Un pacto que se ha convertido en un régimen criminal transnacional y que hemos denunciado ante todos los organismos internacionales por… pic.twitter.com/oOeS2Qd8M1 — Alejandro Moreno (@alitomorenoc) September 2, 2026

He asserted that the government is seeking to “put an end to free media outlets” and “destroy the voices of the opposition, canceling the most fundamental freedoms in our country.”

Moreno went on to say that “the Morena government is impunity disguised as false defense of national sovereignty.”

He accused the Sheinbaum administration of protecting Morena governors and other officials wanted by “foreign governments and mainly the government of the United States.”

Moreno also accused the government of making a “shameful pact” with organized crime, a claim that the Trump administration has also made.

He said that if the government had a “modicum of decency,” it would “break its pact with the organized crime cartels and take away the protection of” López Obrador, Andy López Beltrán, Senator Enrique Inzunza, Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar Ávila and Tamaulipas Governor Américo Villarreal.

“They’ve ruined peace; they’ve destroyed Mexicans’ quality of life.”

Moreno also claimed that the current government “has ruined peace” and “destroyed Mexicans’ quality of life.”

“They systematically eliminated everything that had a stamp of autonomy,” he said, referring to the government’s abolition of various watchdog agencies, including the now-defunct National Transparency Institute.

Moreno asserted that at elections in 2027, “with a large party and citizens coalition,” the opposition will win a congressional majority.

“And have no doubt, in 2030, with the people of Mexico behind us, we’re going to win the presidency of the republic,” he said.

Jorge Álvarez Máynez, national leader of Citizens’ Movement and a former presidential candidate:

“Hospitals and healthcare centers still don’t have medicine.”

In a video posted to social media, Jorge Álvarez Máynez, MC’s candidate at the 2024 presidential election, said that eight years after Morena took power, “Mexico is not making progress.”

Ya son 8 años de Morena en el poder. Y aún con todo el poder, México no está avanzando. El gobierno prometió mucho y ha cumplido poco. Pero México es más que su gobierno. México tiene alternativa. pic.twitter.com/ywiO7JYpsx — Jorge Álvarez Máynez (@AlvarezMaynez) September 2, 2026

“Insecurity continues affecting the lives of millions of families,” he said.

“Hospitals and healthcare centers still don’t have medicine,” Álvarez Máynez asserted.

“And people continue battling to reach the end of the month,” he said, referring to the challenge of making ends meet.

Álvarez Máynez also said that after eight years of Morena governments, “corruption and abuse of power have not gone away.”

“… They promised to be different from the PRI but they failed to deliver on that too,” he said.

“We have a government that promised a lot but which has achieved very little,” Álvarez Máynez said.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How Taiwanese imports are fueling Mexico’s record tech exports
World.content:
Data came out last week showing that Mexico’s exports were worth a record high US $81.4 billion in July, an increase of almost 44% compared to the same month of 2025.

In the first seven months of 2026, Mexico’s export revenue totaled $471.4 billion, a year-over-year gain of 27.7%, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

In July, almost three-quarters of Mexico’s export income came from the shipment abroad of non-automotive manufactured goods. Within that category, revenue from the export of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances soared 134% annually. Among those products are inputs for AI servers and other computer equipment. Mexico is currently shipping large quantities of such goods to the United States.

On the surface, the AI-related export boom appears to be great news for Mexico, but the reality is more nuanced.

As Pedro Casas, CEO of the American Chamber of Commerce of Mexico, wrote in an article that MND published this week, “a significant share of the inputs” in the AI-related products Mexico is exporting is not Mexican, or even North American, but rather Taiwanese. That means that a significant share of the revenue Mexico receives from the export of such products has already been spent on imported inputs.

In a recent LinkedIn post, economist Gilberto García-Vaquez wrote that “a single trailer of servers” entering the U.S. from Mexico “can be worth as much as a thousand cars.”

“But most of that value entered Mexico as imports before the servers ever left,” he added.

In his article, Casas wrote that Mexico, “in many instances,” is “assembling and integrating components that arrive from Asia, then shipping the finished product north.”

“That’s not nothing — assembly creates jobs and keeps supply chains on this side of the Pacific,” he wrote. “But it’s not the same as manufacturing a vertical regional integrated supply chain.”

In that context, this “Mexico in Numbers” article looks at some of the key numbers related to Mexico’s exportation of AI servers and other electronic products — and the Mexican content (or lack thereof) in those goods.

* The data in this article comes from various sources, each of which is mentioned below. In some cases, the numbers cited are estimates rather than proven figures.

More than 1/3 of US server imports come from Mexico

As we reported on Aug. 14, a report by the Economic Studies Department of Grupo Financiero Banamex found that Mexico’s share of U.S. server imports through the first half of 2026 was 34.5%, just behind Taiwan’s 36%. In the second quarter of 2026, Mexico’s share of the U.S. market for imported servers was nearly 40%.

During the first half of the year, Mexico exported more than US $60.4 billion worth of computer servers to artificial intelligence data centers in the United States, according to Banamex. In May, it surpassed Taiwan in sales.

Banamex said that “Mexico has established itself as an assembly platform close to the U.S. market, while design, technological integration and chain coordination activities (for artificial intelligence computing production) remain concentrated in Asia.”

Taiwan’s exports of artificial intelligence servers to the United States were worth $72.2 billion in the first half of 2026, according to Banamex.

As MND wrote last month, “Mexico and Taiwan have captured the U.S. market for artificial intelligence data center servers, which had previously been dominated by China.”

“In 2017, China accounted for 60.4% of U.S. purchases of computer equipment, while in the first half of 2026 its share fell to 2%.”

The vast majority of inputs in computing and other electronic products made in Mexico are foreign

According to a recent report by Swiss multinational investment bank UBS, more than 95% of inputs used in the manufacture or assembly in Mexico of computing and other electronic products are imported, primarily from Asian countries such as Taiwan. In other words, less than 5% of the content in such “Made in Mexico” products is actually Mexican.

“Mexico is capturing an important role in the North American AI supply chain, but much of the value of the products it exports is still generated abroad. Computers and electronics rely heavily on imported inputs, limiting their domestic value-added and employment multipliers,” UBS says in its report.

The bank also says that “a server assembled in Mexico can have a very high export value without generating a proportionally large amount of Mexican income, employment, or local demand.”

Similarly, the Financial Times (FT) reported in August that the “surge in high-value exports is yet to translate into proportional local benefits” in Mexico.

“Each dollar of investment in the highly automated [AI server] plants creates far fewer jobs than more manual sectors such as car parts,” FT wrote, also noting that “Mexico manufactures very few of the parts” used in the country’s AI server sector.

Fernando Alba, deputy economy minister in the state of Chihuahua, told FT that in current conditions Mexico could realistically aspire to reach 3-7% Mexican content in each server, compared to 39% for autos.

“It could do electronics, cooling and product design but making chips was very unlikely, he said, as the country lacks the engineering and design knowhow, as well as enough energy and water,” FT reported.

Alba also said: “A car is a value chain disseminated up and down the country. … It’s much harder to do that with AI servers. We are much less prepared.”

In its report, UBS says that “Mexico does not need to produce advanced chips to capture more value from the AI boom.”

“The more immediate opportunity is to build a broader ecosystem around the manufacturing capacity already being established. Potential areas include electronic components, cooling and power systems, testing and packaging, design, and other specialized industrial inputs,” the bank said.

Mexico’s imports from Taiwan have surged

FT reported in August that “Taiwanese manufacturers are rapidly expanding factories in Mexico to assemble servers, which are now the country’s top U.S. export, overtaking autos that dominated its trade for decades.”

As noted above, the vast majority of the inputs going into servers assembled in Mexico — whether by Taiwanese manufacturers, Mexican manufacturers or anyone else — comes from abroad. Taiwan is a top supplier of those inputs.

“Much of the increase in technology imports is coming from Taiwan,” UBS notes in its report.

Therefore, it is not surprising that official data shows that Mexico’s imports from the East Asian island have significantly increase.

According to Bank of Mexico data, Mexico’s imports from Taiwan totaled US $43.91 billion in the first six months of 2026, an increase of 200.5% compared to the same period of last year. In all of 2026, Mexico imports from Taiwan were worth $46.58 billion, less than $3 billion above the total in the first half of this year.

As Mexico News Daily reported in April, much of the recent significant rise in trade between Taiwan and Mexico is in the semiconductor industry. In other words, Taiwan is sending large quantities of chips and other electronic components and inputs to Mexico, where they are used in the assembly of AI servers and other computer hardware, much of which is sent across the border to data centers in the United States.

World.title: The Colombian Peso Is Having Its Best Year in About a Decade
World.content:
Markets · Colombia

Key Facts — The run The peso has gained about 19% against the dollar in 2026, ranking it among the world’s best-performing currencies.

— The drivers Oil and coal exports, record remittances, and a central bank rate held at 12.0% since July.

— The winners Importers, travellers and dollar earners gain; farm exporters and families living on remittances lose value at home.

— The catch An August earthquake pushed up inflation forecasts, and Colombia’s budget deficit is still 8.2% of GDP.

— The daily Our markets desk tracks the peso and the COLCAP stock index every trading day.

For years, the Colombian peso was the region’s worry, falling first whenever markets panicked. This year it is the exception, rising instead, up about 19% against the dollar so far.

Bogotá’s skyline — the capital of the region’s surprise currency story of the year

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Why the peso is strong

Three flows are lifting the peso this year. Oil and coal exports brought in more dollars.

Colombia’s fuel and mining exports rose 18.6% in the first half of 2026, to roughly US$11.3 billion.

Remittances from Colombians abroad topped US$6 billion in the same six months, a record pace. A third factor is the central bank, which has held its rate at 12.0% since July.

That rate is well above many neighbours’, which keeps foreign money parked in Colombian bonds.

Who wins, who pays

A strong peso cheapens imports — fuel, machinery, medicines — and helps keep inflation on a downward path most of this year. Colombian travellers and online shoppers feel the difference immediately.

Coffee, flower and other exporters earn less in pesos for every dollar they sell abroad. So do the families who depend on remittances, since each dollar sent home now buys fewer pesos than it did in January.

The fiscal shadow

Colombia’s government expects a budget deficit of 8.2% of GDP in 2026, its worst shortfall since the pandemic. Public debt is nearing 63% of GDP.

Markets have mostly looked past both figures so far, while export and remittance income keep flowing in.

That patience is not guaranteed. The peso’s history is full of calm stretches that ended abruptly once investors focused on the deficit instead of the export numbers.

What could break the run

Three risks top the list: a sharp drop in oil prices, unplanned government borrowing, or a shift in US rate expectations. Any of those could pull capital back home.

A newer, fourth risk has already arrived this year.

An earthquake near Armenia on 10 August damaged roads and buildings across Colombia’s coffee region. It pushed the private bank Banco de Bogotá to raise its year-end inflation forecast to 6.8%, up from 6.03% in July.

Colombia’s central bank can smooth swings but has said it will not defend a particular exchange rate. Cutting rates further to protect the peso would carry its own cost for economic growth.

How to follow it

For anyone with money at stake — expats, families receiving remittances, small importers — the standard advice is to convert in stages. Do not bet on hitting one exact exchange-rate level.

The peso’s strength is real and driven by trade flows, but it can reverse. Our markets desk publishes the daily rate; Bogotá’s next budget will publish the harder answer.

The remittance economy

Remittances have become one of Colombia’s largest sources of foreign currency, now outpacing combined coffee and coal export revenue. May 2026 alone brought in US$1.12 billion, the 24th straight month above the US$1 billion mark.

This flow says two things at once. Colombians working abroad are earning well, and many left because pay at home was not enough.

Scenarios into 2027

The base case among analysts is a gradual peso pullback as rate gaps with other countries narrow. A more optimistic case has credit-rating agencies rewarding a credible deficit-reduction plan from Bogotá.

The downside case is an oil-price slide combined with a fiscal shock, a combination that has ended peso rallies before. Timing that turn is guesswork; preparing for it is not.

What the central bank can and cannot do

Banco de la República, Colombia’s central bank, is independent and has held its benchmark rate at 12.0% since 1 July 2026. It can smooth swings with that rate and occasional intervention.

But it cannot hold the peso at a fixed level, and it says so openly.

That honesty is itself a form of credibility, and investors tend to reward central banks that admit their limits. Colombia’s bond auctions this year reflect some of that trust.

The playbook for expats and remitters

A strong peso means every dollar buys fewer pesos than it did last year. That affects expats living in Medellín and Bogotá, along with families receiving money from relatives abroad.

Splitting conversions into weekly amounts smooths out the swings. If you earn pesos and pay bills abroad, this stretch has worked in your favour.

Such periods for the peso have historically lasted months, not years.

The peso’s long memory

Colombians who lived through the peso’s 2022 crash tend to treat this year’s rise as temporary. History mostly backs that instinct.

Strong peso runs over the past 20 years have usually ended with a drop tied to oil prices or politics.

What is different this time is the mix behind the rally. Remittances and services income now make the flow base broader than a bet on commodities alone, though broader does not mean risk-free.

The practical layer: accounts, exchange, timing

Colombia’s peso trades in a single official, liquid market, without the parallel black-market premium seen in Argentina. Banks, exchange houses and fintech apps quote slightly different rates, and on large conversions that spread is worth comparing.

Foreigners opening bank accounts generally find the paperwork easier than the region’s reputation suggests. A cédula de extranjería, Colombia’s foreign-resident ID card, unlocks far more than a passport alone.

Oil-price headlines and scheduled central-bank meetings are the peso’s two most reliable movers. Anyone converting a meaningful sum can plan around those dates rather than guess day to day.

The COLCAP connection

The peso does not move alone. Bogotá’s stock benchmark, the COLCAP index, tends to rise and fall with the same capital flows.

On 4 September 2026, COLCAP closed up 1.81% at 2,534.46 points. The peso traded near 3,140 to the dollar that same day, according to our markets desk.

A fiscal scare tends to hit bond auctions first, then stocks, with the peso reflecting the damage within hours. There is no wall between Bogotá’s politics and its exchange rate.

For Colombian asset holders, watching the peso and COLCAP together, rather than separately, is the more useful habit. When they move in opposite directions — a strong peso alongside weak stocks — that usually signals something has changed.

World.title: Milei Made Inflation Boring; the Bill Is Still Coming
World.content:
Economy · Argentina

Key Facts — The achievement Monthly inflation, 25.5% in December 2023 when Milei took office, was 2.1% in July 2026, INDEC says.

— The bill More than nine in ten Argentine households carry some debt, a private survey found in August 2026.

— The Senate math La Libertad Avanza holds only 19 of 72 Senate seats and needs governors’ votes to pass Milei’s central-bank bill.

— The friction Courts ordered the government to fund universities in June 2026; a broad tax cut has been postponed to 2027.

— The next vote Argentina’s midterms already happened in October 2025. The next election, in 2027, will choose Milei’s successor too.

— The exchange rate The peso trades in a crawling band system; central bank reserves neared US$51 billion in August 2026.

Argentina did what no recent government managed: it made inflation boring. Making stability payable for the households living through it is proving much harder.

Milei Made Inflation Boring; the Bill Is Still Coming

How the inflation fight was won

Economy Minister Luis Caputo used deep spending cuts to force a budget surplus. There was no printing money to cover the gap.

Monthly inflation hit 25.5% in December 2023, the month Milei took office. That is according to INDEC, Argentina’s national statistics agency.

Much of that spike followed his own currency devaluation, days after his inauguration.

By July 2026, monthly inflation had fallen to 2.1%, with prices up 33.8% over the year, INDEC said. June 2026 was even lower, at 1.9%, the best reading in five years.

The debt behind the victory

More than 92% of Argentine households carry some form of debt. That is according to a report by the Institute of Social and Economic Statistics and Trends (IETSE), published August 24, 2026.

Of that debt, 62.5% of credit-card spending now goes toward food, not extras, IETSE found.

Roughly 44% of households now spend more than half their monthly income just paying down debt, IETSE found.

Bank-loan delinquency reached 12.8% in June 2026, up from 2.5% in October 2024. That is according to central-bank data analyzed by the Argentine Center for Political Economy, a research group known as CEPA.

Argentina’s delinquency rate is now the highest in Latin America, well above Brazil’s and Colombia’s, CEPA found.

The central-bank bill and the Senate math

Milei once promised to close Argentina’s central bank, the BCRA. Instead, the lower house passed a scaled-back version on August 26, 2026.

It would ban the bank from printing money to fund the government, Infobae reported.

La Libertad Avanza holds only 19 of the Senate’s 72 seats, even after gains in last year’s midterms. It needs governors’ votes to pass the bill, and they are expected to ask for transfers in return.

Courts, universities, and a tax reform on hold

Argentina’s Supreme Court ruled on June 25, 2026, that the government must fully apply a law funding public universities. The ruling shows that stabilizing the economy by decree has legal limits.

The government has also pushed a broader tax-cut package back to 2027, Argentine outlet Canal26 reported on August 28, 2026. Officials called it a matter of timing, not abandonment.

The exchange rate and reserves

The peso trades in a crawling band system, adjusted on January 2, 2026, that lets it move within pre-announced limits. The gap between the official rate and the informal “blue dollar” rate is the market’s daily verdict on the program.

Central bank reserves reached nearly US$51 billion by August 25, 2026, their highest level since 2019, Infobae reported. The bank’s benchmark interest rate stood at 29% that same month, according to Trading Economics.

The IMF, poverty, and activity

The International Monetary Fund, or IMF, lends struggling countries money in exchange for economic promises. Its US$20 billion program with Argentina requires ongoing budget surpluses and rebuilt reserves.

The IMF’s board completed a second review, plus a broader checkup, on May 21, 2026, releasing about US$1 billion more.

INDEC’s official poverty rate was 28.2% in the second half of 2025, covering 13.5 million people. A separate, private estimate from the Catholic University of Argentina put poverty near 31.7% in early 2026.

That figure is not an official INDEC number, only a university’s own survey.

Monthly economic activity rose 0.8% in June 2026 and 1.9% for the first half of the year, INDEC said. Private economists say it slipped again in July, an uneven pattern some call “saw-tooth.”

One bright spot is energy. A new pipeline is being built to carry crude from the Vaca Muerta shale fields to the Atlantic port of Bahía Blanca.

Exports through it are expected by late 2026, industry outlet ArgenPorts reported.

What already happened at the ballot box

Argentina’s midterm elections happened in October 2025, not this year or next. Milei’s La Libertad Avanza won about 41% of the national vote, well ahead of the main opposition, the Buenos Aires Herald reported.

The party also narrowly won Buenos Aires province, a traditional opposition stronghold, by under one percentage point. That came weeks after Milei’s original candidate there, José Luis Espert, quit the race.

Espert faced allegations of ties to a drug-trafficking case, Infobae reported in October 2025.

Córdoba province also favored Milei’s coalition. Its governor, Martín Llaryora, has since aligned more closely with the federal government on economic policy.

The next elections come in 2027, when Argentines choose a new Congress and decide whether Milei gets a second term.

What to watch

Three numbers matter most through 2027: monthly inflation’s floor, real wages, and the exchange-rate gap. A fourth is how much the Senate charges for its support on the central-bank bill.

None of this is a verdict on Milei’s economic program. It is simply what the debt, inflation, and activity data show so far, drawn from INDEC, the central bank, and independent researchers.

Argentina made inflation boring. Whether it can make the recovery feel real to the families still carrying that debt remains the open question through 2027.

World.title: Chile Supplies a Quarter of the World’s Copper. July Was a Bad Month.
World.content:
Markets · Chile

Key Facts — The position Chile mined 23% of the world’s copper in 2024, more than any other country, per the US Geological Survey.

— The warning Production fell 9.4% in July 2026 after deadly storms hit the northern mining belt.

— The context Copper hit a record US$6.83 a pound in August 2026; it traded near US$6.56 on 4 September.

— The catch July’s drop was weather, not a trend; storms interrupted mines, they did not destroy them.

— The neighbours Peru supplies another 11.3% of world copper; together the two countries produce more than a third.

The energy transition runs on a red metal, and almost a quarter of it comes from one long, dry country. Chile’s copper story used to be about how much it produces; now it is about how hard producing it has become.

Chile Supplies a Quarter of the World’s Copper. July Was a Bad Month.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

One storm season, global consequences

Chile’s national statistics institute, INE, reported July 2026 output of 403,424 tonnes, down 9.4% from 445,322 tonnes in July 2025. INE blamed severe weather in the north and routine maintenance at major mines.

At least 13 people died in the storms, and roads across northern Chile became impassable for days. With global inventories thin, a bad weather week in Chile now moves copper prices worldwide within hours.

The mine-by-mine damage

Codelco, the state mining giant, estimated losses near US$7.5 million a day at El Teniente during the worst of the stoppage. Antofagasta’s Los Pelambres mine halted mining and processing for several days.

Lundin Mining’s Caserones mine suspended operations after snow damaged power lines, with a full restart expected two to three weeks later. Teck’s Carmen de Andacollo plant shut on 17 July after access roads closed.

Escondida, the world’s biggest copper mine, was not reported among the storm-hit sites. BHP, its majority owner, instead blamed a separate 3% annual output drop on falling ore grades, the industry’s slower-moving problem.

The geology problem

Chile’s great mines are old, and average ore grades have fallen for two decades. That means moving more rock, and using more energy and water, for the same tonne of metal.

Codelco carries the heaviest burden: its main mines need multi-billion-dollar projects just to hold output steady. Chile’s treasury also draws directly on Codelco’s earnings to fund public spending.

The demand side of the mountain

Electrification is arithmetic: electric vehicles, power grids, data centres and renewable energy all use far more copper than what they replaced. China still buys the largest share of Chilean output, though the customer base is broadening.

Supply cannot respond quickly, because a new mine takes roughly a decade from discovery to first production. That gap is why many analysts expect copper prices to stay high for years.

Peru, the quiet challenger

Peru produced 11.3% of the world’s copper in 2024, second only to Chile, according to the US Geological Survey. Its output has grown as Chile’s has stalled, and its government elected in 2026 is openly mining-friendly.

Together, Chile and Peru supply more than a third of the copper mined on Earth. For buyers, that concentration in two Andean countries is itself the risk to manage.

What to watch

Three numbers matter most: monthly output after the storm catch-up, Codelco’s investment approvals, and Chinese import volumes. All three are published regularly and can move prices on the day they land.

Chile’s copper century is not ending. It is getting more expensive, and so far the world has kept paying.

Water, energy and the desert

The Atacama is the driest desert on Earth. Mining there increasingly depends on desalination plants and pipelines stretching over a hundred kilometres.

Water rights, more than mineral rights, are becoming the real limit on new mines.

Power is a brighter story. Solar capacity in northern Chile has grown quickly, and new mining projects can now run mostly on renewable electricity.

Buyers increasingly ask about the carbon footprint behind their copper.

The price outlook, without the hype

Copper traded near US$6.56 a pound on 4 September 2026, down slightly from its all-time high of US$6.83 in August. Analysts expect prices to stay high but volatile, moving with Chinese construction data and US interest-rate expectations.

For Chile’s budget, every sustained dollar added to the copper price is worth billions in extra revenue. How much of a rally the finance ministry spends, rather than saves, is a domestic choice no storm controls.

The smelter gap

Chile exports most of its copper as concentrate, sending it to smelters abroad, mostly in Asia. In Santiago, officials debate whether to build more local smelting capacity and capture more value per tonne.

The alternative is to accept the trade-off and keep selling concentrate.

That choice means billions of dollars in capital and decades before it pays off. It is a decision about the shape of Chile’s mining industry for the rest of this century.

What buyers should understand

For manufacturers and investors, the lesson is concentration risk. When a country supplying nearly a quarter of world output has a bad storm week, prices can move before markets even open.

Contracts, inventories and hedging plans should be built around that reality. Chile’s supply is not always as steady as it looks.

Chile’s mining framework, built mainly in the early 1980s, has stayed stable for more than four decades. Contract stability is part of what buyers pay for when they choose Chilean copper.

The glossary of the trade

Ore grade is the share of copper in mined rock; lower grades mean digging more rock for the same tonne of metal. Concentrate is the partly processed product Chile ships to smelters in Asia for final refining.

Codelco is Chile’s state-owned mining company, and the world’s single largest copper producer. CPER is a US-listed exchange-traded fund that tracks copper prices and moves with news from Chile.

The project pipeline

Chile’s answer to falling ore grades is construction, not new discoveries. A queue of expansion projects at the largest northern mines aims to hold national output steady over the coming decade.

Codelco’s own projects, including converting open pits into underground mines, cost billions of dollars and take close to ten years to complete. These projects mainly exist to extend the life of very old deposits.

Private mines run a parallel pipeline, and their expansions increasingly depend on desalination plants and renewable power contracts. Permitting speed is the one lever Chile’s government fully controls, and every administration promises to shorten it.

The storm season’s ledger

July’s storms did not destroy Chile’s mining capacity; they interrupted it, flooding pits and closing haul roads. The 9.4% drop measures days lost, not mines lost, and later figures will show how much output was made up.

What will not return is the world’s margin for error, because global copper inventories remain thin. Every interrupted week now tightens a physical market that prices near-record highs even before accounting for weather.

The industry’s ledger has two columns. On one side: prices near records, demand from electrification, and margins that keep Chilean producers profitable even with rising costs.

On the other: ore grades falling a little further each decade, and desalinated water and renewable power adding real expense. Chile’s finance ministry, meanwhile, competes with schools and pensions for every peso copper brings in.

This storm season did not break Chile’s mining industry. But world copper supply is now so concentrated that one bad month in the Atacama raises costs for buyers everywhere.

That concentration is both Chile’s advantage and its burden.

World.title: Keiko Fujimori’s First Five Weeks and Peru’s 21.6% Rally
World.content:
Economy · Peru

Key Facts — The president Keiko Fujimori won a narrow runoff on 7 June 2026 and was sworn in on 28 July, her fourth run for the job.

— The start Five weeks in, she has 60% approval in the first poll of her term and a market-friendly cabinet.

— The markets Lima’s BVL stock index is up about 21.6% this year to 3 September, among the world’s strongest.

— The signature project A US$20.6 billion plan for four new Lima metro lines is her biggest promise so far.

— The catch Early approval and a hot stock market are not proof of success — they are a test still running.

Peru has had seven presidents ousted by Congress in the past decade. Keiko Fujimori is only five weeks into her term, and markets have already reacted warmly.

Keiko Fujimori’s First Five Weeks and Peru’s 21.6% Rally

The mandate nobody predicted

Fujimori lost runoffs in 2011, 2016 and 2021, the last by fewer than 50,000 votes out of over 18 million cast. Her win on 7 June 2026 completed a comeback few expected.

She inherited a country worn out by improvisation. Between 2016 and her inauguration, Congress removed or forced out six presidents, most recently José Jerí in February 2026.

An interim president, José María Balcázar, held office until Fujimori’s swearing-in on 28 July. Peru’s economy kept growing through all of this turnover.

The market verdict

The S&P/BVL Peru General Index, Lima’s main stock gauge, rose about 21.6% in 2026 through 3 September. Analysts point to fiscal discipline, mining-friendly policy, and hope that the revolving door of presidents has stopped.

Her cabinet was announced on 27 and 28 July, led by Prime Minister Luis Galarreta and Economy Minister Elmer Cuba. Cuba is a former director of Peru’s central bank, part of the market-friendly circle that steadied the country’s finances through the chaos.

Concrete, then credentials

Peru’s state investment agency, ProInversión, put the cost of four new Lima metro lines at more than US$20.6 billion. The government unveiled the plan on 5 August, promising jobs and shorter commutes for a capital of more than ten million people.

It is also a test of whether the state can still build things. In mid-August, flooding overwhelmed drains in Villa El Salvador, a southern Lima district, and forced her hand.

Fujimori responded by ordering a restructuring of Sedapal, the state water utility.

This kind of unglamorous response will decide whether her approval survives its honeymoon.

The Milei axis

On her inauguration day, Fujimori met Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, and the two agreed to deepen cooperation on trade, security and technology. No formal treaty was signed.

For Peru, closer ties mean investment promotion and a friendly neighbour on regional mining questions. For Milei, a meeting with a fellow market-friendly leader is validation of his own approach.

The risks the rally ignores

Congress remains fragmented and transactional, and it has already ousted seven presidents in a decade. Fujimori’s party does not hold a majority, and her father’s record still divides opinion in parts of the country.

The bigger risk is that expectations are outrunning results. A 21.6% stock rally and 60% approval are not achievements — they are a head start that can still be lost.

What to watch

Peru’s 2027 budget, now moving through Congress, is the first real test of Fujimori‘s ability to manage lawmakers. Mining permits and any move on the central bank’s independence complete the list.

Congress has punished nearly every recent president. Her first five weeks suggest she has studied what went wrong for the rest.

The informal economy is her real opposition

Seven in ten Peruvian workers earn a living outside the formal economy, according to INEI, the national statistics institute. They do not track bond spreads; they track bus fares, market prices, and whether police protect their stalls or ignore them.

Fujimori’s 60% approval score lives mostly in this world, not on the stock exchange. Her early focus on water and transport is a sign her government knows where its support actually comes from.

Mining: the promise and the permit queue

Peru is the world’s second-largest copper producer, after Chile. Keeping that rank depends on unblocking stalled projects without reigniting the community conflicts that stopped them before.

Her first weeks brought supportive language from the Energy and Mines Ministry. Whether that becomes real permits, rather than talking points, is still unproven.

Congress: the permanent threat

Congress removed two presidents in the ten months before Fujimori took office — Boluarte in October 2025, then Jerí in February 2026. Her party lacks a majority, so her agenda depends on the same horse-trading that ended her predecessors.

Her one advantage is that lawmakers, too, have been damaged by the churn. For now, both sides need the other to look functional.

The regions versus Lima

The capital votes and invests; the south produces copper and carries the grievances. A CPI poll taken 25-28 August put her approval at just 31.3% in the south.

In the north it was 64.2%, and in Lima 59.4%.

The metro plan and the Sedapal intervention are Lima-focused projects. How the 2027 budget treats the regions will show whether her government sees that gap.

The name she governs under

Every Fujimori campaign carries her father’s record. Alberto Fujimori ruled Peru through the 1990s and defeated hyperinflation and the Shining Path insurgency.

He was later convicted of human-rights crimes. He died in September 2024.

Keiko has spent two decades arguing she is her own politician. Her early record — a technocratic cabinet, market-friendly rules — is a start on that case, not yet its proof.

The score so far

By Peru’s low bar — a government that survives and holds together — her start ranks among the best in a decade.

By the country’s harder problems — extortion, an overloaded judiciary, a mostly informal economy — very little has changed yet.

Markets have delivered their early verdict. The public’s verdict, and the real one, will take longer and will be decided outside Lima’s financial district.

Security in the extortion cities

Extortion, not ideology, is Lima’s most visible problem. Peru’s public prosecutor’s office logged more than 13,800 extortion complaints nationwide between January and July 2026.

Transport firms, market traders and small builders are hit hardest.

Her government’s response so far has been mostly administrative: reshuffled police commands and promises of more prosecutors. Whether complaints fall before the honeymoon ends is the real test.

The water and the floods

Flooding hit southern Lima in her first weeks, a crisis no campaign had planned for. Drains overflowed in Villa El Salvador, and images of the failure spread quickly online.

Her response — ordering Sedapal restructured — was unglamorous and fast. Water in Lima’s hillside neighbourhoods is where the state meets the informal city, and where real approval is quietly built or lost.

Peru’s mining industry, coastal farms and capital all draw on the same stressed river basins. No metro line fixes that problem on its own.

If her first five weeks held one rehearsal for the harder years ahead, this was it. It was a basic service that must simply work, in a country whose institutions have struggled to make that happen.

World.title: Venezuela Sells Its Oil to Washington and Has No Cash
World.content:
Economy · Venezuela

Key Facts — The paradox Venezuela’s oil increasingly flows to the United States, yet cash is scarce at home.

— The deal The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital took a 35% stake in NABEP, a new Venezuelan oil venture, the White House said on September 1, 2026.

— The government Acting President Delcy Rodríguez, not Nicolás Maduro, now runs Venezuela. The US captured Maduro in January 2026 and is trying him in New York.

— The street Venezuela has about 28 million people, per United Nations estimates, and physical banknotes have nearly vanished from daily life.

— The neighbours Brazil alone blocked Venezuela from BRICS membership in October 2024. Chevron and GeoPark are both expanding their Venezuelan operations.

To understand Venezuela in 2026, forget the old question of regime survival. Ask the stranger one that replaced it.

Venezuela Sells Its Oil to Washington and Has No Cash

How does a country send more oil to its former adversary, yet still run out of cash?

Who actually runs the country

US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro on January 3, 2026. They flew him to New York to face drug-trafficking charges, NBC News and NPR reported.

His vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as acting president two days later. The US State Department recognized her as Venezuela’s legitimate leader in March 2026, PolitiFact reported.

Maduro is now fighting his own case. On September 3, 2026, his lawyers asked a New York judge to dismiss it, claiming head-of-state immunity, Al Jazeera reported.

That immunity claim is personal, about his own criminal trial. It is separate from the oil deal described below.

The oil architecture

The centerpiece of the new relationship is NABEP, short for North American Blue Energy Partners. It is Venezuela’s second-largest oil operator, after Chevron, the White House said on September 1, 2026.

The Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital holds 35% of NABEP. The State Department can also buy a fifth of NABEP’s oil at cost, NPR reported.

Rodríguez’s government gave NABEP 100-year rights to 17 oil fields holding an estimated 65 billion barrels. NABEP’s founder, businessman Alejandro Betancourt, pledged US$100 billion (804.81 bolívares per dollar, Venezuela’s central bank, September 3, 2026) in new investment.

Venezuela itself still sits under broad US sanctions. Only specific licenses make deals like this legally possible.

So does the lifting of personal sanctions on Rodríguez, law firm Holland & Knight and CNBC reported.

Where the oil money actually goes

Since Maduro’s capture, every dollar the state oil company PDVSA earns abroad must go into an account the US Treasury controls. That includes royalty payments, Venezuelan outlet La Patilla reported on August 24, 2026.

PDVSA billed US$15.9 billion in the first seven months of 2026. Roughly 40% of that came from sales to the United States alone, La Patilla found.

That is the real answer to Venezuela‘s paradox. The oil money mostly never reaches Caracas to begin with.

Chevron and the wider oil race

Chevron, Venezuela’s largest operator, plans a US$7 billion (804.81 bolívares/dollar) investment to roughly double its output. It aims to go from about 280,000 barrels a day to 600,000, Chevron said on September 2, 2026, CNBC reported.

GeoPark, a smaller operator, wants to nearly triple its worldwide output by 2030. One part of that plan is a Venezuelan field, now producing about 11,000 barrels a day.

The other part is Argentina’s Vaca Muerta shale region, GeoPark said on September 2, 2026.

What Venezuela’s oil actually adds up to

Venezuela now pumps roughly 1.1 to 1.25 million barrels of oil a day, Al Jazeera reported on September 2, 2026. That is far below the 3 million barrels it pumped daily in the late 1990s.

More than 500,000 barrels a day, over 40% of the total, now moves to the United States. That share has grown sharply since Rodríguez took over, the same report found.

China still buys Venezuelan crude too. But the new US arrangement makes that harder, energy analysts at Asia Times wrote on September 2, 2026.

The country without banknotes

Venezuela’s entire money supply was worth 2.59 trillion bolívares, about US$3.3 billion (798.33 bolívares/dollar, September 1, 2026), in late August 2026. Only 2% to 3.5% of that exists as printed cash; the rest is digital.

The largest banknote in circulation is worth 500 bolívares, about US$0.63. An average Venezuelan holds roughly US$3 to US$5 in physical cash, against about US$300 in Brazil and US$1,500 in Mexico.

So people use phone transfers, cards, and worn US dollar bills instead. Roughly US$5 billion in physical dollars now functions as the country’s real everyday cash.

Prices, immunity, and what to watch

Venezuela’s annual inflation rate was 565% at the end of 2025. Economists at a Caracas forum in February 2026 forecast it would ease to about 174% for 2026.

That is still severe, just less so than before.

Separately, the Trump administration wants US courts to grant Rodríguez immunity too, PolitiFact reported. That is in an unrelated civil lawsuit over alleged torture under the Maduro government, a July 2026 Justice Department filing showed.

A hearing on that request is set for September 30, 2026.

Opposition leader María Corina Machado, who won the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize, has long argued that real change should include free elections. A deal with Maduro’s successors is not the same thing, she and her allies have said, NPR reported in January 2026.

Nearly 7.9 million Venezuelans have left the country since 2015, according to the UN-backed regional platform R4V. There is no clear sign yet of that reversing.

Three things will show whether the new arrangement works. Does NABEP’s ownership survive past November’s US midterm elections?

Do banknotes return, and do any migrants come home? For now, oil moves north, and cash stays scarce at home.

World.title: Guyana Opposition Leader Arrested Twice, Then Released
World.content:
