GUYANA · POLITICS

Key Facts —What happened: Guyana opposition leader Azruddin Mohamed was arrested twice on September 3, 2026. —How big it is: Police say a drone was found in his vehicle; a technician said it was his. —What it means: The arrest adds tension to an ongoing US extradition case against Mohamed. —The catch: Mohamed was released without charge, and a court refused a remand application the next day. —Who it hits: Mohamed, his WIN party, and Guyana’s international reputation for rule of law. —What comes next: Extradition hearings on the United States request were listed for September 3 to 10.

Guyana’s opposition leader was arrested twice on September 3, 2026, near the president’s home. Police say a drone was found in his vehicle. He was released without charge.

Who is Azruddin Mohamed?

Azruddin Mohamed is a Guyanese businessman and politician. He leads the We Invest in Nationhood (WIN) party, which he founded in May 2025.

In the September 2025 general election, WIN won 16 seats in Parliament, becoming the main opposition party. This broke a 70-year pattern of dominance by two traditional parties.

On January 26, 2026, Mohamed was formally declared Leader of the Opposition. Opposition MPs chose him unopposed.

His rise was swift and unexpected. He went from businessman to opposition leader in under a year.

The September 3 arrest near the president’s home

On September 3, 2026, police stopped a vehicle near President Irfaan Ali’s private residence at Leonora, West Coast Demerara. They acted after reports of drone activity in the area.

Those taken for questioning included Mohamed, 39, and his driver Eugene Thorne, 35.

Also detained were the technician Dwayne Ross, 25, and Mario Mohamed, 20.

Two WIN MPs, Dr Gordon Barker and Dr Andre Lewis, a regional councillor, a photographer and another driver were also held. They were later released without charge.

Police say they found a DJI drone in the vehicle’s boot, along with four cellphones. They also recovered a second drone at Ross’s home, according to the Guyana Chronicle.

Dwayne Ross told police the drone was his and that his operator’s licence had expired in 2023. Mohamed denies owning or operating it.

Mohamed was released on self-bail, meaning he signed his own undertaking to return. He was then arrested again late that night, after returning to the sea defence area with several people.

He was broadcasting on Facebook Live at the time; police told him to stop the broadcast. An officer, who was not named in reports, told him “it is alleged that you breached security protocol.

He was released without charge.

What his party says

WIN general secretary Odessa Primus said police kept Mohamed’s phone, laptop, and vehicle. She said he was released without charge.

Mohamed denied owning or operating the drone, according to the Guyana Chronicle. His party says the arrest was harassment.

The opposition AFC party publicly accused the state of intimidation after the river arrests. They say the government is targeting opposition figures.

In court on September 4 his lawyer, Siand Dhurjon, gave an account of why Mohamed was at Leonora.

Dhurjon said his client had gone to look into a claim about land next to the president’s home. That is the defence account, not a finding.

The court refuses to remand him

On September 4, special prosecutor Glenn Hanoman asked the court to revoke Mohamed’s extradition bail over the drone investigation. Chief Magistrate Judy Latchman refused, saying a court “cannot act on what is known but can only act on what is proven.”

He was released without charge, but police say the investigation continues. No charges have been filed as of this writing.

The court’s decision is a setback for prosecutors. It means Mohamed remains free while the probe continues.

It is the second time in weeks that Mohamed has been detained and released without charge. His party and the opposition AFC call the detentions harassment; the government says it is enforcing the law.

The August river incident and bail

On August 26, 2026, a Joint Services patrol stopped a boat on the Demerara River at Friendship, East Bank Demerara. Mohamed was on board.

Police say the boat entered at high speed and ignored sirens. They say a bag was thrown overboard during the chase.

Opposition MPs dispute that account. They say the boat was already docked when officers arrived.

Mohamed was released on GY$100,000 bail (about US$478). MP Natasha Singh-Lewis was released on GY$200,000 (about US$956).

The exchange rate is from open.er-api.com on September 4, 2026. No charge over the bag has been reported.

US sanctions and the indictment

In June 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned Mohamed, his father Nazar, and their company, Mohamed’s Enterprise. The Treasury unit that does this is called OFAC.

OFAC alleged the company under-declared gold exports between 2019 and 2023, avoiding over US$50 million in duties. These are US allegations, not proven in court.

On October 2, 2025, a US federal grand jury in Miami indicted Mohamed and his father. Azruddin Mohamed is charged with conspiracy to commit money laundering and wire fraud; his father faces those plus mail fraud.

Prosecutors allege a scheme to evade more than US$50 million in duties on gold exports. An indictment is an allegation, and both men deny wrongdoing.

The extradition case and the Caribbean Court of Justice

Guyana arrested Mohamed on October 31, 2025, in response to a US extradition request. He was released on bail and ordered to surrender his passport.

The extradition case has been moving through the courts. On July 29, 2026, the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) dismissed the Mohameds’ appeal, allowing extradition proceedings to continue.

The CCJ is the region’s highest court. It also turned down a further delay attempt on September 2, 2026.

On September 4 the chief magistrate also refused a defence request to pause the committal hearing.

A separate constitutional challenge sits before the Court of Appeal. It blocks any final extradition ruling for now.

A constitutional challenge to the Fugitive Offenders Act is still before Guyana’s Court of Appeal. Until it is decided, the chief magistrate cannot deliver a final ruling.

Government and police response

Attorney General Anil Nandlall has said the 2025 arrest was a legal obligation under the US extradition request. He frames it as cooperation on financial crime, not politics.

The police have not published a formal press release, but a police account has been given to local media. The Guyana Civil Aviation Authority issued a statement saying unauthorised drone operation is illegal and may constitute a criminal offence.

A special prosecutor asked the court to revoke his bail over the drone investigation. The court refused.

The government says it is meeting its obligations under the extradition treaty. The opposition says it is being harassed.

Why it matters for investors

Guyana is one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, thanks to offshore oil found by ExxonMobil and its partners. Investors watch how the government treats opposition leaders as a sign of rule of law.

The arrest of an opposition leader near the president’s home raises concerns about political stability. Oil investors watch how Guyana treats its opposition.

The extradition case is now the main test of due process. How it unfolds will signal the strength of Guyana’s legal institutions.

The government insists it follows the law. Investors will judge by actions, not words.

What is confirmed and what is not

Confirmed: Mohamed was arrested on September 3 and on August 26, and released both times. Confirmed: he faces US sanctions and an extradition case.

Not confirmed: what, if anything, he will be charged with in the drone probe. Not confirmed: who threw the bag overboard in the river incident.

Mohamed has not been convicted of any crime. He is charged in the United States but maintains his innocence.

The extradition case continues. Watch for new court rulings and any formal charges in the drone investigation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Was Azruddin Mohamed arrested again in September 2026? Yes. He was arrested twice on September 3 near the president’s home and released without charge. What are the US sanctions against Mohamed? In June 2024, OFAC sanctioned Mohamed and his father for alleged gold export tax evasion. The US says they avoided over US$50 million in duties. What is the extradition request about? The US seeks Mohamed’s extradition on charges of money laundering and wire fraud. He was arrested in October 2025 and released on bail. Who is Azruddin Mohamed? He is the leader of the WIN party and Guyana’s Leader of the Opposition. His party won 16 seats in the 2025 election. Why does this matter for investors? Guyana’s oil boom attracts foreign investment. How the government treats opposition leaders signals its commitment to rule of law.

World.title: Uruguay’s Interior Minister Says Death Threats Will Not Stop Him
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

URUGUAY · SECURITY

Key Facts —What happened: Interior Minister Negro received new death threats in early September 2026, also targeting the chief prosecutor. —How big it is: It is at least the third reported threat episode against Negro in 2026, after ones in July and August. —What it means: Organized crime is pushing back against the government’s security crackdown, including prison reforms. —The catch: Uruguay still has lower crime than most of Latin America, but homicides are at their highest since 2018. —Who it hits: Negro and chief prosecutor Mónica Ferrero are the two named targets of the threats. —What comes next: Investigations are ongoing, and Negro says he won’t change his approach despite the threats.

Uruguay’s top security official has received repeated death threats this year, but he says they won’t change how he does his job.

Who is Carlos Negro?

Carlos Negro is Uruguay’s minister of the Interior, the top official in charge of police and public security. He was appointed by President Yamandú Orsi, who took office in March 2025.

Negro has spent over 30 years in public service, mostly in security and justice roles. He is known for a tough stance on crime.

He has been the public face of the government’s response to a recent rise in violence.

The latest threat

On 3 September 2026 the chief prosecutor disclosed the threats to Parliament. Negro spoke publicly hours later.

Negro said the threats come from people linked to organized crime. The threats were made in calls to the 911 emergency line, the same channel used in the July case.

He called the threats an ugly thing to hear. He also said they were not the first in more than thirty years.

They would not change the course of his work, he said, nor that of his team.

What Negro said about the threats

Negro says the threats will not change his work. He told reporters it was not the first time in more than 30 years.

The threats, he said, do not change how he or his team run the ministry.

He said threats of this kind usually come from people linked to organized crime who have serious criminal records.

Previous threats in 2026

In July 2026, a man was detained for threatening Negro’s life during a call to the 911 emergency service. The man, 30, had no prior record and said he was under the influence of drugs.

In August prosecutors began investigating Erwin ‘Coco’ Parentini, a convicted prisoner, over a handwritten letter. Fiscal Graciela Perazza opened the investigation.

It threatened Negro and Ana Juanche, who heads Uruguay’s prison system. Parentini is in prison.

Why Negro is a target

Negro is leading the government’s fight against organized crime and prison gangs. He wants a national security plan that outlasts his term, targeting homicides and prison conditions.

Negro himself links the threats to organized crime, and says they come from people with serious criminal records. No suspects have been named in the September case.

Uruguay’s security picture

That is a 6.6% increase. The interior ministry calls it the highest first-half figure since 2018.

One outlet reported the comparison as reaching back to 2015 instead.

Three in four homicides were committed with firearms. The rise is driven by gang violence.

Negro has described a ‘chain of revenge’ between rival clans going back to 2023. In July 2026 there were ten homicides in a single week.

Regional context

Uruguay has long been considered one of the safest countries in Latin America, with lower homicide rates than many neighbours. But Negro himself has said the rate has jumped from about 5-6 per 100,000 people to around 11-12.

That is still below the rates reported by Brazil and Mexico. Uruguay remains one of the safer countries in the region.

Frente Amplio legislators said after the August threats that ‘democratic institutions will not yield to blackmail.’ Uruguay still has strong courts and low corruption by regional standards.

What happens next

Ferrero told Parliament the people behind the threats had been involved in aggravated murder cases. No names have been made public.

Negro says he will not be intimidated. He has the backing of President Orsi.

Orsi said Negro knows he is exposed but carries on. The open question is whether the government can turn the homicide trend around.

There is a reason threats against these two officials are taken seriously. In September 2025 Ferrero’s home was attacked with gunfire and explosives.

She told Parliament she came within 15 centimetres of death. Eleven people were implicated in that attack.

There is a reason threats against these two officials are taken seriously. In September 2025 Ferrero’s home was attacked with gunfire and explosives.

She told Parliament she came within 15 centimetres of death. Eleven people were implicated.

How a prosecutor became interior minister

Negro’s path to the Interior Ministry began in the justice system, not in politics. He spent decades as a prosecutor before taking the job.

President Orsi chose him in 2025 to lead the ministry. His job is to oversee the national police and set security policy for the whole country.

What the ministry has been doing on prisons and drug routes

Negro has made prison reform a priority, targeting criminal groups that operate from inside. The August threat from a jailed convict shows how much resistance that work faces.

He has also focused on drug trafficking routes, which fuel much of the gang violence. The ministry has increased police operations in areas where clans fight over territory.

How the investigation into the threats is going

Prosecutors are investigating the latest threats against Negro and Ferrero. Ferrero told Parliament the callers had earlier murder cases against them.

The July case led to one arrest, though the final outcome is not yet public. The August letter from Parentini is under separate investigation.

The INR said it would sanction Parentini. The criminal investigation has not reached a court decision.

What this does and does not tell a visitor or a resident

For visitors, the threats against a minister do not mean the streets are unsafe for you. Most violence is tied to criminal groups, not random attacks on foreigners.

For residents, the rising homicide numbers are a real concern, but Uruguay remains safer than many neighbours. The government’s response to these threats will show how seriously it takes the problem.

Uruguay’s prison system and who Ana Juanche is

Uruguay’s prison system is run by the National Institute of Rehabilitation, known as INR. Ana Juanche is its director, and she has been a target alongside Negro.

The INR manages prisons and tries to rehabilitate inmates. Criminal groups inside prisons still run operations, which is why reform is urgent.

The August threat came from a prisoner, showing the challenge. Juanche and Negro are working to break the power of these prison gangs.

What the ministry has changed on policing and drug routes

Negro’s ministry has increased police operations in areas where drug clans fight. This has led to more seizures and arrests, though exact numbers are not public.

He has also pushed for better intelligence sharing between police units. The goal is to disrupt drug routes before violence erupts.

These changes are part of his national security plan. The plan aims to reduce homicides and improve prison conditions over the long term.

How the threats are being investigated and what the prosecution service does

Uruguay’s prosecution service, the Fiscalía, handles criminal investigations. It is independent from the police and reports to the courts.

Prosecutors are now looking into the September threats against Negro and Ferrero. They have not yet named any suspects in that case.

In the July case, the suspect was arrested and handed to prosecutors. The final court decision is still pending.

The August letter from Parentini is also under investigation. Prison authorities plan to sanction him separately.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Negro? Negro is Uruguay’s minister of the Interior, responsible for police and public security. He was appointed by President Yamandú Orsi in 2025. What threats has he received? He has received death threats in July, August, and September 2026. The latest also targeted the chief prosecutor. Why is he a target? He is leading the government’s crackdown on organized crime and prison gangs. His hard-line stance has made him a target. How has he responded? He says the threats won’t change his work or his team’s approach. He has been in public service for over 30 years. What is Uruguay’s security situation? Homicides are at their highest since 2018, with 195 in the first half of 2026. But Uruguay still has lower crime than many regional neighbours.

World.title: Brazil Eases Fiscal Rules for Small Towns
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · FISCAL POLICY

Key Facts —What happened: Brazil’s Congress approved a bill easing the rule. —How big it is: The bill covers towns of up to 65,000 people, most of Brazil’s 5,570 municipalities. —What it means: Small towns with unpaid taxes or unverified accounts can now receive federal transfers and earmarks. —The catch: Congress passed the bill through both chambers in a single day, and the cost is unpublished. —Who it hits: Taxpayers may end up paying, if the change means more spending or less revenue. —What comes next: President Lula must sign the bill or veto parts of it.

Congress passed a bill on 3 September easing the rules on federal money for small towns. Towns with unpaid debts can now receive it.

What the bill does

Brazil’s Congress approved a bill on 3 September that eases the fiscal rules for small towns. The bill is PLP 74/2026, a supplementary bill that needs a higher majority than an ordinary law.

The Chamber of Deputies, Brazil’s lower house, passed it by 346 votes to 46, with three abstentions. The Senate approved it the same day by 66 votes to nil, without changes.

The bill changes the Fiscal Responsibility Law, known as LRF, which sets limits on government spending and borrowing. It also adds a new clause to the LRF.

That clause lets municipalities with up to 65,000 residents receive voluntary transfers from the federal government. These include parliamentary amendments, even if they have unpaid taxes or have not accounted for past funds.

Understanding Brazil’s fiscal rules

Brazil’s Fiscal Responsibility Law, or LRF, has anchored public accounts for 26 years. Economists treat it as a key test of fiscal discipline.

The law caps how much governments can spend on staff and how much they can borrow. It also requires towns to be up to date with their debts and accounts before they get certain federal money.

Voluntary transfers are not automatic payments like pension or health funds. They are one-off grants for local projects, usually negotiated with politicians.

Parliamentary amendments are a type of voluntary transfer that lawmakers can direct to their home towns. They are called emendas parlamentares in Portuguese.

The Fiscal Responsibility Law, or LRF, was created in 2000 to bring discipline to public accounts. It applies to the federal government, states, and municipalities.

The law caps how much governments can spend on staff and how much they can borrow. It also requires governments to publish regular reports on their finances.

Its goal is to prevent governments from spending more than they collect. That keeps public debt from growing too fast.

The LRF has anchored Brazil’s public accounts for 26 years. Economists treat it as a key test of fiscal discipline.

Why small towns get blocked

Under the LRF, a municipality that owes federal taxes is treated as being in default. The Portuguese term is ‘inadimplente’.

It also counts as in default if it fails to file proper accounts. Being in default blocks it from receiving voluntary transfers.

The rapporteur in the lower house was Deputy Isnaldo Bulhões. His report set out the case for the change.

He argued that small towns lose access to money over paperwork rather than over waste.

Small towns often miss deadlines or make errors in their accounts. That marks them as in default, even when the problems are simple paperwork.

What changes for small towns

The new clause covers municipalities with up to 65,000 inhabitants. Those towns can now receive voluntary transfers and parliamentary earmarks even with pending problems.

That includes unpaid taxes, loans and accountability filings. This means mayors of small towns could get federal money in an election year without clearing their debts first.

Congress overrode four of Lula’s vetoes to the 2026 budget guidelines law on 21 May.

That move freed roughly 3,000 municipalities to receive transfers again.

That earlier change also waived compliance requirements for towns up to 65,000 people. The new bill writes the waiver into the Fiscal Responsibility Law itself.

The Redata tax break

The bill does not create Redata, a special tax regime for data centers. That regime was set up by a provisional measure in September 2025 and re-enacted this year.

Data centers are large facilities that store computer servers. They are essential for cloud computing and internet services.

What the bill does is exempt Redata from the 2026 ceiling on new tax breaks. The benefits must still fit the year’s budget target.

The tax break aims to attract investment in digital infrastructure. But it also reduces federal revenue.

Who gains and who loses

The main winners are small municipalities that are in debt. They can now access federal funds for local projects, which may help mayors show progress before elections.

Taxpayers may end up paying, if the change means more spending or less revenue. No official estimate exists.

The main objection is fairness. Towns that paid their taxes on time gain nothing from the change.

Critics argue that loosening the rule is risky. It could encourage irresponsibility and lead to more debt.

What is not yet confirmed

The Senate approved the bill the same day, without changes. It now sits on President Lula’s desk.

Lula has 15 working days to sign or veto. He has not said what he will do.

The government’s budget office has not published a cost estimate for the measure. The full fiscal impact is unknown.

The bill is PLP 74/2026. Its progress can be tracked on the Senate website.

PLP 74/2026 is a package, not a single measure. It also covers the Manaus Free Trade Zone, paternity leave, the Pronon and Pronas health programmes and reinsurers.

That is why no single cost figure has been published. The pieces are costed separately, if at all.

PLP 74/2026 is a package, not a single measure. It also covers the Manaus Free Trade Zone, paternity leave, the Pronon and Pronas health programmes and reinsurers.

That is why no single cost figure has been published.

Why this matters for foreigners

For investors and expats, this shows how money flows to Brazil’s thousands of small towns. It also loosens fiscal discipline in an election year.

Rating agencies monitor Brazil’s fiscal framework. None has commented on this bill.

The move is part of a broader pattern in 2026 of Congress easing rules on transfers to municipalities. That raises concerns about the government’s ability to control spending.

Brazil holds general elections in October 2026. The timing of the bill adds to those concerns.

What a parliamentary earmark is in Brazil

A parliamentary earmark is a type of federal transfer that lawmakers can direct to their home towns. They are called emendas parlamentares in Portuguese.

These earmarks are often used for local projects like paving roads or building schools. They are a key way for politicians to bring resources to their constituents.

In recent years, these earmarks have grown in size and importance. They are now a major part of the federal budget.

The bill allows small towns to receive these earmarks even if they are in default. That makes it easier for lawmakers to send money to their bases.

What critics say about loosening the rule

Critics argue that loosening the rule is risky. It could encourage irresponsibility and lead to more debt.

They also worry about the timing. The bill comes in an election year, which could make it a tool for political gain.

Some say that letting towns with unpaid debts receive money is unfair. It rewards those that do not follow the rules.

Others point out that the fiscal cost is unknown. Without a clear estimate, it is hard to judge the impact on public finances.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Fiscal Responsibility Law? It is a Brazilian law that sets limits on government spending and borrowing. It also requires municipalities to be financially healthy to receive certain federal transfers. Who qualifies as a small municipality under the bill? The bill applies to municipalities with up to 65,000 residents. That covers the vast majority of Brazil’s towns. What are voluntary transfers and parliamentary amendments? Voluntary transfers are discretionary federal grants for local projects. Parliamentary amendments are a type of voluntary transfer that individual lawmakers can direct to specific municipalities. What is Redata? Redata is a special tax regime for data centers. The bill exempts it from the 2026 ceiling on new tax breaks, which could reduce federal revenue. What happens next? Both houses passed the bill on 3 September. Lula can now sign it or veto parts.

World.title: What a Costa Rican migratory alert actually does
World.content:
A judicial notice served on live television this week put an obscure piece of legal machinery in front of all of Costa Rica. Most of what was said about it afterward was wrong. Here is how it played out:

A judicial officer walked up to Pilar Cisneros Gallo outside Casa Presidencial on Thursday afternoon, handed her a document, and ended a two-day story about a measure almost nobody in Costa Rica had heard of a week ago. Earlier that day the Fiscalía General confirmed it had issued a migratory alert against Cisneros, a former legislator who now works without pay as a communications adviser to the Executive.

Prosecutors said they needed to summon her for a declaración indagatoria — the statement a person under investigation is entitled to give — in a case examining the alleged illegal receipt of private contributions during the 2022 presidential campaign. They said they had not been able to reach her. Within hours of the notice being served, the alert was cancelled. That sequence tells you most of what the document is for.

It is not an arrest warrant and it is not an exit ban

This is the part that got scrambled fastest. A migratory alert does not stop you leaving the country, and it does not authorise anyone to detain you. The Ministerio Público said plainly that the measure was neither an arrest order nor an exit impediment, and that it did not require the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería to report each of Cisneros’s border crossings back to prosecutors. The alert existed to help locate her for a summons, nothing more.

An exit ban is a different instrument with a different weight. Under the Ley General de Migración y Extranjería, an authority ordering an exit impediment has to supply the person’s name, nationality, identity document type and number, date of birth and the reason for the restriction. Migración cannot record the impediment if any of that is missing, and cannot lift it without a written order from the authority that imposed it.

None of that applies to an alert. An alert is a flag in a system. An exit ban is a wall.

What happens if you hit one at the counter

The Sala Constitucional examined how these alerts operate in a 2024 ruling, working from the procedure Migración described to the court. When someone carrying an alert is detected at a border post, officers can verify their identity, establish which authority issued the alert, and contact that authority for instructions.

That is the whole mechanism. What happens next depends entirely on what the issuing authority says, and in a case like this one the answer would be that the person needs to be handed a summons. You would notice it as a delay at the counter while an officer makes a call. You would not be handcuffed, and you would not be turned around.

Why this one drew a formal complaint

The Ministerio Público described the request as normal and proportionate, the kind of step taken when a person cannot be located or served. Prosecutors laid out what they said they had tried during August: two attempts at her home and five calls to numbers registered in her name. At one of the home visits, they said, they were told she no longer lived there. On one of the calls, a man who identified himself as her husband said she was out of the country and supplied a second number, and a person answering that number said she was not available.

Cisneros rejected the account. She said she had lived at the same address for 17 years, had kept the same phone number for 25, and worked at Casa Presidencial every day. She called the alert a political attack and a score-settling move by Attorney General Carlo Díaz, and challenged prosecutors to come and serve her, noting the distance between Casa Presidencial and the Fiscalía is about 2.3 kilometres (1.4 miles). Asked by reporters whether she had evidence connecting the measure to the coming selection of a new attorney general and Supreme Court president, she said she had none, but had no doubt either.

Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar then escalated it. In official document MJP-DM-822-2026, addressed to Supreme Court President Orlando Aguirre, he called the measure abusive and disproportionate and asked that the Judicial Inspection, the full Court and the anti-corruption prosecutor’s office examine the conduct of adjunct prosecutor Edith Morera and of the Attorney General in his supervisory capacity. Aguilar argued it was serious to reach for a migratory alert to accomplish something as routine as a notification.

Where it stands

Cisneros was served during a press conference on Thursday afternoon and summoned to appear at 8 a.m. Friday with defense counsel. The Fiscalía emailed Migración the same day to void the alert as she has not been charged. A declaración indagatoria is the stage at which the Código Procesal Penal requires that a person suspected of involvement in a crime be given the chance to speak, and it carries no obligation to answer questions or testify against oneself.

Cisneros lost parliamentary immunity when the 2022–2026 constitutional term ended, which is why the case is no longer handled under the special rules that apply to members of the supreme powers. The Fiscalía said the file is not directed by the Attorney General personally, precisely because nobody currently named in it holds immunity, and that the others under investigation had already given their statements.

The measure at the center of all this lasted less than a day and never restricted anyone’s movement. Whether reaching for it was proportionate is now a question for the Court, and the answer will matter well beyond this one file.

World.title: Watch Spider Monkeys Return to Costa Rica’s Nicoya Peninsula
World.content:
Costa Rica is famous for its biodiversity. There’s an incredible amount of life packed into this tiny country. However, this diversity of species isn’t uniformly present throughout the nation. Many factors, including habitat type and the impact of human beings, affect the presence of a certain species present in a given area.

I’ve spent the last 8 years or so using camera traps to sample the level of species diversity around the country, but I’ve mostly focused on a specific part of the country, Guanacaste. After many camera revisions from locations throughout Guanacaste, I’ve come up with an informal gradient of species diversity that’s based on the animals that my cameras are best at recording, mammals.

Areas with the very highest levels of species diversity are still home to Costa Rica’s largest mammals, the white-lipped peccary, the jaguar, and Baird’s tapir. As the level of species diversity begins to drop, the white-lipped peccaries are the first to disappear, followed by the jaguars and tapirs. In my experience, the first primate species to disappear when dropping down a level of diversity are Central American spider monkeys.

These levels of diversity are nothing official, just patterns I’ve noticed while carrying out camera trap projects throughout Guanacaste. At this point, when I begin a new project, I have a pretty solid idea of what species are going to be missing from the environment based on results from work I’ve done in that general area.

This year, when I had the opportunity to work with a coalition of organizations including the Fondo de Biodiversidad Sostenible and FONAFIFO on a wildlife monitoring project in the Nicoya Peninsula, I thought I knew what species were going to present on the properties. The project is still ongoing, but my assumptions were proven incorrect during the revision of the very first camera.

As I scrolled through species that I knew were going to be present, agoutis, ocelots, nine-banded armadillos, one video stopped me in tracks. It featured two Central American spider monkeys fleeing from the ground up into the trees, either frightened by the presence of my camera or something else nearby.

I was shocked. The nearest property where I had recorded or seen spider monkeys was in northern Guanacaste some 100 kilometers from the place I was sitting. On top of that, I had done some internet sleuthing in the past about locally extinct species on the peninsula and had read that spider monkeys were amongst the species, like jaguars and Baird’s tapirs, that had disappeared decades ago.

Obviously delighted to be wrong, I did some more research when I got home and found that Rescate Wildlife Rescue Center (formerly Zoo Ave) had a reintroduction program that had done some work in the Nicoya Peninsula and one of the species that they had focused on was spider monkeys. Excited about learning more, I reached out to Rescate Program Director Amy van Esch to tell her about my camera trap video and learn more about the program. Amy confirmed that they had been working on wildlife reintroductions for years and even offered to share some more information about their work. Here’s what she had to say –

“Rescate Wildlife has been working in the Nicoya region for over 35 years. Within the foundation we have a large protected area of over 800 hectares (about 2,000 acres) that we use as a release site for many different species.The spider monkey was completely extinct in this region at that time.

In the year 2000 we released a group of 44 spider monkeys, 31 former pets (who came to our rescue center through the pet trade), and 13 born onsite through our endangered species breeding program. Fast forward 26 years and we now have various wild troops with over 100 individuals! It’s pretty amazing to think, this population has all come out of animals that were formerly pets, now living wild, reproducing and dispersing into other areas.

This last year we also started something completely new: we built one of the world’s largest pre-release enclosures, over 4 hectares in size. We currently have a troop of 12 individuals preparing for release (all former pets, some even arriving dressed in baby clothes). This will be the first time we release new spider monkeys in over 15 years.

This enclosure is unique in its size, which is full of large growth trees, allowing them to learn “to fly” between trees and gain real agility before being released into the wild. It’s something we are really looking forward to in the coming year: finally seeing them fully wild!“

How cool is that? Check out the ten second video below that proves that all of their hard work has resulted in spider monkeys once again living wild on the Nicoya Peninsula.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica.

World.title: Why is Daniel Ortega Shutting Nicaragua’s Opposition Out of Elections?
World.content:
Nicaragua approved a constitutional reform that bars the opposition from participating in elections and extends Daniel Ortega’s term in office, a measure aimed at securing a presidential succession within the family of the octogenarian former guerrilla leader.

Ortega and his wife and co-president, Rosario Murillo, tightened their grip further by pushing through the amendment, which closes the door to a political transition after two decades of rule marked by the concentration of power and harsh repression.

What was approved?

The National Assembly, controlled by the Sandinista National Liberation Front (FSLN), voted Tuesday to prohibit “traitors to the homeland,” people linked to attempted coups, or those who call for “military intervention” or “economic blockades” from participating in elections. The couple routinely levels those accusations against all their opponents.

Lawmakers also extended the terms of current elected officials and the heads of the Armed Forces from six to seven years. The reform also granted new powers to electoral authorities to dissolve political parties and sanction candidates. If reelected in late 2028, Ortega and Murillo could remain in power until 2036.

The reform must be ratified during a second legislative session in January 2027. In practice, it would pave the way for a one-party system controlled by the FSLN.

What is the objective?

Ortega, 80, and Murillo, 75, tightened their control over society following the 2018 protests, whose repression left more than 300 people dead, according to the United Nations. The co-presidents describe the demonstrations as an attempted coup sponsored by the United States.

Thousands of people went into exile following the protests, including opposition leaders, intellectuals, journalists and members of the clergy who were stripped of their nationality after being accused of “treason.” During the 2021 election campaign, Ortega’s main rivals were imprisoned before the vote, leaving virtually no domestic opposition today.

Ortega suffers from lupus and kidney problems and has difficulty walking. Most of his children hold key government positions, while opposition figures warn that an internal purge is underway to secure a family succession. Rebecca Bill, president of the Inter-American Dialogue, said Ortega and Murillo do not need tougher measures to win elections because the opposition “has already been crushed and democratic institutions destroyed.”

“The objective is to ensure there is as little uncertainty as possible about what happens after Ortega. Elections create uncertainty, as do independent institutions and a genuine opposition, which is why they have eliminated all three,” Bill said. Extending their terms would also allow the co-presidents to outlast the current period of pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump and postpone any possible negotiations over electoral conditions, according to former Nicaraguan lawmaker Eliseo Núñez.

What could the consequences be?

The United States on Wednesday urged its partners to sever ties with Nicaragua, arguing that “dictatorships” should not enjoy the political and economic benefits afforded to democracies. Washington, Nicaragua’s largest trading partner, has already imposed sanctions on government figures and is pushing for a meeting of foreign ministers from the Organization of American States (OAS) to consider measures against Managua.

The European Union also condemned the amendment before it was approved. “The international community needs to coordinate more effectively and raise the cost of repression in a targeted manner, while avoiding measures that primarily punish ordinary Nicaraguans,” Bill said.

World.title: How El Nino is choking the Panama Canal
World.content:
The Panama Canal will restrict the number of vessels transiting the crucial waterway from Friday for the second time ever due to drought caused by the El Nino climate phenomenon. Five percent of global trade passes through the canal that connects the Pacific Ocean with the Atlantic.

The waterway is set to reduce daily traffic from 36 to 32 ships a day in an effort to conserve water amid a severe drought likely to last until mid-2027. Canal authorities are also reducing the permitted draft of vessels — how deep they sit in the water — from 15.24 to 14.63 meters.

Panama has declared an emergency over El Nino, which raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean and causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions. The canal’s incoming administrator Ilya Espino de Marotta has acknowledged the current “challenging” conditions.

Nothing without water

The 80-kilometer (50-mile) canal draws on freshwater that comes mainly from rainfall and is stored in artificial lakes. Without water, its locks that lift and lower ships at the beginning and end of the journey would not function. Each transiting ship requiers about 200 million liters of water, which is then discharged into the sea.

Water “is the most important resource for operations,” but “between April and August the accumulated rainfall deficit was 35.8 percent below the historical average,” the canal’s water manager Erick Cordoba said. And there are “no signs of recovery in the short term,” Cordoba added.

No signs of recovery

Forecasts indicate that the 2027 dry season, normally between January and April, will start a little earlier than usual and extend into May. In 2023 and 2024, El Nino forced a reduction in daily transits to 22 and the maximum draft to 13.41 meters.

That led to 20 percent fewer vessels and a 17 percent drop in tonnage, not to mention longer lines of ships queuing up. Further restrictions could follow those imposed on Friday. “If we don’t manage to fill the lakes in November, we’re going to have to tighten our belts,” former canal administrator Jorge Quijano said.

Worldwide repercussions

Long-lasting restrictions will lead to “higher shipping costs and longer waiting times” and therefore higher prices for consumers, Rebecca Bill Chavez, president of the Inter-American Dialogue said. A ship loses around 200 containers for every 30-centimeter draft decrease, according to Quijano.

That amounts to hundreds of units for large vessels that can carry up to 16,000. “We’re going to see a significant impact on the container sector,” which is the canal’s biggest source of revenue, he said. But Danish shipping company Maersk believes it is still “too early” to “speculate” about the impact.

The route mainly connects China, South Korea and Japan with the United States — the origin or destination of seven in ten containers that pass through the canal. Rising costs could “potentially affect US trade,” said analyst Natasha Lindstaedt of Britain’s University of Essex. If he wanted to, US President Donald Trump could argue “that trust and reliability in the channel have been lost,” Lindstaedt said.

The US-Israel war on Iran has pushed up traffic in the Panama Canal given the standstill the conflict caused in the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas normally travels. The difficulties on both routes “put real pressure on global supply chains,” noted Bill.

Future-proofing

The canal authority plans to build a new 4,600-hectare reservoir on the Indio River to the west as a way to limit the effects of future droughts on operations. But this project would not be ready before 2031.

The canal’s watershed also supplies drinking water to half of Panama’s 4.6 million inhabitants via infrastructure that was designed almost a century ago.

World.title: A Night With Costa Rica Soccer Fans in Perez Zeledon
World.content:
Perez Zeledon is home to a team in the first division of Costa Rica soccer. Known as Los Guerreros del Sur, the club has been in existence since 1991. As one of the smaller market teams, they are at a general disadvantage compared to the major teams such as Saprissa (San Jose), La Liga (Alajuela), and Heredia. Salaries are much lower, and when a talented player emerges, he will be made a better financial offer by one of the major clubs and depart for the Greater San Jose area.

Los Guerreros play their home games at their stadium in downtown San Isidro del General. It is a cozy facility that seats around 6,000 people. To this day, there is no scoreboard to show time elapsed or even the score of the game. The PA announcer gives the score at the end of each half. As regulation time neared the end of each half, a man on the sidelines held up a digital clock showing the minutes of extra time left to be played.

Back in the 1990s, I was a socio (partner) in the club. For 1,500 colones monthly– about 5 USD at the time– I had a free pass to all home games. (The monthly cost for a socio now is 7,500 colones). The club typically finished in the middle of the standings, competitive but with little chance of winning the title. Across the street was the Stadium Bar, which filled before and after the games, especially on weekends. It was torn down years ago, and a bank now stands where fans once drank their sorrows away.

It had been years since I attended a game, so when I saw that La Liga was coming to town, I bought a ticket in advance. I went in expecting to pay 3000 colones as that was the price I had seen listed for their previous game versus San Carlos. But the cheapest seat for this game was 8000 colones. This ticket was labeled as Sol, though as it was a night game, Luna would have been appropriate. La Liga is the second most successful club in CR league history with 31 titles. Perez Zeledon, by comparison, has one title, won in the opening half of a split season, in 2017.

Entering the stadium, I was patted down by a young security agent. There was heavy security on that side of the stadium, due to the presence of various barras supporting La Liga. Composed mostly of younger men, the barras travel from various areas of the country to loudly support their team, and have a reputation for rowdy, sometimes violent behavior. The side I was on was filled with fans of La Liga, wearing the red and black colors of their club. Banners announced the various locations the barras had traveled from: Grecia, Naranjo, Tres Rios, Rio Segundo, Quepos, Desamparados.

The game was competitive if sloppily played at times. Costa Rican soccer is at a low ebb at the moment and this game did little to showcase a promising future. While La Liga had more talent overall– including World Cup and Spanish football veteran Celso Borges– the overall quality of play left much to be desired.

And the barra surrounding me agreed. I heard the word ‘hijueputa’ shouted a few hundred times, both at the referee and the play of their own team. The final score was 1-all, sort of a moral victory for the outmanned home team. Outside the stadium was a heavy police presence, but there was no violence. The barras packed up and returned to their respective towns, until the next La Liga match.

Read more of Don Mateo’s writing from his newly published ebook.

World.title: Government of Belize launches National Commission for Persons with Disabilities
World.content:
Government of Belize launches National Commission for Persons with Disabilities

The Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs officially launched the National Commission for Persons with Disabilities on September 3, marking an important step in Government’s continued efforts to strengthen the rights, representation, and inclusion of persons with disabilities in Belize.

Held under the theme “Together Towards Inclusion,” the launch brought together persons with disabilities, Government officials, civil society organisations, disability advocates, development partners, and representatives of key national institutions to formally introduce the Commission and begin a new phase in the implementation of the Disabilities Act, 2024.

For the Ministry, the establishment of the Commission represents more than the creation of another national body. It provides an important mechanism through which the commitments contained in the Disabilities Act can be translated into coordinated action, greater accountability, and meaningful improvements in the lives of persons with disabilities.

The Disabilities Act, 2024 provides Belize with a comprehensive legislative framework for advancing and protecting the rights of persons with disabilities, including in areas such as education and training, employment, health care, accessibility, and protection from discrimination.

The National Commission for Persons with Disabilities brings together representatives from Government, civil society organisations serving persons with disabilities, labour, the private sector, and key national institutions. Under the Act, the Chief Executive Officer of the Ministry responsible for Human Development serves as Chairperson of the Commission.

Ahead of the public launch, Commissioners participated in their inaugural working session, beginning the substantive work of the new body. Discussions focused on building a shared understanding of the Commission’s mandate, reviewing the Disabilities Act and Terms of Reference, and beginning discussions on the strategic priorities that will guide the Commission’s work.

During the official ceremony, members of the Commission received their Instruments of Appointment, formally assuming the responsibility entrusted to them under the Disabilities Act.

Delivering the keynote address, Hon. Thea Garcia Ramirez, Minister of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, reaffirmed the Ministry’s commitment to working with the Commission and the disability community to advance greater inclusion across Belize.

The programme also included an overview of the Disabilities Act, 2024 by Mr. Delvitt Samuels, Crown Counsel and drafter of the Act, along with special remarks from Ms. Alisa Fisher and H.E. Rossana Briceño, Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children.

The occasion was attended by representatives from across Government, organisations serving persons with disabilities, members of the disability community, civil society, the United Nations system, development partners, statutory bodies, labour, and the private sector.

The Ministry’s goal is not simply to speak about inclusion, but to help create a Belize in which inclusion is increasingly experienced in the nation’s schools, workplaces, communities, public spaces, services, and institutions.

World.title: 34 RAC technicians receive training on Energy-efficient cooling practices
World.content:
34 RAC technicians receive training on Energy-efficient cooling practices

By Zoila Palma: Thirty-four refrigeration and air-conditioning (RAC) technicians from across Belize are participating in a hands-on training focused on improving efficiency, standards and technical practices in Belize’s cooling sector. The training is being held at Roaring River Resort in Roaring Creek.

The training comes as the refrigeration and air-conditioning industry continues to evolve with the introduction of newer technologies, more efficient equipment, alternative refrigerants and energy-efficiency standards.

The Department of the Environment emphasized that proper installation, servicing and maintenance are critical to ensuring that cooling systems operate efficiently.

Participants are receiving practical instruction on identifying energy-efficient equipment, properly sizing and commissioning systems, diagnosing faults and working with newer technologies. Hands-on exercises are also allowing technicians to examine how common system faults can affect energy performance and overall efficiency.

The training is being led by the National Ozone Unit in collaboration with ARACT, with support from partners in energy efficiency and standards.

World.title: Benque Viejo joins National Sports Leaders at historic Sports Summit
World.content:
Benque Viejo joins National Sports Leaders at historic Sports Summit

By Zoila Palma: Benque Viejo del Carmen Mayor Jorge Rosales and a delegation from the Benque Viejo Town Council attended Belize’s first-ever National Sports Summit, held at the Belize City Civic Center.

Hosted by the Government of Belize through the National Sports Council and the Ministry of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations, the two-day summit was held under the theme “Building Belize Through Sport.”

The forum brought together athletes, sporting federations and regional policymakers to discuss strategies for strengthening and advancing sports development across Belize, with a focus on creating a sustainable roadmap for the sector.

The opening ceremony featured remarks from Minister Anthony Mahler and Prime Minister John Briceño, along with a keynote address by international track star and advocate Marion Jones, who encouraged greater investment in grassroots talent and the development of Belizean athletes for the global stage.

World.title: Six years later, André Bauer finally arrives in Belize as new U.S. Ambassador
World.content:
Six years later, André Bauer finally arrives in Belize as new U.S. Ambassador

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Newly appointed United States Ambassador to Belize Rudolph Andreas “André” Bauer arrived in the country on Friday afternoon, nearly six years after he first thought he would be taking up the diplomatic post.

Bauer, accompanied by his family, arrived at the Philip Goldson International Airport at about 12:40 p.m. and spoke with the media from the VIP room shortly afterward.

“I can’t just tell you how excited my family and I are to be here,” Bauer said, explaining that he hopes his family will become part of the Belizean community during his posting.

Bauer’s journey to Belize began during President Donald Trump’s first term. Trump announced his intention to nominate Bauer as Ambassador to Belize in July 2020, and the nomination was formally sent to the U.S. Senate on July 21 of that year. However, the Senate never confirmed him, and the nomination was formally returned to the president on January 3, 2021, at the end of the 116th Congress.

Trump nominated Bauer for the Belize post again on April 21, 2026, and the U.S. Senate confirmed him on August 7.

Bauer recalled preparing for the assignment back in 2020, including attending diplomatic training and learning about Belize.

“God had a different timing planned for us,” he said. “He planned on us coming to Belize. He just planned on a different time. And so six years later, we’re here.”

The former South Carolina lieutenant governor and businessman said President Trump has sent him to Belize with a mandate focused on “safety, security and opportunities” for both countries.

Among his stated priorities are combating the movement of illegal drugs, addressing immigration issues, supporting opportunities for Belizean youth and seeing the U.S.-funded Millennium Challenge Corporation compact produce tangible results.

Bauer also promised to travel extensively around Belize and engage directly with people, including those who may disagree with him.

“You’re going to see me have meetings all over this country, where people come out and ask me anything they want,” he said.

Bauer said he wants Belizeans, by the end of his posting, to regard the United States as one of the country’s closest allies and to see concrete improvements stemming from the bilateral relationship.

World.title: Belmopan to plant trees as part of 1 million tree initiative
World.content:
Belmopan to plant trees as part of 1 million tree initiative

By Zoila Palma: The Belmopan City Council is partnering with UNDP Student Ambassadors, the University of Belize, the Belize Forest Department and the Small Grants Program for a One Million Tree Initiative Tree Planting Campaign.

The campaign will take place on September 9 at 10:00 a.m. at the Governor General Field in Belmopan, under the theme “Sub Umbra Floreo” — “Under the Shade I Flourish.”

The initiative aims to encourage residents and stakeholders to help protect and nurture the environment, with each tree planted contributing to a greener and healthier city.

The Belmopan City Council is encouraging the community to participate as the capital joins efforts to build a more sustainable future through tree planting and environmental stewardship.

World.title: Ministry of Rural Transformation recognizes 2026 Councils of the Year
World.content:
Ministry of Rural Transformation recognizes 2026 Councils of the Year

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Rural Transformation has announced the Village Councils of the Year 2026, recognizing councils across Belize for their commitment, hard work and efforts toward community development.

The ministry said the councils demonstrated dedication to good governance and service to the public good, while working to meet the needs and expectations of their communities.

The district winners are San Narciso Village Council in Corozal, San Jose Nuevo Palmar Village Council in Orange Walk, and Caye Caulker Village Council in Belize District.

In Cayo, the award went to Franks Eddy Village Council, while Hopkins Village Council was selected for Stann Creek and Bella Vista Village Council for Toledo.

The Ministry of Rural Transformation congratulated all the winning councils and recognized their continued efforts to improve and develop their communities.

World.title: Sports Tourism could drive new visitors, jobs and economic growth
World.content:
Sports Tourism could drive new visitors, jobs and economic growth

By Zoila Palma: Sports tourism could become a major opportunity for Belize to diversify its tourism industry, attract visitors during traditionally slower periods and create new economic opportunities for communities across the country.

During the 1st ever National Sports summit, Belize Tourism Industry Association (BTIA) President Efren E. Perez participated in a panel discussion on “Sports Tourism, Diaspora Engagement and Regional Opportunities,” highlighting the importance of collaboration between government, tourism stakeholders, sporting associations, athletes, communities, event organizers and regional partners.

Perez noted that Belize has the natural assets, cultural diversity, sporting talent and regional connections needed to develop a stronger sports tourism market. He emphasized opportunities to strengthen the national sporting events calendar, improve infrastructure and support local athletes.

The Ministry of Tourism noted that developing travel packages around sporting events could help transform Belize’s sporting strengths into market-ready visitor experiences while promoting tourism, national pride, youth development and inclusive economic growth.

World.title: 56 Student-athletes sign scholarships as UB welcomes a new generation of Black Jaguars
World.content:
56 Student-athletes sign scholarships as UB welcomes a new generation of Black Jaguars

By Zoila Palma: The University of Belize celebrated a major milestone in its athletics program with its Black Jaguar Athletic Scholarship Signing Ceremony, officially welcoming a new generation of student-athletes for the academic year.

Held at the Jaguar Auditorium on the UB Belmopan Campus, the ceremony brought together student-athletes from various sporting disciplines and their families as 56 athletic scholarship contracts were officially signed.

The event was attended by Minister of State in the Ministry of Youth and Sports, Devin Daly, who offered words of encouragement and inspiration to the scholarship recipients as they begin another year of balancing academic and athletic excellence.

UB encouraged the 56 scholarship recipients to represent the Black Jaguar with discipline, determination, pride and excellence on the field and in the classroom.

World.title: UPDATE: Mistrial ruling upheld in case of US mother who killed her children
World.content:
Kevin Reddington, defense attorney for Lindsay Clancy, and Lindsay Clancy look on as Judge William Sullivan (out of frame) instructs the jury to continue deliberating, during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on September 4, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

PLYMOUTH, United States (AFP) — A judge declared a mistrial on Friday in the high-profile case of an American woman who killed her three young children.

Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict in the case of Lindsay Clancy, and an appeals court rejected a last-minute bid by the defence to have a juror replaced.

The jury was deadlocked 11-1, with the majority apparently leaning to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

READ: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case, puts ruling on hold

World.title: Gift from the heart
World.content:
Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton (second right) checks out specialised equipment donated to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) by Abigaye Smythe (second left), founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, on Thursday, as consultant cardiothoracic surgeon Dr Sunil Stephenson explains its function. Sharing in the moment is chief executive officer at UHWI Dr Sydney Powell. The equipment will give surgeons at the hospital the ability to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

A cardiac patient facing her sixth surgery this December has donated US$4,000 in specialised equipment to the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), directly upgrading its training resources and capabilities for minimally invasive open-heart surgery.

Speaking at the handover ceremony of the medical equipment at UHWI on Thursday, Abigaye Smythe, founder and managing director of I Have a Heart Foundation, revealed that leading this initiative is her life’s purpose.

Describing her connection to the project as lifelong, Smythe shared that she has battled heart disease since the age of seven, when she first began experiencing symptoms.

At 19, Smythe was delivered life-altering news when she was diagnosed with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy — the same disease that took her mother’s life. The rare genetic condition causes fat and scar tissue to replace healthy heart muscle, disrupting electrical signals and triggering abnormal heart rhythms.

Since her diagnosis, the philanthropist has undergone five surgeries at UHWI, making this donation a profoundly personal milestone.

“Because of my own journey, and understanding the fact that cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in Jamaica, I don’t advocate for heart disease patients from a distance. I understand what it means to be one [a cardiac patient], and I understand what it means to lose one. So this is my purpose. And that is why today is so meaningful,” she said.

“I’m not simply donating equipment to a hospital, I’m giving back to an institution that has cared for me, from testing and diagnosis in 2011, through five surgeries between 2012 and 2019, several emergency room visits and hospitalisations in-between, and an institution that will care for me again in December when I undergo my sixth heart surgery. I am investing in my fellow heart disease patients. I’m also investing in my country, in Jamaica,” added Smythe.

The donation builds on a partnership between the I Have a Heart Foundation, the Organisation for International Development, and a medical team from New York’s Montefiore Einstein Hospital. Since 2019, this partnership has provided more than $120 million in free open-heart surgeries at UHWI for 60 financially vulnerable patients.

Smythe noted that while this collaboration has been highly beneficial for both the patients and UHWI, she realised the hospital still lacked the capacity to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries without foreign assistance. She highlighted this gap as the driving force behind her efforts to lobby for and secure the new equipment.

“During the 2025 cardiac mission, the international medical team brought their specialised tools to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgery, and this resulted in the first such procedure being performed at UHWI, and possibly the first in Jamaica. They returned [home] and so did their equipment. And they came back in March 2026, for the mission. And when they performed the surgeries, and when they left, so did their equipment again,” she explained.

“So I said, ‘Okay, I want us to be independent, I want us to have our own, I want us to be able to perform minimally invasive open-heart surgeries outside of the mission’. And that is where the begging began. Thanks to our sponsors, we were able to raise the money, and we turned that vision into a reality, and purchased the equipment,” Smythe explained.

Looking ahead, she hopes this contribution will elevate care at UHWI, arguing that the island has no shortage of medical skill or talent but requires some help securing the tools to match that expertise.

“I’m excited to see how this capacity, this capability, will continue to grow. Today is not simply a handover, it is an investment in Jamaican lives, in our health care system, our medical professionals, and the future of cardiac care. My hope is that one day a Jamaican will never have to ask, ‘Can this procedure be done in Jamaica?’ They will simply know that it can be done here, and it can be done here at the University Hospital of the West Indies,” she said.

Expressing gratitude for the donation, Dr Sunil Stephenson, consultant cardiothoracic surgeon at UHWI, told the Jamaica Observer that the equipment was a necessity as the hospital continues to observe an increase in cardiac patients yearly.

“For a year, we perform about 80 to 90 heart surgeries. As a matter of fact, most deaths… in Jamaica are caused by cardiovascular diseases. So we do see quite a bit of patients who require our services and it’s mainly related to lifestyle illnesses. Some are genetic but most of what we do see is related to chronic non-communicable diseases. So there’s definitely an increase,” said Dr Stephenson.

He added that the equipment gave patients greater access to minimally invasive surgery which, he noted, offered significant advantages.

“The benefit in the sense that there’s less pain, they recover much faster. There’s still a shorter time in the ICU, and they need less time on the ventilator. So they recover much quicker and they’re more comfortable. And for females, they prefer the fact that they don’t have an incision in the middle of the chest because they’re very concerned about how the scar would look. So these instruments will actually help us to be able to do these procedures, and extend these procedures to the entire Jamaica, because that’s the population that we serve,” said the doctor.

For his part, Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton thanked Smythe and her team for the donation, and expressed confidence in the quality of staff at UHWI, adding that he had no doubt that the equipment would be put to good use.

“I just want to embrace the concept of ongoing effort to improve, and to make the services more efficient, embrace the concept of volunteerism and charity and gifting, and just say that for health, we have to see ourselves as a community and work together as a community. So thank you again, we appreciate it, and we certainly wish you the very best in terms of your own struggles and work, both as a foundation but also individually,” Tufton said.

World.title: Fit for purpose
World.content:
Mico CARE Centre interventionist Collette Demetrius (right) shows one of the centre’s retrofitted classrooms to (from left) permanent secretary at the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Dr Kasan Troupe; The Mico University College President Dr Asburn Pinnock; and portfolio manager, education and special needs, Digicel Foundation Jamilia Crooks Brown at Thursday’s official opening of the facility that caters to children with special needs. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

AFTER more than four decades of supporting children with special needs, The Mico University College’s Child Assessment and Research in Education (CARE) Centre has upgraded its learning environment, unveiling renovations to five classrooms aimed at creating better spaces for students to learn, develop, and thrive.

The project, valued at approximately $24 million, was done in collaboration with Digicel Foundation and partners and provides classrooms with specialised sensory and occupational therapy equipment designed to aid concentration, emotional regulation, and physical engagement.

“The classrooms before were just regular classrooms. The rooms were very old, wooden floors, old aluminum windows, and so on, which are from the 1980s. Renovating these rooms makes the learning space more modern, more accommodating. So what we’ve done, we have looked at the needs of the clients that we serve,” Micro CARE Centre Director Dr Sharon Anderson-Morgan explained after the official handing over and ribbon-cutting ceremony on Thursday.

“So the rooms are now fit for purpose, they’re not just a regular classroom. We have children who are fidgety, for example, because they have attention-deficit disorder or any kind of disorder that causes them to want to move all the time. So we have the kick bands on the chair, they can put their feet on the chair. We have the wobbly things at the end of it, so they can rock and can move,” she added.

Anderson-Morgan pointed to several challenges faced by the institution prior to its renovation.

“The rooms were very, very hot. When you have spaces that are hot and you have bodies moving around, people are going to get a little agitated sometimes. So we’ve had children who react terribly to the heat. For example, we had some of our kids with autism and it gets hot and they would just start screaming,” she said.

“Also, we could not move the furniture as we would like to, because the old furniture did not allow for us to. If you’re going to move the chairs, it’s going to scrape the floor, some children are sensitive to that. They didn’t fit together the way these fit together,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the lighting at the facility was also an issue.

“We had these old fluorescent lights that also affected some children. There were children who would look up because they’re hypersensitive to visual stimuli. They would get scared because they think they’re seeing patterns in the ceiling. I remember one day we had to cover a portion of the ceiling with paper because the child kept looking up there because he thought he was seeing something else,” said Anderson-Morgan.

She underscored that the renovations will not only benefit students who enter the facility through its intervention programme, but also those who come in for assessment.

“Sometimes children come here for assessment and they are dysregulated. The clinicians now have the centre space to take them, calm them down before they can assess them, because before, sometimes they can’t get to assess them unless they come back because a child is screaming, running all over the place,” Anderson-Morgan said, adding that the centre assesses close to 1,000 children yearly.

She hastened to add that despite the centre being known to conduct assessments, its services extend beyond that.

“We do assessment, we do intervention, not just academic, because we have speech therapy. And we have occupational therapy, behaviour therapy, we have behaviour therapy for one group, and that’s only because we don’t have an on-site behaviour therapist, so we have to bring in the service. And we also have counselling services, we have a counselling centre up there, where even some of our kids in the intervention programme, they also receive counselling as needed, and sometimes their families need it as well,” she explained.

Permanent secretary in the Ministry of Education, Skills, Youth, and Information Kasan Troupe welcomed the upgraded facility and lauded Digicel Foundation and partners for their investment in the special needs sector.

“We’re going to have a room that teachers will be exposed to improve opportunities to train and integrate technology because it is technology-enabled. We’re going to have a room that will build confidence in learners because here they have a safer space, a modern space that they can make mistakes, learn and grow and be strong because they are fully supported with specialists that can train them and support them in the way they should grow,” she said.

“You’re going to have learners who cannot communicate confidently. You’re going to have learners who will learn new skills so they can transform their whole realities in the future. That’s the promise of this investment,” Troupe added.

The Mico University College CARE Centre states on its website that it was established in 1980 as a centre of excellence, dedicated to child assessment and research in education. It was formed through a partnership between The Netherlands and Jamaican governments.

World.title: Malie Donn releases debut album Golden Child
World.content:
Malie Donn.

Dancehall artiste Malie Donn today released his debut studio album, The Golden Child, marking a major milestone for the entertainer who has steadily carved out a place among dancehall’s new generation.

The 21-track project, released through VP Records, follows several years of building his name with songs including Van Cleef, Body Tea, V6, Dirty Mirror, Suspect, Crook and many others.

“The Golden Child represents everything that brought me to this point: the pressure, the growth, the wins and the lessons,” Malie Donn said. “This project gives people a chance to hear more of who I am as an artist, where I want to take the music next and the versatility I bring.”

On Thursday, Malie Donn released the album’s title track, Golden Child, featuring fellow dancehall artiste Squash. The collaboration pairs Malie Donn’s melodic delivery with Squash’s distinctive style, while exploring themes of confidence, ambition and resilience that also run through the wider project.

The official music video for Golden Child also premiered on Thursday, providing the final lead-in to the album. Born Kimalie Hylton, Malie Donn is originally from Jones Avenue, Spanish Town, St Catherine, but grew up in Waterford, Portmore.

His passion for music dates back to his days as a student at Waterford Primary School and developed further while he attended Bridgeport High School. Malie Donn has emerged as one of the acts in dancehall’s newer wave, building a catalogue that has helped expand his audience locally and internationally.

The Golden Child also continues his relationship with VP Records. In 2024, he released The Grand Rising EP through the label, followed by the Leak the Hard Drive EP in 2025.

The album was preceded by Holiday, which arrived on August 7 alongside its official music video and offered listeners an early glimpse of a different side of Malie Donn’s artistry.

For Malie Donn, the release of his first full-length album represents an opportunity to present a more complete picture of himself beyond the individual songs that first brought him attention.

World.title: GOJ TAPS MARKET FOR US$1B
World.content:
The Government of Jamaica (GOJ) has gone to the international capital markets to raise a US$1 billion ($157.62 billion) unsecured bond to support its liability management strategy and budgetary objectives.

The prospectus was published on Wednesday through the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), three weeks after GOJ filed its registration statement to issue debt securities. According to a roadshow document seen by the Jamaica Observer, US$600 million is to be used to fund a tender/exchange offer, with the balance earmarked for general budgetary purposes. A source close to the matter also indicated that the new bond is expected to mature in 2037.

At the same time, GOJ launched the tender/exchange offer for holders of the three existing global bonds, tying the new borrowing directly to its wider effort to manage the country’s external debt.

“The Invitation is part of a broader program of Jamaica to proactively manage its external public debt,” stated the tender invitation to holders of the old bonds/notes.

The Government currently has US$837.53 million outstanding on its April 2028 notes, which carry a 6.75 per cent interest rate. The 2036 and 2039 notes have US$250 million and US$1.24 billion outstanding, respectively.

International Financing Review (ifre.com) reported that GOJ began holding fixed-income investor meetings on September 3, likely in connection with the new bond issuance, which will be listed on the Euro MTF Market of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. Citigroup Global Markets Inc. and Scotia Capital (USA) Inc. are serving as deal managers and joint lead underwriters for the transaction.

If the value of bonds tendered exceeds GOJ’s maximum purchase amount, the government can determine how much of each series it will accept, applying different proration factors where necessary. This means it could accept less than the full amount tendered by holders of any of the eligible notes.

The new tender offer opened on September 2 and will expire on September 9, unless extended or terminated at GOJ’s discretion. Settlement is expected to be completed by September 17.

“The invitation is not conditioned upon any minimum participation of any series of Old Notes but is conditioned on, among other things, the pricing and closing of an international capital markets transaction in an amount and on terms and conditions acceptable to Jamaica,” stated the GOJ release.

The Government last executed a transaction of this nature in October 2023, when it spent US$237.4 million to redeem three notes with a nominal value of US$233.2 million. At the time, GOJ repurchased approximately US$99.7 million in two separate 2025 notes and US$165.15 million of the April 2028 notes. The tender on the 2028 notes represented 11.6 per cent of the amount outstanding before the GOJ offer.

That tender offer coincided with Jamaica’s first Jamaican dollar (JMD)-linked bond issuance on the international capital markets, worth $46.6 billion, or US$300 million. The instrument carried a 9.625 per cent interest rate and matures in November 2030.
