World.title: Saxony-Anhalt: Small parties will be the kingmakers
World.content:
The far-right AfD has good odds of winning an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament this state election, enabling them to govern alone. It all depends on whether other parties make the cut.

It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt. On September 6, 2026, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time.

So far, there has not been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post-World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023.

Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote.

AfD, CDU and Left Party will get into parliament

Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties who can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party, which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR.

All other parties have cause for concern they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany.

This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU).

SPD, Greens, FDP, BSW might not make the 5% mark

The SPD is losing popularity nationwide. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago.

The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback.

The environmentalist Greens are also concerned about returning to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society.

Concern over Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW)

And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election.

The BSW never really recovered from this setback. They went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%.

Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office.

Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole.

What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Small parties could prevent absolute majority for the AfD

The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood of the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone.

On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. This is because in 2018 the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party.

If the CDU sticks to this, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible.

Could the CDU form a minority government?

Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt.

The Left Party is prepared to support Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term.

"In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF.

He pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony, where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party.

Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Germany's alliance against the far right
World.content:
Trade unions, churches and human rights activists are worried about the rise of the far-right AfD. How can civil society protect people who are threatened by far-right extremism?

Fighting for democracy and human rights in Germany today means mustering up a lot of courage. For Felix Pankonin , locking and checking all doors and windows around the house has become practically second nature. Sometimes a hot-tempered lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party shows up on his property; his bicycles have been vandalized; and other times he receives threats that something will happen to his animals. Most recently, his partner was physically assaulted.

Pankonin is the project director of educational programs on political issues, Jewish history and antisemitism at the Hillersche Villa in Zittau, in the eastern German state of Saxony.

The situation is similar for Keerthana Kuperan, who works as a political advisor at DaMOst , the umbrella organization for migrant groups in eastern Germany. Yes, says Kuperan, whose parents are from Sri Lanka, right-wing extremism has had a major impact on her work over the past three years.

"We have completely different security protocols now. After 6:00 p.m., no one is left alone in the office, and when putting up posters in rural areas, security measures are put in place beforehand."

Her work is primarily focused on ensuring the safety of activists. Another aspect of her work involves dealing with challenges from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which files parliamentary information requests, often on migration, in order to delay political proceedings and highlight issues that should not really be controversial.

Ahead of the state election in Saxony-Anhalt, numerous business owners with a background of migration went on strike against racism and fascism, and in support of a free and democratic society Image: Peter Gercke/dpa/picture alliance

In Saxony-Anhalt, a federal state with a very low proportion of foreigners, state legislative elections will be held on September 6. DaMOst observes that the political landscape has shifted to the right. This has led to the discrediting of democratic networks, which has affected their funding and job opportunities.

Green Party politician becomes target of hostilities

Miriam Zeller, a councilwoman in Stendal (a city of 37,000 in Saxony-Anhalt), is a member of the environmentalist Green Party and is running in the state election on September 6. Zeller told DW that the hostility was even more intense when the Greens were in power.

Her daughter stopped being invited to birthday parties, and she herself was viciously accused of being a warmonger. From the very beginning, the Greens had declared their solidarity with Ukraine after it had come under attack from Russia.

"It can't get any worse than this," says Zeller.

However, she pointed out that, fortunately, as a teacher, she is a civil servant and therefore cannot lose her job.

For others, the specter of losing one's job — should the AfD come to power — is very real.

Miriam Zeller, a Green Party candidate, is feeling the impact of the shift to the right in her private life as well Image: Miriam Zeller

Alliance for Democracy: Educating people on how to defend themselves

People like Pankonin, Kuperan and Zeller need more protection. The Together for Democracy alliance aims to support individuals or institutions that are being attacked or threatened by far-right extremists.

The aim of the group's Solidarity Agreement — which over 80 groups have signed, including labor unions, the major Christian churches, sports organizations, human rights groups as well as social and environmental organizations — is to ensure that anyone who is targeted for their commitment to democracy will not be left alone. The groups joined forces in 2024 to form an alliance against the far right when it became clear that attacks on democracy were intensifying.

Now, alliance members want to also offer help and support in the event of attacks on youth or cultural centers, hate campaigns against people who speak out publicly, or when volunteers are threatened — whether through public expressions of solidarity or by providing legal or financial support. The alliance includes powerful actors such as the German Trade Union Federation (DGB) and environmental organizations like Greenpeace.

Yasmin Fahimi, the head of the DGB, which has over five million members, took the opportunity to present the new agreement in Berlin. When asked by DW whether the AfD, in the event of an election victory, could actually fire all public employees, Fahimi was clear.

"This fantasy of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt — to carry out a complete personnel shake-up in government agencies, ministries, courts and the police — is completely unlawful," Fahimi said. "We are making it clear to our members that they can fight back against this. It is also a manifestation of an authoritarian mindset to believe that one can simply issue a decree and do as one pleases. That's not how our democracy works."

That is why the DGB is training its members both in constitutional law and civil service law so they can defend themselves, Fahimi said. The trade union leader calls for more commitment from politicians.

"We must ensure — especially in regional areas, but also within our institutions — that people cannot simply be forced to comply with unlawful orders. I believe it would be good for the Conference of Interior Ministers to discuss how to provide clear information, seminars and workshops on these issues, so that public servants, ministry employees and staff at institutions governed by the rule of law are not left to fend for themselves," Fahimi told DW.

Threats, abuse to German mayors hurting local government To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hope for help for queer people following the Berlin attack

"Of course, this alliance can mean more protection for queer people who are active on the ground," says Andre Lehmann, from the Queer Diversity Association (LSVD+) — a civil rights organization that has represented the interests and concerns of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans* and intersex queer people (LGBTQ+) since 1990.

"Right now, we're seeing a lot of attacks on Pride events all over Germany. In some cases, local organizers don't even know what to do in such situations. That's where an alliance like this can step in," Lehmann said in an interview with DW.

The Islamist attack on the Pride event in Berlinhas deeply unsettled the queer community, said Lehmann. On top of that, many democracy projects are being financially bled dry right now of all times.

The alliance will hardly be able to make up for the lack of funding for democracy projects that has resulted from the federal government's cuts and restructuring. However, teaming up with other organizations helps build strength, says Sophie Lampl, who works for Greenpeace.

"That is certainly one of the strengths we can bring as an environmental organization: our ability to campaign. To provide support when civil society organizations or individuals are attacked, to publicly stand up for them and to bring this injustice to light," Lampl argues.

Will the alliance also be able to help in rural areas?

Felix Pankonin has often helped the Together for Democracy alliance — by providing legal advice, funding for security and moral support. Pankonin would like to see more involvement from major organizations in rural areas.

Green Party politician Miriam Zeller reports that she has also received aid from small local networks. She believes that a large network, with its newfound solidarity, can make a big difference and could be a vital source of support, even in rural areas.

Andre Lehmann sounds determined: "We will defend our democracy and, if necessary, guide our local people through this valley," he says.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Nigeria: Suspected oil thieves dead after inhaling fumes
World.content:
A Nigerian environmental group says that at least 37 people died trying to siphon crude oil off a ship illegally. Police acknowledged a fatal incident but gave fewer details, saying investigations continued.

A Nigerian environmental NGO says that at least 37 people died in an attempt to tap oil from a loading vessel in the south of the country illegally.

Most of them died as a result of inhaling hazardous fumes, the Youth and Advocacy Centre said.

Nigerian authorities were yet to issue a death toll but had acknowledged a fatal incident in which people were killed, apparently while trying to steal crude oil.

What do we know about the case?

The incident took place overnight on Thursday in Okrika in Rivers State in the oil-rich Niger Delta in the south of the country.

The environmental group said it happened at a jetty as a vessel was loading oil from the Indorama Eleme Petrochemical through the Port Harcourt Refinery. The people who died were "suspected oil thieves" trying to siphon the commodity off into boats at an "illegal tapping point."

The Youth and Advocacy Centre NGO said that other people were still missing, potentially lost in the water, quoting a network of volunteers.

Police acknowledged an incident but said they continued to investigate the details.

"The Rivers State Police Command can confirm the deaths. The victims were allegedly attempting to steal crude oil," said spokesperson Blessing Agbabe.

Africa's fuel crisis: Is Dangote the answer? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Oil theft is fairly common in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, Africa's biggest oil producer, with oil mining areas hotspots for poverty and environmental degradation.

The Nigerian government estimates that oil theft causes losses worth several billion dollars annually and has been trying to clamp down on the practice.

The tapping process can also cause leaks and environmental damage.

If confirmed this would be the worst fatal accident on record connected to attempted oil theft since at least October 2023.

However the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps said that the casualty figures circulating remained unverified, saying it was working with other security agencies to clarify the details.

World.title: Germany, partners aim to finalize 'return hubs' by year end
World.content:
German Interior Minister Dobrindt said "technical discussions" were underway with non-EU countries to establish controversial "return hubs." Rights organizations have questioned the legality and morality of the plans.

Germany and other European Union countries are aiming to finalize so-called "return hubs," detention centers outside the bloc where they wish to send migrants whose asylum requests have been rejected, by the end of the year.

The European Parliament in June approved tougher migration rules that paved the way for the creation of "return hubs."

"We want to reach an agreement with third countries this year," which would then enable the establishment of so-called "return hubs," said German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt after a meeting with his counterparts from Denmark, Greece, Austria and the Netherlands in Copenhagen on Friday.

He added that "technical discussions" were currently underway with countries outside the EU, but did not name such countries.

What did the EU ministers say on 'return hubs?'

The five EU countries whose ministers attended the Copenhagen meeting are seeking a deal with an undisclosed non-EU country to host the "return hubs."

Uganda and Rwanda in particular are seen as possibilities —two autocratically ruled countries.

"Around New Year, we expect to have a common understanding with a partner country outside of the European Union," said Danish Migrations Minister Morten Bodskov.

Both the Greek and Danish migration ministers said they wished for the "return hubs" to become operational by 2027.

"We do not accept that foreigners staying illegally in Denmark should be rewarded because of our difficulties in returning them," Bodskov said in an earlier statement.

How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The controversial scheme had already been briefly adopted by the United Kingdom under the former conservative government, but has since been scrapped after the social democratic Labour Party came to power.

In Italy, the right-wing government of Giorgia Meloni reached a similar deal with Albania which currently faces legal challenges.

Are EU 'return hubs' legal?

The legality of the plans for the so-called "return hubs" remains unclear under EU law.

A legal appraisal issued by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in April concluded that the controversial Italian deportation centers in Albania do not violate European law.

EU law does not in principle prohibit member states from establishing such centers outside their own territory.

However, it stipulates that deportees continue to receive legal counsel and linguistic support, and are able to maintain contact with their families and the relevant authorities.

Andreas Grünewald, a migration expert with the German evangelical charity Brot für die Welt (Bread for the World), questioned the feasibility of the plans, calling them "practically difficult to implement and highly problematic in terms of human rights."

He said ministers risked running into "political dead ends."

Rights organizations criticize EU 'return hubs'

The highly controversial plan has been met with wide rejection from rights groups, including children's charities and church organizations, who have criticized the plans for what they see as the "criminalization of migration."

Marta Welander from the International Rescue Committee (IRC), a global humanitarian aid, relief and development NGO, said the plans risk "normalizing detainment in prison-like facilities" and warned that deportees may face "persecution, torture or worse" in their destination countries.

Caritas, a Catholic charity operating in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Slovakia, said that migrants risked becoming trapped in a "legal grey area" if "arbitrarily and indefinitely detained" in the hubs.

Spain's Ceuta grapples with aftermath of border chaos To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Florian Westphal, CEO of Save The Children Germany, warned of the risks faced in particular by children and young people.

"The planned return centers in third countries are places of uncertainty and carry the risk of massive violations of children's rights," he said.

"Transferring children to states with which they have no connection, and where they face the risk of deprivation of liberty and are cut off from key figures in their lives, cannot be in their best interests. Children deserve unconditional protection, no matter where they come from or where they live."

Edited by: Zac Crellin

World.title: Nepal flood disaster puts climate justice under spotlight
World.content:
The devastating Himalayan glacial floods have raised broader questions about who should bear the costs and responsibility for the impacts of climate-related disasters.

Days after devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trisuli river basin, the true scale of the disaster is still emerging.

More than 1,250 people have been confirmed dead and almost 4,000 are still missing.

Buildings, bridges, roads and more than a dozen hydropower facilities have been destroyed, causing an estimated $2.6 billion (€2.24 billion) in damage to public and private infrastructure, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).

Search and rescue operations for missing people remain underway, with families still hoping for their safe return.

The exact cause of the glacial collapse remains unclear, but experts say climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risk of such disasters.

Nepal floods trap hundreds in hydropower tunnels To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A global responsibility?

For Nepal, the disaster has raised a question that goes beyond rescue and reconstruction.

It's about climate justice and who should bear the costs and responsibility for such environmental disasters when the Himalayan nation contributes only a tiny fraction of global greenhouse gas emissions yet faces increasingly severe climate-related risks.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said responding to the catastrophe is a "global responsibility."

"As we work tirelessly to address the damage caused by this sudden and massive disaster, a deeper question has also emerged: How did this destruction happen to us?" Shah asked while addressing Parliament this week.

"Mitigating and managing its impacts is regarded as a shared responsibility of the international community," he stressed.

Kathmandu is planning to raise climate justice issues in the upcoming United Nations General Assembly session in New York, where Prime Minister Shah himself is likely to lead the Nepali delegation.

"We will make our case about the impact of climate change and seek global support and moral obligation to tackle it," Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told DW. "We will also take the initiative of building a coalition of climate-vulnerable countries to raise our collective concerns."

After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Highly vulnerable to climate impacts

Nepal, a largely rural nation of 30 million people, has contributed little to the greenhouse gas emissions driving global warming.

The country accounts for just 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions and emits about 0.5 tons of CO₂ per person each year, making it a "negligible contributor to climate change," according to the World Bank.

But the landlocked Himalayan nation is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change, with flooding, landslides, glacier-related hazards and other environmental risks threatening lives and livelihoods.

Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment.

The country's government estimates that implementing adaptation priorities between 2025 and 2035 could require as much as $18 billion to $20 billion. And Kathmandu wants international climate finance to provide most of these funds.

Nepal has spent years arguing in global climate forums that vulnerable mountain countries need greater support for adaptation and resilience.

In December 2009, Nepal held a historic Cabinet meeting at Kala Patthar, near Mount Everest base camp, at an altitude of 17,192 feet, to highlight the threats that climate change and glacial melting pose to Nepal and other mountainous nations.

Bimala Rai Paudyal, a former Nepali foreign minister, said the latest disaster meant "this is an opportune time for us to highlight glacier melting and climate justice issues in international climate forums."

"Earlier, we were only advocating about climate impacts. Now, we are heavily suffering from it," she told DW.

Paudyal believes Nepal is well positioned to lead an alliance of vulnerable countries, given its exposure to climate risk as well as its expertise and contribution to the climate justice effort.

In Nepal, families cling to hope as thousands still missing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An opportunity for global climate action?

Kathmandu has formally approached the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC)-backed "Loss and Damage Fund" for assistance over the latest floods.

But the fund, set up by the UN in 2025 to aid the impacts of climate change, has not yet begun distributing its limited cash.

The fund also relies on voluntary contributions and lacks legally binding commitments under current international climate agreements, leaving major emitters such as China, India and the US under no direct obligation to compensate for climate change impacts.

Still, some observers and climate advocates believe Nepal can present a strong case for urgent global climate action.

"Nepal can turn this tragedy into an opportunity for global climate action," Dinesh Paudel, professor of sustainable development at Appalachian State University in North Carolina, told DW. "For which, Nepal needs to build a consensus among national stakeholders and maneuver cautiously, considering geopolitical factors."

According to him, Kathmandu can create an ethical movement for climate justice by highlighting the recent flood. This could then lead to creating an effective and legally binding mechanism to deal with climate impacts in the future.

Ashok Swain, professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University and also UNESCO Chair on International Water Cooperation, shares a similar view.

"Nepal should not be left to pay for a climate crisis it did little to create or for regional non-cooperation over which it has limited influence," he said. "This is not a question of charity. It is fundamentally a question of climate justice and a fair distribution of responsibility."

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: How can African retailers compete with Shein and Temu?
World.content:
Shein and Temu are expanding across Africa with low prices and vast product ranges. Businesses and unions warn the growth could come at a cost for local jobs.

A T-shirt for a few dollars, along with jewelry, shoes and accessories — all delivered straight to your door. For many young people in African cities, shopping no longer starts in a store.

They scroll through Instagram or TikTok, see influencers showing off their latest purchases, and place an order with just a few clicks.

This combination of extremely low prices, a huge selection and aggressive social media marketing has made Chinese company Shein one of the world's most successful online fashion retailers.

Temu, also from China, follows a similar model with an even broader range of products.

For Africa's young, urban consumers, the appeal is obvious. But as more purchasing power flows directly to Asia through these platforms, another question is becoming increasingly important: What happens to local retailers, manufacturers and jobs?

South Africa shows the impact

South Africa is currently the clearest test case. Shein launched there in 2020, followed by Temu in 2024.

According to a study commissioned by the Localization Support Fund, the two platforms generated around 7.3 billion rand (about $405 million) in 2024. That represents 3.6% of the total market for clothing, textiles, footwear and leather, but already around 37% of online sales in the sector.

The study also estimates that 2,818 manufacturing jobs and 5,282 retail jobs failed to materialize during that period, a combined impact of about 8,100 jobs. By 2030, more than 34,000 additional retail and manufacturing jobs could be at risk under the study's modeled scenarios.

China's fast-fashion giant Shein opens first store in Paris To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Simon Eppel, a research director with the South African Clothing and Textile Workers' Union (SACTWU), sees this as a growing threat to the domestic industry.

He says Shein and Temu have gained a significant market share in a short period of time and put local manufacturers under pressure.

"They sucked up billions of rands […] in sales, and undercut local manufacturers," Eppel said.

The union is calling for stricter controls.

"In fact, we propose to ban these apps in South Africa," added Eppel, noting that the SACTWU sees such a move as one possible measure to counter the effects of the price pressure.

Aggressive price competition

Industry experts have cautioned that online giants such as Shein can operate at a speed that is difficult for a small African retailer to match.

Digital data shows which products are in demand, while influencers, discounts and a constant stream of new offers encourage consumers to buy.

For users, the line between entertainment and shopping is becoming increasingly blurred. But price is a crucial factor for many consumers.

Tsonam Cleanse Akpeloo, chairman of the Association of Ghana Industries, Accra chapter (AGI Accra), stresses that the offers are particularly attractive in price-sensitive markets.

"Their prices are attractive in price-sensitive economies where consumers naturally look for products that fit their budgets," he told DW.

Local business owners say that problems arise when they can no longer compete on price.

Companies that rely on high-quality materials and higher standards are put at a competitive disadvantage.

In Ghana, Akpeloo has observed similar developments in sectors such as aluminum and hardware.

Nigeria: Cheap imports for urban youth

Nigeria is also an important market for the major Chinese online retailers. Temu has a dedicated platform for the market there, while Shein is building its reach primarily through influencers and fashion content.

The appeal is clear: a wide selection, low prices and access to international trends. But Nigeria has already experienced what cheap imports can do to a local industry.

For governments, therefore, the issue is not just fashion. It is also about the conditions under which local businesses can compete with global platforms.

New tariffs on low-cost goods from China To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Shein and Temu do not have a direct presence everywhere in Africa. Their strongest presence so far is in countries such as South Africa and Nigeria, and to some extent in Ghana and Kenya. But their products also reach customers indirectly in many other African countries.

So-called freight forwarders play an important role. They provide customers with a delivery address in a country where Shein or Temu delivers directly. The package is initially sent there and then forwarded to other places across Africa.

This is how it works for Mariama Sow from Guinea-Bissau. She orders shoes, accessories and human hair for hair salons from Shein. She uses a freight forwarder in Portugal, which then forwards her orders to Guinea-Bissau.

"Underwear, shoes, clothes and school supplies, and above all the human hair, live up to their promise," Sow said.

At the same time, she says she has heard complaints from other customers about poor quality or incorrect sizes. Another problem, she says, is that local retailers are losing customers, particularly younger ones.

The tax dispute shows the political dimension

For governments, the issue is also about taxes and fair competition. South Africa has therefore tightened the rules governing small online imports. The government wanted to prevent international platforms from enjoying a tax advantage over local retailers.

For a local retailer who pays rent, staff costs and taxes, such differences can be significant.

The conflict is therefore not simply a matter of China versus Africa. It is about whether local businesses can compete under comparable conditions.

Akpeloo from AGI Accra is also calling for better controls.

"We need stronger action against smuggling, better enforcement of customs and quality standards," he told DW.

Goods entering the market without the required duties and taxes can put additional pressure on local businesses.

Beyond cheap imports

Despite all the criticism, it would be too simplistic to portray the platforms solely as a threat.The key question is where the economic value is created.

A delivery driver earns money from an order placed in China. A textile worker, by contrast, can support an entire local value chain — from the fabric producer to the sewing factory and retailer.

For African governments, the challenge will therefore be to provide access to affordable products and digital commerce without weakening their own industrial base.

The real competition is no longer just between Shein, Temu and local retailers. It is also over the shopping habits of a young generation — and over whether Africa will remain primarily a consumer in the new digital economy or become a producer itself.

World.title: Begoña Gómez pide su absolución y defiende que no influyó en los cargos de la universidad ni en ninguna autoridad para crear la cátedra
World.content:
Begoña Gómez, esposa del presidente del Gobierno, ha presentado este viernes un nuevo escrito de defensa —firmado por su nuevo abogado— en el que pide una vez más su absolución en la causa contra ella por, supuestamente, haberse valido de su condición de esposa del presidente del Gobierno para impulsar su carrera. Gómez, que afronta una petición de cárcel de 13 años por tráfico de influencias y malversación en el marco de la cátedra extraordinaria que promovió y codirigió en la Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM), argumenta en el escrito que ni se aprovechó de ser la mujer de Pedro Sánchez para influir en los cargos de la universidad, en autoridad o funcionario alguno para conseguir la creación de la cátedra, ni obtuvo beneficio de ella.

La acusación popular liderada por HazteOír basa su petición de cárcel en tres supuestos actos delictivos: el tráfico de influencias para conseguir no solo que se creara la cátedra, sino codirigirla —por el que solicita una condena de dos años—; la malversación de fondos públicos en usar a su asistenta en La Moncloa para cuestiones profesionales —tres años— y la supuesta apropiación de un software desarrollado dentro de la cátedra —otros ocho—, canalizada a través del registro a su nombre de la web y de una marca.

Para defenderse de la primera de las acusaciones, el nuevo letrado de la esposa del presidente del Gobierno, el penalista Jaime Campaner, hace un repaso pormenorizado de la carrera profesional de Gómez antes de que se constituyese la cátedra, y hace especial hincapié en que trabajó en la UCM “mucho antes de que su marido accediera a la presidencia del Gobierno” y en que su participación y nombramiento como codirectora se produjeron dentro de la norma.

El letrado defiende en este sentido las reuniones que tuvo con autoridades de la universidad o empresarios —que la acusación considera pruebas del tráfico de influencias— como la que mantuvo en 2020 con el rector de la UCM, Joaquín Goyache, que se produjo en La Moncloa, un hecho especialmente relevante para HazteOir, pero también para el instructor del caso, el polémico Juan Carlos Peinado. La defensa aduce que, si el encuentro se produjo allí, en la residencia de Gómez, fue porque el lugar inicialmente señalado estaba cerrado por la pandemia. Allí surgió la idea de la cátedra, afirma.

La “apropiación” del ‘software’

Sobre el hecho de que la propia Gómez registrase a su nombre la marca del software, su abogado sostiene que el registro con su correo se produjo “con el único fin de dar a la plataforma una identidad inicial hasta que el proyecto estuviera terminado y pudiera estar registrado a nombre de la UCM”. En este sentido, insiste el letrado, Gómez lo registró con su correo de la universidad e indicó expresamente que formaba parte de la cátedra.

A renglón seguido, el escrito aborda otra de las tesis de la acusación: que la esposa del presidente del Gobierno quiso apropiarse del dominio web de la cátedra. Desde la universidad, afirma la defensa, informaron a Gómez y sus colaboradoras que ellos no podían inscribir el dominio, “en la medida en que la UCM nunca había registrado” uno, y que tenían que hacerlo ellas. Así lo hizo Blanca de Juan, coordinadora de la cátedra, en septiembre de 2022. En julio de 2023, tras cesar de su cargo, transfirió los dominios a la esposa del presidente del Gobierno, que estuvo pagando su mantenimiento. “La actuación de Begoña fue funcional y provisional, con ánimo de impedir que terceras personas pudieran hacerse con el dominio y utilizarlo hasta que el proyecto estuviera finalizado y pudiera registrarse a nombre de la UCM”, concluye el letrado.

“Begoña en ningún momento actuó con ánimo de enriquecerse y no se apropió de la plataforma tecnológica (primera tesis de la acusación popular) ni la destinó a usos privados sin ánimo de apropiársela (segunda tesis de la acusación popular)”, recalca el escrito. Y añade: “La UCM no sufrió perjuicio patrimonial alguno. Los gastos relacionados con el desarrollo de la plataforma se financiaron con las aportaciones realizadas por las entidades colaboradoras, según lo acordado en la cláusula sexta del convenio”. Además, insiste el letrado, la universidad, tras el cese “abrupto” de la cátedra, se quedó con un remanente de 29.685 euros.

Más información El nuevo curso judicial aumenta la presión al PSOE con las causas a Zapatero, Cerdán y Begoña Gómez

Además, el letrado defiende que la asistente de Gómez en La Moncloa, Cristina Álvarez —también imputada—, la ayudase puntualmente en sus gestiones profesionales. En el escrito, de unas 50 páginas, Campaner subraya en primer lugar que el ámbito de las tareas de los asistentes no está delimitado: “Desde la llegada de la democracia (hace ya más de 50 años) ha sido costumbre que las cónyuges del presidente necesariamente cuenten con personal de apoyo de carácter eventual”, remacha. Sus funciones, aunque no tasadas, incluyen el “apoyo en todas las actividades que han sido tradicionalmente realizadas por la cónyuge del presidente, tanto de carácter institucional como de naturaleza privada o profesional”, subraya la defensa de la esposa del presidente del Gobierno.

Para sostener su argumento, el abogado va más allá y aporta como evidencia Mis ocho años en La Moncloa (2004), las memorias de Ana Botella, exalcaldesa de Madrid y esposa del expresidente José María Aznar, donde esta relataba cómo su asistente “le acompañaba en su día a día, tanto en actividades institucionales como estrictamente privadas (por ejemplo, participó en los preparativos de la boda de su hija, la acompañó a desfiles de moda y recorrió con ella el Camino de Santiago)”. E, incluso, fotografías del que fue asistente de la esposa de Mariano Rajoy, Jaime de los Santos (ahora en la ejecutiva popular), portando bolsas de una tienda.

Aunque técnicamente la anterior defensa de Gómez ya había presentado sus conclusiones a la polémica investigación del juez Juan Carlos Peinado —que concluyó con la esposa del presidente del Gobierno y su asistente de camino a un jurado popular—, este nuevo escrito responde a que, el pasado julio, la Audiencia Provincial de Madrid le retiró dos de los cuatro delitos de los que se le acusa y dejó solo el de tráfico de influencias y el de malversación. Tras esta modificación, la acusación popular liderada por Hazte Oír tuvo que rebajar su petición de condena de 24 a 13 años de prisión, y ahora responden las defensas. La Universidad Complutense de Madrid, que está personada como perjudicada, reclama 113.000 euros. La Fiscalía, por su parte, ha avanzado que solicitará la absolución tanto de Begoña Gómez como de Cristina Álvarez.

World.title: Que nadie se quede fuera
World.content:
La voluntaria Pepi Solana durante una clase de refuerzo a niños en en la asociación Juniors en el barrio de la Viña (Cádiz), en uno de los programas de acción social de CaixaBank.

Personas mayores activas, emprendimiento local, población que vive en el entorno rural... La sociedad cambia y los servicios financieros se adaptan a colectivos con las mismas necesidades que el resto. El compromiso social de CaixaBank pone el foco en la atención al cliente esté donde esté y la integración de personas en situación de vulnerabilidad

“Son cuestiones básicas que pueden cambiar la vida de una persona”. Así resume Pepi Solano (San Fernando, Cádiz, 58 años) lo que supone aprender conceptos y poder adoptar costumbres de economía básica entre los más jóvenes. Solano, a través de Voluntariado CaixaBank, participa desde 2015 en distintos programas sociales en Cádiz, desde apoyo escolar hasta acompañamiento a personas mayores, y este tipo de consejos los imparte a alumnos de 4º de la ESO. Por ejemplo, que el ahorro comienza si guardan dos de los cinco euros de su paga, o que “las tarjetas no se prestan a nadie”. “Alguno se queda con cara de: ‘¿Cómo?’. Otros directamente se justifican: ‘Bueno, es que es mi amigo...’. Y rápidamente les tienes que decir que eso no se hace”, describe.

La visión del voluntariado que da Solano es uno de los espejos del propósito social de CaixaBank: conseguir que cada uno transforme su realidad con algo de ayuda. El banco, desde sus inicios en 1904 como Caja de Pensiones para la Vejez y de Ahorros de Cataluña y Baleares, se creó con el objetivo de que la población pudiera ahorrar, y hoy mantiene actualizado su compromiso social. Entre sus principales acciones están las de adaptarse a las necesidades de las personas en situación de vulnerabilidad (canaliza ayudas a más de 5.000 entidades sociales en todo el país a través de la colaboración con la Fundación “la Caixa”), facilitar a las personas mayores la gestión de su dinero, llegar a aquellas zonas rurales más aisladas o ayudar en el impulso a los emprendedores que lo necesitan. Como la propia entidad afirma, sus productos financieros se conciben para ofrecer oportunidades, favorecer la integración y fortalecer el bienestar colectivo.

Los ejes de CaixaBank que modelan una banca más humana Accesibilidad, también en zonas rurales Sus 4.200 oficinas dan cobertura en más de 3.700 municipios de toda España, con una presencia en el 99% de localidades con más de 5.000 habitantes, según datos de CaixaBank. La entidad también está presente en las zonas rurales: Es el único banco en 460 pueblos, y sus oficinas móviles llevan servicios financieros a más de 1.420 localidades sin sucursal bancaria o con acceso limitado en las que residen más de 630.000 personas.



Fotos: CaixaBank Acompañamiento personalizado a personas mayores CaixaBank ha desarrollado un protocolo de atención especial para las personas mayores, que incluye la formación de más de 30.000 empleados en atención preferente, más de 11.000 cajeros de uso fácil, horario de caja sin restricciones, adelanto del pago de pensiones al día 24 y asistencia personal por teléfono y WhatsApp con más de 600 agentes. La oferta la completa su programa Generación+, con servicios como la planificación del ahorro, el acompañamiento para la jubilación o la gestión de la prestación de dependencia. Inclusión social para grupos vulnerables La entidad financiera ofrece servicios personalizados para colectivos en situación de vulnerabilidad. Unos 400.00 clientes tienen cuentas de pago básicas y la entidad tiene oficinas, cajeros y plataformas digitales accesibles y fomenta el lenguaje económico claro. Para las personas con discapacidad auditiva, ha desplegado en toda su red el servicio de videointerpretación en lengua de signos SVisual, que permite a este colectivo acceder a la información bancaria de manera autónoma. Un sostén para los emprendedores El banco social del Grupo CaixaBank, MicroBank, cerró 2025 con cerca de 280.000 operaciones por más de 2.400 millones de euros. Sus funciones han favorecido el emprendimiento, la creación de empleo y la igualdad de oportunidades. Esta propuesta se suma a otras iniciativas, como los Premios EmprendeXXI para startups de alto potencial; la imaginPlanet Challenge de imagin para jóvenes con proyectos de sostenibilidad; o el programa Tierra de Oportunidades, que fija población y crea empleo en el entorno rural para hacer frente al reto demográfico.

Esta idea tan amplia de inclusión real se traduce directamente a pie de calle en medidas concretas, como que la mayor parte de las oficinas de CaixaBank estén diseñadas para ser accesibles físicamente, con rampas, puertas automáticas y mostradores adaptados para personas con movilidad reducida. Sus cajeros también están adaptados a personas con discapacidad, con opciones como un teclado en braille y navegación guiada por voz para personas como problemas visuales, menús fáciles de entender y pantallas con alto contraste. Con estas medidas, CaixaBank trata de establecer un equilibrio entre el negocio y diferenciarse con la dimensión social.

Su consejero delegado, Gonzalo Gortázar, sostiene que “CaixaBank es una entidad con valores profundos, capaz de tener éxito en el negocio y, al mismo tiempo, aportar una dimensión social fundamental”. Y añade: “Tenemos una manera de hacer banca diferente, centrada en la inclusión financiera, tanto por nuestra presencia territorial, con una red extendida por toda España, como por nuestro compromiso en no dejar a nadie atrás”, explica el CEO del banco.

Una nueva visión de las personas sénior

A veces, son las oficinas las que llegan a los usuarios, y no al revés. El servicio de las 32 oficinas móviles de CaixaBank permite realizar las operaciones bancarias más habituales (sean o no clientes de la entidad) a casi 630.000 personas que viven en más de 1.420 pequeñas poblaciones sin oficina bancaria o con restricciones que limitan el acceso a los servicios financieros. Casi 270 de estas localidades tienen menos de 100 habitantes. Estas oficinas sobre ruedas suponen un importante impulso a la inclusión financiera, recorriendo cada mes más de 75.000 kilómetros en 17 provincias de siete comunidades autónomas.

Hay un colectivo que se ve más beneficiado con el servicio de oficinas móviles: el 70% de usuarios de oficinas móviles son personas de más de 65 años. Cuatro de cada 10 clientes de este segmento en España confían en CaixaBank, según datos de la entidad. Y es probable que la cifra aumente, si se tiene en cuenta que dentro de 50 años el 30,9% de las personas residentes en España tendrán 65 años o más, según el Instituto Nacional de Estadística (INE).

Para adaptarse a esta evolución demográfica, CaixaBank ha rediseñado su propuesta de valor. La entidad trata de fortalecer a este grupo de edad que, más o menos activo, no solo necesita que se le pongan las cosas fáciles ―por ejemplo, a través del protocolo de atención especial―, sino también productos adaptados a la mayor longevidad.

A través de programas como Generación+, CaixaBank proporciona asesoramiento patrimonial, apoyo en la dependencia y soluciones financieras adaptadas a las necesidades de cada etapa vital. Ramiro Elena

A través de programas como Generación+, CaixaBank ofrece asesoramiento integral del patrimonio, ayuda en la tramitación de la dependencia, rentas vitalicias para complementar la pensión sin renunciar a la herencia o se encargan de elaborar testamentos y garantizar que se respeten las voluntades. Su enfoque se basa en la diversificación y en moldear las soluciones al ciclo vital de cada cliente, de manera que la planificación financiera evolucione con sus necesidades (y con sus circunstancias). El objetivo, señalan desde la compañía, es combinar eficiencia fiscal, liquidez, rentabilidad y protección.

La apuesta por considerar a este grupo demográfico como personas activas también se respalda en el emprendimiento sénior, y los microcréditos pueden servir de incentivo. Durante 2025, MicroBank, el banco social de CaixaBank (como ellos lo denominan), financió 2.303 proyectos de emprendimiento liderados por personas de 55 años o más, por un valor total de 36,5 millones de euros. Su importe medio se ha situado en cerca de 15.900 euros: la mayoría (el 77%) solicitó financiación para ampliar su negocio, mientras que el 23% lo ha hizo para abrir nuevas iniciativas empresariales.

Emprendedores rurales, al frente

Esos microcréditos del banco social llegan, además, a otras generaciones, y el año pasado destinaron financiación principalmente a cinco sectores: restauración, transporte por carretera, belleza, albañilería y reformas y talleres mecánicos. La estrella fue el primero, la restauración, que implicó más de la mitad de los 4.477 nuevos negocios que se alcanzaron gracias a la entidad en España en ese periodo de tiempo.

Enfocada en emprendedores rurales con proyectos activos, la entidad bancaria impulsa además el programa Tierra de Oportunidades, que busca fijar población y empleo en la España rural, a través de ayuda económica, formación y acompañamiento. Una de las iniciativas beneficiadas en la última edición fue la empresa Gurevet, en Mezkiritz (Navarra), que presta atención de servicios veterinarios de animales de compañía a domicilio en toda la Comunidad Foral. Al principio, en 2021, Teresa Etxarri (32 años, Mezkiritz, Navarra) empezó sola en su furgoneta adaptada (cuenta un quirófano para hacer cirugías urgentes o sencillas). Con el tiempo, se incorporó su hermana como auxiliar y gerente y, desde hace un año, cuentan también con otra veterinaria porque abrieron una clínica.

Mi hermana y yo somos de un pueblo muy pequeño, del Pirineo navarro. Los servicios llegan en furgoneta: el panadero, el carnicero, el pescadero... y dijimos: ¿por qué no también la veterinaria? Es una forma de poder ayudar a diferentes zonas. Teresa Etxarri, veterinaria y empresaria de Gurevet (Mezkiritz, Navarra)

Pero la cualidad de sus servicios reside en que Etxarri se desplaza hasta los hogares para vacunar, realizar consultas o chequeos o aplicar cuidados paliativos, entre otras cosas, sobre todo a perros y gatos. “Hay cosas que empiezan siendo algo leve que, si no tuviésemos este servicio, se quedarían sin atender y acabarían siendo cosas graves; la gente es más consciente de tener las vacunas al día o de esterilizar a sus animales”, detalla. La relación con el cliente es más cercana, se basa en la confianza, y ellos responden. “Queremos dar a las zonas rurales el mismo servicio que tendrían en una ciudad”, incide.

Gracias a la aportación de CaixaBank, la emprendedora consiguió un apoyo no solo económico, sino también visibilidad: “Por ejemplo, nos ayudaron a hacer vídeo en condiciones para redes sociales. La verdad, es que nos han ayudado a coger confianza con determinados clientes”. En definitiva, Tierra de Oportunidades les sirvió de “acompañamiento y de difusión”.

La veterinaria Teresa Etxarri (derecha), atiende a un perro dentro de su furgoneta. Cedida por CaixaBank

La “inquietud de ayudar”

La vocación de ayudar es una especie de “inquietud” que se lleva dentro siempre, califica Pepi Solano. “Sabes que quieres hacer algo, pero no sabes cómo ni dónde”, describe. Esta andaluza ha podido desplegar esa energía de la mano de Voluntariado CaixaBank. “Por mediación de su voluntariado, ellos enseguida te localizan y te dicen: ‘Pepi, mira, nos están pidiendo ayuda en tal sitio’. Y yo respondo: ‘Ahí estamos”.

Mi marido, que trabajaba en CaixaBank, sabía que yo tenía la inquietud de probar un voluntariado y me enseñó las oportunidades que daba el banco. Nos metimos juntos a ayudar y, desde hace más de 10 años, colaboro con distintas entidades sociales. Pepi Solano, colaboradora en proyectos de Voluntariado CaixaBank en Cádiz

Desde hace más de una década ha participado en talleres de cocina online para jóvenes migrantes, actividades para niños con discapacidad, visitas a las residencias de mayores o apoyo escolar a chicos de un barrio vulnerable de Cádiz. “Algunos de los que ayudé de pequeños ya son mayores de edad y seguimos en contacto. A veces, vamos a tomar un café o me llaman, me van contando su vida”, describe, con cariño. La han acompañado (se han contagiado de su entusiasmo) su marido, sus dos hijas y algunos amigos. Todos han tenido la misma sensación: “Siempre sales de allí feliz y piensas: esto hay que repetirlo”.

Como ellos, un total de 24.000 personas participaron en actividades de voluntariado en 2025, más de 19.000 eran empleados ―el 45% de la plantilla―. Además, entre mayo y junio de este año se ha celebrado la cuarta edición del Mes Social que, gracias a la colaboración de unas 1.400 entidades sociales locales, ha beneficiado a más de 155.000 personas en situación de vulnerabilidad y ha permitido impulsar más de 4.600 actividades solidarias en todas las comunidades autónomas. Solano afirma que las personas a las que ayuda responden con rotundidad: “Siempre te dan mucho más de lo que tú das”, asegura.

World.title: Tengo tres trasteros en un edificio en el que no resido. ¿Pueden los vecinos negarse a darme una copia de las llaves del portal?
World.content:
Pregunta. Tengo tres trasteros que compré mientras estaba de alquiler en un edificio. Me fui de ese piso y perdí la llave del portal, fui a la comunidad a pedir otra y me la niegan porque dicen que no soy propietaria ni estoy alquilada en ningún piso de ese edificio. ¿Tengo derecho a tener una llave del portal para poder acceder a los trasteros? J. García

Respuesta. Si es propietaria de tres trasteros en ese edificio tiene derecho a acceder a ellos. La propiedad de un trastero lleva aparejada una cuota de participación en los elementos comunes del edificio, de conformidad con la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal y, por lo tanto, una obligación de contribuir al mantenimiento de los gastos comunes.

Ello significa que, en la medida en que el portal, las escaleras, los pasillos o el ascensor sean necesarios para acceder a los trasteros, tiene derecho a utilizarlos en las mismas condiciones que el resto de los propietarios. Por lo tanto, la comunidad de propietarios no puede negarle un medio de acceso alegando únicamente que no es titular de una vivienda en el inmueble. Si el acceso a los trasteros únicamente puede realizarse a través del portal, la comunidad debe facilitarle una llave sin perjuicio de que pueda repercutirle el coste de la copia o del dispositivo, si ello está previsto o resulta razonable.

Lo recomendable es presentar una solicitud por escrito al presidente o al administrador de la comunidad acreditando su condición de propietaria mediante una copia de la escritura o una nota simple registral. Si, pese a ello, la comunidad persiste en su negativa, podría estar vulnerando el derecho al uso y disfrute de su propiedad, lo que le facultaría para reclamar judicialmente el reconocimiento de su derecho de acceso y exigir el cese de una actuación que le impide disfrutar de sus trasteros en condiciones normales.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Calpe, renovarse a la sombra del Peñón
World.content:
Además de por su paquidérmica y famosa formación rocosa, la ciudad alicantina merece una visita por las Salinas, el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina y una gastronomía en la que destaca la gamba blanca

Siempre que vuelvo a Calpe (cosa que pasa menos veces de las que querría) me sorprende y me exalta la colosalidad irredenta del peñón de Ifach. Esta paquidérmica protuberancia, ocasionalmente envuelta de nubes como la aureola de un santo, parece siempre a punto de saltar sobre el mar, que le es refugio y no abismo. Y, en efecto, ese tosco poliedro es una prolongación de la cordillera Bética, que se sumerge audazmente bajo las olas para dirigirse a Mallorca. Un tótem prodigioso, una ofrenda desmesurada y, quizás, en su priapismo cósmico, un tabú.

El parecido de esta gran roca con la de Gibraltar ha propiciado teorías diversas, normalmente descabelladas pero siempre amenas. Que Gibraltar e Ifach estuvieron unidos físicamente antes de abrirse el Estrecho es una de esas leyendas. Sí que es cierto que, en la antigüedad, el nombre Calpe designaba al peñón de Gibraltar. En un tiempo tan dado a las supercherías y otros golpes en el pecho de la ignorancia suprema me extraña que nadie haya propuesto que este titánico pedrusco pueda ser una ofrenda a algún dios. O quizás un monumento obra de los extraterrestres, como algunos partidarios desaforados del delirium tremens dicen que son las pirámides de El Cairo. Ajeno a todas nuestras elucubraciones, el Peñón sigue aquí, como el dinosaurio de Monterroso: una erección ciclópea, una insurgencia calcárea insolente y retadora, un desorbitado capricho morfológico.

Con este atractivo paisajístico, la ciudad alicantina necesita poco más para atraer visitantes. Y, sin embargo, las calidades de su oferta no dejan de aumentar. Ya se sabe que desde hace décadas recibe un elevado número de turistas extranjeros (muchos, hoy, residentes permanentes), principalmente procedentes del Reino Unido, Alemania, Bélgica y los Países Bajos. Este carácter cosmopolita no le ha hecho perder personalidad. Su casco antiguo con restos de los muros medievales resulta muy evocador, con sus calles estrechas, sus plazas tradicionales y edificios históricos como la iglesia Antigua (del siglo XV) y el Torreó de la Peça (baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla). A esto une una variada oferta de restauración y comercio, amén de las actividades náuticas de su puerto deportivo o el senderismo que puede practicarse en el Peñón.

Torreó de la Peça, baluarte defensivo de la antigua muralla, en Calpe. TONO BALAGUER (GETTY IMAGES )

Entre sus atractivos naturales están las Salinas y el conjunto arqueológico Baños de la Reina. Las Salinas son parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. La explotación de sal se cerró en 1988, así que, clausurada la industria, ha florecido la biodiversidad: allí viven 173 especies diferentes de aves. En cuanto a Baños de la Reina, es un yacimiento arqueológico, anexo a las Salinas, donde debió vivir un noble romano. Además de su lujosa villa, incluye una piscifactoría (donde se llevaba a cabo la salazón del pescado), unas termas, una noria y cuatro aljibes.

Esta antigua actividad pesquera ha llegado hasta la actualidad. A diferencia de otros destinos muy orientados exclusivamente al turismo, Calpe ha mantenido una flota de arrastre significativa. Su puerto alberga una de las lonjas más importantes de la zona, donde se realiza la ancestral e imprescindible subasta del pescado y el marisco locales.

Vista de Las Salinas, parte de una antigua bahía cerrada por una barrera de dunas que unía el Peñón con el continente. Jacek Krysciak ( GETTY IMAGES )

Su gran tesoro marino es la gamba blanca. Aunque la gamba roja de su vecina Dénia tiene una fama más consolidada, las propiedades de la blanca (su dulzura natural, su carne firme y sedosa, el suave aroma a yodo acabada de pescar) no son precisamente despreciables. Desde 2025, este fruto del mar goza de marca de calidad propia. Según el Portal Agrari de la Generalitat, ese año se capturaron y comercializaron más de 1.600 toneladas de gamba blanca en la Comunidad Valenciana (casi toda en la costa de Alicante). Es la tercera especie local en número de capturas (después del boquerón y de la sardina): genera 13,5 millones de euros, superando a la gamba roja y al boquerón, que hace años lideraban el ránking marino. Y ahora ese tesoro, que era cuantitativo, ha empezado a volverse cualitativo.

Parte de los Baños de la Reina, un yacimiento arqueológico anexo a Las Salinas. Teo Moreno ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Es precisamente en la gastronomía donde Calpe ha afinado más su renovación en los últimos tiempos. La versatilidad culinaria de ese prodigioso crustáceo ha llamado la atención de los chefs más reputados de la zona. Dos ejemplos: los restaurantes Onami y Beat.

Marisco fresco expuesto en el puerto pesquero de Calpe, Alicante. Manoli Perez ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Onami abrió este pasado mes de junio en el hotel AR Diamante Beach. Este imponente establecimiento ya disponía de otros dos locales de restauración, el Audrey’s (el primer local con estrella Michelin de Calpe) y el Amas. Onami comparte chef con Amas: Diego Laso. La diferencia entre los dos —inspirados ambos en la cocina japonesa— es que en Onami no hay carta y se come en la barra. El servicio está concebido como un menú degustación al estilo kaiseki-ryori: la forma más refinada y tradicional de la alta gastronomía japonesa. Onami es un juego de palabras entre ona (ola, en valenciano/catalán) y nami (mismo significado en japonés). Esto da la medida de su filosofía: ofrecer un diálogo entre la cocina valenciana y la nipona. De aquí la receta de gamba blanca en Amas (curada con sake y servida con crema inglesa y algas de Galicia), o el nigiri de este mismo crustáceo en Onami, simplemente pelado y servido sobre arroz.

Segundo ejemplo: el restaurante Beat (una estrella Michelin), ubicado en The Cookbook. Este hotel acaba de renovarse en profundidad. En Beat reina desde hace diez años José Manuel Miguel, el único cocinero valenciano que ha obtenido estrellas Michelin en Francia y en España. Si en Onami dialogaban la cocina local con la nipona, aquí la fusión está protagonizada por lo valenciano y lo francés. El gran referente de José Manuel Miguel es Paul Bocuse, emblema de la nouvelle cuisine gala. El bogavante lo cocina a la manera de la Salade de homard à la française de Bocuse, pero la gamba blanca no requiere mayor transformación: su hechizo radica en la ausencia de cocción.

Con todo esto ya se puede volver a visitar Calpe y saborear algo más que la siempre imponente vista de su Peñón. Tradición y modernidad, lo llaman.

World.title: Amsterdam travel app leaked users’ personal data for months
World.content:
Polarsteps, an Amsterdam-founded travel app used by more than 23 million people, left users’ photos, locations and home addresses reachable by anyone through an unsecured data feed – including trips put on private mode – and had known about the flaw for months, an investigation by Follow the Money (FTM) has found.

The investigation found that anyone could connect to the free app’s data feed and pull users’ names, 230 million photos and videos, and 1 billion GPS locations from nearly 2 million trips – enough to plot journeys on a map and follow many of them close to real time.

More than a million of those trips had been shared only with followers. Even accounts set fully to private gave away who a user followed, who followed them and which device they logged in from. And once FTM held the link to someone’s trip, removing it as a follower changed nothing.

Home addresses were among the most sensitive details exposed. FTM pinned down dozens from the exact location saved inside users’ photos – a shot of packed suitcases taken at home, for example, and worked out many more from the spots people returned to each night.

That photo-location data appeared nowhere in Polarsteps’ privacy policy, and was missing from the file the company released when FTM asked to see its own records.

A year’s warning

The problem was first flagged last year by a French cybersecurity researcher who said Polarsteps told him it already knew what was happening. He took his findings to FTM, which said the data stayed exposed for at least six months.

Marc Schuilenburg, a professor of digital surveillance at Erasmus University, called the company negligent, and warned that leaked location data can be used to stalk, harass or threaten people.

The leak was not from a hack – no passwords were taken and no accounts entered. Anyone with basic technical skill could connect to Polarsteps’ servers and scrape the data, with none of the request limits, CAPTCHAs or login walls.

Company response

Polarsteps, which has grown from 1 million users in 2019, said no passwords or accounts were compromised and that it is in contact with the AP.

Chief executive Clare Jones, appointed in 2024, said the company should have caught the problem itself and was working out what went wrong. It has since tightened its systems, and noted that much of the exposed data had been made public by users’ own choice.

The company’s own website warns travellers that sharing location details in real time “can make you a target.” FTM said a second part of its investigation, on dozens of military personnel it tracked to bases and missions at home and abroad, would follow on Saturday.

World.title: Prosecutors hold 32 over Overasselt attack, including two minors
World.content:
Public prosecutors are detaining 32 people on suspicion of murder or manslaughter in connection with the killing of a security guard in Overasselt on Tuesday.

Thirty-four people were initially arrested in the area surrounding the Gelderland village but two were released as there was insufficient evidence to hold them. CCTV footage shows dozens of masked men getting out of a truck outside the property, some heavily armed, before one shoots a man sitting in a car.

They also opened fire on police shortly afterwards, injuring two. Of those arrested, two are minors aged 16 and 17, the rest are men from France, Netherlands, Algeria, Libya, Belgium and Ukraine – all aged between 18 and 32.

Footage emerged online after the attack purportedly by a drugs gang, threatening the resident of the property that was attacked and saying that he had stolen a large quantity of goods from them.

That man, known as Jan G. Jr, has been barred from entering the council around Overasselt for at least two weeks and will not be allowed back to live in the property for at least a year.

He has been linked to the drugs trade before and the house was shot at last year with an AK-47 by a young man from Amsterdam, said to be a drug addict who was paid to carry out the attack. He never named who paid him.

World.title: Public officials among those abusing Jetten online, AD finds
World.content:
A council official, a police employee and a member of the Dutch air force are among thousands of people posting homophobic abuse under prime minister Rob Jetten’s social media messages on X, an investigation by the Algemeen Dagblad (AD) has found.

The paper analysed 45,860 replies to 323 posts sent from the prime minister’s official account during his first six months in office. One in 20 – 2,293 replies – was homophobic, it said.

The abuse appeared under routine posts, from a congratulatory message for Queen Máxima to a post about Amsterdam Pride, and did not depend on the topics Jetten was writing about.

AD identified two recurring forms of abuse. The first was crude slurs and the second, far more common, was a single insinuating question posted in Dutch hundreds of times: “Did you tell them you’re gay?”

Hard to prosecute

Most of the accounts did not belong to anonymous trolls, AD said. The large majority left a single homophobic reply and never returned, and the 10 most persistent accounts together produced less than 6% of the total.

Only a handful of repeat posters could be traced, among them the council, police and air force employees. Marloes van Noorloos, a professor of criminal law at Leiden University, told the paper that the insinuating questions were hard to prosecute as hate speech or criminal insult, because it depends largely on wording and context.

Civil servants, she said, could face disciplinary action under the rules governing public employees.

Jetten’s response

Jetten is the Netherlands’ first openly gay prime minister, and has said he files a police report every week over the abuse he receives about his sexuality. At the WorldPride conference last month he said big social media companies were “barely moderating content for hate speech”.

X’s own rules prohibit attacking users over their sexual orientation, but the company has taken little action, according to AD.

Dutch acceptance of homosexuality has stalled after years of progress. Jetten has said the Netherlands needs to get back on track and return to the top 10 countries for LGBTQI+ rights, from where it fell to number 13 after 2018.

World.title: Farmers face livestock cuts as nitrogen plan falls short
World.content:
Dutch farmers are still facing a compulsory cut in the number of animals they can keep as livestock, after the government’s environmental assessment agency found the cabinet’s nitrogen plan would fall just short of its own 2035 target.

The agency, PBL, assessed the €20 billion nitrogen plan at the cabinet’s request and called it an important step that could bring the farming emissions target within reach.

But it found the measures worked out so far leave a gap, and that an across-the-board cut of 5% to 10% in farmers’ livestock rights, the permits that cap how many animals a farm may hold, is still needed.

The coalition has always said that a blanket cut is a last resort, to be used only if the targets are missed in 2035. Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen called it an “emergency brake” on Friday and “a no-go for the cabinet.”

Farmers must reduce ammonia emissions by 42% to 46% by 2035, against 2019 levels, under the package agreed in June. PBL expects the herd to shrink further regardless as farms adapt to those rules, with some businesses forced to close.

The agency was more positive about the plan’s benefits for the environment, but warned the nitrogen problem will not just disappear. On more than half the area of the most sensitive protected sites, deposition is still expected to breach the critical threshold in 2035.

Nature groups called the plans the minimum needed to start repairing decades of damage. The farmers’ party BBB and the farm lobby LTO said the extra cut was unacceptable, though LTO is staying at the table to negotiate the rest of the package.

World.title: Dutch soil scientist wins Ig Nobel for burying 1,000 underpants
World.content:
A Dutch scientist has won the Ig Nobel prize for conducting a study that involved burying around 1,000 pairs of underpants and digging them up two months later.

Marcel van der Heijden, a soil scientist at the University of Zurich, shared this year’s Ig Nobel for soil science with three colleagues. The annual prizes, a parody counterpart to the Nobels, reward research that “first makes people laugh and then makes them think.”

Volunteers buried identical cotton underpants across more than 25 countries, then dug them up after two months and recorded what was left. The more the fabric had rotted, the healthier and more biologically active the soil.

“Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” van der Heijden said in a statement, adding that healthy soil was crucial for fertility and for the wider ecosystem.

This year’s ceremony was held in Zurich, the first time it has taken place outside the US after more than three decades in the country.

Organisers said they could not in good conscience ask winners or visiting journalists to travel to the US this year, a decision widely assumed to be down to American immigration policy. Next year’s event will be in Antwerp.

Dutch researchers are Ig Nobel regulars. According to broadcaster NOS, they have won 22 times since the first ceremony in 1991, including last year’s award for showing that a drink can improve people’s foreign-language skills.

World.title: Dutch road traffic CO2 falls for first time since pandemic
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Emissions from road traffic in the Netherlands fell in 2025 for the first time since the Covid pandemic, according to figures from the national statistics agency CBS.

Vehicles produced 26.6 million tonnes of CO2 last year, 1.6% less than in 2024 and 2.2% below the level of a decade earlier.

Passenger cars account for almost 58% of the total. Their emissions fell 1.9% on the year even though the distance driven rose slightly. Fully electric cars produce no CO2 while being driven, and around 7.4% of cars on the road were fully electric in 2025.

The saving covers tailpipe emissions only, not the CO2 released to generate the electricity used to charge those cars.

Emissions from vans and lorries, which together make up 40% of the road total, also fell, mainly because commercial vehicles were driven fewer kilometres.

The longer-term picture is more mixed. While car emissions were 9.1% lower than in 2015, those from vans and lorries were higher, as the distance driven by commercial vehicles rose over the decade.

The Netherlands remains well short of its climate law target of a 55% cut in greenhouse gas emissions on 1990 levels by 2030.

World.title: Rents rise 4.4% nationally, Rotterdam hit hardest
World.content:
Rents in the Netherlands rose by an average of 4.4% in July compared with a year earlier, national statistics office CBS has reported, a slower increase than in either of the past two years.

The rise was lower than the 4.9% recorded in 2025 and the 5.4% in 2024, then the steepest increase in more than 30 years. Most landlords in the Netherlands raise rents once a year, in July.

The average covers two different things. Tenants who stayed where they were saw a 3.8% rise but rents rose faster when a new tenant moved in.

Where rents rose most

Among the four big cities, rents rose most in Rotterdam, at 4.7%, and least in Amsterdam, at 4.3%. The Hague saw 4.4% and the city of Utrecht 4.5%. By province, the steepest rises were in Overijssel and Noord-Brabant, both at 4.6%, and the smallest in Friesland, at 4%.

The government sets annual caps on rents for each part of the market, at 4.1% for social housing this year. Rents can still rise above the cap when a home is re-let, or when higher earners are charged an extra €50 or €100 a month.

For private-sector tenants, housing already takes a bigger share of income than for any other group, up to 35% for those entering the market, CBS reported earlier this year.

World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains.
