World.title: Our goal is to build one of the leading modern private banks in Uzbekistan - Interview with Bank ABB Chairman of the Management Board Abbas Ibrahimov
World.content:
–On August 23, the ABB Davr project was officially launched with the participation of the Presidents of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan. The key question many people are interested in now is: when will the bank begin operating under the ABB Davr brand?

–Yes, August 23 became a historic day for us. With the participation of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, and the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, the ABB Davr project was officially launched. The President of Azerbaijan described this event as the entry of a leading Azerbaijani bank into the Uzbek market. For us, this is both a great source of pride and a great responsibility.

We would like to express our gratitude to the Presidents of Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan for their strong support for this project. We would also like to thank the government institutions of both countries that have supported us throughout all stages of the project implementation – including the central banks, the Ministry of Economy of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of the Republic of Uzbekistan, as well as the Committee for Development of Competition and Protection of Consumer Rights of the Republic of Uzbekistan.

Prior to the official launch of the project, all necessary approvals had been obtained and the share purchase agreement had already been signed. At the next stage, in accordance with the legislation and procedures stipulated by the agreement, the legal transfer of ownership rights to the shares will be completed and the relevant changes will be made to the shareholders’ register. Once this process is completed, Bank ABB will become the main shareholder of Davr Bank. We expect this process to be finalized within the next 7–10 days.

Operations under the ABB Davr brand will begin immediately after the completion of the official procedures related to changing the bank’s name. believe that we will see the ABB Davr brand already around October.

–How will the rebranding process take place?

–First of all, we will begin with corporate communications and digital channels. The transition of branches, ATMs, cards, and other physical customer touchpoints to the ABB Davr brand will be carried out gradually. This is exactly the approach outlined in our transition plan.

Our goal is not simply to change the name and signage, but to bring to Uzbekistan the service quality, technologies, innovations, and institutional expertise that stand behind the ABB brand.

–Why did you choose Davr Bank specifically to enter the Uzbek market?

–We were looking for a bank and a platform on the basis of which we could create even greater value. During our search, we carefully studied the history of Davr Bank, its operations, products and services, partnerships, and international relations. We concluded that the bank meets our criteria in many aspects, including its development dynamics, international connections, service network, customer segments, and sustainable high growth rates.

Today, Davr Bank has more than 2 million customers, over 1,800 employees, and 43 branches and service centers in the capital and regions. Its assets exceed 2 billion manats. The bank plays an active role in financing small and medium-sized businesses.

For us, the numbers were not the only important factor. The partnership approach was equally important. At Davr Bank, we saw a strong foundation, an effective business model, a capable team, and a partner that shares our vision and is moving in the same direction. Our views with the existing shareholders and the bank’s team regarding its future and further development priorities were largely aligned.

Davr Bank is not simply a platform for entering a new market. It is an established Uzbek bank with a strong team, customer base, and deep understanding of the local market. Our task is to further develop this foundation by combining Davr Bank’s local market knowledge, team, and existing strengths with Bank ABB’s capital, technologies, and institutional expertise.

–What kind of bank will ABB Davr become?

–Our ambitions are clear. We want ABB Davr to be, first and foremost, an Uzbek bank – one that is close to local customers and entrepreneurs, while at the same time leveraging international experience, modern technologies, and the capabilities of a larger financial group. ABB Davr will be a universal bank serving individuals, small and medium-sized businesses, as well as corporate clients. We see particularly strong potential in such areas as working with small and medium-sized businesses, digital banking, payments, documentary operations, and corporate financing.

At the same time, over time we aim to adapt to the Uzbek market our successfully developed Beyond Banking experience from Azerbaijan.

I would like to emphasize one very important point here. We do not intend to simply transfer Bank ABB’s model in Azerbaijan to the Uzbek market in an unchanged form. Banking is largely a local business. The Uzbek market is large, dynamic, and has its own unique characteristics. Taking this into account, we will adapt our products and services to the needs and behavior of local customers, as well as to the specific characteristics of the market.

That is why the needs of Uzbek customers, market specifics, and the knowledge and experience of the local team are of fundamental importance to us. We will combine Bank ABB’s technologies and expertise with these local insights and competencies.

–What contribution can ABB Davr make to the development of economic relations between Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan?

–More than 470 companies with Azerbaijani capital are registered in Uzbekistan, while Azerbaijan has more than 130 companies with Uzbek capital. These figures alone demonstrate that a strong business ecosystem has already been established between the two countries. As mutual trade and investment continue to grow, the demand of these companies for financial services is also increasing.

ABB Davr can become a financial bridge for this ecosystem. Settlement services, trade finance, documentary operations, as well as financing of new business and investment projects, will create additional opportunities in this area.

At the same time, ABB Davr will first and foremost be a local bank serving the Uzbek market and Uzbek customers. We intend to make a real contribution to the country’s economic development, support entrepreneurship, and particularly foster the growth of small and medium-sized businesses.

–What is the strategic significance of this project for Bank ABB?

–This is the first major step toward achieving the goal of geographical expansion outlined in Bank ABB’s 2026–2028 development strategy. It is especially important for us that we are beginning this journey with our brotherly Uzbekistan.

As the ABB Financial Group, we will now serve around 5.5 million customers, while the potential audience we can reach will increase from approximately 10 million to 50 million people.

However, I would not measure the significance of this project solely by numbers. We are bringing not only capital to Uzbekistan. We are also exporting the knowledge, experience, and solutions that we have developed in Azerbaijan over recent years. We will have the opportunity to apply our digital solutions, artificial intelligence models, risk management approaches, corporate governance practices, and the capabilities we have created in services beyond traditional banking on a much larger scale.

Another strategic advantage is the effect of scale. A larger customer base will allow us to invest more in technology and artificial intelligence. Any digital solution or AI model that we create in the future will be able to benefit millions of customers across a much broader geography, rather than being limited only to Azerbaijan.

There is another very important aspect here. This project will transform not only Davr Bank, but Bank ABB itself. For the first time, we will apply the banking model we have developed in Azerbaijan across a broader geography, acquire new competencies, and learn to operate as a regional financial group.

In this sense, the ABB Davr project – represents the expansion of Azerbaijan’s financial brand, technologies, and banking expertise into a new international market.

World.title: Just like an Italian piazza, this community garden has grown a community
World.content:
Thirty years ago, Mario Minuzzo looked at an overgrown patch of land behind his suburban Adelaide home and saw something special.

"In amongst all of that was vermin and snakes," Mr Minuzzo said.

"The critical thing that started me was when a red-bellied black snake ended up in our house amongst the children on Christmas morning."

Mr Minuzzo sought and was given permission to mow and maintain the land on Aqueduct Reserve at Highbury.

Mario Minuzzo says the community garden is a place for people to connect and share stories. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Growing interest from neighbours led to the establishment of the community garden in 1996.

Today, the 88-year-old is celebrating the legacy of the Pioneer Court Community Garden — a place where generations have grown together.

"I recall standing on the mound thirty years ago and thinking this would make a great community garden," Mr Minuzzo said.

"My heritage is Italian and in Italy, local people often meet in the piazza.

" They gather, walk, share stories, and connect, so my original vision for the garden was to create a sense of community and place — just like a piazza. "

The Pioneer Court Community Garden has bloomed from a hectare-large plot in Highbury into multiple patches growing food for the local area. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

The community garden is home to more than 40 plots, 75 members and almost 400 fruit and nut trees and vines — from pomegranates and bananas, to grapes and macadamias.

It is on just under one hectare of land leased from the Department for Environment and Water and is one of the larger community gardens scattered across the state.

The garden's 'secret power'

Mr Minuzzo wanted the garden to be somewhere people could meet, share stories and connect.

"Australia in my view is one of the best multicultural examples in the world," he said.

Their membership spans generations, cultures and gardening experience, with long-term members sharing their knowledge with people just starting out.

Marina Birch says their members are from all ages and backgrounds. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Chairperson Marina Birch, who took over the reins from Mr Minuzzo in 2022, said she was proud of the garden.

"The secret power of our garden is actually the retired community," she said.

"They keep it going and without them we wouldn't be anywhere.

"But we do have a mix of families with young children, people not quite yet at retirement and a good variety of people from different countries as well."

Laura Fleming says the members have put a lot of effort into the garden. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

Laura Fleming is the garden's youngest member.

"It has been so nice to meet local residents and learn from them and grow things I've never grown before," she said.

"It's clearly a huge legacy for Mario and all the people that have been involved.

"It's not been without a lot of hard work and I'm really grateful that they've put this effort in."

A helping hand

The garden's impact also extended beyond its boundaries.

Members grow produce specifically for charity and donate surplus fruit and vegetables to Pathway Community Centre, which partners with OzHarvest to help feed families in need.

The garden members has also been recognised for its contribution to the community, including winning the 2022 City of Tea Tree Gully Australia Day Award for Outstanding Community Group of the Year.

There are already plans for the next chapter, including a proposed native nursery to help restore areas affected by the giant pine scale infestation.

World.title: Risk v reward: Was the NSW premier's trade mission to India worth it?
World.content:
There was a moment on the streets of Mumbai this week when New South Wales Premier Chris Minns probably wanted to be somewhere else.

As he was squinting into a pair of virtual reality goggles for a photo opportunity, police in Sydney were building a clearer picture of the gang violence which had shocked the city.

The murders of Marco Tapia and Joshua MacDonald both appeared to be cases of mistaken identity, marking a new escalation in the city's gangland war.

In the hours that followed, the premier withdrew from a planned media appearance as part of his trade mission to India.

Rather than being photographed enjoying saffron-infused rice pudding as part of a scheduled food tour, he wisely left that task to his wife Anna and Treasurer Daniel Mookhey.

Mr Mookhey and Ms Minns eating rice pudding during the trip. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Instead, he used the time to get a briefing on the situation from NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon.

The decision was a symptom of his own nagging sense of discomfort at leaving the state on a week-long trip like this one.

Part of that comes from past experience.

But some of it is a product of his own making.

From a distance

Chris Minns at Haji Ali Dargah in Mumbai. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Minns knows the feeling of being thousands of kilometres from home when he is needed at his post.

When the deadly Bondi Junction stabbings occurred in 2024, the premier immediately returned from a family holiday to Japan, which had barely even begun.

The premier was on a four-day visit to India to "attract investment". (ABC News: Nick Dole)

In doing so, he avoided any trace of the criticism that was levelled at former prime minister Scott Morrison, who was pictured holidaying in Hawaii as bushfires took hold back home.

While this week's gangland violence did not match the scale of those crises, it still demanded the government's attention.

Speaking to reporters in Mumbai on Thursday, the premier agreed Sydney's gang war was out of control in the eyes of those affected by it.

However, he said his physical absence was inconsequential.

"We can, for example, speak to the police commissioner on a Teams call," he said.

"That's what I would be doing if I was back in Sydney."

He said his trade mission was equally important.

"We have to be able to walk and chew gum," he said.

Pressure to deliver

The premier took time out of his trip to get a brief about the Sydney gangland shootings. (ABC News)

Significantly raising the stakes of this trip was Minns's mockery of the trade mission his predecessor made.

In 2022 while then-premier Dominic Perrottet was on a visit to Japan, South Korea and India, the Coalition was enduring days of negative headlines over former Nationals leader John Barilaro's appointment to a plum trade role.

At the time, Minns saw an opportunity.

"NSW is embroiled in scandal and Dominic Perrottet seems to be on an extended Contiki tour through south-east Asia," he posted on social media.

"We deserve better."

Current NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane has avoided the temptation to downplay the significance of Mr Minns's trip.

She had expressed her own desire to embark on a trade mission here, so criticising the premier would be hypocritical.

Mr Minns met with Indian Bollywood producer Sajid Nadiadwala during the four-day trip. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

Early in his term, Mr Minns had little appetite for an overseas trip, preferring to focus on bread-and-butter issues like health, education and housing.

Three and a half years in, he is convinced that face-to-face meetings can help build momentum in the trading relationship.

"The Indian economy is the fastest-growing major economy in the world and they want what NSW has," he said.

"But we've got to work at it."

Was it worth it?

Before he flew home on Friday, Minns met with Indian Bollywood producer Sajid Nadiadwala at a studio, announcing that three films would be shot in NSW, including a sequel to the 2007 film 'Heyy Babyy'.

Earlier in the trip, the government signed a deal to provide state-owned traffic management technology to Indian firm, HCLTech.

The premier also launched Western Sydney University's India campus and held a series of meetings aimed at boosting investment in the state's critical minerals.

Mr Minns visited a Bollywood studio. (ABC News: Nick Dole)

However, there were no deals with Indian airlines to secure direct flights to Western Sydney airport.

And tourism leaders repeatedly told the premier that Australia's visa process was frustrating for Indian tourists, restraining growth in that sector of the market.

The new face of 'disorganised crime' Young, cheap and dumb. Sydney's crime bosses are hiring teenage help, but it is leading to tragic consequences.

While the trip was focused on trade, Mr Minns would be hoping to take a political dividend from this visit.

As debate over immigration rages, Labor hopes voters, particularly those in Western Sydney, remember his enthusiastic embrace of the India-NSW relationship.

If he wins an election in March, the once travel-averse premier could soon be on a plane again.

World.title: What are the World Nomad Games and why are Australians competing?
World.content:
The horse is already moving when Sezim Jumabekova draws her bow.

She has three targets to hit before the track runs out.

She grips the horse with her thighs, twists at the waist, and shoots.

Ms Jumabekova, 29, from Kyrgyzstan, has been riding competitively for only three years.

"I've fallen off many times and torn my clothes learning new tricks," she said.

Sezim Jumabekova tries out new tricks ahead of the opening ceremony. (Supplied: Sezim Jumabekova)

Despite being a relative newcomer to the sport, she is competing in horseback archery in the World Nomad Games from August 31 to September 6 in Kyrgyzstan.

Kyrgyzstan launched the World Nomad Games in 2014 as a stage for the traditional sports and cultures of Central Asia's nomadic peoples.

What began with 20 countries and 10 traditional sports has grown, in just over a decade, into an international competition of about 100 countries competing across 43 events.

Repackaging heritage as sport

An eagle hunter, also known as berkutchi, competes. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

Some of the sports are obscure outside the region, like eagle and falcon hunting and Kok-boru, where a horseback team wrestles for a sheep.

"It's like AFL and the NRL here in Australia, but on horseback," said Ahmed Kharat, captain of the Australian team competing in archery events in this year's games.

Many of the sports have cultural significance and local audiences.

Eagle hunting on command traces back to the Mongol conquests of the 12th and 13th centuries.

Falconry is a traditional sport with hunting assisted by Taigan hounds. (Reuters: Pavel Mikheyev)

Other events trace a long lineage.

An 11-kilometre horse race is among some of the equestrian events that have a rich history in neighbouring Mongolia and Kazakhstan.

Another is Er enish, a traditional Kyrgyz horseback wrestling sport.

The team from Kazakhstan unseated opponents to win gold in both the 60-kilogram and 70-kilogram categories this year.

Two teams compete in Kok-Boru, throwing a stuffed sheepskin into a goal for points. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

There are several other competitions competed on foot.

One times how quickly teams put up a yurt, a traditional portable nomadic dwelling used by nomadic families moving between pastures.

In another event called Ordo, teams use sheep knucklebones to flick opposing pieces from a marked ring.

Eagle hunting dates back to the Mongol Empire days. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

From Soviet torpedo factories to Insta-stan famous

The World Nomad Games is more than entertainment.

Regional commentators also point to their political and economic purpose.

Kyrgyzstan is a young state, which became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991, building its national identity from its nomadic past.

It was deeply integrated into the Soviet industrial machine, with one of its largest factories producing torpedoes for the Soviet navy.

The 6th World Nomad Games kicked off this week in Kyrgyzstan. (Reuters: Pavel Mikheyev)

When the Soviet Union collapsed, so did those jobs.

"Kyrgyzstan is quite unique as it experienced a lot of outward migration to the countryside after the collapse," said Kiril Nourzhanov, an associate professor in Central Asian Studies at the Australian National University.

"The economy of Kyrgyzstan was hit for six, and it experienced deindustrialisation, so more people began to engage in agriculture, including the traditional nomadic pastoralism," he added.

A service economy has emerged in the gap, and tourism now ranks among the country's most valuable sectors.

Tourism has soared in recent years, with tour companies such as Intrepid Travel reporting a 900 per cent increase in bookings to Kyrgyzstan this year compared to last year.

Delegates from Russia and Iran attended the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan this week. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

Gulshat Rozyyeva, a research scholar from the Australian National University's Centre for Arab and Islamic Studies, called the Games "a major identity booster".

She said it was an opportunity for Kyrgyzstan to appear as more than "one of Central Asia's poor countries".

"It doesn't have the natural resources like Kazakhstan or Turkmenistan," she said.

"But it has mountains, and a horse culture, and so the World Nomad Games are important economically, too, as people book hotels, and support local businesses."

Horse tricks were performed during the opening ceremony. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

The Kyrgyz government has invested heavily in that image: horses grazing on a backdrop of snow-capped mountains and pristine blue lakes.

This year the World Nomad Games double as a diplomatic stage, hosting delegates from Russia, Iran, India, and China at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan's capital, Bishkek.

Ms Rozyyeva said the balancing act was a familiar one for Kyrgyzstan — asserting a distinct national identity while leaning economically on its larger neighbours.

China invests in infrastructure in the country under the Belt and Road Initiative, while migrant workers in Russia send remittances back home to Kyrgyzstan.

A digital revival of an analogue culture

Ms Jumabekova grew up in Bishkek, far from the high mountain pastures traditionally associated with the country's nomadic culture.

She was teased for being a city girl, but was drawn to learning about horses and became a guide leading horseback tours, learning acrobatics and trick riding.

She said she was passionate about rediscovering skills from semi-nomadic life.

"Nowadays young people are interested in the digital world," she told the ABC.

"Each year it gets harder to save our nomad culture, perhaps because it brings in less money."

Participants from the UK take part in a tug-of-war competition. (Reuters:Pavel Mikheyev)

The irony is that the digital world and Instagram videos from tourists may also be helping preserve it.

Australian archer Daniya Aziz, 23, said that these sports haven't just seen a revitalisation in Central Asia.

"I think in the age that we are in, because we're so social media heavy, so technologically dependent, there has been … an urge to sort of disconnect from that," she said.

"There's no better way to do that than through these cultural sports because they have that element of physicality and an element of being outdoors.

Speed yurt assembly is one of the more traditional sports in the games. (AFP: Vyacheslav Oseledko)

" It's a really nice way for us, from diverse backgrounds in Australia, to connect back to that culture identity. "

Ms Aziz said she was attracted to horseback archery for its challenge.

When contestants arrive in Kyrgyzstan, they pick sticks from a hat as part of a lottery and are allocated a horse at random.

"What's really cool about horseback archery is that it's building that connection between horse and archer so that when you are going down a track, you're going down as one unit," she said.

Kyrgyz archer Asel Sadyrova believes these sports also promote aspirations for girls today, building strength and confidence while keeping alive history that may otherwise be forgotten.

Asel Sadyrova is teaching girls in Kyrgyzstan traditional wooden bow archery. (Supplied: Asel Sadyrova)

"Epics and tales passed down preserve our nation, and my grandfather's stories about heroic, courageous women who defend their people from enemies make me remember we are the heroines of the modern age," she said.

"I believe young people want to follow in the footsteps of these heroines."

World.title: Sabalenka interrupts US Open match over cannabis smell
World.content:
Aryna Sabalenka had an unusual interruption during her US Open third-round match, stopping play to ​alert the umpire to a strong smell of cannabis drifting onto Louis Armstrong Stadium court.

The world number one, who secured a 6-3, 6-4 win against Uzbekistan's Kamilla Rakhimova, ​raised the issue during her ‌second service game, pointing out the smell before play resumed.

"Someone is smoking weed," top seed Sabalenka told umpire Eva Asderaki-Moore as she was serving 30-0 up.

"Do you mind? Because it's ‌so strong."

Sabalenka later told reporters she was not objecting to anyone enjoying themselves but pleaded for the smoking to be kept away from the ‌court.

"I was like, 'Guys, you can ​do whatever, you can ‌smoke whatever, you can relax as much as you can, but please not do it around the tennis courts,'" a smiling Sabalenka said.

"It's a bit tricky to handle that smell while you're trying to compete at your best."

The odour of ​cannabis ‌has become a familiar — if unwelcome — feature at Flushing Meadows, with players complaining about the distraction in the past.

While smoking is not permitted inside the grounds, ⁠recreational cannabis is legal for adults over ‌21 in New York.

Smoke from people in the surrounding Flushing Meadows-Corona Park can drift into the tennis complex and ‌on to the courts.

Sabalenka said she had previously smelled cannabis at the tournament but never so strongly during a match, with the wind ‌apparently ​carrying the odour into ⁠the stadium.

"I don't know if it was coming from the crowd or was from the outside because the wind blows it into the stadium," she said.

"I just hope they ⁠are a bit more aware of that stuff."

As her post-match media conference continued, Sabalenka laughed when questions returned to the subject.

"Come ‌on, guys. I ‌think there is nothing else to say about weed," she said.

"I'm just ​asking people not to smoke it next to the tennis court."

Pegula advances to fourth round

Jessica Pegula rallied from behind to beat fellow ​former US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez 1-6, 6-4, 6-3 and make the fourth round.

Third seed Pegula faces Sorana Cîrstea in the last 16 and will need to iron out some of the flaws in ​her game after a sluggish ‌start against Fernandez.

But the American showed the resilience and composure that have made her one of the title contenders.

Back at Arthur Ashe Stadium, where her dream run ended against Emma Raducanu in ‌the 2021 final, Fernandez seized the initiative and rarely allowed Pegula ⁠to find any rhythm early in the contest.

Jessica Pegula moved through to the fourth round after defeating Leylah Fernandez. (Getty Images: Al Bello)

"It was really tough ‌today. I always feel it's hard ​to play her. I ‌never feel comfortable when I play her, even when I have won," said Pegula, who was the 2024 US Open runner-up.

"I was going to have to dig deep. I'm glad I was able to find somewhere there in the second set to turn it around.

"She's a great player, so ​it ‌was really hard. A lot of it revolves around my serve. My serve percentage was pretty bad."

Romanian 16th seed Cîrstea, 36, extended her impressive farewell-season campaign with ‌a ​clinical 6-3, 6-3 win over ⁠Italy's 19th-seeded Jasmine Paolini.

Ukraine's ‌Marta Kostyuk, seeded 11th in New York, advanced to the fourth round with a straight-sets 6-3, 6-2 victory over Russian ‌Ekaterina Alexandrova.

In the men's draw, defending champion Carlos Alcaraz underlined his status as the player to beat with a ruthless 6-3, 6-4, 6-1 victory over China's Wu Yibing.

The victory extended Alcaraz's match-winning streak at the majors to 17 following his triumph at Flushing Meadows last year and his Australian Open ‌win in February.

The two-time US Open victor next faces American 20th seed Tommy Paul, who defeated 15th-seeded Alexander Bublik 6-4, 3-6, 6-7 (4/7), 6-1, 6-3.

Meanwhile, Russian seventh seed Daniil Medvedev overpowered Frenchman Arthur Rinderknech with a ​6-4, 6-4, 6-4 victory.

Reuters

World.title: Behind the seven-year fight to get the AFLW off the ground
World.content:
Growing up in Melbourne, Suzie Miller's family was footy mad.

But because there were no girls in the AFL, she felt excluded from the game and boycotted the sport her family loved.

She didn't give it much thought until 2017.

Internationally acclaimed playwright Suzie Miller's Strong is the New Pretty explores the formation of the AFLW. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

"When they finally announced there was going to be a women's league, I thought, 'oh my goodness this is something I never even imagined,'" Miller said.

" I remember as a girl thinking, 'I can't even imagine girls being allowed to play football.' "

The Australian playwright was invited to attend the first grand final of the AFLW on the Gold Coast in a match-up between the Brisbane Lions and the Adelaide Crows.

Leah Kaslar and Sarah Perkins during the first AFLW grand final on the Gold Coast in 2017. (AAP: Dan Peled)

"Women were running out into a green field under a beautiful blue sky and all these little girls were cheering them on, and I just thought 'this is a generational shift,'" Miller said.

"There was just this air of joy throughout the evening, people were crying and laughing".

In awe of the inaugural grand final, Miller went to work interviewing various people involved in the AFLW to get a better understanding of how the league came to fruition.

From that moment, the idea for Strong is the New Pretty was born.

Lions fans Karina Smith and Ashley Lamb 2017 AFLW grand final. (ABC News: Matthew Eaton)

'Passing the baton'

Miller has more than 40 acclaimed plays to her name, including sell-out 'RBG: Of Many, One' international phenomenon Prima Facie and Inter Alia which starred actress Rosamund Pike.

Her new production is a fictional re-imagining of the true events that led to the formation of the women's league and has made its world premiere at the Brisbane Festival.

The production is part of the Brisbane Festival program. (Supplied)

In 2010, a report into the state of the sport commissioned by the AFL recommended the creation of a professional national women's competition by 2020.

The play explores the seven-year battle to turn the idea of a women's league from a dream to reality.

Freshly drafted Brisbane Lions player Ally Anderson was among the first group to take part in the inaugural season of the league.

Ally Anderson has won two AFLW premierships with the Brisbane Lions. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

"Growing up, I never thought I would a professional athlete," Anderson said.

"In that first year I kept thinking this is a one-time thing, I remember at the end of the first season I took so many pictures of the change room, the Gabba and the girls".

At a crossroad, Suzie Miller took the risky path In 2009, Suzie Miller had a choice between becoming a magistrate in Australia or a residency at the National Theatre in London.

Since that first season, Anderson has won two premierships, been the AFLW's best and fairest and is the AFLW's games record holder.

More than just sport

The play's premiere comes in the fourth round of the AFLW's 11th season.

After she finished writing the play, Miller attended an under 9s girls game in Sydney where she witnessed young girls playing with their brothers cheering them on.

The play will be performed in Canberra, Geelong and Sydney. (Supplied)

"Australian rules football might be the great saviour of that great gender debate because these young boys will see these girls running around as strong competitive players, and they'll see them with strong bodies and loud voices," she said.

"They won't grow up thinking of girls as weak or other or not equal to them, and that's what I hope people can take from this play — everyone should get a fair go".

The play tours around Australia, heading to Canberra, Geelong and Sydney next.

World.title: Africa bigger, US smaller as UN votes to adopt a new world map
World.content:
The United Nations General Assembly has voted to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.

Aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the US voted against it and six other states abstained.

The new map — known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection — "is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world", the resolution said.

The new map was supported by 164 countries, while the US voted against it. (AFP)

It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.

Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said: "[Maps] guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions.

"They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation."

The US, however, slammed the resolution, saying such moves are "the reason this institution is losing its credibility".

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems … this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.

'Distorted representation'

The Mercator projection focused on accurate depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses, but their relative sizes were often inaccurate, in part due to the challenge of rendering a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional map.

It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America.

A group of cartographers launched the Equal Earth projection in 2018.

It makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.

Why do most world maps depict north up top? My map of the world displays the southern hemisphere at the top but it's actually not upside-down, writes Gary Nunn.

"Equal Earth preserves the relative surface areas of continents and, as much as possible, shows their shapes as they appear on a globe," one of the cartographers, Bojan Savric, told AFP in 2025.

France — which co-sponsored the resolution in support of the new map — announced Friday that it would abandon the Mercator projection.

"[In that map] the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or south-east Asia, [while] Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

"Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world.

" But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth. "

The initiative comes as France is seeking to improve relations with Africa, particularly in former colonies with which it has prickly ties.

AFP

World.title: Documentary brings stories of 150yo shipwreck to life
World.content:
It has been 150 years since she was wrecked off SA's south-east coast, but the story of the Geltwood is still being told.

The ship came to grief in June 1876 in a storm, described at the time as a hurricane, hit on its maiden voyage from England.

The 31 passengers and crew aboard were presumed to have drowned.

Lyndal Redman's family connection to the Geltwood inspired the documentary. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

The wreck was not found until the 1980s and, more than 40 years later, former local Lyndal Redman brings the tale to the screen.

Ms Redman's connection to the shipwreck is familial. Her father Kym dived on the wreck and used his boat to help recover artefacts from the ship.

"I stumbled across some amazing footage that my dad had filmed back in the 80s," she said.

" I just knew that I needed to do something with it to preserve the story of the Geltwood. "

Artefacts and depictions of the Geltwood are on display in Millicent. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Decades of intrigue and controversy

Millicent local Lisa Braes, who provided historical background on the wreck for the documentary, said while many people knew of the Geltwood, they did not know much about it.

She said because of significant looting and auctioning of parts of the wreck that washed ashore in 1876, artefacts had found their way into many people's lives.

"So many local people have been touched by the story," she said.

" Because of those looters, many people have got wood from the Geltwood in their shearing shed or in the farmhouse. "

Lisa Braes was part of the documentary. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Ms Redman said the controversy, and her familial link, made it a quick documentary to put together.

"I knew there was such history and such shame around it because [of] the looting that happened," she said.

"I knew so much about the Geltwood already that it was quite an easy process for me."

Iain Stewart, Brian Foster and Kym Redman all dove on the Geltwood wreck. (Supplied: Lyndal Redman)

Among the people telling the story of the Geltwood was Rendelsham's Brian Foster, whose father-in-law Mick Galpin discovered the wreck.

"I went down with Mick to have a look at it, just using conventional scuba gear," he said.

"Everyone had heard about the Geltwood Beach, but that was basically all I knew."

Looting of the wreck of the Geltwood is depicted at the Millicent museum. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Preserving, not looting

The divers brought up artefacts from the wreck, many of which are still on display at museums in Millicent and Beachport on the Limestone Coast.

However, contemporary media reporting was not kind to their preservation efforts.

"The local divers were also accused by the Adelaide media of looting the ship," Ms Braes said.

"They felt so embarrassed and ashamed that they could be thought to be looting.

"They were only bringing the things up off the wreck for prosperity."

One of the Geltwood's anchors is on display at the Millicent museum. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Ms Braes said the divers eventually received an apology from the local papers.

"They were in a way honouring the people … that lost their lives," she said.

Ms Redman said the release of the documentary had brought even more artefacts with a connection to the Geltwood to light, even overseas.

"I got an email from a lady in Poland; she said, 'I've just stumbled across this family bible that was from … one of the mates on the Geltwood,'" she said.

"It's amazing that we have this local connection with this history."

The documentary has received strong support from the community. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Huge support for local history

The documentary has struck a nerve with many people across the region, surprising even Ms Redman.

"The first screening we had in Millicent, we had over 280 people," she said.

"It got to the point where we had to put extra chairs out to fill the space.

"The biggest thing for me was just that support from the community — the people that came to see it, the people that came up to me afterwards and said, 'This is an amazing part of our history, and thank you for capturing it.'"

Three unknown sailors and a passenger are buried near the Millicent hospital. (ABC South East SA: Josh Brine)

Mr Foster said he had been very impressed by both the reception and the documentary itself.

"It's good to have it preserved for the future, because we're not going to be here forever, but Lyndal's documentary should be," he said.

" People still associate with the wreck of the Geltwood, and it's remarkable how many people have a story. "

World.title: Jai Arrow's last NRL game was the second of a lifetime
World.content:
The record books will show that Jai Arrow’s last game as a South Sydney Rabbitoh lasted exactly one second.

It was one second not for a career, but for a footballing life as rugby league gave him everything it could, which was everything it had.

This was one second that really mattered in a way a century of Rabbitohs-Roosters matches never could. Their hatred, which flared up later on, felt insignificant.

Normally the NRL defines and destroys itself according to such bitterness but for one second it felt so easy to stow away that pettiness. Never has so much been fit into that second.

There was room for Arrow to run onto the field, to wave to his wife Berina and his daughter Ayla Rae in scenes that summoned an emotion deeper than description can provide.

There was room for former Rabbitoh brothers-in-arms to line the tunnel to cheer him on, lustily and loud, just how he would have wanted it.

Some of them are still playing in the NRL now. Was it really just a year ago they last met Arrow under the bright lights?

South Sydney's rivalry with the Roosters was put aside for the night for Arrow. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

His last two weeks are Arrow’s bravest as he’s brought up his 99th and 100th game for South Sydney following his motor neurone disease (MND) diagnosis, but his final full season was certainly his toughest.

He carried a series of injuries through a rotten Bunnies campaign to earn a place of high honour in winning the club’s player of the year award, leading from the front in many a footballing battle that was lost long before kick-off.

Some of those who lined the tunnel left such fights behind many seasons ago, former teammates and greybeards alike, but they shared a desire to return to give their mate a send off nobody could have ever imagined he'd ever need.

All of them were there when it mattered to slap his back, to shout his name, to make him feel like the player he has always been and was again one last time.

The Rabbitohs ran out big winners in Arrow's final match. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

There was room for Arrow to walk on with hope in his heart and perhaps, just for a second, to hear the sweet, silver song of a lark as the emotion fell down upon him.

There was room for a moment with Cody Walker, who just last week Arrow begged to spray him as he left the field against Gold Coast so things could feel like they used to be.

The brotherhood between the two men was palpable and their embrace was proof deeds are truer than words and that while it’s easy to tell somebody you love them it’s more important, if you can, to try and show them.

There was room for an embrace with Wayne Bennett, who has done so much for so many men in his half century of coaching but has never had to grapple with something like this.

Last week he helped Arrow put his boots on. This week he just held him.

Arrow’s face had been fighting the tears since the moment he hit the lights of the stadium and they welled up when he met Walker but only when he found Bennett’s arms did they flow, nakedly and unashamed, before his coach held his hand and led him to his family.

Arrow's journey has led to an outpouring of emotion across rugby league. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

He sat on the bench for the final 79 minutes and 58 seconds, wrapped in a coat and chatting to Souths players about nothing and everything as he became a footballer for one more second, a second the game will carry forever.

Sport often drifts towards self-importance but this is a case where it can be actually important.

For proof of that rest assured that result of the match, which the Rabbitohs won 50-20, did not mean all that much.

It was a fine enough way to spend a Friday evening. A lot of things happened therein, from tries to bizarre refereeing calls to a face off between Keaon Koloamatangi and Spencer Leniu that Arrow would have loved, especially since South Sydney got the better of it.

None of it mattered as much as the first second, a second that had to happen now if it was to happen at all.

Arrow’s degeneration since his public revelation of his diagnosis in May is already plain to see, even as there is no doubt he will continue on as bravely as a person can.

There is no known cure for motor neurone disease. Even with the assurance that anything that can be done for Arrow will be done, the hardest of days loom.

But on Friday night, there was still some time.

Time for an ancient rivalry to seem small as it was postponed for something that really mattered.

Time for men, some of whom might not know their emotions all that well, to embrace as brothers and bear their hearts to one another, bleeding and raw and full.

Time to feel the love and to show it, to share the things we too often do not say.

Time for the sport that has been such a part of Arrow’s life to give him the greatest gift it could muster, all wrapped up in just one second.

World.content:

A total fire ban is in effect for Sydney on Saturday, with the city set to reach up to 33 degrees just five days into spring.

An extreme fire danger has also been recorded for the region stretching from the coast to Mount Victoria, coming days after Sydney experienced its warmest winter in 167 years of records.

The dazzling beauty of Sydney’s floral displays is arriving earlier each year due to climate change. Steven Siewert

Sydney is forecast to record 27 degrees at noon on Saturday, stretching to 33 degrees by 1pm.

The Bureau of Meteorology said “fresh to strong and gusty northwesterly winds” were due to develop on Saturday morning, and, when combined with the “dry, unseasonably warm conditions”, would lead to elevated fire dangers across the city.

World.title: Kings of the close ones: How the Western Bulldogs found a superpower after losing a superstar
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Kings of the close ones: How the Western Bulldogs found a superpower after losing a superstar Andrew Wu September 5, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Ryley Sanders’ first emotion when he realised Sam Darcy had wrecked his knee was sadness. Once that initial heartache dulled, it soon became apparent to the third-season midfielder how much tougher this season would become for the Western Bulldogs. “When you lose someone of Darce’s calibre, you know that it’s got to be harder to win a premiership,” Sanders told this masthead this week. “We can definitely still contend without him. Obviously, having him would make it more likely.” Ryley Sanders has ridden the ups and downs of the Bulldogs 2026 campaign. Chris Hopkins As far as injuries go, few hit a club harder than an ACL tear to a star key forward. Unlike midfielders, their scarcity makes them nigh on impossible to replace. In the weeks after Darcy’s injury, the Bulldogs had the look of a team that was learning how to play the game again. The Bulldogs may finally have unlocked the formula to not only cope without Darcy but, at times, thrive. It has come in the nick of time.



Luke Beveridge’s men were the flavour of the month in the heady days of March after beating three of last year’s finalists in their first three games. Just weeks later, their season was spiralling amid a four-game losing streak where heavy defeat was compounded by injuries to their spine. Sam Darcy ruptured his ACL against Geelong in April. Getty Images Ruckman Tim English hurt his knee on Easter Sunday against Essendon. Then came the disaster in Geelong when Darcy ruptured his ACL, skipper Marcus Bontempelli hyperextended his knee, midfield heartbeat Tom Liberatore was concussed and key defenders Rory Lobb and James O’Donnell strained hamstrings. The following week, key forward Aaron Naughton landed on his head attempting a speccy. He was fortunate to escape without any structural damage to his neck. “We went through a pretty traumatic period after the Geelong game,” Dogs coach Luke Beveridge said this week.



While fans in the stands mourned the loss of a star player for the year, the human element was felt inside the locker room. “Losing him as a player is very sad, it’s more the person he is,” Sanders said. “He’s such a great guy. He’s such a loving teammate for everyone. He gives the time of day for everyone. He’s such a presence around the club. View post on X “Everyone was a bit just devastated for him because he puts so much work into his craft, and he’s such a competitor. I think the way he was training in the preseason, everyone was like ‘Oh, this bloke’s ready to absolutely explode’. “To lose him was pretty devastating, but it’s good that he’s on the road back now.”



Darcy’s absence on the field was just as keenly felt. From rounds one to six, the 208 centimetre forward was the most targeted Bulldog inside 50m – by a considerable margin – with 26.8 per cent of all entries aimed at him, ahead of Naughton at 17.1 per cent. “Losing Darce up forward was a big one, just because he’s such a presence, and a lot of our entries go to him. So we were kind of learning how to play without him. We had to learn a few different things,”Sanders said. Naughton sent shockwaves through the Bulldogs camp after his frightening fall against Sydney in late April. Fans had their hands to their head in shock as Naughton lay motionless on Marvel Stadium while medical staff carefully loaded him onto a stretcher. “I think most of the boys were a bit rattled,” Sanders said. “You always think the worst. I remember being right there. I was like, “F---, you just hope he’s OK. It was pretty sickening.”



Remarkably, Naughton lined up the following week. It has not affected how he plays. He still throws himself into marking contests. Months down the track, he can see the funny side. “I have watched it back, I’m still flat that they didn’t pay the mark on that one,” Naughton quipped. Aaron Naughton was instrumental to the Bulldogs’ win in the wildcard final against Collingwood. Getty Images There is no player arguably more important to the Bulldogs’ premiership hopes than Naughton, who is contracted until the end of 2032. In Darcy’s absence, he has become the man in attack for the Dogs. Since round seven, Naughton is the target of 27.1 per cent of the Bulldogs’ entries inside 50m. Next are mature-age rookie Will Lewis (21.5 per cent) and youngster Jordan Croft (10.2 per cent).



Though Lewis’s return from injury takes some of the load off Naughton, the Dogs are hardly stacked with proven tall targets. Their loss to North Melbourne four weeks ago prompted a rethink. The Dogs needed to be bold – or fold. It has worked. Their scores in the past three weeks have been their highest across a three-game stretch since rounds one to three when Darcy and Naughton ruled the air. Small forwards Arty Jones, Cody Weightman and Rhylee West have hit form. “I reckon the last three or four weeks we’ve been a bit more aggressive with our ball movement.,” Sanders said.



“We’ve realised we don’t have the kind of big fellas ... especially when it’s only Naughts up there. If Lobby [Rory Lobb] is playing ruck or back or whatever, we have to play different to what we would if we had Darce there or another key forward. “Bevo and all the coaches are really giving us a licence; take the game on because that’s the way we’re going to win. It’s like very uplifting and empowering. “We’ll make mistakes sometimes, but we need to take the game on ... to be damaging. After that North game, everyone kind of went a bit into their shells during the game. “It wasn’t great at the time, it’s been a good blessing in disguise having that game. We actually needed to change, otherwise we might not have made [last week’s] wildcard [final], or if we did, we wouldn’t have been any kind of danger.”



This has been a year of living dangerously for the Dogs, who have won eight from eight in games decided by a single-digit margin. Related Article Analysis

Naked City The night Hawthorn refused to die The footy gods have played a part, Sanders conceded, as seen in Tim Membrey’s miss after the siren last week. But there is more to it than just luck. Every club has a save-the-game mode they train during the year – and the Dogs have done it better than anyone. “It’s very psychological,” Sanders said. “Those close games, it’s almost like Collingwood a couple years ago when it felt like they couldn’t lose those close games. You just get confident. You’re like, ‘Oh boys, we’ve already done this’ because big games or close games at the end you can tighten up. “But I feel like our boys are really relishing being in high-pressure environment.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Boots on the ground as first Australian rescue team arrives in Nepal
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods Boots on the ground as first Australian rescue team arrives in Nepal Michael McGowan September 5, 2026 — 6:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kathmandu: A team of specialist drone operators from New South Wales and Queensland has arrived in Nepal, the first Australian rescue workers to reach the disaster-stricken nation since a deadly tidal wave tore through the country last week. The team, including 10 Fire and Rescue NSW personnel, landed in the capital, Kathmandu, late on Friday night (Saturday AEST) following a plea for help from the Nepalese government. A team of NSW and Queensland drone specialists arriving at the Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu on Friday night. The 15-member team are the first Australian specialist search and rescue personnel to arrive in Nepal since the devastating floods struck last week. Michael McGowan They are part of the federal government’s $11 million humanitarian support package, and will be joined by disaster victim identification officers from the Australian Federal Police on Saturday. Chief Superintendent Jeremy Stubbs from Fire and Rescue NSW said the unit, which included personnel who had experience in the 2011 Christchurch earthquake and Japanese tsunami, would meet with their Nepalese counterparts on Saturday before being deployed to help the rescue effort.



“It’s humbling to have our offer of this type of capability accepted,” he said, as Nepal’s search and rescue effort enters its 10th day. “I think it demonstrates the relationship that Nepal has with Australia, and also the respect that the Australian community has had for Nepal seeing them go through this type of disaster.” Related Article Floods In Nepal, hope gives way to grief. Few are counting on miracles Families of some of the 36 Australians still unaccounted for have expressed angst at the lack of new information from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Two Australians were removed from the list of those unaccounted for on Friday, sparking hope for some families, but DFAT declined to publicly provide their names or specific locations. Speaking outside the Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu late on Friday night, Australia’s ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, defended the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s policy of not releasing details. He said privacy laws limited the agency’s ability to disclose people’s identities.



“We can’t do anything differently,” he said. “We can’t talk about them. We can’t disclose their names. We can’t disclose any details that would make them identifiable,” he said. “They’re quite at liberty to talk to you if they wish to. But we, I can’t do that. Chinese experts (in orange) with specialist equipment arrive at a Nepalese base in Bidur to assist in the effort to rescue the tunnel workers. Kate Geraghty “We generally communicate with the next of kin. Now there are times when people don’t want people, even in their immediate circle, to know where they are.” While the expectation of finding survivors may be fading, there are still glimmers of hope. Nepalese authorities revealed two people had been rescued alive from a hydropower tunnel on Friday, nine days after the floods hit.



Asked whether authorities still had hope of finding the missing Australians alive, Ernst said: “we do”. Related Article Floods This valley was the last known location of a Sydney family. Then a wave 100 metres high hit But Ernst said no decision would be made about where the Australian experts would be dispatched until meeting with Nepalese authorities on Saturday. “They will contribute to the overall Nepali operation, but they’re not a standalone outfit,” he said. “This is part of Australia assisting Nepal, and there’ll be discussions tomorrow about where they deploy and the focus.”



Of the missing Australians, about 15 were part of a tour group undertaking a Hindu pilgrimage up Mount Kailash near the border between Nepal and Tibet when the floods hit. Some of their families have travelled to Nepal and have asked for rescue efforts to be directed to areas where phone pings were detected after the floods. Ernst said Australia had “specifically asked” Nepalese authorities to search those locations. Fire and Rescue NSW Chief Superintendent Jeremy Stubbs (right) with Australia’s ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst (left), speaks to reporters outside the Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu. Michael McGowan “I think we’re getting to the point now where individual areas, pieces of ground have now been searched multiple times,” he said. While he did not believe authorities had struggled to obtain information from telecommunications companies, it was a question of “whether the data actually helps take forward the investigation or not, or the search or not”.



“In some cases, it does. In some cases, it’s inconclusive,” he said. “But it’s a pretty obvious question, and we can be confident we’ll be, you know, making that particular, our particular interest in that location known, as we already have.” Related Article Graphic content

Floods Quicksand and rotting flesh: No words can capture the devastation in Nepal Other Australian help has arrived since the glacial collapse near the border with Tibet sent an inland tidal wave tearing through the country last week, including aid supplies aboard Royal Australian Air Force plane on Wednesday. However, the drone specialists are the first dedicated rescue team to arrive. While there have been questions over why Australians had not deployed sooner Ernst said it was a response to requests from the Nepalese government.



“They don’t need more boots on the ground, so to speak,” he said. They need technology and expertise and that’s part of what our team is.” “Access has been very difficult, so pouring more people into it doesn’t necessarily help with the issue.” The team has arrived with two sets of drones. One, Stubbs said, was small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, and could be used to fly inside damaged homes and tunnels. “The benefit of that is we have a structural engineer with us. That structural engineer will do an assessment of what they can see and determine whether it’s safe for us to go in, but the imagery is fantastic as well,” he said. The larger drone conducts what he called a “broad area assessment” which can quickly provide mapping to the Nepalese government and emergency workers.
