World.title: Not buying it: Melbourne’s build-to-rent boom comes at a high price
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Built by Melbourne developer Gurner Group for $300 million, Beach House bills itself as a place to “live like a millionaire, mortgage free”.

“But for context on that – because that’s a big number – it’s a beautiful apartment,” he says. “I have Albert Park views, beach views, city views, so it’s one of the top-tier apartments.”

The 28-year-old property investor and social media identity sold his apartment and moved into a two-bedroom pad in Beach House, a 297-unit build-to-rent development that towers over St Kilda’s northern gateway.

But Fein didn’t buy the view; he leased it.

On an upper floor in one of St Kilda’s tallest towers, his unit’s floor-to-ceiling windows give an uninterrupted view of the patchwork of open spaces around Albert Park Lake, Middle Park’s multimillion-dollar cottages far below and the curved shoreline of Port Phillip Bay beyond.

Travis Fein’s St Kilda Junction apartment has one of the most seductive views of Melbourne that money can buy.

But some experts say the influx of high-priced housing is doing nothing to ease Melbourne’s rental affordability crisis.

Governments desperate for solutions to the housing crisis have laid out the welcome mat for some of Australia’s biggest builders, including Lendlease, Mirvac, Grocon and Salta, along with operators from the US, Japan and Singapore.

Footloose, financially flush and renting because he wants to, Fein could be a poster child for Melbourne’s burgeoning build-to-rent housing market, which has burst out of the ground and into the city’s skyline with a promise to make renting simultaneously more glamorous and more secure.

“To be able to just use a sauna, ice bath and the whole wellness area and then go home to sleep, you’d need to spend $30,000 to $40,000 to have that at home privately,” Fein says. “You’re not paying for a normal rental. You’re paying for a nice lifestyle, which would cost a shit-ton of money otherwise.”

The opulent complex is part of Melbourne’s first wave of build-to-rent developments, inner-city buildings marketed at lifestyle-conscious renters happy to pay over the odds for a central pad with perks.

Its amenities would not be out of place on a cruise ship: a heated pool lined with banana lounges, dimly lit billiards room, 10-pin bowling alley, cinema, plush private bar with city views, day spa, pet spa.

In the 12 months to July 2026, an estimated 8200 new apartments were built in Melbourne. More than half of them, 4400, were build-to-rent.

In 2021, an estimated 14,000 new apartments were built in Melbourne. Not one was a build-to-rent unit.

One set of numbers, calculated by property advisory firm Charter Keck Cramer, captures the seismic shift under way.

But the model is muscling in on Melbourne’s struggling apartment sector so rapidly that some property analysts predict it will soon grow to be a major player in the rental market.

Meanwhile, some tenants interviewed for this story have said the experience does not live up to the glamorous sales pitch, or justify the high-end rents.

An analysis by The Age of 12 months of rental data from hundreds of listings at 14 completed build-to-rent developments bears out this criticism: they are 20 to 70 per cent more expensive on average than other nearby rental homes.

Plans for a 39-storey CBD office tower on Lonsdale Street were also dumped in August in favour of build-to-rent. Multiple BTR high-rises have just been approved around Arden underground station.

Projects that had previously stalled are being revived and repurposed as build-to-rent: Southbank’s STHBNK, conceived and sold off-the-plan as Australia’s tallest apartment building, were altered last month to a smaller build-to-rent tower .

Several thousand more are in the pipeline, funded by a mix of domestic and foreign institutional capital that is swooping in to take advantage of federal and state tax breaks and friendly planning laws aimed at buoying investment in build-to-rent (BTR) housing.

Build-to-rent towers have sprung up around Docklands, South Melbourne and Southbank, near train stations and tram lines in Kensington and Brunswick, and along the city’s hippest high streets in Fitzroy and Collingwood.

It’s the first time the incipient housing model has overtaken the delivery of conventional (or build-to-sell) apartments in Melbourne, or any other Australian city.

“We drive to a house in Preston We see police arresting A man with his hand in a bag How’s that for first impressions? This place seems depressing It’s a California bungalow in a cul-de-sac.”

“People still need a place to live, and a lot more of them are just being forced to rent.”

“I remember the good old days in 2016 and 2017, when we did 19,000 [new apartments a year]; that’s really the level that we should be building to bring Melbourne back into balance,” Charter Keck Cramer national executive director Richard Temlett says.

But housing analysts warn the boom is a symptom of a dysfunctional housing market in which the annual number of new apartments being built in Melbourne has shrunk to lows last seen in the global financial crisis, while the city absorbs well over 100,000 new residents each year.

It’s a remarkable rise for a sector that barely existed in Australia five years ago.

Melbourne singer-songwriter Courtney Barnett’s 2015 tune Depreston was a forlorn indie anthem for a generation who believed ever-escalating property prices – up more than 400 per cent in Melbourne since 2000 – had denied them the Australian dream.

Renting has historically been a transitional form of housing for most Australians, Dr Tom Alves, acting managing director of the Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute, says. But in the 21st century, a growing cohort of lifelong renters has emerged.

This is particularly so among younger adults. In two generations, Australians aged 25 to 34 have changed from mostly home owners to mostly renters. Ownership rates have also fallen below 50 per cent among low-income Australians aged over 45.

“There obviously always were a bunch of people who were renting for their whole lives, but that was a small group, whereas now it’s become fairly mainstream and not necessarily by choice,” Alves says.

Australia’s steadily declining home ownership rate has “prepared the ground” for the recent boom in BTR housing, Alves says. As home ownership falls out of reach for more people, it offers those on good incomes an opportunity to lease a style of housing they could not afford to buy.

The new wave of BTR accommodation, overwhelmingly leased at a premium, has also emerged at a time when rental affordability is the worst on record, according to federal government advisory body, the National Housing Supply and Affordability Council.

An analysis by The Age of 1223 listings in 14 operational BTR developments, between July 2025 and June 2026, found that median rental rates in those buildings are 20 per cent to 70 per cent more expensive than other apartments in the same suburb.

Beach House, in St Kilda, listed its units at 66 to 70 per cent above St Kilda’s median. Realm in Caulfield North is similarly high-priced, leasing some of its one-bedroom apartments for more than double the suburb’s $455 weekly median.

Even Local, an operator that has sought to differentiate itself as a rare provider of affordable build-to-rent accommodation, listed units in Kensington at 37 to 48 per cent above median for the suburb.

Only one development, Spotswood’s Union Quarter, offered rental accommodation in line with the suburb’s median.

“What’s this doing in terms of affordability? I think very little is the answer. If anything,” Alves says.

Victoria’s Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny visited Preston in late April to officially launch the maiden Melbourne apartment building for BTR brand, WeAreLiving.

WeAreLiving opened its newest build-to-rent development in Preston in April.

Standing on a 16th-storey rooftop BBQ area with a view of the CBD skyline behind her, Kilkenny gushed about the building to an audience of property and superannuation stakeholders being served finger sandwiches, Portuguese tarts and developer-branded cans of carbonated water.

“What a beautiful building it is. The bold red brick as you enter downstairs, I must say it’s one of my favourites,” Kilkenny told the crowd before helping to cut the ceremonial ribbon.

“This is exactly the type of development we want to see: great homes, well-built, secure, in fabulous locations, offering choice and diversity.”

Melbourne’s worsening housing affordability challenge “can only be met by boosting supply”, Kilkenny said, before listing the planning and tax changes she has steered through parliament to stimulate housing development.

“We’re also, of course, really proud to be the nation-leading build-to-rent capital, and we’re going to continue to support build-to-rent developments with 50 per cent reduction on land tax and, of course, the exemption from absentee surcharge.”

The absentee land tax surcharge is blamed by the property industry for driving foreign investors away from Melbourne’s apartment market. BTR buildings are exempt.

WeAreLiving ticks all the high-amenity boxes of Melbourne’s BTR boom. The building’s handsome red brick ground floor and basement levels include a gym, sauna, steam room and cold plunge pool, and a bookable dining room.

The building adds a splash of style to the cluster of grey high-rise apartment buildings that have been wedged into the narrow triangle of land between gentrifying High Street and the route 86 tram corridor on Plenty Road.

Rental units range from $545 a week for a studio apartment to $1390 for a three-bedroom townhouse, putting the development at the top of the range for Preston.

The building does not include any affordable housing.

This omission was a calculated decision. To do so would jeopardise the returns of the 1.2 million Aware Super members who have financed the project, one of its developers said.

“Our starting position here was a return for Aware and return for their members,” Barings Real Estate Head of Residential Warwick Dowler said. “So, from our perspective, that’s number one. To hit that minimum return hurdle here it had to be market rent.”

The project was financed with the assistance of a 50 per cent concession on land tax.

The government has established a four-month, accelerated approvals timeline for projects that include at least 10 per cent affordable housing. But Dowler said this inducement would do little to tackle the level of unmet need for lower-cost rental housing.

“Quite honestly ... if [the government] want to see more affordable product, they need to look at subsidy programs,” he said.

Not chicken feed

Monday afternoon is Sasha Sheko’s rostered time to feed and water the four resident hens at 15 Thompson Street, a 197-room build-to-rent development run by Assemble in Kensington.

“I’m so inner-north I’m blanching kale stems to take to my chickens,” Sheko says.

Sasha Sheko enjoys the communal aspect of build-to-rent, but has been disappointed in the service standards. Ruby Alexander

Sheko moved into a two-bedroom apartment in Thompson Street last year, saying a wistful goodbye to their old CBD apartment, where they paid a private landlord bargain-basement rent of $440 a week.

The new home is no bigger but is more modern and has communal amenities: including a common room where new friendships have been made, and a rooftop basketball court they almost never use. It costs $605 a week.

Sheko says it’s decent value for the area, although they have been so underwhelmed by the standard of maintenance that they expect to move out within a year.

“Just the whole Assemble model, ‘we’re ethical, we’re sustainable, blah blah blah’, I think it maybe raised my expectations in terms of what it would be like dealing with property management.

“I’m at the point where if I have any more issues I will ignore them and probably won’t be there in six months, which is a shame because the community is really lovely.”

Assemble is positioned at the affordable end of the build-to-rent market, with fewer amenities than most other BTR developers offer. It has also bought heavily into federal and state government schemes to deliver subsidised affordable housing.

Even so, Sheko’s weekly rent is more expensive than the $550 weekly median price for a two-bedder in Kensington.

University of Melbourne Professor of Property Piyush Tiwari has researched Melbourne’s first wave of BTR developments, and says the financial feasibility of the sector “hinges on the ability of units to be leased at higher than market rents”.

Communal amenities such as wellness rooms, swimming pools, gyms and cinemas have been included to attract tenants willing to pay the steeper rents necessary to make a profit.

“The original proposition was that BTR provides a higher end rental offering, including amenities, so the rents would be higher,” Tiwari says.

“Generally, the providers were expecting a rent to be 20 to 25 per cent above the market.”

Build-to-rent housing is mainstream in parts of Europe and in the US, where it accounts for roughly 4 per cent of the housing market, and caters more for lifelong renting families.

Tiwari says that if Australia follows these countries, mid-market build-to-rent housing will emerge. But two years after his research paper was published, most BTR buildings in Melbourne are even more expensive than the 20 to 25 per cent premium the first wave was financed on.

The Age calculated rental rates for Melbourne’s BTR developments using Homer, a property app that tracks the prices over time of all Australian properties on the market.

Homer chief executive Henry Pedersen had personal experience with Melbourne’s premium-priced BTR sector while looking for a rental home for his family of three in 2024.

Henry Pedersen, chief executive of Homer, could not justify the rental premium of leasing a build-to-rent apartment. Steven Siewert

Pedersen and his wife considered leasing a three-bedroom apartment at Home in Richmond, but baulked when they found a modern four-bedroom townhouse in the same suburb for $250 a week less.

“The amenities of those things are really cool and that somewhat inflates the value, but at the same time I didn’t think it was worth that much of a difference in price personally; maybe if money was a bit looser,” Pedersen said.

He suspects many renters, aspiring to own a home one day, would make the same calculation.

“Paying 10 to 20 per cent more doesn’t help you save to enter the property market.”

Edward McAuliffe is director of BTR operations at Salta, which operates Fitzroy and Co, a boutique BTR in Fitzroy North, and has two large projects in development in Richmond and Docklands.

Median rental rates at Fitzroy and Co exceed the median rental in Fitzroy North by about 50 per cent, The Age and Homer’s analysis found.

McAuliffe agreed that most BTR housing in Melbourne is relatively expensive to rent, but said that was the only way to make the developments stack up financially.

“You know, we’re creating housing,” he said. “Yes, some of it’s at the premium end at the moment, but that’s a function of what you need to do to get a project to become viable, get the funding you need to build it and get it operating.”

‘It felt like a student campus’

Where younger renters have baulked at BTR, some operators have turned to international students to fill their new buildings, satisfying their financiers but undermining the premium rental experience.

The first few months living in Mirvac’s LIV Aston building in Docklands were pleasant for David Powlett. The apartment was comfortable, the neighbours were friendly and the address on the Yarra’s north bank was convenient.

The rent was high compared to other places he’d considered, but the single father and IT service designer needed a spacious and well-built apartment for himself and his two children, and was prepared to pay a premium for it.

“I was a bit fussy about cupboards that don’t open and noise levels and things like that, and the Mirvac apartment was actually very quiet, very comfortable, the build quality was very high,” he says of the three-bedroom unit he rented, initially for $1270 a week.

Powlett was one of the building’s first tenants.

The communal swimming pool inside LIV Aston in Docklands is typical of the amenities of Melbourne’s premium-priced build-to-rent first wave.

“I was almost the only person on my floor,” he says. Even so, the small community of residents were socially lubricated by regular, catered gatherings thrown by management in one of the building’s common areas.

But six months in, the community in LIV Aston changed dramatically as scores of vacant units were filled with international students, seemingly within a matter of days.

“It really changed the whole atmosphere … I know quite a few people left because they felt the vibe had changed a bit too much. It just didn’t feel like premium accommodation, it felt like a student campus,” Powlett says.

Amenities such as the building’s cinema room, media room and dining spaces were booked out, sometimes for months.

“We didn’t use the amenities anywhere near as much as we thought we would … People just had them constantly booked, so it was just a nightmare to try and get in there,” Powlett says.

He stayed until the end of his 12-month lease, but left when the company sought to increase his rent by more than $300 a week.

On the other side of the CBD, in Mirvac’s LIV Munro building, Alaisdair Leith’s experience was almost the same: a luxurious lifestyle in a near empty building soured after the building rapidly filled up with overseas students.

Mirvac is in dispute with the valuer-general over LIV Munro, its build-to-rent project in the CBD. Justin McManus

Leith and his partner moved into a two-bedroom apartment facing Queen Victoria Market just three months after it had opened, paying $700 a week.

“The first six months there was incredible; no issues,” Leith says. “There was a really good blend of tenants; people in their 30s, retirees.”

But the building was clearly well below capacity until it was filled with international students, leading Leith to question the value in his premium accommodation.

“It was near impossible to book anything because they would book six months in advance. So it was like, well, I can’t use the amenities. So why am I paying this?”

They moved out earlier this year.

Melbourne University’s Tiwari says that international students are an easy market for BTR operators to tap.

But he says the fact they are doing so is also an indication that one of the key selling points for the BTR sector – the offer of long-term, multi-year leases instead of standard, 12-month leases – is attracting relatively few takers.

A Mirvac spokesperson said its BTR buildings attract different resident profiles depending on location, with some drawing in more students, others appealing to professionals, families, key workers or downsizers.

Mirvac is pursuing legal action against Victoria’s valuer-general in the planning tribunal, arguing that LIV Munro’s land value for tax purposes should be slashed by more than $32 million, due to “the deterioration in property market conditions and economic uncertainty over the past 12 months”.

But its 2026 annual report, published in August, presents a more bullish position about its build-to-rent growth strategy, telling investors that Australia’s housing crunch is fertile ground.

Low housing supply, historically low rental vacancy, increased migration and population growth, all support the company’s BTR expansion strategy, the report noted.

Charter Keck Cramer’s Temlett says the BTR boom is delivering desperately needed housing for Melbourne at a time when far too few conventional apartment developments are being built.

“We’ve got the fastest growing population other than WA, we’ve got a chronic shortage of rental stock, so that all points to the fact that rents will continue to rise.”

But in chasing the upper tiers of the market, Melbourne’s BTR boom has left the renters most in need of an affordable place to live out in the cold, Tiwari says.

“At the end of the day, millennials are budget conscious, and their experiences are very different. They are not necessarily looking for all those amenities, they’re looking for a decent home.”

World.title: At a time of global peril, Jeopardy! is the only thing that can save us
World.content:
CultureTV & radioThe Verdict At a time of global peril, Jeopardy! is the only thing that can save us In this column, we deliver hot (and cold) takes on pop culture, judging whether a subject is overrated or underrated. John Saxby September 5, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An adage I’ve long tried to live by, with varying degrees of success, is that it’s better to remain quiet and be thought a fool than to open your mouth and remove all doubt. Certain situations – being asleep, being underwater, intubated – are easy. Being awake, in a conversation, or watching Jeopardy! – less so. The long-running US game show, which airs in Australia weeknights on SBS and SBS2, has clues arranged into categories, presented in the form of answers. Contestants must phrase their response in the form of a question. The best thing on TV right now is a quiz show hosted by a Mormon brainiac. Sydney Morning Herald Were the category “Opening Lines”, for example, this is what it might sound like on the couch at our place: Clue: “Before we proceed any further, hear me speak”.

Me: “Hamlet! No. Sorry. What is Hamlet? No. Macbeth! What is …”

Wife: “What is Coriolanus?”

Me: “D’oh!”



Most winners enjoy one or two victories, pocket a few thousand dollars and bow out. Recently there was a new winner every night for 11 nights. Five wins in a row earns an invitation to the Tournament of Champions. Ken Jennings, aka “the Michael Jordan of trivia”, won a record 74 games in a row before becoming Jeopardy!’s host. Host Ken Jennings, himself a former contestant, won 74 games in a row, a record that still stands. He is also a Mormon, something I thought remarkable until I learnt that Johnny Gilbert, who introduces Ken and the three contestants, is 98 years old. Until 2025, Jennings also held the US record for being the highest-earning game show contestant ever – more than $US4.5 million ($6.8 million) from Jeopardy! alone. Slate magazine called him “the Michael Jordan of trivia” and “the Seabiscuit of geekdom”. The title of his 2006 memoir was Brainiac: Adventures in the Curious, Competitive, Compulsive World of Trivia . “I was aware, from a young age, about being a know-it-all,” Jennings once told The New Yorker. “You immediately realise that America doesn’t like that, that it’s not a hit with girls in your class to know Captain Kirk’s middle name … It is kind of silly to know this weird stuff but we can have a good time with it. It’s better than not knowing it, right?”



As a contestant, Jennings knew enough weird stuff and more to provide thousands of correct responses. But it is a single incorrect answer that still haunts him. The year was 2004, the category was “Tool Time” and the clue was: “This term for a long-handled gardening tool can also mean an immoral pleasure seeker”. Jennings, who looked then, as he does now, like the Mormon missionary to Madrid he once was, answered: “What is a hoe?” “No,” responded Alex Trebek, the show’s then-host. Pause. “Ooooh … they teach you that in school in Utah?” he quipped. “What is a rake?” another contestant replied correctly. In the US, where the show attracts 20 million viewers a week, fans online endlessly dissect and relive such moments (as well as debate whether Jennings will ever match the still-beloved Trebek, who appeared in 37 seasons before he died of pancreatic cancer in 2020).



Recent chatter concerned Bevin Blaber, a writer originally from Schenectady, New York, whose tendency to sway when answering made viewers at home dizzy. Klay Frappier, an accountant from McHenry, North Dakota, also drew attention for solving clues one category at a time, a strategy known as the “Forrest Bounce” for reasons nobody will remember, were they to read them here. It will surprise absolutely no one to learn that the median age of the audience in the US is 70. But the show is also a beacon of inclusiveness, insight and intelligence at a time when America appears light on all three. From 40-game winner Amy Schneider (the first openly transgender contestant and first woman to win more than $1 million in a regular season), to a guy the other night who was more excited about the Beyonce concert he was going to after the taping than being on the show itself, to stay-at-home dad Andrew He and stay-at-home son Brendan Liaw (who attends 12-hour gin rummy marathons with his three retired aunts), what often makes these people interesting is not their cleverness – some are just as clueless as me – but their ordinariness. Related Article The Verdict Other people’s dreams bore me rigid. So why are films and TV shows full of them?

World.title: He was the ‘Baron of Blacktown’ – then his empire fell apart
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Five years ago, he was lauded as the “Baron of Blacktown”. Bathla Group founder Bhart Bhushan’s irresistible migrant success story – from a taxi driver to reclusive multimillion-dollar property developer – was celebrated across western Sydney. His company was credited with changing the face of the region by building thousands of properties at prices that appealed to first home buyers. Bathla became a major sponsor of the Western Sydney Wanderers soccer club, while family members set about building a palatial spread in the city’s rural north-west. The red Bathla logo became omnipresent on fences, signage and cranes at sites from Box Hill and Marsden Park to Schofields, Castle Hill and beyond. Today, however, all of it – his reputation, the fortunes of Bathla Group, and his family members’ dream home – lies in tatters. Harris Mazoudier purchased a Bathla home that he says is full of defects. Sitthixay Ditthavong The company went into voluntary administration with $3.4 billion of debt last week. It was the news many had dreaded, but expected, for weeks. The collapse leaves thousands of victims, including buyers with money tied up in unfinished developments, residents of homes with defects, as well as unpaid subcontractors, tradies, suppliers and staff, with little to no recourse. “We’ll be left in the dust,” said McDonald’s restaurant manager Harris Mazoudier, who has a Bathla apartment in Schofields that he says is riddled with defects.



The scale of Bathla’s debt is so extraordinary – equivalent to the cost of 17 of Australia’s futuristic F-35 fighter jets and their support systems, training, weapons, and infrastructure – that it poses the question: how did it come to this? Indian-born Bhushan and his brother Rajinder Mohan founded the Universal Property Group, now known as Bathla, in 1997. It was good timing. Western Sydney was undergoing rapid population growth, inflation was low, interest rates were falling and a new generation of migrant families was looking to buy. While his formal qualifications are unknown, the then-33-year-old Bhushan was ambitious, shrewd, charismatic and a skilled negotiator. He took the lead while the quieter Mohan was said to be content to work behind the scenes. The following year, they celebrated their first development of five red-brick townhouses in Girraween, the multicultural western suburb where their company headquarters is based. Located around the corner from the highly ranked and then soon-to-be-selective Girraween High School, it was a smart move to attract the aspirational migrant buyers and members of the Indian diaspora they were targeting for sales.



Over the next decade, the brothers transformed the family business into an aggressive and fast-paced development machine, buying up swaths of land and completing 1000 townhouses, duplexes and houses before turning their attention to apartments. Related Article Exclusive

Bathla collapse Abandoned sites and missed deadlines: The boulevard of broken dreams Bathla left behind Key to their success was value in a price-conscious market. “They gave people opportunities in the cheaper end of the market,” said Blacktown MP Stephen Bali, whose electorate is home to many of Bathla’s developments. “Low-cost housing has a role and people pay what they can afford.” Now aged 62, Bhushan is described as “an enigma”. He never gives interviews, there’s only one official photo of him online, and he kept a low profile even when it came to his involvement with the Western Sydney Wanderers, which was terminated last week. Bathla is also a long-term platinum sponsor of the Sydney Sikhs Sports Club, with an untagged Facebook photo from 2022 depicting Bhushan holding up a poster for an awards night. “He’s reasonable to deal with, and he supported charitable organisations, which makes him human,” said Bali, who met with him several times. “But as a businessman, he was ruthless.”



Those who know him say he dreamt of a legacy family business and that he aspired to elevate the status of his company, moving into higher-quality homes. But with a business model that was too risky for the banks, Bhushan financed his operations with loans from a string of private lenders that charge notoriously high interest rates. They included Ray White Capital, which reportedly lent Bathla $240 million, Centuria Capital and La Trobe Financial. A rare photo of Bhart Bhushan, who likes to stay out of the limelight. So what went wrong? Bhushan would describe “a perfect storm” of softening sales, the federal government’s May budget and the falling confidence of key markets. Spiralling construction costs also played a role. Western Sydney Leadership Dialogue chief executive officer Adam Leto says he’s not alone. Many developers in the area are struggling with tightening margins amid rising costs and falling demand. “It’s a lot easier to sell a $1.5 million apartment east of Sydney Olympic Park than it is west of Sydney Olympic Park,” he says. “That’s the grim reality of it.” In truth, there had been warning signs about Bathla for years. Growing debt. Unpaid contractors. A chorus of buyers disgruntled over unfixed defects. Court cases and tribunals.



When the end came, it came very suddenly. On August 25, the company made an announcement on its website and on social media titled “Bathla seeks orderly restructure of business”, and entered voluntary administration. Bhart Bhushan (centre), the man at the top of the Bathla construction empire, which sponsored the Sydney Sikhs Sports Club. Facebook In its second decade, the company really hit its straps: by 2008, it had built 1000 homes; 10 years later, that figure had ballooned to 5000. Insiders say Bhushan was a master of efficiency and frugality in those years, keeping as much skilled work in-house as possible to control costs and driving a hard bargain on everything else. Many of his staff were family, including his children and nephews, or foreign workers on working visas. He was said to work 18-hour days; to be a micromanager who maintained a tight grip on control of all aspects of the business; and yet who dressed more like a labourer than a senior executive. And he loved to make a deal. But the business was not without controversy. An investigation by corporate regulator ASIC raised flags over vendor finance Bhushan was offering to vulnerable buyers, many of whom were immigrants from non-English-speaking backgrounds, between 2004 and 2009.

World.title: It took two Aussie entrepreneurs six years to build a cult sunscreen brand. Then it came crashing down
World.content:
Dubbed “SunscreenGate”, the entire affair made global headlines as sunscreen experts, scientists and skincare girlies picked apart the merits of sunscreen testing, the role of medicine regulator the Therapeutic Goods Administration and the validity of Choice’s SPF results, not to mention Ultra Violette’s defiant initial response – quickly followed by a sudden volte-face – and then whether it was worth wearing sunscreen at all.

Choice’s initial investigation morphed into a kind of national sunscreen scandal, sowing doubt about the efficacy of sunscreen altogether in the country with the highest rates of skin cancer in the world.

“A trust rebuild is not an interesting story,” says Chandler-Matthews. “It’s not as interesting as a sunscreen scandal where there are interesting players. It became us versus Choice.”

Nine months since co-founders Chandler-Matthews, 40, and Bec Jefferd, 50, first agreed to this interview – after cancelling and rescheduling twice – the Melbourne-based friends turned business founders have flown to Sydney for the day for their first sit-down media interview since the story broke. They arrive at a North Sydney cafe in late July bearing a selection of designer tarts from Melbourne – a peace offering after the rescheduling – ready to talk about how they found themselves in the eye of the storm and how they climbed out of it.

It’s been more than a year since consumer advocacy group Choice published that investigation into sunscreen that would upend the industry. On June 12, 2025, Choice reported that 16 out of 20 Australian sunscreens failed to meet their SPF claims of 50 or more, implicating plenty of household names including Banana Boat, Invisible Zinc, Neutrogena and the Cancer Council. Among them, none suffered the kind of fallout that cult favourite brand Ultra Violette did: its “Lean Screen” product, a mineral zinc sunscreen and one of the most premium products in the cohort (a 75ml tube retailed for $52), trailed the pack with a woeful SPF score of 4 – the only one to score in the single digits.

For Ava Chandler-Matthews, one half of the duo behind Australian suncare brand Ultra Violette, what preceded the fall that would plague her company was the stuff of bucket lists: a private dinner with billionaire beauty founder Hailey Bieber . What came after would throw this high into sharp relief.

In every dramatic fall from grace, there is a before, and there is an after.

Neither are scientists – they enlisted a force of product developers, in-house regulators and chemists to build Ultra Violette – but their marketing backgrounds were pivotal in the brand’s sharp rise, enlisting influencers like Gen Z-favourite Sophia Begg (@sophadophaa to her 1.5 million TikTok followers).

Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd, alumni of household names like L’Oreal and Napoleon Perdis, met while working at beauty retailer MECCA – Jefferd as head of product development, Chandler-Matthews as brand manager – and they departed in 2017 to build what would eventually become Ultra Violette.

Of all 16 sunscreens that failed Choice’s testing, the fall of Ultra Violette was the steepest. In the six years between launching the brand in 2019 and the Choice investigation in 2025, its sunscreens had become a darling of the Australian beauty industry – a cult favourite among young women for its pastel-hued packaging and its lightweight, tinted formulas that felt more at home in an upmarket beauty retailer than a chemist. ( The Australian Financial Review credited the brand with “making sunscreen sexy” .)

The pair will tell you the past 14 months have been “triggering” and “traumatic”. Chandler-Mathers puts it more bluntly: “It’s been the hardest year of my life. So often I would come home and I was mute. I couldn’t talk to my husband. I couldn’t talk to my best friends. I couldn’t talk to my mum.”

The fallout is ongoing: the TGA’s investigation into the other 15 sunscreens that failed Choice’s testing is yet to wrap, and in March, it opened up consultation for how sunscreen is regulated in Australia, the results of which are expected to be published by the end of the year.

And because the TGA doesn’t conduct its own testing (except in select circumstances), Choice has historically been the only body in Australia to conduct testing independent of brands. Its last report on Australian sunscreen, published in 2015, found four out of six products tested failed to meet their advertised SPF level.

In Australia, most non-cosmetic sunscreens are regulated as medicines, meaning to get on the market they need TGA approval. To do so, brands send a product to a laboratory of their choosing to be tested according to the Australian and International standard. If approved, this is typically the first and only time in a product’s lifecycle it is tested.

Acknowledged by the TGA and the sunscreen industry, the current standard for SPF testing in Australia and internationally is inherently variable. This method ( in vivo ) involves applying sunscreen to 10 to 20 human subjects, who are then exposed to UV light. A trained tester observes this process, noting the time it takes for skin to redden (an assessment procedure which is itself prone to error), to determine the product’s SPF.

What the saga partially succeeded in doing was exposing the public’s limited understanding of how sunscreen works – and just how volatile the testing process can be.

Doors opened for them with financial injections from private equity and the support of beauty retailers such as Adore Beauty, Sephora, Net-A-Porter and Harrods. They had just launched in the US market when Choice’s report forced them to focus not on thriving, but simply surviving.

After dinner, Chandler-Matthews returned to her hotel room to tackle customer service queries until the early hours. The next day, she mentally parked everything for a meeting with Sephora US before filming a video to respond to the Choice report and flying home. Fielding calls and messages from retail partners, brand ambassadors, customers and the media over questions the pair didn’t have the answers to, they were shocked to see 15 other brands had also failed their SPF claims.

Meanwhile, Ultra Violette had received the results of two of its additional SPF tests – sent to Princeton Consumer Research, an SPF certification lab based overseas founded by two British reality TV stars, with no connection to Princeton University – with scores of 61 and 64. Ultra Violette shared these numbers with Choice, to little effect. “We asked a few questions, but we weren’t engaged,” says Chandler-Matthews. “It was not like we were talking every day.”

The SPF figure that Choice’s testing (conducted at Eurofins Dermatest in Sydney) arrived at – 4 – was incomprehensible to them. “We genuinely could not understand how that result was even possible,” says Jefferd. ” ‘Is this true? Have we been damaging our customers?’. That was our first response. Like, ‘That can’t be right. Have we had any cases of people being sunburnt?’.” Choice was confused, too. When it sent a different batch of Lean Screen to a lab in Germany, it returned a score of 5.

Ava Chandler-Matthews was in California at The Business of Fashion’s The Business of Beauty Global Forum in June just before Choice’s report dropped.

Choice released its report at midnight AEST, and although Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd had known it was coming, they hadn’t been told exactly when. The advocacy group had alerted Ultra Violette about its test results in March, three months prior to its public release, prompting Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd to order additional testing on every batch of Lean Screen then on the market. They revisited manufacturing records and asked Choice for more detail on its testing methods.

When the worst year of her life began, Chandler-Matthews was in California’s Napa Valley, dining with beauty mogul Hailey Bieber, having just spoken at The Business of Fashion’s global beauty forum, headlined by the influencer.

“We did a full 180,” says Chandler-Matthews. “There was no choice,” Jefferd says. “The product was not safe to keep on the market.”

Meanwhile, additional test results returned with figures below 50 – and then another, and another (in Australia, products advertising SPF50+ must actually test at 60 or above). On August 22, the company apologised to customers and announced a voluntary recall of Lean Screen. It looked like a total capitulation – because it was. “We are deeply sorry that one of our products has fallen short of the standards we pride ourselves on and that you have come to expect of us,” their statement read. The next slide on the carousel was a chart of eight test results, returning SPF levels of 64, 61, 60, 33, 26, 21, 10, 4.

It did little to assuage public concerns. Some looked at Ultra Violette’s distinct blue and purple colour scheme and concluded that the entire range must also be similarly defective (the pair later retested the entire range and said they found no issues beyond Lean Screen). Others accused Jefferd and Chandler-Matthews, who couldn’t help but read every comment on social media, of diluting their product to squeeze more out of their customers.

Chandler-Matthews doubled down the following day. In an eight-minute video uploaded to TikTok and Instagram, she pointed to Ultra Violette’s own SPF test results of 60-plus from the same batch Choice tested. “What we do know about Choice is they’re not a regulator. They are not the ACCC. They are not the TGA. They are not the ones who approve sunscreens,” she said to her iPhone camera in the video filmed in her US hotel room. “We stand by the tests we’ve done.”

On paper, though, they were less incredulous and more recalcitrant. Ultra Violette engaged a reputation and crisis management consultant to distribute a forceful statement condemning Choice’s results as “not even remotely accurate” and “scientifically impossible”, suggesting that what was most likely to have happened was “human error and the mix-up of samples”. The way the product was decanted, their statement said, may have led to destabilisation (Choice later published all its SPF tests and stood by the validity of the test results).

While the recall was announced in late August, Ultra Violette had started refunding customers after Choice published its report. Some sunscreen brands tarred by the same investigation reached out to Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd for advice on how to handle the recall process (one copied their statement so closely that it still contained Ultra Violette’s specific product number). About $1 million evaporated, squeezing cash flow at a time when the company was trying to fund its US expansion. Its chief financial officer, alarmed at the amount of money going out the door, tried to put some limits on the refunds, but the founders say they were refunding just about anyone who asked. “It was absolutely in doubt,” Chandler-Matthews said of the business’ financial viability at the time.

So what actually went wrong with Lean Screen? Why were the results that low?

Unlike other sunscreens in Ultra Violette’s range, Lean Screen was the only product not developed in-house. The zinc sunscreen used a base formula made by Wild Child Laboratories, a formula which, ABC investigations revealed, was shared by 20 other Australian sunscreens that were all recalled, paused or under TGA review. The TGA would later find that this base formulation was “unlikely to have an SPF greater than 21”, triggering a domino effect of product recalls by brands that hadn’t been called out by Choice’s report.

Further ABC investigations cast a shadow on the integrity of the whole sunscreen industry. Sunscreen experts and whistleblowers called into question the data emerging from Princeton Consumer Research, which had tested and certified three of Ultra Violette’s SPF results – the ones they presented to Choice to counter its 4 – and at least seven other sunscreens in Choice’s report. Former employees said they resigned over the lab’s “tendency to cut corners”. In late September, the TGA said it found “significant concerns about the reliability” of Princeton’s SPF testing, and urged sunscreen brands to get their products tested elsewhere.

While there’s no suggestion it occurred in this case, fraudulent testing isn’t unheard of. In 2019, the regulator began reviewing sunscreens tested by American lab AMA, whose owner was arrested by US authorities for a scheme involving fabricated test results.

Perhaps no business suffered more from the saga than Wild Child. Ultimately, a TGA investigation didn’t find any manufacturing deficiencies that explained why the formula could only ever achieve an SPF of 21 and it pointed to variability in SPF testing as the potential cause. “Our investigation did demonstrate that materially different SPF results were generated when the formulation was tested by different laboratories,” says Wild Child chief executive Tom Curnow.

But the negative attention sparked by Choice’s investigation had done its damage; the Perth manufacturer collapsed, was acquired by a group of investors, and rebranded to Heliora. “The publicity, recalls and resulting loss of customer and market confidence in SPF testing caused significant commercial damage,” said Heliora chair Paul Waldren.

Ultra Violette stopped working with Heliora, which has ceased production of the recalled base formula, but the manufacturer managed to retain all 20 brands subject to recalls as clients and kept all 70 of its staff employed.

Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd accept responsibility for what they put out on the market, but they aren’t keen to say much more about what went wrong with the product. “We still don’t know. It wasn’t our formulation,” says Jefferd. “It’s a manufacturer’s formula. It’s up to them,” says Chandler-Matthews.

Princeton Consumer Research did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Good Weekend.

Fair or not, Ultra Violette’s tarnished brand became synonymous with faltering trust in Australian sunscreen as a whole, a $270 million-plus market that had been regarded highly by international consumers whose own regulators (like the US’s Food and Drug Administration) are less stringent than the TGA’s.

It didn’t help that this came at a time when the sunscreen “scepticism” movement, popularised by right-wing figures like RFK Jr and Joe Rogan who claim sunscreen contains “toxic” ingredients and prevents vitamin D generation, had been gaining traction on social media, alongside tanning culture.

“Regardless of whether people buy Ultra Violette or not, the fact that trust in sunscreen in general was shaken was really disastrous,” says Jefferd.

Chandler-Matthews hopes they can win back as many customers as possible, but she says some have turned their back for good. “For some people, it may take longer,” she says. “For some people, not at all.”

Chemist Dr Michelle Wong, a science educator known to her social media followers as @labmuffinbeautyscience, has followed the scandal closely. The founders’ approach – which took aim at the validity of Choice’s results – worked against, not for them, Wong believes. “I think a lot of the lack of trust actually came from Ultra Violette themselves and how they responded,” she says. Their claim that Choice’s results were “scientifically impossible” turned out to be untrue.

“If you compare Ultra Violette’s response to every other brand in the original Choice article, theirs was just out of line,” says Wong, who was paid to copywrite for the brand in 2021. “While I think a lot of what they did behind the scenes to sort out the issue was commendable, publicly it seemed like they were trying to influence their way out of this situation.”

Swathes of social media users have expressed that waning confidence in the brand was less because of Lean Screen’s failure in Choice’s report, and more because of their subsequent handling of it, which they claim included deleting unsavoury comments, blocking users and enlisting influencer friends to rage against Choice.

How Ultra Violette handled (or mishandled) its response became a PR lesson on how not to handle a crisis, inspiring multiple think pieces and LinkedIn posts on the topic. (It’s normally an excellent strategy to mobilise people in your network to defend you, opined crisis management consultant Sally Branson, but in this instance, Ultra Violette’s ecosystem of beauty influencers and TikTok creators were doing so “without bulletproof information to support it”.)

By speaking to customers in a video on social media, Chandler-Matthews had wanted to address customers directly and personally. Given the chance, they’d “absolutely” do things differently, they say now. “There’s a lot to be said for that classic PR response,” says Chandler-Matthews. “By doing that video, did I think I would become the face of a global sunscreen scandal? No, I didn’t. It was defensive.”

“We wouldn’t have operated on a platform of as much certainty,” says Jefferd. “We felt we were on really solid footing, and what turned out is that we weren’t.”

But while hindsight may offer the gift of perspective, both are emphatic they acted in good faith as passionate founders doing the best with the information they had. “This is not our business,” says Jefferd. “This is our life, and we care deeply about this.”

Despite the wreckage to Ultra Violette’s reputation, its cash flow crisis and its social licence to operate, Chandler-Matthews and Jefferd don’t regret the changes catalysed by Choice’s SPF testing. “I think [Choice] shone a light on an important area that needed to be talked about. We wouldn’t be having this discussion about regulatory change if they hadn’t,” says Jefferd.

The scale of the problems across the supply chain led the TGA itself to the conclusion that there were broader issues with the current regulatory framework for sunscreens, rather than isolated product failures. A TGA spokesman said this includes addressing known limitations in SPF testing reproducibility, laboratory oversight, and life-cycle quality assurance.

In March, the TGA opened up a consultation group seeking feedback on proposed regulatory changes – before its investigation into sunscreens that failed Choice’s testing has been published, which it said would be online “before the end of the year”. The public, and politicians, are getting impatient. When independent senator David Pocock tried to press for answers from a TGA official at a Senate Estimates hearing in June (he was not the first to do so), he was told the investigation was “nearing completion”.

“I think a lot of the lack of trust actually came from Ultra Violette themselves and how they responded,” says chemist Dr Michelle Wong.

Wong, who is part of the TGA’s consultation group, says industry insiders had been raising the alarm on issues with SPF testing with the regulator for years, without much progress. Choice’s investigation made the problems too big to ignore. “I think Choice felt like they needed to stir up some attention to get the TGA to act,” she says, “which, I think, is kind of justified.”

The consumer advocacy group, formed in 1959 at a Sydney Town Hall meeting, enjoyed a level of national exposure and attention it hadn’t had in years. For the first time, Choice was nominated for a Walkley Award, typically reserved for journalism, for its sunscreen investigation.

Without it, defective sunscreens would have stayed on the market and regulatory reform may have never happened, said Matt Steen, Choice’s director of reviews and testing. “The existing regulatory system, which relies heavily on companies certifying their own compliance, is clearly not working and cannot continue.”

One industry group that had been lobbying for regulatory change is Accord, representing the hygiene, cosmetic and personal care industry, of which Ultra Violette is a member. The organisation would like to see the TGA adopt in vitro [lab-based] test methods to validate results, particularly given many labs operate overseas under different regulatory frameworks. In vitro testing has since been approved for use in Australia, but it has yet to be implemented across the industry. Early analysis shows it is at least as reliable as in vivo testing, says Accord executive director Damien Mitsch, and it is a preferable alternative as it’s cheaper and faster (machines don’t need to be recruited and paid to have their skin burned).

Mitsch describes the way Choice handled its publication as “sensationalistic”. “Getting the sunscreen conversation into the public domain was in some ways helpful,” he says. “But at the same time, to throw it out into the ether and watch the chaos ensue is probably not the best way to manage a significant public health issue.”

All stakeholders Good Weekend spoke to agree the regulator needs to do more – particularly around eliminating issues with testing variability – but opinions diverge on the nitty gritty about exactly how this might play out.

Ava Chandler-Matthews, left, hopes changes they’ve implemented will help Ultra Violette rebuild as a leader in the sunscreen industry and rehabilitate the reputation of Australian sunscreens. Jason South

Ultra Violette has come full circle. In mid-August, 361 days after the company pulled Lean Screen from shelves, it released Velvet Screen, a mineral zinc sunscreen that has gone through two rounds of testing from separate laboratories and is manufactured at a different, TGA-approved third-party manufacturer.

The number on the bottle has been lowered to 40 – unlike its predecessor’s SPF 60 claim – a decision Jefferd says was made in the hope consumers take a little extra time in applying sunscreen properly (mineral sunscreens are heavier, meaning users are more likely to apply insufficient amounts), and despite testing returning results in the high 40s and 50s. Velvet Screen’s development has heralded broader changes across the brand, aimed at reducing SPF testing’s inherent variability.

They have also engaged French photobiologist Sebastien Miksa, whose job it is to review the validity of test results through his company Suncert and identify potential anomalies. Ultra Violette is pushing for the TGA to have someone perform this role in-house.

“The trust in the rest of the range should probably be stronger than ever, because we’ve implemented all of those changes,” says Jefferd.

Chandler-Matthews hopes these changes will help Ultra Violette rebuild as a leader in the sunscreen industry and rehabilitate the reputation of Australian sunscreens. “It’s actions and not words at this point,” she says. “It’s just consistency. I think we’ve done the work.”

The drama has bruised, but not hamstrung, Ultra Violette’s ambitions to expand across the globe. Despite the public tumult, Ultra Violette didn’t lose any retail partners, and new US investors had come on board some weeks before Good Weekend sat down with the pair. The day after Choice’s investigation came out, Chandler-Matthews met with Sephora US, which renewed its deal and gave them four times more shelf space.

This time last year, they were asking themselves why they had bothered to make sunscreens at all.

“We could have made a blush,” says Jefferd. “We could have made a f---ing fantastic moisturiser.”

World.title: The rebirth of Hawaii’s first beachfront resort is not to be missed
World.content:
★★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews The rebirth of Hawaii’s first beachfront resort is not to be missed Rob McFarland September 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel Moana Surfrider Some things haven’t changed at Moana Surfrider, like the porte-cochere that greets guests on arrival. Check-in When it opened in March 1901, the Moana Surfrider became the first luxury hotel on Honolulu’s Waikiki Beach, heralding a new era of sophistication on the Hawaiian island of Oahu. In March, the property celebrated its 125th anniversary with a major refurbishment, refreshing all 791 guest rooms and its Victorian-era lobby. One thing that hasn’t changed is the grand porte-cochere that greets guests on arrival – still one of the loveliest welcomes on the island.



The look 



My Deluxe Ocean room in the Tower Wing has an elegant residential feel, with plenty of natural wood, modern furnishings and ocean-inspired artwork. The en suite doubles as a dressing room with refillable jasmine-infused toiletries. The real wow-factor comes from the balcony, which offers a screensaver-worthy panorama of Waikiki Beach, the mouthwash-blue ocean and the forested slopes of Diamond Head. Watching surfers glide toward the shoreline while Hawaiian music drifts up from the bar below quickly becomes one of my favourite pastimes. Food + drink The courtyard banyan tree is an enduring feature at Beachhouse, the hotel’s main restaurant. The property’s main restaurant, Beachhouse, is a versatile venue that offers a solid breakfast buffet, an indulgent afternoon tea and an upscale three- or four-course surf-and-turf dinner. Nab a table at the ocean end of the verandah and you’ll have one of the finest dinner settings in Waikiki – a prime beachfront view of the sunset followed by a front-row seat for the nightly live music and light show that illuminates the banyan tree. Other options include the casual all-day Beach Bar, a poolside cafe and Vintage 1901, an intimate lobby bar with a live pianist at weekends, and A-grade people-watching from the rocking chairs on the verandah near the entrance. Out + about



A stroll along the palm-tree-dotted oceanfront is always invigorating. It’s hard to quibble about the hotel’s compact pool when you’re steps away from Waikiki’s inviting waters. If you can tear yourself away from the sand, take a stroll along the palm-lined promenade towards Diamond Head. Along the way you’ll pass an entertaining procession of skaters, cyclists and lei-festooned holidaymakers. Admire the towering banyan trees in the beachfront parks and look out for endangered Hawaiian monk seals basking on Kaimana Beach. The hotel offers free morning yoga and meditation classes, but for something more energetic, tackle the winding ascent to the summit of Diamond Head for glorious coastal views (book a timeslot online in advance). For historic context, don’t miss the curated display of hotel artefacts on the Moana’s first floor, including a guest ledger from 1905, when rooms cost just $US1.50 a night. The verdict A thoughtful refresh of a much-loved classic. No other Honolulu hotel matches Moana’s elegance, ambience and historical significance. The essentials





Relaxing in the jacuzzi at the hotel’s beachfront spa after an invigorating signature massage. Lowlight Frustratingly patchy internet. Free portable Wi-Fi hotspots are available, but it’s a needless inconvenience for a luxury resort. The writer was a guest of Moana Surfrider and Hawaii Tourism Oceania.

World.title: Total fire ban in place for Sydney as city set to reach 33 degrees
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

A total fire ban is in effect for Sydney on Saturday, with the city set to reach up to 33 degrees just five days into spring.

An extreme fire danger has also been recorded for the region stretching from the coast to Mount Victoria, coming days after Sydney experienced its warmest winter in 167 years of records.

The dazzling beauty of Sydney’s floral displays is arriving earlier each year due to climate change. Steven Siewert

Sydney is forecast to record 27 degrees at noon on Saturday, stretching to 33 degrees by 1pm.

The Bureau of Meteorology said “fresh to strong and gusty northwesterly winds” were due to develop on Saturday morning, and, when combined with the “dry, unseasonably warm conditions”, would lead to elevated fire dangers across the city.

World.title: Kings of the close ones: How the Western Bulldogs found a superpower after losing a superstar
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Kings of the close ones: How the Western Bulldogs found a superpower after losing a superstar Andrew Wu September 5, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Ryley Sanders’ first emotion when he realised Sam Darcy had wrecked his knee was sadness. Once that initial heartache dulled, it soon became apparent to the third-season midfielder how much tougher this season would become for the Western Bulldogs. “When you lose someone of Darce’s calibre, you know that it’s got to be harder to win a premiership,” Sanders told this masthead this week. “We can definitely still contend without him. Obviously, having him would make it more likely.” Ryley Sanders has ridden the ups and downs of the Bulldogs 2026 campaign. Chris Hopkins As far as injuries go, few hit a club harder than an ACL tear to a star key forward. Unlike midfielders, their scarcity makes them nigh on impossible to replace. In the weeks after Darcy’s injury, the Bulldogs had the look of a team that was learning how to play the game again. The Bulldogs may finally have unlocked the formula to not only cope without Darcy but, at times, thrive. It has come in the nick of time.



Luke Beveridge’s men were the flavour of the month in the heady days of March after beating three of last year’s finalists in their first three games. Just weeks later, their season was spiralling amid a four-game losing streak where heavy defeat was compounded by injuries to their spine. Sam Darcy ruptured his ACL against Geelong in April. Getty Images Ruckman Tim English hurt his knee on Easter Sunday against Essendon. Then came the disaster in Geelong when Darcy ruptured his ACL, skipper Marcus Bontempelli hyperextended his knee, midfield heartbeat Tom Liberatore was concussed and key defenders Rory Lobb and James O’Donnell strained hamstrings. The following week, key forward Aaron Naughton landed on his head attempting a speccy. He was fortunate to escape without any structural damage to his neck. “We went through a pretty traumatic period after the Geelong game,” Dogs coach Luke Beveridge said this week.



While fans in the stands mourned the loss of a star player for the year, the human element was felt inside the locker room. “Losing him as a player is very sad, it’s more the person he is,” Sanders said. “He’s such a great guy. He’s such a loving teammate for everyone. He gives the time of day for everyone. He’s such a presence around the club. View post on X “Everyone was a bit just devastated for him because he puts so much work into his craft, and he’s such a competitor. I think the way he was training in the preseason, everyone was like ‘Oh, this bloke’s ready to absolutely explode’. “To lose him was pretty devastating, but it’s good that he’s on the road back now.”



Darcy’s absence on the field was just as keenly felt. From rounds one to six, the 208 centimetre forward was the most targeted Bulldog inside 50m – by a considerable margin – with 26.8 per cent of all entries aimed at him, ahead of Naughton at 17.1 per cent. “Losing Darce up forward was a big one, just because he’s such a presence, and a lot of our entries go to him. So we were kind of learning how to play without him. We had to learn a few different things,”Sanders said. Naughton sent shockwaves through the Bulldogs camp after his frightening fall against Sydney in late April. Fans had their hands to their head in shock as Naughton lay motionless on Marvel Stadium while medical staff carefully loaded him onto a stretcher. “I think most of the boys were a bit rattled,” Sanders said. “You always think the worst. I remember being right there. I was like, “F---, you just hope he’s OK. It was pretty sickening.”



Remarkably, Naughton lined up the following week. It has not affected how he plays. He still throws himself into marking contests. Months down the track, he can see the funny side. “I have watched it back, I’m still flat that they didn’t pay the mark on that one,” Naughton quipped. Aaron Naughton was instrumental to the Bulldogs’ win in the wildcard final against Collingwood. Getty Images There is no player arguably more important to the Bulldogs’ premiership hopes than Naughton, who is contracted until the end of 2032. In Darcy’s absence, he has become the man in attack for the Dogs. Since round seven, Naughton is the target of 27.1 per cent of the Bulldogs’ entries inside 50m. Next are mature-age rookie Will Lewis (21.5 per cent) and youngster Jordan Croft (10.2 per cent).



Though Lewis’s return from injury takes some of the load off Naughton, the Dogs are hardly stacked with proven tall targets. Their loss to North Melbourne four weeks ago prompted a rethink. The Dogs needed to be bold – or fold. It has worked. Their scores in the past three weeks have been their highest across a three-game stretch since rounds one to three when Darcy and Naughton ruled the air. Small forwards Arty Jones, Cody Weightman and Rhylee West have hit form. “I reckon the last three or four weeks we’ve been a bit more aggressive with our ball movement.,” Sanders said.



“We’ve realised we don’t have the kind of big fellas ... especially when it’s only Naughts up there. If Lobby [Rory Lobb] is playing ruck or back or whatever, we have to play different to what we would if we had Darce there or another key forward. “Bevo and all the coaches are really giving us a licence; take the game on because that’s the way we’re going to win. It’s like very uplifting and empowering. “We’ll make mistakes sometimes, but we need to take the game on ... to be damaging. After that North game, everyone kind of went a bit into their shells during the game. “It wasn’t great at the time, it’s been a good blessing in disguise having that game. We actually needed to change, otherwise we might not have made [last week’s] wildcard [final], or if we did, we wouldn’t have been any kind of danger.”



This has been a year of living dangerously for the Dogs, who have won eight from eight in games decided by a single-digit margin. Related Article Analysis

Naked City The night Hawthorn refused to die The footy gods have played a part, Sanders conceded, as seen in Tim Membrey’s miss after the siren last week. But there is more to it than just luck. Every club has a save-the-game mode they train during the year – and the Dogs have done it better than anyone. “It’s very psychological,” Sanders said. “Those close games, it’s almost like Collingwood a couple years ago when it felt like they couldn’t lose those close games. You just get confident. You’re like, ‘Oh boys, we’ve already done this’ because big games or close games at the end you can tighten up. “But I feel like our boys are really relishing being in high-pressure environment.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Boots on the ground as first Australian rescue team arrives in Nepal
World.content:
WorldAsiaFloods Boots on the ground as first Australian rescue team arrives in Nepal Michael McGowan September 5, 2026 — 6:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kathmandu: A team of specialist drone operators from New South Wales and Queensland has arrived in Nepal, the first Australian rescue workers to reach the disaster-stricken nation since a deadly tidal wave tore through the country last week. The team, including 10 Fire and Rescue NSW personnel, landed in the capital, Kathmandu, late on Friday night (Saturday AEST) following a plea for help from the Nepalese government. A team of NSW and Queensland drone specialists arriving at the Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu on Friday night. The 15-member team are the first Australian specialist search and rescue personnel to arrive in Nepal since the devastating floods struck last week. Michael McGowan They are part of the federal government’s $11 million humanitarian support package, and will be joined by disaster victim identification officers from the Australian Federal Police on Saturday. Chief Superintendent Jeremy Stubbs from Fire and Rescue NSW said the unit, which included personnel who had experience in the 2011 Christchurch earthquake and Japanese tsunami, would meet with their Nepalese counterparts on Saturday before being deployed to help the rescue effort.



“It’s humbling to have our offer of this type of capability accepted,” he said, as Nepal’s search and rescue effort enters its 10th day. “I think it demonstrates the relationship that Nepal has with Australia, and also the respect that the Australian community has had for Nepal seeing them go through this type of disaster.” Related Article Floods In Nepal, hope gives way to grief. Few are counting on miracles Families of some of the 36 Australians still unaccounted for have expressed angst at the lack of new information from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Two Australians were removed from the list of those unaccounted for on Friday, sparking hope for some families, but DFAT declined to publicly provide their names or specific locations. Speaking outside the Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu late on Friday night, Australia’s ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst, defended the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s policy of not releasing details. He said privacy laws limited the agency’s ability to disclose people’s identities.



“We can’t do anything differently,” he said. “We can’t talk about them. We can’t disclose their names. We can’t disclose any details that would make them identifiable,” he said. “They’re quite at liberty to talk to you if they wish to. But we, I can’t do that. Chinese experts (in orange) with specialist equipment arrive at a Nepalese base in Bidur to assist in the effort to rescue the tunnel workers. Kate Geraghty “We generally communicate with the next of kin. Now there are times when people don’t want people, even in their immediate circle, to know where they are.” While the expectation of finding survivors may be fading, there are still glimmers of hope. Nepalese authorities revealed two people had been rescued alive from a hydropower tunnel on Friday, nine days after the floods hit.



Asked whether authorities still had hope of finding the missing Australians alive, Ernst said: “we do”. Related Article Floods This valley was the last known location of a Sydney family. Then a wave 100 metres high hit But Ernst said no decision would be made about where the Australian experts would be dispatched until meeting with Nepalese authorities on Saturday. “They will contribute to the overall Nepali operation, but they’re not a standalone outfit,” he said. “This is part of Australia assisting Nepal, and there’ll be discussions tomorrow about where they deploy and the focus.”



Of the missing Australians, about 15 were part of a tour group undertaking a Hindu pilgrimage up Mount Kailash near the border between Nepal and Tibet when the floods hit. Some of their families have travelled to Nepal and have asked for rescue efforts to be directed to areas where phone pings were detected after the floods. Ernst said Australia had “specifically asked” Nepalese authorities to search those locations. Fire and Rescue NSW Chief Superintendent Jeremy Stubbs (right) with Australia’s ambassador to Nepal, Simon Ernst (left), speaks to reporters outside the Tribhuvan International Airport in Kathmandu. Michael McGowan “I think we’re getting to the point now where individual areas, pieces of ground have now been searched multiple times,” he said. While he did not believe authorities had struggled to obtain information from telecommunications companies, it was a question of “whether the data actually helps take forward the investigation or not, or the search or not”.



“In some cases, it does. In some cases, it’s inconclusive,” he said. “But it’s a pretty obvious question, and we can be confident we’ll be, you know, making that particular, our particular interest in that location known, as we already have.” Related Article Graphic content

Floods Quicksand and rotting flesh: No words can capture the devastation in Nepal Other Australian help has arrived since the glacial collapse near the border with Tibet sent an inland tidal wave tearing through the country last week, including aid supplies aboard Royal Australian Air Force plane on Wednesday. However, the drone specialists are the first dedicated rescue team to arrive. While there have been questions over why Australians had not deployed sooner Ernst said it was a response to requests from the Nepalese government.



“They don’t need more boots on the ground, so to speak,” he said. They need technology and expertise and that’s part of what our team is.” “Access has been very difficult, so pouring more people into it doesn’t necessarily help with the issue.” The team has arrived with two sets of drones. One, Stubbs said, was small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, and could be used to fly inside damaged homes and tunnels. “The benefit of that is we have a structural engineer with us. That structural engineer will do an assessment of what they can see and determine whether it’s safe for us to go in, but the imagery is fantastic as well,” he said. The larger drone conducts what he called a “broad area assessment” which can quickly provide mapping to the Nepalese government and emergency workers.
