World.title: The rebirth of Hawaii’s first beachfront resort is not to be missed
World.content:
★★★★½ Reviews & adviceHotel reviews The rebirth of Hawaii’s first beachfront resort is not to be missed Rob McFarland September 5, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hotel Moana Surfrider Some things haven’t changed at Moana Surfrider, like the porte-cochere that greets guests on arrival. Check-in When it opened in March 1901, the Moana Surfrider became the first luxury hotel on Honolulu’s Waikiki Beach, heralding a new era of sophistication on the Hawaiian island of Oahu. In March, the property celebrated its 125th anniversary with a major refurbishment, refreshing all 791 guest rooms and its Victorian-era lobby. One thing that hasn’t changed is the grand porte-cochere that greets guests on arrival – still one of the loveliest welcomes on the island.



The look 



My Deluxe Ocean room in the Tower Wing has an elegant residential feel, with plenty of natural wood, modern furnishings and ocean-inspired artwork. The en suite doubles as a dressing room with refillable jasmine-infused toiletries. The real wow-factor comes from the balcony, which offers a screensaver-worthy panorama of Waikiki Beach, the mouthwash-blue ocean and the forested slopes of Diamond Head. Watching surfers glide toward the shoreline while Hawaiian music drifts up from the bar below quickly becomes one of my favourite pastimes. Food + drink The courtyard banyan tree is an enduring feature at Beachhouse, the hotel’s main restaurant. The property’s main restaurant, Beachhouse, is a versatile venue that offers a solid breakfast buffet, an indulgent afternoon tea and an upscale three- or four-course surf-and-turf dinner. Nab a table at the ocean end of the verandah and you’ll have one of the finest dinner settings in Waikiki – a prime beachfront view of the sunset followed by a front-row seat for the nightly live music and light show that illuminates the banyan tree. Other options include the casual all-day Beach Bar, a poolside cafe and Vintage 1901, an intimate lobby bar with a live pianist at weekends, and A-grade people-watching from the rocking chairs on the verandah near the entrance. Out + about



A stroll along the palm-tree-dotted oceanfront is always invigorating. It’s hard to quibble about the hotel’s compact pool when you’re steps away from Waikiki’s inviting waters. If you can tear yourself away from the sand, take a stroll along the palm-lined promenade towards Diamond Head. Along the way you’ll pass an entertaining procession of skaters, cyclists and lei-festooned holidaymakers. Admire the towering banyan trees in the beachfront parks and look out for endangered Hawaiian monk seals basking on Kaimana Beach. The hotel offers free morning yoga and meditation classes, but for something more energetic, tackle the winding ascent to the summit of Diamond Head for glorious coastal views (book a timeslot online in advance). For historic context, don’t miss the curated display of hotel artefacts on the Moana’s first floor, including a guest ledger from 1905, when rooms cost just $US1.50 a night. The verdict A thoughtful refresh of a much-loved classic. No other Honolulu hotel matches Moana’s elegance, ambience and historical significance. The essentials





Relaxing in the jacuzzi at the hotel’s beachfront spa after an invigorating signature massage. Lowlight Frustratingly patchy internet. Free portable Wi-Fi hotspots are available, but it’s a needless inconvenience for a luxury resort. The writer was a guest of Moana Surfrider and Hawaii Tourism Oceania.

World.title: Nelson community 'shocked' by shooting
World.content:
A Nelson MP says the community is shocked after two people died in a shooting in the suburb of Tahunanui yesterday afternoon.

A man and a woman were found dead at a house on Parkers Road after a report of a shotgun being stolen in nearby Annesbrook.

Police say the two people were known to each other and they are investigating the circumstances of the deaths.

Acting Tasman District Commander Superintendent Blair Macdonald said it was an isolated incident and there was no ongoing threat to public safety.

However, Nelson MP Rachel Boyack says the seaside suburb isn't used to such incidents, and people are concerned.

Rachel Boyack is the MP for Nelson. Max Frethey / LDR

"People are reassured there's no risk to public safety but, you know, we have a really caring community and when these types of incidents occur people are really concerned about their friends, their family, their community," Boyack told RNZ.

"Our love and thoughts go to the family and friends of those involved," she wrote on Facebook.

World.title: Magnitude 4.9 earthquake felt in Wellington
World.content:
Thousands of people have been jolted awake by an early morning quake in Wellington.

The magnitude 4.9 tremor hit at 6.34am on Saturday, centred about 30km north-west of Paraparaumu, and 26km deep.

GeoNet described the shaking as moderate.

More than 21,000 people reported feeling the quake immediately afterward, with reports concentrated from the Marlborough and Nelson areas in the South Island, up to the Central Plateau - and the strongest reports from the Kāpiti Coast, Wellington, Wairarapa, and top of the South Island.

An RNZ reporter in Lower Hutt said the furniture began shaking against the wall in her house, and neighbourhood dogs soon started barking, with the shaking going for some time.

GeoNet posted that their team also felt it: "The earthquake was felt in our National Geohazards Monitoring Centre in Lower Hutt, who heard the quake coming and report it had definite primary and secondary wave arrivals, which makes the quake feel longer."

A Raumati South man said: "I was asleep, but woken by a noise you could hear coming... like a close freight train.

"Then a decent shake for about 10 seconds and a wobble. During the wobble, my phone alert went off, despite my phone being on silent. No damage, and I have felt stronger quakes here..."

GeoNet earth sciences seismologist Sam Taylor-Offord said this earthquake's distinct primary and secondary wave arrivals would have been very noticeable to many people who felt the shaking.

"Often with earthquakes, people don't feel the primary wave. It's the smaller, faster wave. You might see it in like the rattling of glass or lights, but it's the secondary wave that has a lot more of the energy, and that's what people typically feel.

"And when you feel both of them, it's going to make the earthquake feel possibly twice as long, rather than just a jolt. It's a real rolling motion."

World.title: SH6 near Wānaka partially reopens for the weekend
World.content:
A section of State Highway six near Wānaka is reopening during daytime hours this weekend, after a week of closures and limited access following flooding, while Milford Road remained closed into Saturday morning due to snow.

SH6 near Wānaka partially open for drivers to use without convoys

The Transport Agency says more than 30 slips along State Highway 6, between Lake Hāwea and Makarora, had now been cleared.

And this weekend, travellers can use the road between 8am and 5.30pm, without having to be escorted by pilot vehicles, as long as the weather cooperates.

Caution was still advised for drivers, Waka Kotahi said: "Road users are advised to take extra care as lane closures and temporary speed restrictions will remain in place."

The section would close at night time, as fresh slips could come down in the dark, it said.

During the week, the section would revert to limited access via convoys.

A Road Snowfall Warning for Milford Road has been extended for two hours longer than expected, into Saturday morning.

The road, between Te Anau and Milford (SH94), would now remain closed from Hollyford Junction and Donne River Bridge until 10am.

MetService forecast that 1-2cm of snow could accumulate above about 800m.

World.title: League fans fuming after Sky cuts to betting ad as Jai Arrow walks out for 100th game
World.content:
Rugby league fans are fuming after Sky Sport cut to a betting  just as Jai Arrow was due to walk onto the field for his 100th game for the Rabbitohs.

The 31-year-old retired from rugby league earlier this year - just two games shy of his hundredth match - as he battles motor neurone disease.

Following his diagnosis, the NRL approved a special one-off rule change that would allow Arrow to reach the milestone with his former club; being named as an additional player on the team list and interchange rotation.

New Zealand audiences missed the emotional walk on as, instead, an ad for Betcha began to roll.

Their screens returned to the pitch right on the kick-off whistle.

Livid fans posted on social media, calling the move "unbelieveable", "disgusting" and "disrespectful".

"My wife died of motor neurone disease and tonight I sat with my two children to watch Jai Arrow in his 100th game walking on to the field. This was suppose to be a special moment to remember my wife and their mum, but we had to watch a betting advert. I am hopeful that Sky tv issues an apology to Jai Arrow and MND New Zealand, and to my devastated children. I am so very disappointed," one person wrote.

Others threatened to cancel their subscriptions to Sky and their Betcha accounts.

In a statement, a Sky spokesperson said the ad break was due to a scheduling error.

"We apologise to fans who missed part of Jai Arrow's post-match celebration during our coverage and share their disappointment," they said.

"We know how important this moment was to fans and we regret that the full celebration wasn't shown live.

"To ensure fans can enjoy the moment as it happened, we have shared the full celebration across our social media channels and will also make it available to watch on demand."

Comments on the post were turned off.

RNZ has also approached Betcha for comment.

Arrow's exemption saw him lead the Rabbitohs onto the field at Cbus Super Stadium for his 99th game last weekend, arm-in-arm with teammate Cody Walker, and greeted by a standing ovation.

He was then taken off three seconds after kick-off against the Gold Coast Titans - despite jokingly trying to wave off the call from Rabbitohs co-captain Cameron Murray. He was permitted to remain on the bench in his playing kit for the remainder of the match.

Prior to the game, footage from the changing sheds showed veteran coach Wayne Bennett helping Arrow pull up his socks on and lace his boots.

Before medically retiring at the start of the year, Arrow played 178 NRL matches. His first-grade career started in 2016 with 24 games across two seasons for the Brisbane Broncos, followed by 56 games for the Gold Coast Titans, then finally 98 games for South Sydney from 2021 - 2025.

World.title: Mum calls for mandatory e-scooter helmets after crash leaves son with fractured pelvis and memory loss
World.content:
A collision with a ute while on his e-scooter left her son with a fractured pelvis, internal bleeding and a large bump to the head, but Riana Grobbelaar fears it would have been much worse had he not been wearing a helmet.

Her son, 15, has spent more than a week in hospital following the incident, which occurred while he was out delivering newspapers in Greymouth on August 29.

Have you been impacted by an e-scooter accident? Email melanie.earley@rnz.co.nz

"My son delivers papers on the main road, State Highway 6, in the Paroa area. He crosses that main road a few times and the speed goes from 100km/h to 80 so vehicles coming in to Paroa area go quite fast.

"He said he was waiting to cross and looked and didn't see anything, but after that he woke up with a lot of people around him.

"He can't remember what exactly happened."

Despite the injuries her son did receive, Grobbelaar believed if he hadn't been wearing a helmet he would've ended up with a serious head injury - or worse.

Doctors had been looking at whether he had a concussion, which could account for his memory loss.

"His helmet took a big hit. That was a rule in our house: no helmet, no scooter. He was really lucky, but he has a slow and long road to recovery.

"The helmet is full of bumps and scratches through the side."

The helmet following the crash. RIANA GROBBELAAR / SUPPLIED

Grobbelaar decided to speak out after seeing RNZ's earlier coverage of a psychologist calling for helmets to be made compulsory for e-scooter riders in New Zealand.

The e-scooter was wrecked, along with a puffer jacket he had been wearing which had helped prevent more extensive bruising and cuts on his upper body.

Her son was using crutches and a wheelchair, and the family had spent Thursday having a ramp installed at the house for him.

Grobbelaar said she didn't want any other families to go through what hers had been through.

Seeing other young people riding around Greymouth without helmets since the accident worried her, especially given the speed they were able to go at.

"A lot of the kids are driving on pathways and the speed they are driving at... a vehicle could just back out of their driveway and imagine what accident that could cause."

ACC figures released earlier this year have shown claims for e-scooter injuries are on the rise, with children and young people among the most affected.

Earlier this week psychologist Chris Parsons told Morning Report he was one of many people in the industry who believed attitudes towards e-scooter safety were generally too relaxed.

He said the country's legislation was lagging behind other countries.

"In Australia, it's mandatory to wear a helmet on an e-scooter.

"Queensland is looking at bringing in a range of measures, including the possibility that you have to have a learner's licence and have to be over 16 before you ride an e-scooter. We're in a situation where the law has to catch up with technology."

He said there needed to be nationwide social education, particularly for young people, to prevent more "catastrophic" e-scooter accidents.

"For anyone with a serious brain injury, we're looking at long-term rehabilitation and sometimes lifelong effects. The consequences are very serious.

"The brain is a very soft organ, the consistency of tofu, inside a boney structure of the skull, and people are moving at speed on an e-scooter and if it suddenly stops the brain keeps moving with catastrophic results."

World.title: When does our job as parents end? – Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

My daughter is planning on going to uni next year. Hopefully she will get a scholarship but she should also qualify for a small amount of student allowance. If she doesn't get a scholarship she will keep living at home in west Auckland. I guess she could get student loan living expenses, too. She will also probably work about four hours a week. How do other parents go about deciding how much to keep paying for their children even once they have turned 18? She won't be working full-time so obviously can't afford to pay for everything but when does our job as parents end? Maybe it doesn't. Things are tight so I would love for her to start managing and paying for some things by herself. She is good with money but I'm wondering what to do about mobile phone charges, paying for car running costs - we are looking to buy a car which would be a joint purchase but she would use mostly, clothes, etc. I currently make her earn and pay for make-up, alcohol or treats, concerts, non-essential clothing, things like that. Any advice on how to get a good balance?

I asked Liz Koh, who is the founder of Enrich Retirement about this.

Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

She said a good starting point is for your daughter to do a budget of her likely living costs.

"The next step is to look at how the budget is funded. There are three options: working, borrowing - assuming the student is eligible for a student loan for living expenses - and parental support," she said.

"There is a limit to how many hours a student can work without interfering with studies and that needs to be agreed. Then it's a matter of deciding the balance between borrowing and parental support."

You could work through this together, and maybe share your own budget, if that's appropriate, so your daughter gets a sense of how the bigger picture fits together.

She said you shouldn't feel bad about expecting her to take a lot of this on herself if there isn't a lot of room in your own budget.

"Debt from a student loan is nothing to be concerned about if it is managed properly and if the debt is incurred for the right reasons. In effect, student loan repayments are like an extra tax paid once the student has completed their studies. From a financial perspective the student loan is an investment in personal development that results in higher earning power which offsets the cost of the debt.

"One of the best ways in which parents can help their children is to teach them how to be financially independent and make good financial choices."

My partner and I are looking to buy our first home and would have enough deposit through KiwiSaver for the purchase of a modest property, however, because my partner worked in Australia many years and has ported half his KiwiSaver from there, we are unable to use that part of it so therefore have nowhere near enough. This money is here sitting now in KiwiSaver in New Zealand. This is a ridiculous and unfair situation, the government has made this rule that any KiwiSaver earned in Australia can't be used as a deposit to fund a first home purchase. Are the government going to change this rule or look at it ? If the NZ government say that they want to encourage Kiwis back home to live and work so it would seem an obvious step to take to encourage this.

I can see this would be really frustrating but I think this is a situation where the problem lies with the Australian rules, rather than New Zealand's.

Ana-Marie Lockyer, chief executive of Pie Funds, said Australian funds moved to New Zealand are still governed by some of the Australian restrictions and that's why they can't be withdrawn.

"This restriction is also written into the KiwiSaver Act, so it's not something a KiwiSaver provider can choose to waive. Any change would likely need to come through the Trans-Tasman arrangements, with corresponding changes to NZ law."

She said it could be the case though that the investment returns earned on the transferred money could be withdrawn.

People who move KiwiSaver to Australia are sometimes able to withdraw some of it, but there are more restrictions there, too. Australians are only allowed to withdraw voluntary contributions up to a maximum $50,000 if they qualify for a first home withdrawal from super.

I was wondering why one can only pay 3.5 percent, 4 percent, 6 percent, 8 percent and 10 percent to KiwiSaver? Why can't I pay 5 percent?

The Retirement Commission says this is because the rates are set under the KiwiSaver Act.

"Employees can only contribute at specified rates that can be deducted from salary and wages provided for in the legislation," a spokesperson said in an email.

"Retirement Commissioner David Boyle feels this could have been because of employer payroll constraints back in 2007 when KiwiSaver was introduced. As payroll systems have improved over the past 20 years this might be area that could be revisited to support more flexible KiwiSaver contributions options in the future."

World.title: Mum left stranded with baby after British Airways refuses boarding for mistake it admits
World.content:
It's a parent's nightmare - being stranded unexpectedly at an airport with a small child.

Fleur Lonsdale was travelling in late May with her son, Oakley, one, from New Zealand, where she lives, to Europe for her mum's birthday.

After flying to Auckland Airport, she arrived at the check-in counter three hours early for her next flight to Geneva.

But she missed it after being told her son couldn't board because of a mistake on his ticket - a mistake she had been assured wouldn't matter by the airline.

"I've been in some fairly stressful situations, you know, I've worked for the military. I've worked with some very high-level people - and that had to be one that had to top some of them," she said.

Three months earlier, in February, Lonsdale had booked her flights on British Airways' (BA) website. Her one-year-old would be travelling on her lap for free but he needed his own ticket.

However, the ticket that had been generated looked strange, she said. Only the first letter of his name and four of his surname appeared.

Lonsdale was sure it wasn't her mistake.

"If that had been my mistake, then it would have been a one-letter mistake ... but there's no way that I would have put 'O' and then four letters of his last name."

She said she went to the company's online chat for help, in which an agent reassured her that this was a known system error and would not cause any problems with boarding.

However, when she made it to the airport, this turned out not to be the case.

BA declined to share the chat history or call logs with customer service with her, which Lonsdale is entitled to under the UK's General Data Protection Regulation laws.

RNZ has contacted its customer service and can confirm it records calls for monitoring and quality purposes.

In an email seen by RNZ from the airline to Lonsdale, BA appeared to admit fault for a system error which caused the misprint of her son's name.

"I also understand your frustration that the matter was ultimately acknowledged as stemming from a system-related issue rather than any error on your part," a customer service agent wrote to Lonsdale.

But when asked about this directly by RNZ, it did not provide an answer.

It also did not answer questions on whether such a system error was known about, or whether there were plans to fix it.

British Airways appeared to admit fault for the system error in an email seen by RNZ. AFP

The flight's operator, which was not British Airways, told Lonsdale she would need a form from British Airways to change her son's name to be allowed to board.

Lonsdale said she spent hours on the phone with British Airways' customer service, but nobody could help her.

She told RNZ that an agent left during the call to go home for the day.

"They've literally just kept me on hold, complete carelessness and just gone: 'Oh, well, I'm going to go home now. Screw this girl who's waiting at the airport with her one-year-old'."

Lonsdale said she was becoming increasingly distressed at missing her flight - and potentially her mum's birthday celebrations.

"It was just blame, blame, blame, your fault, your fault, your fault, you're going to have to pay for it."

Eventually, she broke down in tears, despite usually being calm, she said.

"I was just so shocked, I think. How is this even happening? Are you kidding me?

"Like I'm at the airport for a 35-hour flight with my one-year-old by myself and you're telling me that you can't get me on my flight when you told me you could?"

The agent then escalated the matter, and another told her they would book her on to a flight the next day.

She arrived in Europe a day late but in time for the party.

After complaining to the airline, and months of back-and-forth emails, it paid for the expenses incurred as a result of the delay, including accommodation for the extra night in Auckland and food.

It also provided compensation and a gift voucher, as a goodwill gesture.

But there was no mention of fixing the system error.

This prompted Lonsdale to share her story: she said she didn't want this to happen to another parent.

"This is about every mother who has to travel with her child. This should never be allowed to happen at any airline, not just them."

World.title: NZ First to campaign for conservation land to be open for economic development
World.content:
New Zealand First says it will be campaigning for conservation land to be opened up for economic development.

The party's deputy leader and resources minister Shane Jones said he fought hard to retain a controversial clause 6ea in the Conservation Amendment Bill, which says the Department of Conservation (DOC) should recognise and enable "economic opportunities" on conservation land to "the greatest extent practicable".

This sentence is in the latest draft of the bill, which is still before the Environment Select Committee.

Conservation minister Tama Potaka backed down from other proposed changes earlier this year which could have made 2.8 million hectares of conservation land eligible for sale.

Jones said he would campaign for economic activities like mining and quarrying on conservation land - apart from in national parks.

"We, NZ First, rejects the notion that [conservation land is] some type of Camelot lotus land feature of New Zealand that can never ever be used or developed.

"That drove us to introduce into legislation that there has to be priority and status given to economic development."

He said whether the clause in the bill survived, was strengthened or diluted would come down to the results of the election.

Conservation minister Tama Potaka. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Critics say the clause undermines the very purpose of conservation law.

Greenpeace said this week that conservation land should be protected from "economic exploitation", and so that native wildlife could thrive, as well as for the public and future generations to enjoy.

Jones rejected the criticisms, saying he wanted to drive for jobs, economic development and export earnings.

Jones also said he would campaign on re-structuring DOC so that areas which processed concessions, permits and rights of access were potentially run separately to other functions, or given to another entity less driven by conservation.

In statements provided to RNZ this week, Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said he wrote to the Environment Select Committee in June to ask the committee to work with relevant NGOs, iwi, and sector groups to ensure section 6(ea) supported "strong and enduring conservation outcomes".

He said he also wrote to the committee to say the government had changed its position on the bill's provisions relating to land exchange and proposals, and sought to have these removed as part of the re-drafting process.

He said the committee had started hearing oral submissions but did not expect to finish that during this parliamentary term.

World.title: Adelaide returns to scene of finals flop to face biggest test of growth
World.content:
Every week it seems like there is history being written in the AFL.

Some of this is welcomed, memorable and celebrated, such as when Scott Pendlebury broke the games record earlier this year, or when Lance Franklin notched the 1,000-goal mark in 2022.

Moments like these are cherished throughout each club's fanbase and reflects the long history of the league and sport.

Other slices of history are far more trivial. Last week, Sam Walsh set the record for the most disposals in the Wildcard Finals round. While the stat is interesting, it is not necessarily illustrative of a feat of great importance.

Nonetheless, it provides colour to the rich tapestry that is Australian football.

Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks is hoping to avoid an unwanted slice of history this weekend. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

And there are some feats that players and coaches avoid like the plague.

Many football fans know the tale of Kevin Murray. The former Roys stalwart managed to play 333 games, all without winning a single final — a league record.

While his career was rich and storied, eventually earning him Legend status in the Hall of Fame, the achievement underscored the futility of playing for Fitzroy through most of the second half of the 20th century.

Though never winning a VFL final, Murray did manage to play in a finals win during a lucrative mid-career stint at East Perth in 1966 on the way to a losing Grand Final against Perth.

This Saturday night Adelaide coach Matthew Nicks is set to, at least temporarily, claim his own slice of footballing ignominy.

Nicks will join Alec Hall as the coaches to steer their sides through the most VFL/AFL games without winning a final.

For those who don't immediately recognise the name Alec Hall, his last game as coach came more than a century ago.

Over the last two years Nicks's Crows have won the second most regular season games. Last year's minor premiership season was cut short with a straight sets exit.

This year the Crows are already on their last chance with a rampaging Bulldogs ahead of them.

Nicks has quietly rebuilt his side's biggest question mark. But in the Bulldogs, the Crows face a test designed to test this weakness in full.

Mayhem in the middle

The Crows midfield was bossed by Jai Newcombe and Hawthorn in last year's semifinal loss at home. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed)

Fresh in the mind of Nicks, and all Crows fans, is how their 2025 season came to an end.

Like all sides who fall short of their end goal, reflection on their failings quickly sets in.

For Nicks, the message on what went wrong was clear, and last year's disappointment has put them in a stronger place for this year.

"I think we're ahead of last year," Nicks said after their round 24 win over the Giants, despite being "a little lower on the ladder."

"We've been doing a lot of work around what it was we didn't get right last year. Under that immense pressure that Collingwood and Hawthorn brought last year we weren't able to execute and deliver our game on our game plan."

That pressure around the contest is arguably what brought their once-promising 2025 season undone. Against Hawthorn, the Crows struggled both at contests both at stoppage and in general play, with the Hawks midfield unit gaining control of the game.

Starved of opportunity with ball in hand, the Crows' defence could only do so much to hold the wave of Hawks back.

The Hawks ended that final with a six-clearance advantage and 20 more post-clearance ground ball gets. Starved of the ball, the Crows were left passengers in a finals series that they were meant to drive from the front.

At the most basic level, only part of the contest game needed adjustment from the outside. The Crows finished the 2025 season leading for post-clearance ground ball gets and contested possessions.

They were relatively weak at stoppage, however, with a negative clearance differential across the year.

But that hid a slide against the best of the best.

The Crows struggled more against good opposition midfields than most other contenders, perhaps the canary in the coalmine for their finals struggles.

This is despite their units at either end of the ground largely holding up their ends of the bargain.

The Crows defence in 2025 and 2026 has actually gotten stronger against the best sides in the league. They conceded just 1.47 points per inside 50 this year — better than any team's full season record.

The figures were even starker last year. While the Crows concede more in games against good sides, this has largely been down to an increased volume of inside 50s their defence has to protect against.

It's yet another mark of honour for the severely underrated Adelaide backline. Over the past two years the Crows defence has arguably been the strongest defensive unit in the league, despite the lack of individual acknowledgement.

Only one Crows defender, Wayne Milera, has made the All-Australian team in this time despite the depth and strength of their taller options.

While their forward line has had a rotating list of players contribute it has been a little stronger when it matters most.

The territory battle at the contest, particularly up the ground and at stoppage, is so important for one of the Crows' other weaknesses.

Despite their defensive miserliness, their backline has struggled to transition the ball from defensive 50 and the defensive half to create scoring opportunities.

It means the Crows can absorb the pressure of opposition attacks, but sometimes struggle to get the game back on their terms in this way.

Without the benefit of winning the territory battle, or control of the footy at the contest, it can make a spellbinding side look pedestrian at best.

The shift

Izak Rankine has had an excellent season after missing last year's finals through a self-inflicted suspension. (AAP: Matt Turner)

This has spurred the Adelaide brains trust into action. Throughout this year Nicks has experimented with different looks up the ground.

Bodies have floated through the middle and up forward to try to execute when it matters most.

The highest profile change through the year was one involving a player who missed last year's finals altogether.

Since he entered the league with Gold Coast, Izak Rankine has long been viewed as one of the game's most damaging attacking players. He is the type of player that makes the hair stand up on the back of your neck, or your eyes quickly dart back to the TV if the commentator mentions his name in excited tones.

His 2025 season ended not due to form or injury, but rather as a consequence of using a homophobic slur towards a Collingwood player in round 23. Suspended for four matches, Rankine admitted his mistake and apologised publicly and privately.

It is always difficult to judge atonement and sincerity from a distance, but Rankine has made further efforts to build a relationship with the Rainbow Crows supporter group, which has in turn praised the progress made.

Some fans, both of Adelaide and the sport more broadly, may need more time to evaluate his response to the incident.

Others, particularly a large cohort of Crows fans, believed the punishment to be too severe from the outset.

Regardless of your stance, Rankine appears to be choosing his own course in making amends for his grave misstep.

AFL bans Rankine for four games over 'highly offensive' homophobic slur Adelaide Crows star Izak Rankine has been suspended for four matches for using a homophobic slur against a Collingwood opponent during last weekend's AFL match at Adelaide Oval.

Rankine's on field evolution in 2026 is far easier to evaluate than anything off field.

This year Rankine has been deployed full time in the middle of the ground for the first time in his career. The results have been dramatic.

Since the shift, Rankine has been about the most damaging player in the competition, with his previous skill in limited opportunities scaling up when foisted around the ball more often.

The tipping point for Nicks to throw Rankine through the middle more was making sure the young Crow fit with the defence first mindset of the side.

"I've always wanted to play midfield." Rankine told AFC.com.au earlier this month.

"I just had to fix up my two-way running, understanding the game, and when the opposition gets momentum against us how to mentally stay in the game and not get frustrated.

"I've found that the way I can get more of those opportunities is really delving into the defensive side of the game, getting back and helping the defenders, and being an option for them when they get stuck."

It's hard to overstate the growth in Rankine's game. Rankine has moved his predominantly front-half game to impact across the ground.

Defensively, Rankine has increasingly involved himself at contest and tracked his opponent while retaining that attacking flair that makes his game so appealing.

In that time, Adelaide has become even stronger at the contest without suffering on the defensive side. Rankine provides an explosive attacking strength that few other sides can boast, and his improved defensive effort has cost the Crows little the other way.

Rankine is not the only adjustment the Crows have made in the middle through the year.

The Crows have exposed players like Jake Soligo and Brayden Cook at the contest, with other experiments along the way. Instead of direct results on a week to week basis, it appears that Nicks is attempting to expose a wider group to action in the middle in order to maximise his options come September.

Perhaps the last shift might be their biggest, as over the past month the Crows have shifted recent draftee Dan Curtin to the guts in order to provide a vastly different look.

At 197cm and with the build of a key position player, Curtin may be the league's biggest full-time midfielder.

If it sticks, Curtin might provide a midfield option that few other sides have seen before.

Daniel Curtin has averaged a career-best 15.5 disposals per game this season. (Getty Images: James Elsby)

"He's still got so much upside in his game. We haven't really scratched the surface there yet," Nicks said.

"I think we see Dan as a midfielder moving forward. We feel like he's got the football intelligence, the execution and the awareness that you need to be a midfielder.

"He's unique in that he's such a big body, so he's a tough match-up. He's still a very young player that's still learning a fair bit about the game. But it's exciting for us."

Curtin presents opponents a rare challenge of raw size alongside unquestioned footballing ability, similar to Patrick Cripps and experiments with ruck-mids such as Mark Blicavs and Luke Jackson.

Curtin's exposure to different roles across his short professional career has also gifted him with a sense of defensive responsibility when running through the middle — key to executing the Crows' game plan.

A meeting with the biggest midfield test

Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli (pictured) and teammate Ed Richards present a challenge to Adelaide's midfield. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Given how much of their focus has been on building their game at the contest, it is somewhat fitting that their first finals test comes against arguably the league's most damaging contested side on their day.

While the Bulldogs are entering September with a depleted forward line and a defence with more questions than answers, few can question the raw ability and system of their midfield unit.

For a side entrenched in the mid-table hustle over the last two years the Dogs are a side few want to see when the footy starts to get serious.

It's that ability in the middle of the ground, led by All-Australian duo Marcus Bontempelli and Ed Richards, that is set to stress test Nicks's personnel changes.

While the Crows have improved their work at the contest as the year has progressed, the results across the whole year paint a similar picture to that of 2025.

Looking at the entire season likely undersells where they sit right now. While they lost the clearance battle to Fremantle in round 23, they dominated the post-clearance contested battle — crucial to maintaining field position.

Despite Adelaide's strong performances over the last two years, rumbling from Victoria has suggested that Nicks must steer the Crows to victory to retain his job.

"I understand the narrative, it's part of this industry, [but] it's probably not something I could talk to," Nicks said.

If, for whatever reason, the Crows do the unthinkable and remove Nicks from his post after the season, it would be a move without little recent precedent.

The most recent coach to lead his side to at least 33 wins over his last two seasons in charge before leaving his role was Mick Malthouse in his "negotiated handover" to Nathan Buckley at Collingwood.

Few, if any, coaches have been legitimately sacked in league history with so many home and away wins immediately prior to their removal.

While it is likely just a rumour spread wild, the game on Saturday night presents a chance to silence the speculation of the doubters.

World.title: Jai Arrow makes emotional 100th Souths appearance, Souths thrash Roosters
World.content:
Tears flowed as Jai Arrow made his 100th Rabbitohs appearance, with his Souths teammates helping crush the reserve team of their arch rivals, the Roosters.

Arrow choked back tears when he was hugged by Wayne Bennett as the forward was given a hero's reception at a sold out Sydney Football Stadium.

The 31-year-old father of one was diagnosed with motor neurone disease (MND) this year and, until two weeks ago, was stranded on 98 NRL games for the Bunnies.

At Bennett's initiative, the NRL allowed Souths an extra interchange against the Gold Coast last week for game number 99 and again on Friday against the Roosters.

"It was pretty emotional," Cam Murray told Channel 9.

"I'm just so happy that everyone was able to get around him and he's been able to feel all the love.

"I know he really appreciates it and we love to see it.

"We all love him and happy he was able to notch up 100 games."

Arrow led his teammates out to the sound of the Gerry and the Pacemakers rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone, with 14th Immortal and dual-club legend Ron Coote ringing the Rabbitohs' bell.

The former Queensland State of Origin forward was given a guard of honour by more than 100 Souths old boys, including members of the 2021 grand final squad Arrow was a member of and his family, who all sobbed along with him and plenty of others in the stands.

"It was emotional," Roosters captain Connor Watson said in his post-match press conference.

"It was very touching. Things like that are bigger than rugby league."

Jai Arrow presented a stong face to the Rabbitohs crowd. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

In the subsequent match, the Rabbitohs ran in 10 tries to pummel the Roosters 50-20, who had rested 10 of their star players with a top four spot secure.

But in completing the win, Souths have themselves earned a home finals spot, and will face Newcastle at either the Olympic Stadium or Sydney Football Stadium next week.

Campbell Graham scored twice for the Rabbitohs, who had nine different try scorers on the night, including Alex Johnston, who crossed for the 30th time this season.

Latrell Mitchell was one of them, scoring on his return to the starting line up while mixing his sublime skill with fearsome physicality, most notably when he flattened Toby Rodwell in the closing stages, standing over the stricken half like Mohammed Ali over Sonny Liston in their 1965 rematch.

If Mitchell's performance was heartening — a poor 5/10 kicking rate aside — Roosters firebrand Spencer Leniu will have raised concerns from coach Trent Robinson in the first half.

Leniu squared up to Keaon Koloamatangi after the Rabbitohs prop smashed him in a tackle twice in the same set, the second time tossing the ball away and giving away a penalty.

Titans fume over questionable calls

Earlier, the Dolphins hung on to beat the Titans 24-20 on the Gold Coast.

It was the Dolphins' seventh-consecutive win, but almost didn't happen as the Titans fought back late on and were unfortunate not to come away with the win.

The Titans were left fuming when, while leading 14-0, they had Keano Kini sin-binned in the 23rd minute for a very soft push on Dolphins winger Tevita Naufahu.

Josh Hannay was fuming after that call, and a trio of others in the closing minutes, went against his side.

"I thought it was incredibly harsh and not long after that they get a try from a knock-on," Hannay said.

"You talk about momentum swings — they don't get much bigger than that. Moe [Moeaki Fotuaika] got smacked in the face at the end and ends up in the bin for retaliating.

"[Jamayne Isaako] throws a leg out to trip [AJ Brimson] in the act of a potential try-scoring play and it is just a penalty.

"It was probably more sin-binnable than Keano's play.

"You stack all those things up and you lose by four points, you have got to be proud of your team's effort."

With AAP

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Clear and present Danger as Cats sweep aside Carlton
World.content:
Geelong has ended Carlton's fairytale season with a solid win, after withstanding an early challenge to run away with their elimination final.

In the first finals meeting of the two teams since the 1995 grand final, Carlton got the early jump but could not keep control, as Geelong secured the win by 33 points on a rainy night at the MCG.

Geelong skipper Patrick Dangerfield led the way with five goals in his 378th AFL game.

The loss ended Carlton's season after a monumental run of 12 wins and a draw out of 16 games to get to the elimination final under new permanent coach Josh Fraser.

Geelong will travel to Perth to face Fremantle next week in a cut-throat semifinal.

Look back at how the action unfolded in the live blog below.

World.title: Fancy cars and hanging with mum, the paradox of Aussie's EPL teen dream
World.content:
Lucas Herrington has gone to number one with a bullet in 2026, at a speed so dizzying it would leave many teenagers' heads spinning.

Turning 19 this weekend, he is fresh off a breakthrough World Cup, has a multi-million-dollar contract in the best football league in the world, and has fans fawning over him.

But true to his persona on the pitch, the central defender is calm, level-headed and capable of tackling any challenge.

"My parents have always instilled that factor of humility in my life and having that humbleness to stay grounded and just to keep working hard," he told Australian media on a call from Hull.

"I'm always trying to get better. So I think it's always having that positive mindset that I've still got a lot of things to work on. And I'm not the finished product."

Herrington was one of Australia's best players throughout the recent World Cup. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Herrington made his bolt-from-the-blue Socceroos debut in March, which turned into a maiden World Cup appearance a few months later.

His impressive efforts in North America captured interest from some of the biggest clubs in the world including Barcelona and Liverpool.

But he settled on Hull City, newly promoted in the English Premier League, and a five-year deal for a transfer fee reportedly worth $33 million with add-ons, to become the most expensive Australian player ever.

Alessandro Circati recently joined that rich list with his transfer from Parma to Benfica.

Herrington with his manager, Buddy Farah, after signing his record deal with Hull City last month. (Supplied: Hull City)

The money is astronomical for an Australian footballer, and despite his down-to-earth nature, even Herrington was lured in by the EPL stereotype of fancy, fast cars.

"It's a nice car park. I do have a car right now; it's nice. I'm enjoying it," he laughed, almost sheepishly.

But when he speaks about his off-field highlights in his few weeks in England, the teenager goes back to keeping it real.

"Mum's here at the moment. She leaves soon, so I've just been exploring around with her," he said.

"So that's been really nice, some great quality time with her."

Advice from a legend

Herrington made his debut for the Tigers off the bench in their upset win over Manchester United.

"It was only a week and a couple of days from when I landed to that game against Man United," he said.

"Great moment for the city and for me personally, with my mum and my agent in the stands, it was a super proud moment for me.

"And it was a great match, very grateful for the opportunity to be there."

Herrington celebrated the Tigers' upset win over Manchester United to open their season. (Getty Images: Molly Darlington)

He was again used as a substitute in a win over Coventry, while he started the EFL Cup penalty shootout win against Stoke.

A strong show of confidence for the youngster, who is the only Australian in England's top flight.

"It's probably the best league in the world. So to be here at 18 is super special," he said.

"I've always wanted to play in the Premier League, so I'm very grateful for the opportunity from the coaching staff and the club to do so. And I've loved my first three or so weeks here.

"It's a league with the best players in the world, so to be up against them every week is really special and a great challenge for me as a young defender.

"It's just about trying to learn as much as possible from the older boys in the team and just try and take every game as a lesson."

And don't mistake his modesty for meekness; he knows he belongs.

A message reinforced by former Sweden international Zlatan Ibrahimović, who publicly supported Herrington after missing a penalty in the Socceroos' World Cup round of 32 shootout loss to Egypt.

Herrington received plenty of public support after Australia exited the World Cup. (Getty Images: Alex Slitz)

“This is just the beginning of your career," Ibrahimović said on Fox Sports USA's post-game analysis.

"You stepping up there, you show a lot of courage. Not everybody would do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here."

Ibrahimović made good on his promise and ended up calling the Queensland product himself.

"He just said, really don't fear anyone. I'm here for a reason, so just go enjoy," Herrington said.

Dreams do come true

Herrington's meteoric rise means he has not yet played for Australia in his home state.

Herrington is hoping to play in the Socceroos' upcoming friendlies against Brazil in Queensland. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

Something the former Roar product hopes to do in the Socceroos' friendlies against Brazil later this month, in Townsville and Brisbane.

"It'd be a dream come true to play for the Socceroos in Brisbane," he said.

"Something that I've always wanted to do, and to play in front of hopefully a packed-out Suncorp would be a dream, and in front of my family and friends would be awesome."

And he is happy to be a role model for others.

"Just trying to be an inspiration for all the young Australians that there is really a pathway to the Premier League," he said.

"I think a lot of young footballers in Australia like me wake up at all hours in the morning to watch the Premier League.

"So hopefully I can make them proud, make Australia proud.

"Just to keep working hard, enjoy the process, and to have big dreams because dreams do come true."

World.title: Tigers coach defends Luai amid 'irrelevant' criticism over PNG trip
World.content:
Benji Marshall insists Jarome Luai is entitled to spend his downtime as he pleases, dismissing "irrelevant" criticism of the Wests Tigers star's recent trip to PNG.

When Luai asked to change his flight out of Townsville following last week's loss to North Queensland, Marshall was unaware his star player would be travelling to his future home country to attend a golf tournament.

The trip came only days after Pepsi unveiled Luai as a brand ambassador ahead of his arrival at the Chiefs for their first NRL season in 2028.

Luai's trip to Port Moresby, and the first of what is likely to be many promotional opportunities with PNG brands, come while he remains on a seven-figure salary with the Tigers.

Loading Instagram content

The five-eighth will also join Parramatta on a one-year deal before his first pre-season with the Chiefs, which begins in more than a year.

Marshall described media concerns over the optics of Luai's enthusiastic PNG links as "irrelevant to me".

"He paid to change his flights [from Townsville] and not come back with us, which happens quite often with players," Marshall said.

"From my opinion, it's his time off.

"What he chooses to do in his time off, that's up to him. In one week's time, he's not going to be here anymore and we're not going to have to worry about any of those things."

In signing Jarome Luai, Papua New Guinea's power has become real Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

Marshall said, in time, Luai's move to the Chiefs could help transform him from villain to hero in the public's eye.

"He always gets painted as the villain for some reason," Marshall said.

"But he's about to walk into a country in about 12 months' time where he's about to be the hero, so it's going to change for him."

Four-time premiership winner Luai arrived at the Tigers last year with hopes of finally reinvigorating the long-struggling joint venture.

Instead, Luai's decision to sign with the Chiefs coincided with a sharp downturn in form that consigned the Tigers to a 15th consecutive year out of finals.

Marshall previously admitted he had let the saga become a distraction for the 15th-placed Tigers, who had been in the top four when Luai signed with the Chiefs.

Benji Marshall (pictured) has no problems with Luai spending time in Papua New Guinea in his downtime. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"There's obviously a lot of things probably both sides wish went a little bit better, but we are where we are and we've got to move forward," Marshall said.

Marshall still believed Luai's signing was a success for the Tigers, who face top-two side Penrith in their last game of the season.

"There's no regrets from our side about bringing him here whatsoever because he did the job we needed him to," he said.

"I'm sure a lot of people probably have their opinions about what he hasn't done here, but all I've seen are the things he has done here and the impact he has had on the club.

"I'm sure he would admit himself that he would have liked to have contributed more on field performance-wise but all in all, he'll leave here having had an impact on our club."

AAP

World.title: How Swans midfielder is supporting banned housemate amid trade rumours
World.content:
Sydney's James Rowbottom says he must "separate the person from the problem" in trying to support suspended teammate Nick Blakey amid a club crisis and finals campaign.

Blakey is one of five Swans players stood down for the remainder of the season for breaching the club's behavioural standards in a post-AFL match hotel party in August.

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordon and Riley Bice have also been suspended from Sydney's finals campaign.

As the club mulls a call on the group's playing future, Blakey is reportedly searching for a trade following a deterioration in his relationship with the Swans.

Nick Blakey is reportedly keen on a trade out of Sydney as he sits out of this year's finals. (Photo by Morgan Hancock/AFL Photos/via Getty Images)

Swans midfielder Rowbottom says he has only spoken to close mate Blakey about his welfare.

"I haven't spoken to Nick about any sort of details [about a trade]," Rowbottom said today.

"It's been a challenging period for him, and I'm just sort of reaching out as a friend.

"Living with him is another layer to the situation, and so I've reached out as a friend but, no, we haven't spoken about any of those sort of specifics.

"You've got to sort of separate the person from the problem when you live with someone, to try and offer support.

"I've been trying to do that."

The player suspensions are separate to a police investigation into sexual assault allegations and the events at East Melbourne's Pullman Hotel after Sydney's round 23 game against Essendon on August 16.

No charges have been laid and there is no suggestion of any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

Rowbottom would not be drawn when asked if he was open to the five players returning to the club before the end of the season.

The group won't be at the SCG for the club's qualifying final against Brisbane on Saturday, but have individually spoken to teammates in the lead-up to the clash.

Rowbottom (right) and teammate Errol Gulden (left) will be relied upon heavily in the absence of Sydney's suspended quintet. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"It's a lot more complex than what I think or believe," Rowbottom said.

"The club is working through that with them and the relevant party. Honestly, it's above my pay grade."

Heeney and Warner's absence has meant Rowbottom has taken on the bulk of the midfield work with Errol Gulden and Jai Serong.

Rowbottom had returned to the side for the round 24 clash against North Melbourne after missing two weeks with a broken hand.

"For me, personally, I just do what the team needs and I have done that for the last eight years or so," the 25-year-old said.

"My role has been ever-changing this year. I've played a lot of half-forward, a lot of midfield, a bit of wing.

"Football's ever-changing, and I'm happy to take it as it comes."

AAP

World.title: Fan-built roller-coaster sets new standard in match-day choreography
World.content:
Tifo displays have long been a ubiquitous sight in football stadiums around the world.

Typically displayed before kick-off at major matches, fan-led displays have become increasingly elaborate as rival supporters look to outdo one another with the scale of their devotion.

But German second-tier side VfL Osnabrück have taken things to an entirely new level.

Ahead of their German Cup tie against defending champions Bayern Munich, the supporters created a fully functioning roller-coaster in the stands of their 16,100-capacity stadion an der Bremer Brücke.

VfL Osnabrück fans truly surpassed themselves on this occasion. (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

A track was built in sections and had a cart, complete with dummy passengers, which was towed around the track on repeat.

To one side of the stand, a separate "photo" banner was displayed after the cart passed a flashing camera, delivering the authentic experience of what the supporters called the "Funpark Bremer Brücke".

Loading Instagram content

Accompanied by a sign saying "VfL Osnabrück — a roller-coaster ride!" the not-so-subtle message was that supporting the club, based in Germany's north-western Saxony region, was full of ups and downs.

The club has only just been promoted back to the 2. Bundesliga after a five-year stint in the 3. Liga and has a reputation as a club that yo-yos around the leagues.

VfL Osnabrück brought the pyro to their party against Bayern Munich. (Getty Images: picture alliance/David Ebener)

Welcoming Bavarian giants Bayern in the first round of the DFB Pokal was always going to be a tough ask, but the roller-coaster theme continued when the hosts took a shock 1-0 lead thanks to a 30-yard shot by Robin Meißner after just five minutes.

The defending champions soon hit back though, Harry Kane scoring twice either side of goals to Tom Bischof and Michael Olise to give the record 21-time winners a path through to the second round.

But Bayern, who are not strangers to spectacular tifos of their own at their cavernous Allianz Arena home, will have to up their game if they are to manage something as impressive as this for their next home game, against Bodø/Glimt in the Champions League.

Bayern are partial to the odd display of mass choreography. (Getty Images: sampics/Stefan Matzke)

Germany has been something of a trendsetter when it comes to tifos in recent years, although the practice originated in southern Europe and Italy.

Starting out as supporters holding up cards to create a display across a grandstand, Australian fans can think of a tifo as something similar to the fan-made banners AFL teams run through pre-game, only on a much larger scale.

Tifo is short for tifosi, the Italian for supporter, and has become known as a way for fans to display their passion or to mock their rivals.

Tifos originated in Italy, with San Siro home to some of the best. (Getty Images: AC Milan/Diego Puletto)

In 2017, Western Sydney Wanderers provoked the ire of Football Australia, then known as Football Federation Australia, for displaying a homophobic banner during the Sydney derby.

The banner, depicting a blue-faced man giving oral sex, was put up in the Wanderers' support area during the second half of the game.

"FFA is aware of the unauthorised and totally unacceptable banner that was displayed in the Western Sydney Wanderers area during Saturday night's Sydney derby at ANZ Stadium," then-A-League chief Greg O'Rourke said.

"The discriminatory nature of the tifo has no place in society and will not be tolerated in the A-League."

Not all of Western Sydney Wanderers' tifos were vile, most were excellent. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Clubs can play a role in the content of tifos, but often they are ways for fans to make their point about an issue they feel strongly about.

Given the increasingly elaborate designs, Arsenal were heavily criticised by their own fans for a bland rectangular tifo ahead of a Champions League match at the Emirates against Paris Saint-Germain in April 2025.

PSG are known for their extravagant displays — particularly in the Champions League — so perhaps it was fair for Arsenal to be mocked.

Paris Saint-Germain fans are increasingly keen on displaying tifos. (Getty Images: UEFA/Stuart Franklin)

However, since then they have upped their game significantly.

Still, we're yet to see a roller-coaster of any sort at the Emirates, so there's clearly still room for improvement.

As fans of Lechia Gdansk know, the devil is often in the detail. (Getty Images: Mateusz Slodkowski)

World.title: Shifting Ayrton Senna plaque a sign of things to come for Adelaide's MotoGP
World.content:
A plaque installed after F1 driver Ayrton Senna died in 1994 is among a swag of changes to Adelaide's famed street circuit for the MotoGP next year, but an industry stalwart says it represents "transition" rather than the end of an era.

The government wants to return parts of the circuit to its original F1 layout, including the 900-metre Brabham Straight along Dequetteville Terrace, but is also proposing to shift Senna Chicane further into Victoria Park and dump popular Supercar components.

This includes the "staircase" and its challenging succession of 90-degree turns along the CBD's east edge.

"It's a new life, a different life for one of the best locations for a motor racing circuit in Australia," said Motorsport Hall of Fame chairman and longtime industry journalist John Smailes.

The Senna Chicane is a historic turn in the Adelaide Street Circuit that harkens back to the F1 days. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"It still sits in Victoria Park where [track designer] Bob Barnard placed it in 1985, so you're talking about a rich 41-year history of Victoria Park hosting probably the best Grand Prix that's ever been held in the Southern Hemisphere for cars.

"It's so close to town; it really does involve the whole city and, to that end, whatever the layout may happen to be, the geography remains pretty much the same."

A popular circuit

After the Grand Prix moved to Melbourne in 1996, the circuit was reduced to 3.2 kilometres for the 1999 Adelaide 500, which became the most well-attended leg of the Supercars Championship and grew a reputation for challenging corners, bumps and upsets.

Loading...

One of the Adelaide street circuit's major drawcards, however, is that spectators can be seated close to the action for much of the course.

The MotoGP, on the other hand, requires very large gravel traps along the far edge of corners to slow a dismounted rider safely, meaning spectators will be set a significant way back for bigger stretches of the circuit.

Mr Smailes pointed out there were parts of the current Phillip Island MotoGP course where "you can get up close and personal with the bikes", and expected the same in Adelaide.

The proposed MotoGP street has wide gravel pits along much of the course. (Supplied: SA government)

Viewing areas for the current Adelaide street circuit are largely close to the action. (Supplied: Daniel Kalisz)

"There'll probably be places where the aficionados will scope out the best parts to stand where they can still get the buzz of being close," Mr Smailes said.

" And when you cop the full force of a 320 kilometre-per-hour MotoGP bike pushing the air in front of you, it's like being hit by a glove from a heavyweight boxer. It's amazing. "

The state government said the MotoGP track will be reconfigured for the Supercars Grand Final, which will take place about 10 days later.

Five-time Supercars champion Mark Skaife said the kerbs would remain "punishing and the walls will be inches away".

"The new Senna Chicane will be unforgiving," he said, and the track will be "super quick, with lots of overtaking opportunities".

MotoGP bikes are expected to hit speeds of 340 kilometres per hour on the Adelaide Street Circuit. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

A larger sticking point

The MotoGP's larger footprint, however, is behind its most controversial sticking point for a lot of Adelaideans, which is its requirement to remove trees from the city's national heritage-listed Parklands.

Angered by tree removals for a revamped golf course, a large protest movement has emerged that marched in the thousands on August 23, while a petition of 43,784 signatures tabled in state parliament has triggered an inquiry.

The state government has responded by promising to replace every tree 10 to one, and arguing that of 377 trees that needed removal, 42 were significant, 88 would be transplanted, and the rest were either "unregulated, invasive species, dead or in poor health".

A protest against tree felling for the MotoGP in late August drew thousands of people. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Mr Smailes believed the issue was of bigger consideration than Senna's memorial plaque.

"I don't think Ayrton Senna would be at all concerned if you moved his plaque to another place. I think that's a very small consideration," he said.

A spokesperson for the South Australian Motor Sport Board said the plaque "commemorating the life of three-time World Champion Ayrton Senna was a part of the folklore of the Adelaide Circuit".

The plaque is currently located adjacent Senna Chicane in Victoria Park. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

"The intention is to keep it adjacent to the Senna Chicane, but the exact location won't be determined until the consultation process has concluded and the final circuit design is confirmed," he said.

A 'spectacle for sure'

Adelaide motorsport fan, Simon, told the ABC he was a "car guy, but the MotoGP is probably the most exciting motorsport to watch at the moment, given F1 has become so sanitised and tech-driven", and he would most certainly be attending.

"I'd prefer the F1 to come back, but MotoGP is a spectacle for sure and has a huge global following," he said.

"I also like the fact the infrastructure could be used for the Adelaide Motorsport Festival [AMF] as well, and could see that event become Australia's answer to the Goodwood Festival of Speed [England].

"[AMF owner/CEO] Tim Possingham is a very switched-on guy and I'm sure he has a vision for the AMF to grow and succeed."

A map showing the design for the MotoGP street circuit in Adelaide. (Supplied: SA government)

Mr Possingham said he had been in constant communication with the state government about the incoming MotoGP and was working with it closely with respect to its build times and how the AMF would fit in.

Adelaide MotoGP circuit gets lukewarm motorsport review Adelaide's new $96 million MotoGP track has received mixed reviews from motorsport fans and riders.

"We're also mindful that the Formula One calendar hasn't been released yet, so there's a couple of moving parts we need to fit in with," he said.

"Anything that remotely comes to look like the great track we had in the 80s and the 90s and, in some way, shape or form, brings back that grandeur of a truly international event here in the city of Adelaide is very, very powerful.

"I think that that will be realised maybe after a year or two of the event being delivered here, and I think there's some foresight there of what might come in the future, and the government's looking further afield than national events with MotoGP."

Works have begun for the Adelaide Street Circuit in its current configuration for the final time. (891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton)

A public consultation period for the proposed MotoGP track is open until September 20.

Tech.title: The White House is making arcade games racist
Tech.content:
is a policy reporter at The Verge covering surveillance, the Department of Homeland Security, and the tech-right.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The PR masterminds at the White House just released a series of vaguely policy-themed “arcade” games, some of which are racist — and modeled on real games whose copyright holders may not be too happy to be associated with the MAGA agenda.

The Tetris Company has already responded to “Build the Wall,” which is obviously modeled on the famous puzzle game. In the Trump administration’s game, the player has to stack interlocking shapes to stop a “zombie border siege” along the southern border. Aliens — the administration’s preferred term for noncitizens, and the subject of previous grotesque attempts at humor — run across the screen, trying to get to America before the gates are shut.

In a statement to The Verge, Tetris spokesperson Kerri Brusca clarified that the company wasn’t involved in the creation of Donald Trump’s game. “For more than 40 years, Tetris has brought people together across generations and cultures through play and joy. The objective of the game has always been to stack with purpose to clear as many lines as possible,” Brusca said. “We are currently reviewing the matter.”

The various companies whose brands the White House ripped off to make and promote these games — including Sega, Nintendo, Xbox, and the Flappy Bird Foundation Group — did not immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.

Previously, the Trump administration has gotten in trouble for infringing on others’ copyrights. The Department of Homeland Security has had to delete some of its racist, fancam-esque posts after receiving DMCA takedown requests.

The purpose of Trump’s interminable memes, games, and other gimmicks is manifold: to drum up support for Trump’s policies, to entertain his groyper fans, and, of course, to troll the libs. (One game, “Rio Run,” is like snake, except the head of the snake is a Border Patrol agent who collects migrants as he moves across the screen. Ha ha, get it? The president is deporting people.) But the games also inadvertently highlight the administration’s policy failures, not to mention the hypocrisy of Trump’s agenda.

Trump’s efforts to build a wall through protected lands in the Southwest, including Big Bend National Park, has been met with mass opposition — even from Republicans in deep-red Texas who form a key part of the MAGA coalition.

Other games are similar reminders of how Trump’s policies are backfiring, even on the right.

There’s “Flappy Bill,” a play on Flappy Bird that involves getting a bald eagle to deliver a piece of legislation to the National Mall. Cute! Except the administration has rolled back protections under the Endangered Species Act, the landmark legislation that helped rescue bald eagles from the brink of extinction. The administration’s supposed revamping of the National Mall has also been unpopular.

In “Supply Line,” reminiscent of the game Tapper, you have to knock processed foods — those filled with additives, seed oils, and artificial colorings — off a conveyor belt before they get fed to schoolchildren. But Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. hasn’t managed to do any of that. Besides issuing a likely AI-drafted report for his Make America Healthy Again commission, RFK Jr.’s main role at HHS has been to roll back vaccine recommendations and food safety regulations. The administration’s gutting of the Food and Drug Administration made it harder to investigate the spread of cyclosporiasis, the so-called explosive diarrhea parasite, earlier this year.

If anything, these games serve as a great reminder that our well-being is a big joke to the president and the people who surround him.

Tech.title: GoPro says it’s still committed ‘to your collective stoke’
Tech.content:
To our GoPro community, fans and customers,

We understand there’s some concern about GoPro’s post-merger commitment to continue developing market leading cameras for consumers and professionals. Making amazing cameras for all of you is our core DNA and reason for being and that will never change! We’re fired up about what’s ahead for GoPro and want to share a little more about what our proposed merger with Starman means for our future.

Thanks to the improved financial strength this merger will provide, we’ll be in a much better position to innovate, invent and advance the future of consumer and professional content creation. And importantly, Starman shares our passion for the GoPro brand, developing market leading products and our commitment to your collective stoke.

We’ve accumulated more than 2500 patents over the last 24 years which tells you we’ve been busy innovating, and this merger will ensure we’re able to innovate for many more years to come. We expect this merger will make GoPro a stronger, more capable camera company than ever before.

Our goal is to become a more diversified company which can make us stronger financially, enabling GoPro to become as awesome as we (and you) want us to be. We plan to bring you more innovative cameras, smarter accessories, and more powerful software and services designed to make capturing, editing and sharing your experiences easier and more exciting than ever. We see opportunities to improve the products you already love while developing new tools and experiences that help you create, connect and share in entirely new ways.

We have so much more to do, so much more to invent, and so much more we want to bring to the GoPro community. We appreciate all of you who have been on this journey with us and we’re excited about where we’re headed. We’re going to keep doing what we do best - making the world’s highest-performance cameras and building the products, services and innovations that help you capture life’s most exciting moments. It’s what we were founded to do and it’s what we will always do. Be a HERO…GoPro.

With respect and appreciation — Nick

GoPro Founder & CEO

Tech.title: Roland is getting into generative AI music with Melody Flip
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

It’s not quite the “push button; get song” of Suno, but Roland’s new Melody Flip tool marks the company’s foray into generative AI music. Available as a plug-in for your digital audio workstation (DAW), Melody Flip offers around 250 “Palettes,” which are essentially themed collections of musical ideas sorted by genre. You can start from scratch and ask it to generate any combination of melody, chord progression, bassline, or drums. Or you can feed it a reference track and have it build off the melodic ideas from that.

Unlike Suno or Udio, Melody Flip doesn’t spit out fully polished songs with vocals and full arrangements. Instead, it offers simple musical loops meant to serve as a creative spark for you to build on. There are fairly limited control over the outputs. You can’t feed Melody Flip a text prompt like “acoustic country rock with clean male vocals, literate singer-songwriter, gentle brushed drums, and sparse pedal steel at 98BPM” and get a Jason Isbell ripoff. Instead, you basically just choose a genre, note density, BPM, musical key, and take what you get. Though the genre options are pretty fine-grained, going from standard fare like “80s disco” and “90s R&B” to esoteric things like “Kawaii Future Bass” and “Anime World.”

The sound selection is further proof that you’re not supposed to use Melody Flip outputs out of the box. The presets available are mostly the sort of general MIDI tones you’d find in ‘90s video games. It seems like the intended use is to export the MIDI data from Melody Flip directly into your DAW to manipulate and pair with other, more powerful synth plugins.
